3.3.3. Why MoE saves compute but not KV cache memory
The compute savings are straightforward: if only na = 12.8B of nt = 47B total parameters are active
per token, the FLOP count drops by the active fraction relative to a same-size dense model. But note
the active fraction for top-2-of-8 routing is ~12.8/47 ≈ 27%, not single-digit — so the relative saving
is about 5.5× versus the canonical 70B dense comparison, not 20× or 30×. Concretely,
FLOPMoE/token = na × 2 FLOP/param = 12.8 B × 2 ≈ 0.0256 T
which is 0.0256/0.14 ≈ 0.183× of the dense 70B figure — roughly a 5.5× reduction in compute
per token. (It is also 12.8/47 ≈ 27% of a hypothetical dense model of the same 47B total; the 5.5×

Understanding the Model

38

figure uses the book’s canonical 70B dense as the comparison, so always state which baseline the
ratio is against.)
The KV cache story is the surprising part. Recall from Chapter 1 (KV cache as a concept)
that the KV cache stores one key and one value tensor per token, per layer. The cache size per
token scales with the canonical Chapter 1 formula (the full-MHA case, where n_KV-heads × head_
dim = hidden_dim; for a GQA/MQA model substitute n_KV-heads × head_dim), KVper-token =
2 × nlayers × (nKV-heads × dhead ) × bytes-per-value (full-MHA special case: nKV-heads × dhead = dhidden ).
Critically, the attention mechanism processes every token in the context densely — each
token’s query attends to all previous tokens’ keys and values, regardless of whether the model is
dense or MoE. MoE sparsity operates in the feed-forward sub-layer; it does not change the attention
sub-layer’s behavior.
Therefore, for the canonical dense 70B (80 layers, hidden 8192, full MHA — Ch 7) and for the ~47B
challenger’s own attention shape (32 layers, hidden 4096, GQA with 8 KV-heads × 128), at 8K–9.2K
input context:
• Dense 70B: KV cache ~1.31 MB per token × 9,200 tokens ≈ 12.06 GB (at 8-bit, the raw tensor
byte-halving figure = 1.31 MB/token, exactly 50% of FP16 — the block-overhead and ‘54%’
ITL-slope caveats are stated once in Ch 1; see Ch 7) or ~24 GB (at FP16 precision for the
key/value storage pattern discussed in Ch. 7).
• ~47B MoE challenger (Mixtral 8x7B class): KV per token = 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 = 65,536 B =
0.0655 MB/token at 8-bit, so 9,200 × 0.0655 MB ≈ 0.60 GB (≈1.2 GB at FP16) — smaller than the
dense 70B’s ~12 GB, and the whole difference is the attention shape, not the routing: 32 layers ×
a 1,024-wide GQA KV width instead of the canonical 80 layers × 8,192 full-MHA width. The
attention layers still emit one key and one value per token per layer; routing neither reduces
nor increases that count: the fact that only 12.8B of 47B total parameters are active in the
feed-forward layers changes nothing about the keys/values the attention layers store. A dense
model with the challenger’s 32L/4096H GQA shape would hold the same ~0.60 GB — hold the
attention geometry fixed and dense vs MoE KV is identical.
In other words: MoE sparsity = compute sparsity (fewer FLOPs per token). MoE sparsity ≠
memory sparsity (KV cache still grows linearly with context length, exactly as a dense model’s
does at the same attention shape). Only changing the attention mechanism itself (e.g., hybrid/linear
attention) can stop the cache from growing — KV offload changes where the cache resides, not how
fast it grows. MLA-style latent attention does not stop the growth: it cuts the bytes/token constant
(~50–60× for DeepSeek-class geometry [DERIVED]) but the cache still grows linearly with length. It
belongs to Ch 1’s reduced-width per-token family, not the constant-state family. This distinction —
compute-sparsity versus memory-sparsity — is one an architect has to get exactly right.
Key takeaway: MoE provides compute sparsity (far fewer FLOPs per token because
a fraction of experts is active), not automatic weight-residency sparsity — the full

39

Understanding the Model

expert set normally remains resident unless it is explicitly offloaded or sharded in a
way that changes residency. And the KV cache budget must be provisioned from the
model’s own attention shape — and, where that shape is not known, at the full-MHA
rate for the same layer count and hidden width (the conservative bound). Do not assume
MoE reduces KV cache memory — routing never does; only a different attention shape,
cache dtype or context length changes the bytes — and do not confuse active-compute
savings with a residency saving. (This restates at the parameter level the sparsity lesson
introduced conceptually in Ch 1 and developed arithmetically for the canonical model
in Ch 7; each chapter teaches it at its own rung of the spine.)
Boxed rule — two distinct accounting lines. Keep two numbers separate and never
blur them: 1. total parameters → weight residency. The resident weights (all experts,
for MoE) are what the GPUs must hold. For a 70B dense model this is ~140 GB FP16; for a
~47B MoE this is ~94 GB (full expert set) unless experts are explicitly offloaded. 2. active
parameters/token → approximate compute per token. The routed top-k fraction
(e.g. ~12.8B active) sets the FLOPs per token (~25.6 GFLOP) and the active weight-read
traffic (~25.6 GB of weights read per batch-1 decode token, amortized across a batch).
This is not a memory-freeing lever unless offloading is in play.

3.4. Measurement
How do we determine the total-versus-active split for a model we haven’t trained?
1. Model card inspection. Most model vendors publish the total parameter count. The activeper-token count is harder to find; it requires reading the architecture documentation for the
routing mechanism (top-k, top-1, importance-based). If the model card says “70B parameters”
without qualification, assume dense unless it explicitly describes an MoE layout.
2. Runtime measurement. For a given input, profile the number of FLOPs or the memory
footprint of active weights. Infer the count from the execution, e.g. with torch.profiler
(record_shapes / with_flops) summing the shapes of the matmuls actually run, or a router hook
that logs the experts selected per token; this is an empirical measurement, not a first-party
spec.
3. Architecture diagram. For MoE models, the number of experts × parameters-per-expert
gives the total; the routing hyperparameter (top-k) × parameters-per-expert gives the active
per token. This is a derived fact from the source code/release, not always on the model card.
Practical habit: When we encounter a model quoted in “X billion parameters,” pause
and ask: is this total or active? For dense models they are the same; for MoE models they
diverge. Misreading this is the most common source of weight-residency and compute

Understanding the Model

40

underestimation — and, through the “sparse therefore smaller KV” shortcut, of KV-cache
underestimation as well.

3.5. Common Mistakes
• Assuming total parameters = active parameters per token. This is one of the costliest
misreads. For a MoE model, the quoted several-hundred-billion or 47B is the total across all
experts; the active count per token is a fraction. The two counts drive different budgets: the
total count sets weight residency (the full expert set must be resident — the quoted total × 2
bytes, not just the active footprint), while the active count sets compute per token (only the
routed experts are read). Sizing weight memory from the active count under-provisions it (the
un-routed experts still occupy HBM); sizing compute from the total count over-provisions it (the
un-routed experts are not read per token). The opposite error — sizing for active parameters
while forgetting that MoE routing does not reduce KV cache size — under-provisions the KV
budget.
• Confusing compute sparsity with memory sparsity. MoE reduces FLOPs per token because
fewer parameters are active. It does not reduce the number of keys/values written to the KV
cache. An architect who assumes MoE shrinks KV cache will be blindsided by memory pressure
at long context lengths.
• Using MoE as a free lunch for long-context workloads. The compute savings from MoE
are real, but the memory cost (weights + KV cache) must be provisioned at the total-parameter
scale for weight residency and at the-full-context scale for KV cache. Neither benefit is “free”
in the other domain.
• Ignoring routing overhead. Top-k routing itself requires computing routing scores (a softmax
over expert assignments). This adds a small but non-zero compute cost that is sometimes
omitted from published FLOP counts. It is usually negligible compared to the feed-forward
arithmetic but should be acknowledged.

3.6. Architecture Consequence
Knowing whether a model is dense or MoE, and whether the quoted parameter count is total or
active, directly changes three architectural decisions:
1. Weight residency budget. For a dense 70B model, provision 140 GB of FP16 weight memory
per host. For an MoE model with ~47B total and ~12.8B active, distinguish two numbers: the res­
ident budget (the full expert set, ~47B × 2 bytes ≈ 94 GB, unless experts are offloaded/swapped)
and the active per-token footprint (~12.8B × 2 bytes ≈ 25.6 GB read per token). The active
number governs compute; the resident number governs whether the weights stay on device.
Routing does not lower that floor by itself — residency is set by the total count, so a same-total

41

Understanding the Model

dense model holds the same bytes; this challenger’s floor is lower only because its total (47B)
sits below the dense 70B’s: 94 GB vs 140 GB, a 46 GB (~32.9%) saving. Offloading inactives is a
further option, priced in bandwidth.
2. KV cache provisioning. Provision the KV cache as for a dense model of the same context
length, hidden dimension and attention shape. Do not apply a MoE sparsity factor to the KV
cache. If we are running a 9.2K-token input on a model with the canonical 80L/8192H full-MHA
shape (dense or MoE), the KV cache memory is the same either way — plan accordingly; a
model with a smaller or GQA shape (like the ~47B challenger, ~0.6 GB at 8-bit) needs fewer
bytes, but that is its shape, not its routing.
3. Parallelism and routing strategy. MoE deployment requires a routing strategy (e.g., expert
placement, dispatcher, switchboard) and often expert parallelism across GPUs. This adds
infrastructure complexity (cross-GPU communication for expert routing) that dense models do
not have. The architectural choice between dense and MoE is therefore not just a parametercount decision; it is a deployment-complexity decision.
3.6.1. The 2026 baseline shift: same framework, new constants
The 2026 trend signal (forward-looking; an interpretation of the sample we surveyed,
not an established industry-wide convergence). By August 2026 the four frontier open-weight
families surveyed for this edition share a notable pattern, and it is not more of the same dense
scaling: extreme MoE sparsity (single-digit active-parameter fractions — Qwen 6B of 125B, Kimi
K3 104B of 2.8T) coupled with hybrid attention (compressed/sparse/linear hybrids such as Gated
DeltaNet + sparse attention) has become a common way to make long-context inference affordable.
Appendix A documents these at full depth with first-party provenance; what matters here, in the
model-understanding chapter, is that this is not a competing mechanism but the same dense-vs-MoE,
total-vs-active, KV-vs-compute machinery this chapter just taught — with new constants. We hold
that view explicitly as the forward-looking direction the architect should size toward, and flag
it below as continuing future work (the frontier moves; this handbook is a living document, and
Appendix A is where the moving part lives).
Why the trend signal should not be read as “dense is dead”. This pattern among the four
frontier families we surveyed describes the top of the market — the ~100B-and-up tier that includes
the ~2.8T-parameter frontier models (e.g. Kimi K3, 104B active of 2.8T). It is not a claim that dense
models have disappeared. On the contrary, the smaller, denser tier is alive and actively shipping
in 2026 for exactly the constrained-deployment reasons this chapter teaches: Qwen3.8-27B ([1P]
[FACT], source: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B) is a dense 27.8B model whose 4-bit weights fit on a single
24 GB consumer GPU, and Muse Glimmer 30B ([2°][FACT], source: Meta via vLLM-Recipes) is
a dense 29.6B local-agentic model that runs in ~18 GB at ~5-bit weights. These exist because the
dense-vs-MoE trade is itself a deployment decision, not a date: MoE buys active-parameter efficiency

Understanding the Model

42

at the cost of total-parameter memory and routing complexity — worthwhile when serving many
requests from a large pool of resident weights, but hard to justify when the whole budget is one
consumer GPU whose total weights already overrun. That is precisely why this book keeps its
canonical on the dense tier: the canonical must serve the architect whose whole fleet is a handful of
boxes, not only the one sizing a 2.8T datacenter model. The framework does not change between
tiers — total vs active, KV per-token, and residency budgeting apply identically to a 27B dense laptop
model and a 125B/6B MoE fleet model.
Why the rest of this chapter’s canonical stays a dense full-MHA model. If the trend is MoE
+ hybrid, why does this book’s canonical still size a dense 70B full-MHA workload? Because a dense
model with full multi-head attention gives the cleanest single-constant KV formula (2 × layers ×
hidden × bytes) and the largest KV footprint — the conservative worst case an architect should

always size against first. Teaching against that bound means the reader learns the framework on the
hardest memory case and then relaxes it. It is a deliberate teaching simplification, not a claim that in
2026 an enterprise RAG fleet really runs on dense 70B.
One verified 2026 transfer: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. The model card [1P][FACT] (source: HF
Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) is the Qwen4-architecture preview: 125B total / 6B active (plus a
separate 51B of offloadable N-gram embedding parameters), 512 MoE experts (10 routed + 1 shared
per token), and hybrid attention — Gated DeltaNet (GDN) on three of every four layers plus Qwen
Sparse Attention (QSA) on the fourth. This is exactly the “125B/6B active MoE + Gated DeltaNet/QSA”
class of model a 2026 architect actually considers. Stepping through this book’s own arithmetic:
• Weight residency (Ch. 7’s floor): the active-weight working set for Qwen is ~6 × 10⁹ params
× 2 bytes/param = ~12 GB read per batch-1 decode token — ~12× less per-token weight traffic
than the canonical dense 70B (140 GB → 12 GB), and ~21× less than Qwen’s own total weight
footprint (~250 GB → 12 GB). But this is a compute/bandwidth statement, not a residency one:
the total weights dominate the memory ceiling, ~125 × 10⁹ params × 2 bytes/param ≈ 250 GB
(plus the offloadable N-gram). So the total-vs-active split of this chapter is not a footnote —
it is the difference between fitting on one host and sharding across several, and the ~250 GB
total (not the ~12 GB active working set) is what must be resident unless experts are explicitly
offloaded.
• KV cache (Ch. 7/8): the canonical 2 × layers × hidden × bytes KV formula is the fullMHA bound. Qwen’s hybrid attention attacks the KV constant at the mechanism level: GDN
layers keep a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing per-token cache, so only the
remaining full-attention layers contribute per-token KV — the GDN state and the attentionlayer fraction are what change stored KV. QSA’s sparse micro-block attention cuts attention
reads; it does not change the bytes stored per token. So per-token KV no longer follows the
dense formula, and no KV metric for this model is stated anywhere in this book. Chapter
7 works a configuration-backed version of exactly this two-term budget — Qwen3.8-27B’s
16 full-attention layers priced separately from its 48 Gated DeltaNet layers — into its own

43

Understanding the Model

history-state arithmetic, so we do not re-derive it here. The framework question (“does it fit?”)
is unchanged; the function plugged in for KV is not the dense one.
• Compute (Ch. 8): active-parameter FLOPs drop to ~2 ×6B per token, but the QSA/GDN layers
ride different roofline points than a dense 70B prefill/decode split, so the throttled-resource
conclusion must be re-derived per model (Ch. 8’s measurement discipline, not a one-time
number).
The architect’s move is unchanged. For the canonical dense model this book sizes memory,
compute, and fleet with one clean constant set. For a 2026 MoE/hybrid model the architect does
the same decision loop — read the model card, get total vs active, get the KV scheme’s per-token
function, size residency and roofline, then decide parallelism (Ch. 10) and serving (Ch. 11). Only the
constants differ; the framework does not. Appendix A walks the four frontier models through exactly
this re-derivation and flags which vendor numbers still carry a verify-on-own-hardware caveat.
Recorded as future work. This forward-looking view is intentionally a pointer, not
the full treatment — the complete, current analysis of the 2026 frontier lives in Appendix
A. Because the frontier moves quickly and every vendor figure in it carries a verify-onown-hardware caveat, we treat the trend as a living section to be updated against new
model cards, rather than a set of frozen gospel numbers. An architect should re-check
Appendix A before any capacity decision — the constants, not the framework, are what
change.
3.6.2. An expert can be selected by noise stage
Wan2.2 A14B is a useful counterexample to treating every mixture of experts as per-token top-k
routing: its high-noise and low-noise experts are selected from the current timestep rather than by a
per-token gate, at about 27B total and about 14B active parameters as published (Wan2.2 source).
The implementation-level inspection (which function picks the expert, and what offload costs) is in
Appendix A’s alternative-inference note. [1P][FACT]
The reusable distinction is total weight storage versus active execution — the same two accounting
lines this chapter keeps separate for language MoE, applied to a selection rule that is not per-token
top-k. The language-model cache conclusion stays scoped to the attention geometry and execution
path that produced it: noise-stage selection does not establish an autoregressive KV cache for a video
denoiser, and the canonical dense/MoE arithmetic above is untouched by this case.

• Exact active-fraction per token for commercial MoE models. Model cards rarely publish
the precise top-k routing distribution under real workloads. We know the architectural top-k
(e.g., top-2 from 8 experts), but which experts are active varies with prompt content and token

position; the number of active parameters per token is fixed by top-k and expert size under
standard routing. Effective active count can vary only under variable-k, capacity dropping, or
expert-unavailable fallback — an implementation-specific exception, not the default.
• Whether router latency offsets MoE compute savings. The cost of computing routing
scores and dispatching to experts is not always included in published FLOP counts. On some
hardware the routing overhead can be significant enough to narrow the compute gap between
MoE and dense.
• KV cache behavior under MoE with expert swapping. Expert swapping does not change
KV cache size; size is set by attention geometry and sequence length. But expert weight
transfers compete with KV offloading for the same host-transfer path. The open question is the
bandwidth contention between expert weight transfers and KV transfers at a given PCIe/NVLink
budget. It is workload- and implementation-dependent.
These flags exist because home-lab measurements are not reference per the evidence taxonomy;
each is an open empirical question a team should validate against its own target workload, not a
claim the handbook has settled.

3.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Total vs. Active Parameters, and the KV Constant
(Continuous scenario — chained from the enterprise Q&A thread.)
An architect is fleshing out the design of the internal Q&A tool described in Chapter 1’s mini-case.
The team’s standing decision from Chapter 2 is the dense 70B model; a MoE model with 8 experts
(roughly 47B total params, ~12.8B active per token) is the challenger under consideration. They ask:
“If we go MoE, can we cut our GPU memory budget?”
From the model-understanding chapter, the architect can answer: Active-compute memory yes
— only ~12.8B of the ~47B total is active per token, so ~25.6 GB of active weight footprint is read per
batch-1 decode token vs. 140 GB for a dense 70B. Resident memory yes as well, for this challenger —
but for a reason worth stating precisely. An MoE model normally keeps its full expert set resident
— the non-active experts still occupy HBM unless we explicitly use expert offload/swapping (Ch 3 §6,
Ch. 18), which itself costs bandwidth — so the resident budget is ~47B × 2 bytes ≈ 94 GB rather than
140 GB: a drop of 46 GB, ~32.9% of FP16 weight memory. That drop is earned by the challenger’s
smaller total parameter count (47B vs 70B), not by routing itself — a dense model of the same 47B
total would hold the same 94 GB — and offloading some experts is a further, bandwidth-costed option
on top. And KV cache memory no — routing does not change it: the attention layers still process
every token densely and emit one key and one value per token per layer, so at a fixed attention
geometry the 9.2K-context budget is the same whether the model is dense or MoE. The challenger’s
own shape (32 layers, hidden 4096, GQA 8 KV-heads × 128) needs only ~0.6 GB at 8-bit (~1.2 GB at
FP16) for that input — but that is its attention shape, not its routing, and a dense model with the
same shape holds the same bytes; where the shape is not known we provision at the dense full-MHA

Understanding the Model

46

rate, ~12 GB (at 8-bit) or ~24 GB (at the precision pattern discussed in Ch. 7) per request, as the
conservative bound. We’ll also need expert-routing infrastructure on top of that.
The architect’s decision therefore rests on two findings, both stated plainly. (a) Resident weights
do drop: ~140 GB (dense 70B) → ~94 GB (the ~47B MoE) — 46 GB, ~32.9% of FP16 weight memory
— earned by the challenger’s smaller total parameter count, not by routing a same-size model. (b)
Routing does not change the KV bytes: with the same attention geometry the 9.2K-context budget
is unchanged; the challenger’s own 32L/4096H GQA shape would need only ~0.6 GB (8-bit) / ~1.2 GB
(FP16), and where the shape is unknown we provision at the dense-70B full-MHA rate (~12 GB at 8-bit,
~24 GB at FP16) as the conservative bound; when the shape is known, use the model’s own shape
(~0.6 GB for the challenger). What this accounting does not settle is whether the challenger is the
better system. Routing and expert dispatch are integrated in serving runtimes — vLLM, for example,
dispatches experts over all-to-all communication behind a runtime flag (Expert Parallel Deployment)
— so a GPU dedicated to the routing dispatcher is an optional design hypothesis [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[ASSUMPTION], not an unavoidable requirement; the real added cost is placement, and it must be
compared on an actual arrangement — on the canonical single 8×H100 host (640 GB, Ch 4 Table
4-2) both 140 GB and 94 GB of FP16 weights fit, so the 46 GB saving buys KV headroom rather than
feasibility, while an expert-parallel layout across GPUs trades that headroom for cross-GPU all-to-all
traffic (§6). The team therefore does not select the challenger yet: quality at equal task performance,
placement on the actual single-host or expert-parallel arrangement, and measured service goodput
under the target workload remain unresolved [UNRESOLVED]. The Chapter 2 dense 70B decision
stands as the provisional choice, and the KV cache budget is provisioned at the dense-model rate
either way.

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to take a vague deployment ask — “thousands of employees
asking questions over internal documents” — and turn it into a measurable workload across six
concrete dimensions. We will trace the arithmetic from user concurrency through traffic, token
profile, latency, economics, and operational constraints, ending with a workload characterization
that directly enables system architecture decisions. After this chapter, the question “which model
should we choose?” can be answered with numbers, not intuition.

4.1. Concept
4.1.1. The Six-Dimension Workload-Characterization Framework
A workload is defined by six dimensions (Table 4-1 applies the framework to the canonical workload).
Together they form a complete specification that — jointly, not taken alone — constrains model
selection, system architecture, and economic feasibility. No single dimension is sufficient; the architect
must characterize all six before committing to a design.
1. Quality — the fidelity, accuracy, and capability the workload demands of the model. Includes
reasoning depth, tool-use requirements, modality (text‑only, multimodal, etc.), and any accu­
racy thresholds (e.g. >85% factual accuracy on internal Q&A). Quality is the goal; the other
dimensions are the constraints within which quality must be delivered.
2. Traffic — the request rate the system must sustain, expressed in requests per second (rps) or
queries per second, plus concurrency levels and burstiness. Traffic, combined with the token

51

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

52

profile and the latency SLO, determines the compute and memory bandwidth required to keep
the serving pipeline saturated without excessive queuing.
3. Token profile — the distribution of input length, output length, and context length per request.
This is the workload’s “shape” in token space: how many tokens arrive in the prompt, how
many the model generates, and whether the prompt is dense (long context) or sparse. The
token profile is the primary driver of memory (KV cache) and prefill cost.
4. Latency — the time budget for different stages of request processing. Typically split into
time-to-first-token (TTFT), which encompasses retrieval and prefill, and time-per-output-token
(TPOT), which governs decode speed (the rate of token generation, not the number of tokens
generated). Latency budgets feed directly into SLOs and serve as the key differentiator between
serving configurations (e.g. continuous batching vs. discrete batching).
5. Economic constraints — the cost budget denominated in tokens per dollar, dollars per million
tokens, or cost per request. This dimension translates traffic and token profile into a recurring
cost line, and it determines whether a given infrastructure choice (single node vs. multi‑node,
FP16 vs. FP8) is affordable at scale.
6. Operational constraints — availability, privacy, locality, and update frequency. Multi‑region
deployment for fault tolerance. Data‑privacy requirements that force on‑prem or VPC‑local em­
bedding models. Update frequency that dictates how often embeddings or model weights must
be refreshed. These constraints often interact with traffic and economics to force architectural
compromises.
The framework is deliberately dimensional: a workload that is “high‑quality, high‑traffic,
long‑context, low‑latency, cost‑sensitive, private” is fundamentally different from “low‑quality,
low‑traffic, short‑context, high‑latency, cost‑abundant, public,” even if the raw text looks the same.
The framework prevents the architect from optimizing one dimension at the expense of others — a
common failure mode.

4.2. Mental Model
The six dimensions are best read as the axes of a six‑dimensional space in which every AI
workload resides. A workload’s position in this space is its fingerprint. When an architect says “we
need a model for enterprise Q&A,” that is only a descriptor of the quality dimension. To make the
statement actionable, we must project the workload onto all six axes: what quality level, how much
traffic, what token profile, what latency SLO, what economic ceiling, what operational constraints? The
intersection of these projections is the workload point that drives every downstream decision —
model selection, infrastructure sizing, serving configuration, and TCO.

53

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

The mental model is not a checklist; it is a lens. Looking through it, the architect sees which
dimensions are tight (binding) and which are loose (permissive). Tight dimensions become the design
drivers; loose dimensions offer optimization freedom. The goal is to identify the binding constraints
so that resources are allocated where they matter most.

4.3. Worked Example
4.3.1. Characterizing the Canonical Enterprise-Q&A RAG Workload
RAG is retrieval-augmented generation: the system retrieves relevant passages from a document
store and prepends them to the user’s question as context, so the model answers from evidence
rather than memory. The canonical workload below is the book’s running example of such a system
(the Preface defines the term; this is where it becomes a quantified workload).
We now apply the six‑dimension framework to the canonical enterprise‑Q&A RAG workload
used throughout this handbook. The canonical numbers are the fixed reference set for Part II; all
arithmetic in this chapter traces to them. Table 4-1 states the six-dimension characterization; Table
4-2 gives each value’s provenance.

The canonical workload’s operational constraint and SLA (this box: Multi-region deployment
(active-active), 99.9% availability) state the requirement; the follow-on TCO and fleet arith­

metic in Ch 16–17 prices a single-region deployment with N−1 single-host failover, not multiregion active-active. These are different provisioning problems: multi-region active-active re­

consistent state/data replication across regions — none of which is priced or validated anywhere in
this book’s cost arithmetic. The canonical cost figures (Ch 16 $/1K req, Ch 17 host counts) therefore
understate the cost of the canonical workload’s own stated 99.9% availability requirement.

Note 1 (Table 4-2) — the three label axes, and why the change log does not mix them.
Axis 1 provenance — where the number came from: [1P] first-party (vendor spec, method pa­
per), [canonical scenario] the book’s own fixed reference set (this table), [ILLUSTRATIVE] a
non-canonical hypothetical worked example, [2°] reputable second-hand (textbook, survey, inde­
pendent benchmark), [LAB] measured on the author’s own hardware. Axis 2 epistemic status
— what was done to it: [FACT] stated by the source, [DERIVED] computed from stated inputs,
[ASSUMPTION] a deliberately chosen scenario input, [HYPOTHESIS] reasoned but not yet vali­
dated, [UNRESOLVED] left open. Axis 3 measurement status — how far it has climbed the mea­
surement hierarchy: ANALYTICAL / ILLUSTRATIVE / MODELED / MEASURED, or UNMEASURED.
A label pair takes one item from Axis 1 and one from Axis 2 (e.g. [1P][FACT], [canonical scenario]
[DERIVED], [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]), with Axis 3 riding along. Hence the change log’s
rule: a hypothesis is tagged [HYPOTHESIS] (Axis 2), never [ILLUSTRATIVE] (Axis 1); and
[LAB] / [2°] are provenances, not validation stages — validation is the Axis-3 MEASURED
step, which a [2°] number may or may not have reached. Within [canonical scenario] an
input or parameter assumption (traffic, latency target, price, token count) is [canonical scenario]
[ASSUMPTION]; a value arithmetically derived from those inputs (an occupancy, a tokens-per-second
rate, a cost-per-request) is [canonical scenario][DERIVED]; a vendor hardware constant (e.g. the
H100 footprint) is [1P][FACT], never [ILLUSTRATIVE]; and [canonical scenario] is distinct from
[ILLUSTRATIVE], which is reserved for a non-canonical hypothetical and uses the same ASSUMP­
TION/DERIVED split. (Full definitions: Preface; Sources, Method, and Reproducibility.)

Arithmetic Walk‑Through: From Users to Declared Traffic and Derived Occupancy
The step from “~2,000 registered users” to “~10 rps average” is the key connective tissue that makes
the continuous scenario concrete. Here is the declaration-plus-occupancy walk-through, traceable
line by line:
1. Concurrency: a fraction f of the N registered users are active at any moment. With f = 0.05
and N = 2,000:

C = f · N = 0.05 × 2,000 = 100 concurrent users
2. Request completion time (service time W ): the average end‑to‑end time from request
submission to answer delivery. We deliberately keep TWO named values, and the distinction
matters: a planning round number of ~10 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill ~1.08 s + decode
~7.5 s, rounded up to a comfortable planning figure) versus the derived model-execution
service time of ~8.6 s (prefill 1.08 s + decode 7.5 s, without the retrieval/plumbing term) that
the later fleet chapters use in Little’s-law sizing. The two differ by the retrieval/pipeline room
and by rounding; they are not a numerical contradiction. Whichever we use, we must use it
consistently — the canonical ledger pins the fleet-sizing service time at ~8.6 s (Chapters 16–17
use it for Little’s-law occupancy; Chapter 8 gives the prefill + decode decomposition), and the
~10 s figure is the coarser planning-round headline.
3. Arrival rate — a declared traffic assumption, NOT a Little’s-law derivation from the
active-user population: Little’s Law, L = λW , relates the average number of requests in the
defined system L, the arrival rate λ, and the mean time in system W . It cannot be applied to a
count of active people — 100 recently-active users is not the same as 100 requests in the serving
system. So the ~10 rps average is declared as a scenario input (≈ 2,000 registered users ×
one request ~every 200 s → ~10 rps), not solved for from the 100-user population.
4. Peak arrival rate: ~40 rps is the same behavior scaled to a burst/traffic spike — again a
declared scenario input (see step 3).
The walk-through makes the distinctions explicit: the ~100 active users are a population/activity
measure, not a request-occupancy count; the ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak are declared traffic
assumptions (scenario inputs), not derived from the user count; the ~86 / ~344 execution occupancy
is derived from those arrival rates via Little’s Law (L = λ × Wexec , Wexec ≈ 8.6 s). The point of the
exercise is to keep population, arrival rate, and occupancy separate, not to claim that a registereduser count empirically determines an arrival rate. Change any one assumption and the others shift
accordingly; the architect recomputes them when the requirement changes. If the architect starts
from a measured 10 rps instead, the relation runs the other way (it yields ~86 in-flight at W ≈ 8.6 s,
not a user count).

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

66

Before moving on, it is worth naming the four distinct quantities so they are not collapsed:
registered users are the population; concurrent users are the activity state (active users in the
modeled window, not in-flight requests); arrival rate (λ) is requests per unit time; and service
time (W) is the end-to-end duration of a request. Little’s Law, L = λW, relates only the request-level
quantities — L (in-flight requests), λ, and W — not the registered- or active-user population; the
architect must estimate or measure request concurrency, arrival rate, and service time — none is a
fixed property of the workload. Two further separations matter for KV planning and are easy to
collapse, so we hold them apart here too:
“Concurrent users” here means active users, not simultaneous in-flight inference re­
quests. The 5% figure gives ~100 active users in the modeled activity window — people who are
using the tool over the window — not 100 requests that are all mid-execution at the same instant. The
in-flight request concurrency is a different quantity, computed from Little’s Law with the derived
service time W ≈ 8.6 s. The two operating points are distinct rows, not one figure reconciled by an
unstated multiplier:

The reason these columns differ in kind is that active-user population and request occupancy
are different state variables. Active users is a population measure — how many people engaged the
tool over the modeled window. Request occupancy is an instantaneous Little’s-law quantity — how
many requests are resident in the serving system at a moment. They are related only through the
arrival rate and service time, not through a per-user request multiplicity. So at the average operating
point the population (~100) and the occupancy (~86) happen to be close, while at the peak they differ
(400 vs 344); neither gap needs a “one user issues several requests” reconciliation, and we do not
claim one. Whenever the book says “concurrent users,” read “active users in the modeled activity
window”; whenever it needs the request-level occupancy that a host’s KV budget must absorb, use
the Little’s-law λ·W figure for that specific operating point.
The ~40 rps peak is assumed sustained over the provisioning burst interval — long enough
for Little’s Law and service-time occupancy to reach the modeled steady state (sustained for at least
the service-time scale, Wexec ≈ 8.6 s — not a one-second or few-second spike), not a one-request 40-rps
spike. A one-second spike would not populate the queue to λ·W; the fleet sizing deliberately treats
40 rps as the sustained burst the system must absorb. A load generator reproducing this workload
should emit the same sustained arrival process, not merely target the same average rps.
• Concurrent users ≠ concurrent requests. “100 concurrent users” is a statement about the
population’s activity, not about how many requests are in flight at the scheduler at any instant.

67

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

The two are different state variables, and they need not be close — at the average operating
point they happen to be (~100 vs ~86), at the peak they differ (~400 vs ~344).
• Requests in flight ≠ KV-resident sequences. A request in the queue, or one whose prefill
is not yet admitted, is “in flight” from the user’s perspective but does not yet hold a KV slot.
In-flight concurrency upper-bounds the KV-concurrency the system must serve, but the KV
budget is sized by the number of resident active sequences — which is what the concurrency
ceilings in Ch 17 count. Little’s Law gives the in-flight number; the KV budget is a separate,
residency-side quantity obtained by multiplying the resident sequence count by per-token KV.
Keeping these three apart (in flight vs resident vs per-token KV) is what prevents the “100
users → 100 KV slots” leap.
The “5% active” and “10 s duration” are deliberately simple scenario assumptions
([canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]), not externally verified facts; in a real engagement the archi­
tect replaces them with observed concurrency, measured latency, and a burst profile from telemetry.
Getting this separation right is what turns traffic modeling from a guess into a reproducible arithmetic.
Token Profile in Detail
The canonical workload’s token profile is input‑heavy, which has direct consequences for system
design:
• Per‑request input: 1,200 tokens (enterprise query, possibly reformulated) + 8,000 tokens
(retrieved context from vector DB) ≈ 9,200 tokens. The [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]
provenance traces to the canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2).
• Per‑request output: ~300 tokens (the generated answer, possibly with citations).
• Input‑to‑output ratio: 9,200 ÷ 300 ≈ 30× more input tokens than output tokens. This ratio is
[canonical scenario][DERIVED] from the canonical numbers and sets the relative prefill‑ver­
sus‑decode work split; the 9,200‑token absolute context length is what sets KV residency per
request and therefore the concurrency ceiling. The canonical workload is KV‑capacity‑ and
prefill‑dominated because of that long context, not because of the ratio (KV residency also
scales with context length × concurrency × bytes/token, and decode throughput must still be
checked at the target batch size and SLO).
• At 10 rps: input tokens/s = 9,200 ×10 = 92,000 tokens/s; output tokens/s = 300 ×10 = 3,000
tokens/s. At peak 40 rps, input spikes to ~368,000 tokens/s and output to ~12,000 tokens/s.
These [canonical scenario][DERIVED] numbers are the Canonical Workload box’s derived
rates (above).
The input-heavy profile means the system’s dominant resource demands are prefill compute
and KV-memory capacity; under the canonical timing assumptions prefill is not the dominant wallclock component of an individual request. Prefill takes about 1.08 s, while generating the 300-token
answer takes about 7.5 s (300 × 25 ms/TPOT) — so decode is the dominant per-request wall-clock

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

68

component (~87% of the ~8.58 s total). A model that processes the 9.2K-token input in ~1.08 s of prefill
is important to keep the prefill leg within the 1.2 s TTFT budget, but it does not make prefill the
latency bottleneck; that distinction is a resource-regime statement (in the canonical long-prompt,
low-batch regime, prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound), not a wall-clock latency
ranking. Architecture choices must be based on phase-specific demand, measured utilization, and
SLO-goodput, rather than the input/output token ratio alone. This is why the token profile is the
primary architectural driver for this workload.
Latency from SLO
The latency dimension is specified through Service Level Objectives, which translate user‑experience
goals into concrete time budgets:
• TTFT (time-to-first-token): budget of 1.2 s, comprising retrieval (~120 ms for vector search
and reranking on a local GPU) + prefill (~1.08 s for 9,200 tokens across the 8×H100 canonical
host, ≈8.5K tokens/s prefill — below the host’s ~19,800 tok/s sustained-planning prefill rate
(a planning rate, not a ceiling) and far above what a single H100 alone could sustain, per
Ch 2 and Ch 8). p95 TTFT must stay ≤ 2 s — a tail ceiling above the 1.2 s target budget,
allowing occasional cache misses or network jitter to land between the 1.2 s target and the 2 s
ceiling. TTFT_e2e convention (used throughout): TTFTe2e = retrieval+admission/queue+
tokenization/transfer + prefill. Here the 1.2 s budget names the two dominant modeled terms
— retrieval (~120 ms) + prefill (~1.08 s) — and the 1.08 s is therefore a two-term-only upper
reach, NOT a feasible deployed prefill target: it leaves zero allowance for admission/queue
and tokenization/transfer, which are positive. Write it as budget_prefill ≤ 1.08 s − B_
other until measurement supplies B_other; every “meets 1.2 s” statement needs a named tested

workload and end-to-end timing (see the “Prefill compute budget — two-term-only upper
cap, NOT a feasible deployed prefill target” row in Table 4-2). The 1.2 s is an aspirational
SLO budget (a sub-2-second user-experience target), not a demonstrated p95 TTFT from
a benchmark; the ≤2 s p95 is the budgeted ceiling, and the demonstrated value under load
requires an actual measurement.
• TPOT (time-per-output-token): budget of ~25 ms/token. A 300‑token answer therefore
takes ~7.5 s of total decode time. p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms/token provides headroom for batching
variability.
These budgets are [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] from typical enterprise Q&A user ex­
pectations (sub‑2‑second feel) and from the hardware’s published prefill/decode rates. They are the
latency constraints that every subsequent architectural decision must respect.

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

Economic Constraints
The economic dimension translates the token profile and traffic into a cost structure:
• Infrastructure: A single host with 8×H100 GPUs (640 GB total GPU memory, 140 GB model
FP16 weights fit with room for KV cache). On-demand rental (operating) cost ≈ $20/hour
($2.50/GPU-hr), or ~$2,500/month reserved (illustrative committed-use discount; a ~83% dis­
count on H100 on-demand is unusually deep and differs from the on-demand basis the canonical
box uses) — the canonical box uses the on-demand basis.
• Token pricing: ~$1.20 per million input tokens and ~$2.00 per million output tokens as a
mid-tier managed-API list price (2026 snapshot) — a provider’s price for a hosted service, not a
rate for the canonical H100 instance, which is priced separately at ~$20/hr on-demand (see
the Infrastructure bullet). The frontier-class API used in the Ch 16 TCO comparison is priced
higher (~$2/$8 per 1M) — a different provider tier, not the same line item.
• Throughput per dollar: At 10 rps average, the system processes ~92,000 input tokens/s +
~3,000 output tokens/s. The dollar denominator must be the whole fleet that serves this
rate, not one host. At the ~6-host average the whole-fleet spend is ~$120/hour (≈ $0.0333
per second), so ~92,000 / 0.0333 ≈ ~2.76 million input tokens per cloud dollar and ~3,000 /
0.0333 ≈ ~90,000 output tokens per cloud dollar — the active-hours basis (the ~$120/hour
spend over the ~173.3 active hours/month is $20,800, matching the 6.24M active-hours request
volume); on the wall-clock paid-occupancy basis ($87,600/month for the same month’s
~57.4B input tokens) the same volume gives ~655K input tokens per dollar. These are
modeled, whole-fleet figures (before SLO/headroom/failover). A separate quantity is a single
host’s sustained-planning prefill rate (~19,800 tok/s at 35% MFU, Ch 8 — a planning rate, not
a ceiling: the peak-derived ceiling is ~56.5K tok/s): ~19,800 × 3,600 / $20 ≈ ~3.56M prefill
tokens per host-dollar — a different denominator and a different rate, and not a claim that
one host serves the offered load. Never present a tokens-per-dollar figure with the offered
workload rate divided by a single-host price. (Chapter 5 expresses the same economics on a
GPU list-price basis as tokens per dollar; see its throughput-basis reconciliation note before
cross-chapter comparison — Chapter 5’s 9,000 tokens per dollar is single-stream (50 tok/s),
while this chapter’s ~2.76M input tokens per cloud dollar (~2.85M combined) is whole-fleet
aggregate.)
• Cost per request: At 10 rps, each request carries ~9,500 tokens (9,200 input + 300 output). At
the per‑million rates, cost per request ≈ ($1.20 × 9.2 + $2.00 × 0.3) / 1,000 ≈ $0.01164 ≈ $0.012 per
request per inference cycle. At 40 rps peak, cost scales linearly. Basis note — two different
cost bases, not interchangeable. The $0.012 figure is derived from per-token market/API list
prices ($1.20/M in, $2.00/M out) for the mid-tier managed API; it is a cloud-provider price a
customer would pay per request on that hosted API. (The frontier-class API used in the Ch 16
TCO comparison is priced higher — ~$2/$8 per 1M, ~$0.0208 per request; see the token-pricing
bullet above for the tier distinction.) It is not the fleet owner’s marginal infrastructure cost.

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

70

The owned-fleet cost is nearly all fixed capex/opex and barely scales per request, but it must
be computed on the whole fleet, not one host: the $20/hr is the price of a single 8×H100 host,
while the canonical 10 rps average / 40 rps peak needs ~6 hosts at average and ~21 at peak
(Ch 16/17). So the owned per-request cost on the active service-hour basis (the sidebar’s
$87,600/month, by contrast, assumes the fleet is paid for all 730 wall-clock hours) is (N_hosts
× $20/hr) ÷ (rps × 3600) ≈ (6 × $20) ÷ (10 × 3600) ≈ ~$0.0033 per request at average, and (21 ×
$20) ÷ (40 × 3600) ≈ ~$0.0029 per request at peak (6/21-host full-util basis; the 9/32-host policy
basis gives ~$0.0050 / ~$0.0044) — the two no longer coincide exactly, because the floor-17 KV
screen rounds 10 rps up to 6 hosts and 40 rps up to 21 (6/10 ≠ 21/40), so the peak lands slightly
cheaper per request. (Dividing one host’s $20/hr by the whole workload’s 10 rps would give
~$0.00056, but that is dimensionally wrong: one host cannot serve 10 rps of this workload.)
Keep the two bases separate: use the per-token price for a hosted/API cost model, and the fleet
$/hr ÷ fleet rps for an owned fleet. The two are juxtaposed in the cost-basis table below (§4.3)
only to show the hosted-API pricing basis, not as an owned-fleet marginal cost.
The economic constraint is what makes the workload real: a 70B FP16 model on one host is
analytically feasible against the per‑request latency SLO (TTFT/TPOT) under the first-order Ch 2
model — and only in that model’s two-term (retrieval + prefill) form, with B_other unmeasured
(Table 4-2) — end-to-end timing must be confirmed by benchmark (per the TTFT bullet in §4.3) —
but the capacity question, how many hosts absorb the ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak arrival, is a
separate computation. As Chapters 8 and 16–17 show, a single 8×H100 host holds ~17.5 KV‑resident
requests (436 GB KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9.5K-token resident request ≈ 17.51, §6; the conservative
integer floor is 17), so it cannot carry the ~40 rps peak (~344 in flight); the canonical workload needs
on the order of ~6 hosts at the average and ~21 hosts at the peak. Scaling to higher traffic or longer
contexts pushes the host count further, and the cost line must be re‑evaluated.

4.4. Measurement
For this chapter, measurement is about quantifying the six dimensions so the workload can be
communicated definitively and used to drive architecture decisions. The token-counting habits of Ch

73

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

1 §1.4 apply unchanged (run the model’s own tokenizer, split input from output, log the distribution
not just the mean) — rather than restate them, the three things the six-dimension view adds are:
1. Quantify each dimension with a number, not a label. For the six dimensions (quality,
traffic, token profile, latency, economic constraints, operational constraints), attach a concrete
measured or derived figure. “RAG” is not a load; “1.2K prompt + 8K retrieved, 300 out, 40 rps
peak, p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s” is.
2. Tie the token split to the bottleneck it drives. An input-heavy profile (like RAG’s 30×
ratio) means prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure dominate; an output-heavy profile
would dominate decode. State which side dominates, because it decides where the money and
the architecture effort go (Ch 8).
3. Record the peak and the tail, not just the average. A workload that averages 9.2K input
but has a long tail (e.g. 32K peak contexts) sizes the fleet very differently. Log percentiles (p90,
p99) alongside the average and size against the peak.
These habits answer the book’s recurring question, “what would I actually measure here?” —
and they let the six dimensions be stated as numbers an architecture decision can be defended on.

4.5. Common Mistakes
• Treating “5% concurrency” as the throughput. Concurrency is a snapshot of simultaneous
users; throughput depends on how long each request takes. 100 concurrent in-flight requests
with a 200 s service time yield 0.5 rps, not 10 rps. The binding connection is through request
duration (Little’s Law). Catch this by always asking “how long is each request in system?”
before quoting a concurrency-derived throughput.
• Using the ~10 s planning round as Little’s-law W. The planning round (~10 s) is not the
execution service time (W_exec ≈ 8.6 s); plugging ~10 s into L = λW gives occupancies of
100/400 — exactly the active-user population — and conflates people with requests. Use W_
exec for occupancy (the tokenizer-side traps — token ≈ word, context window as free capacity
— are Ch 1 §5’s; measure there, not re-derived here).
• Ignoring the input–output asymmetry. An input-heavy workload like RAG tends to in­
crease prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure — it does not by itself make the system
“memory-bandwidth-bound.” In the canonical model, prefill is compute-bound under the
analytical roofline, while long input raises KV residency, which constrains sustainable concur­
rency (a capacity constraint, distinct from bandwidth). An output-heavy workload is decodedominant (bandwidth/runtime per generated token). Raising aggregate decode throughput
(output tokens/s across the fleet, e.g. via more batching) on an input-heavy workload moves
the needle negligibly — the binding constraints are KV residency and prefill, not output rate;
but per-request decode rate and TPOT are reciprocals, so reducing TPOT does shorten service
time and host count — the same lever read per request, not a different one. The real win is
prefill reduction, prefix/KV reuse, or increasing effective carrying capacity.

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

74

• Sizing KV and the fleet from the mean context and the average fleet. The 9.2 K mean
hides the tail (a 32 K context costs ~84 GB of KV per request, §7), and the ~6-host average fleet
is not the ~21-host peak fleet — size against the tail context and the peak rate, not the mean.
• Overlooking operational constraints. Multi–region deployment adds replication cost;
privacy requirements may force a more expensive on-prem embedding model. These are often
the true binding constraints, not the per-token price.

4.6. Architecture Consequence
The six‑dimension characterization informs and constrains the architectural path for the canonical
enterprise‑Q&A RAG workload:
• Model selection: A 70B FP16 dense model (140 GB weights) fits on a single host with 8×H100
(640 GB GPU memory). The model is large enough to follow instructions and synthesize
retrieved context without task‑specific fine‑tuning (factual accuracy still depends on retrieval
quality, context, and evaluation), but the 140 GB footprint means KV cache for 9.2 K context
adds ~20–30 GB of GPU memory per request at peak, leaving headroom but not abundance.
• Serving configuration: One host is the per-request latency baseline, not the capacity answer:
at 10 rps the offered prefill load is ~92,000 tok/s against one host’s ~19,800 tok/s sustainedplanning rate, so prefill alone needs ≥5 hosts at average; the KV-residency screen (86 in-flight ÷
17 slots = 5.06) is the binding bound and raises this to ~6 hosts (§4.3). On each host, continuous
batching (e.g. vLLM) is nearly mandatory under this load to hold the 1.2 s TTFT budget: it
reduces queueing and improves utilization under concurrency (it does not shorten a single
request’s 9.2 K prefill); without admission scheduling, queued prefills can push p95 TTFT
past the 2 s ceiling — chunked prefill and priority scheduling are the levers that address
prefill/decode interference directly. The input‑heavy token profile (30× more input than output)
makes continuous batching especially effective: with long prefills and short outputs, decode
slots would otherwise sit idle between admissions, and continuous batching keeps them filled.
The benefit of many requests sharing the same retrieved-context prefix belongs to prefix
caching — a distinct mechanism (Ch 2 §1, developed in Ch 11) — not to continuous batching.
• Memory planning: KV cache for 9.2 K context on the canonical model — a 70B full-MHA
reference model (every query head has its own K,V, so K/V width = hidden_dim = 8192) — is
2 × layers × hidden × bytes = 2,621,440 B ≈ 2.62 MB/token (Chapter 7), giving ≈9,200 ×2.62
MB ≈ 24.1 GB of initial KV per request; a resident request also holds its 300 output tokens, so
the slot-counting basis is 9,500 ×2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB. This is the MHA upper-bound baseline; a
GQA model (8 KV-heads, d_head=128) would carry only ~0.33 MB/token, ~8× less (Ch 7). At 10
concurrent full-context requests the MHA figure is ~241 GB of KV on top of the 140 GB weights
— 381 GB of the 640 GB pool — and the pool presses well before concurrency reaches 100 (~17
full-context requests once the ~64 GB runtime is reserved: 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5, floored to
17 — the input-only 24.1 GB figure above would give 436 ÷ 24.1 ≈ 18 before the output tokens

are counted). The architecture must therefore limit concurrency, quantize KV (FP8 → ~1.31
MB/token, ~12.06 GB/request at the same 9.2K context), or use a GQA architecture. This is the
same KV-residency discipline developed fully in Chapters 7 and 17.
• Economic feasibility: Two cost bases meet here and are not interchangeable: ~$20/hour per
8×H100 host (owned/self-host basis) and ~$0.012 per request at mid-tier API list prices (from
$1.20/M input × 9.2 K + $2.00/M output × 0.3 K — an API-basis figure, not a self-host TCO).
On the API basis the request cost is driven by the 9.2 K input tokens: if the input token count
could be reduced to 2 K (e.g. tighter retrieval/reranking to fewer chunks, context compression,
or prefix caching), cost per request drops to ~$0.003, and the same traffic fits within a much
lower budget. This is the lever the architect pulls when TCO is the binding constraint.
• Operational topology: Multi‑region deployment (active‑active) provides region-failure toler­
ance at an illustrative ~2× infrastructure cost (unvalidated — see caveat below); 99.9% availability
alone does not require it, since a single-region multi-AZ design can meet 99.9% depending on
the failure domains. If the SLA requires region-failure tolerance, the architecture must absorb
a separately modeled active-active cost — not necessarily 2×. If it is negotiable, a single-region
with graceful-degrading fallback may suffice. The operational constraint thus directly sets the
economic floor. Caveat — this multi-region active-active topology and the 2× cost here
are UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED in this book’s TCO/fleet arithmetic (Ch 16–17),
which prices a single-region N−1 deployment instead; multi-region active-active is
a different provisioning problem (cross-region capacity duplication, region-failure
tolerance, data locality and traffic routing, state/data replication) and must be costed
separately before the 99.9% SLA is met — see the canonical-box availability-topology
note.

4.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• Tokenizer exactness for technical domains: While the “one token ≈ 4 characters” rule of
thumb is convenient, enterprise Q&A prompts may contain code, JSON, or domain‑specific
terminology that tokenizes differently. The exact per‑token count for a given prompt distribu­
tion is [UNRESOLVED] and would require running the model’s tokenizer on a representative
sample of real user queries.
• KV cache scaling with longer contexts: The canonical scenario uses ~9.2 K input tokens. If
retrieval quality degrades and context lengths grow to 32 K or 128 K, the KV cache memory
per request grows linearly. Be precise about what breaks. A single 32 K canonical request
costs ~84 GB of KV, which — with the ~140 GB weights and ~64 GB runtime/workspace
[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] (the runtime/NCCL/activation reserve derived in Ch 7,
which subtracts it to reach the ~436 GB KV budget) — still fits the nominal 640 GB aggregate
host as a single request (~288 GB total, well under 640 GB). What fails is not one-request fit but
a particular concurrency/SLO requirement: at the canonical ~40 rps peak and ~8.6 s service

77

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

time, the in-flight occupancy (~344 requests) demands far more than one host’s aggregate KV
budget once per-request KV grows to 32 K or 128 K (at 128 K a single request alone needs ~335
GB of KV, leaving little for any concurrency). So state the exact breakpoint in terms of the
maximum concurrent requests and the per-rank/aggregate feasibility, not as “a 32 K or
128 K context no longer fits.” The specific breakpoint is workload‑ and SLO‑dependent and
must be checked per‑rank (Chapters 17, 20), not asserted as a universal constant.
• Impact of reranking on latency: The TTFT budget assumes retrieval (~120 ms) plus prefill.
If a late‑stage reranker is added to the pipeline, the retrieval component’s latency may increase,
eating into the TTFT budget and potentially requiring a wider SLO margin or a faster retriever.
The magnitude of this effect is [UNRESOLVED] and should be measured before production
deployment.
• Economic durability at scale: The tokens‑per‑dollar numbers are derived from 2026 on‑de­
mand H100 pricing. Spot instances, reserved contracts, or custom cloud agreements could shift
the economics significantly. The durability of the economic model across provider changes is
[UNRESOLVED].

4.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: A Six-Dimension Workload Characterization
An architect is brought into the early design of an internal Q&A platform. The stakeholder says: “We
have thousands of employees who want to ask questions over our internal documents. We need it to
be accurate and fast, but we don’t know how many thousands or how fast is fast enough.” Before
any architecture can be defended, the architect does the workload characterization that this chapter
walks through.
Using the canonical scenario as a starting point — ~2,000 registered users, ~5% concurrency, ~10
rps, ~9.2 K input + 300 output tokens — the architect projects the enterprise’s actual headcount. If
the company has 5,000 employees and expects 10% concurrent activity during peak Q&A periods
(after a policy rollout), that gives 500 active people — a population measure, not 500 requests
currently occupying the inference service. An arrival rate requires its own traffic assumption or
observation. Suppose user research and demand modeling independently set the busy-period peak to
50 requests/s (a declared scenario input at this growth scale, not a figure derived from the 500-user
count — Little’s Law cannot convert an active-user population into an arrival rate without knowing
in-flight request occupancy). With the illustrative ~8.6 s engine response duration, Little’s Law
implies approximately 50 × 8.6 ≈ 430 requests in the system across the fleet at that rate — distinct
from the 500 active people. It is the arrival rate, not the user count, that sizes the fleet. Using the
canonical per-host bound from Chapters 15–20 (a single 8×H100 host serves ~2.0 rps at full modeled
utilization, i.e. the whole-slot floor 17 KV-resident requests ÷ 8.6 s = 1.977 — C ≈ 17.5 (= 436 GB
÷ 24.9 GB, the 9.5K-token resident basis of §6) is the analytical quotient, floored to 17 deployable
whole-context slots per the book’s whole-slot convention, Chapters 14/16/17), the fleet rounds up by
the same whole-slot ceiling the canonical 40 rps case uses (⌈344/17⌉ = 21):

not a measured duty cycle) depending on purchase mode and duty cycle (the canonical self-host

dollars per million — and can engage the rest of the team on model selection, serving configuration,
and TCO with concrete numbers rather than vague assurances.
The specific sizing — turning “thousands of employees” into a characterized workload across all
six dimensions — is the payoff of Ch. 4’s framework. Each dimension carries an arithmetic (quality
→ accuracy target and its validation; traffic → offered load and occupancy; token profile → KV and
prefill demand; latency → service time and SLO; economics → $/token and $/request; operational
→ availability topology, data locality, refresh cadence) that the later chapters plug specific numbers

79

The Anatomy of an AI Workload

into. Until a workload has numbers on all six axes, any architecture chosen against it is being chosen
against a category, not a workload.

chapter 5.
From Workload to Model Selection

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to reason about model selection as a consequence of workload
characterization, not as a first question. We should also be able to walk the two-part selection
that defines a RAG system: (a) choosing an embedding model for the retrieval leg, and (b) choosing
a generation model for the answer leg. The chapter works toward showing that “which model is
best?” is the wrong first question; the right first question is “what job does this system do, and how
quantitatively?”

5.1. Concept
Model selection proceeds across five surfaces, each derived from the workload characterization (Ch
4, Table 4-2):
1. Capability / quality needed — does the workload require multi-step reasoning, tool use,
or modality handling? A workload that needs chain-of-thought reasoning needs a different
model class than one that only needs fact retrieval.
2. Latency / compute budget — can the system meet TTFT and TPOT SLOs with the candidate
model on the target hardware? This surface determines whether we need a dense 70B, a
distilled 13B, or a MoE variant.
3. Context / KV cost — how much memory does the input context consume in the KV cache, and
what does that mean for feasible context length on the target infrastructure? An 8K-context
workload has a very different cost profile from a 32K-context one.
4. Cost per token — what is the $/million-tokens for the full request (prefill + decode) on

80

81

From Workload to Model Selection

the target infrastructure? This surface makes the economic difference between model sizes
concrete.
5. Retrieve-then-generate vs end-to-end — does the system architecture split the job into a
retrieval leg (embedding model + vector search) followed by a generation leg (base model +
prompt), or does it use a single model that jointly retrieves and generates? This architectural
decision drives the embedding‑vs‑generation model contrast.
The core reframe — modeled in Chapter 4 — is that model selection is a consequence of
workload characterization. When the workload is specified in token counts, request rates, latency
budgets, and economic constraints, the feasible model space narrows naturally. The architect does
not start with a model and reason forward; they start with the workload and reason backward into
model space.
5.1.1. A model candidate includes its deployment precision
A model name alone does not identify a deployable candidate. The same checkpoint can produce
different quality, memory use and execution paths under different quantization recipes.1,2 We
therefore compare a base-model revision together with its tensor precisions, calibration or recovery
procedure, export schema and serving backend. The quality gate applies to that exported deployment,
including its tokenizer, prompt template and modality branches. A language-only quantization result
does not establish that a vision encoder, projector or tool-use workload retains the same behavior.
The mechanism and byte accounting appear in Chapter 7; Chapter 14 supplies the acceptance test.
[1P][DERIVED]
5.1.2. Inference mode is a candidate, not a selection verdict
The same task can favor different inference modes at different concurrency levels. Parallel refinement
(diffusion-style decoding that updates many token positions per step) is worth investigating when lowbatch latency or constrained infilling dominates, but neither advantage follows from a model-family
label. AR fill-in-the-middle (FIM) models — autoregressive models trained to infill a marked span —
are a necessary editing baseline. For the canonical RAG workload, the inference mode is standard
autoregressive generation; the selection question reduces to whether the chosen AR model, tokenizer,
and serving runtime meet the SLOs. For workloads that might use non‑AR generation (editing,
infilling, image‑to‑text), the mode itself becomes an additional selection dimension. Structured
output adds another gate: an API that documents JSON-schema generation and a self-hosted backend
that rejects grammar constraints are not interchangeable candidates.3 The selection question is

5.2. Mental Model
Model selection is really system design, not model picking. The workload is the architect’s input;
the model is a component that must satisfy the workload’s constraints. If the workload is inputheavy (9.2K average input, 300-token output, ~30× more input than output), the system is first-order
memory‑capacity‑bound (the KV cache’s HBM footprint limits how many concurrent requests fit
— KV HBM capacity limits concurrency, not bandwidth — at the Ch 17 concurrency screen) and
prefill‑dominated in FLOPs — a first-order tendency to verify per workload, not a consequence of
input-heaviness alone. If the workload were output‑heavy, the token/FLOP mix shifts toward decode,
which often makes decode bandwidth or latency critical — the actual bottleneck must be measured
on the target stack. The mental model holds both profiles in view: the same “which model?” question
produces opposite answers depending on the token profile.
A useful image for the full pipeline:
Workload → Selection surfaces → Model category → Specific model
The arrow from workload to selection surfaces is the one the architect must keep in focus. Every
other arrow follows from it.

one 8×H100 host. TTFT budget 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill), TPOT ~25 ms/token; p95 TTFT ≤ 2

overstates compute — most for the smallest model (MiniLM’s table is ~51% of its params). Body-parameter
ratios are the truer cross-model comparison (mpnet/MiniLM ~7.7× body-only vs 4.8× by total params), so
the proxy overstates each model’s compute most for the smallest, and the proxy ratio (4.8×) is a lower
bound on the true body-only compute ratio (≈7.7×), not an upper bound. [DERIVED]
[HYPOTHESIS] : within a given embedding family or a controlled dimensionality experiment,
reducing the embedding dimension may trade retrieval quality for lower index storage and query‑time
projection cost (the encoder’s compute is essentially unchanged) — e.g. a 384‑dim variant of the same
model family can halve the index storage of a 768‑dim one (the encoder’s compute is essentially
unchanged, since only the final projection shrinks). Dimension alone is not a cross‑model quality
metric: a 1024‑dim embedding model is not intrinsically better than a 768‑dim one merely because its
vector has more dimensions; retrieval quality depends on model architecture, training objective/data,

corpus/query distribution, normalization, and retrieval strategy. Assume, as a scenario input rather
than a measured result, a quality‑vs‑dimension uplift of up to ~15% MAP (an assumption, not a cited
finding — no study is invoked here); any such relationship is domain‑ and corpus‑specific and must
be validated on the target corpus.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: for a 1 M‑chunk corpus (a Ch 5‑local illustrative input, not part
of Table 4‑2), the index storage for a D‑dim float32 vector corpus is bytes = nchunks × D × 4. For
768‑dim: 1×106 × 768 × 4 = 3.07 GB; for 384‑dim: 1×106 × 384 × 4 = 1.54 GB; a difference of
~1.5 GB. At 10× the corpus (10 M chunks), that difference grows to ~15 GB. Small relative to a 140 GB
base model, but not negligible at large corpus scale: storage is a persistent footprint that scales with
corpus size, not a one‑time cost that vanishes.
[HYPOTHESIS] : for the canonical 2,000‑user workload with ~10 rps average, the incremental
per‑request compute cost of the 768‑dim (all‑mpnet) vs 384‑dim (MiniLM) embedding models — a
cross‑model difference, not a dim‑only sweep — is ~11.1 GFLOP per 64‑token query (2 × params × L:
14.08 − 2.94 GFLOP, the Table 5‑1 embedding table’s own rows; a same‑family 384‑dim variant halves
index storage (encoder compute ~unchanged)) — ~186–371 ms if encoded on a single CPU core at
~30–60 GFLOP/s sustained (~200 GFLOP/s is the AVX‑512 theoretical peak, not a sustained rate), but
only ~1.1 ms on a ~10 TFLOP/s GPU, which is the basis the ~120 ms retrieval budget already assumes
(vector search and reranking on a local GPU, Ch 4).
On that basis the incremental cost stays well within the ~120 ms retrieval budget; single‑core
encoding fits only above ≈92.8 GFLOP/s sustained per core (11.14 GFLOP ÷ 0.12 s), beyond the
typical sustained range (371 ms at 30 GFLOP/s vs 186 ms at 60 GFLOP/s) — conditional on measured
single-core throughput.
The decision hinges on whether the top‑of‑range ~15% MAP gain (a [HYPOTHESIS] scenario
input, and a within‑family / controlled‑dimension upper bound that cannot be assumed to transfer
across model families — §5.3(a)) translates into sufficient answer‑quality improvement to justify the
~4.8×FLOP cost (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP per 64‑token query, Table 5‑1). The same bar that rules out
bge‑large applies here: the mpnet‑vs‑MiniLM quality gap must be measured on the target corpus
before the ~4.8× FLOP cost is paid — a workload‑specific tradeoff, not a universal rule.
Takeaway for the canonical RAG workload: 768‑dim (all‑mpnet‑base‑v2) is the recommended
embedding model. It balances compute, storage, and expected quality as a mid‑range candidate —
compute and storage alone favour the 384‑dim option — and the quality claim itself is the §5.3(a)/§7
item still to validate on the target corpus, and it introduces no per‑request latency that threatens the
TTFT SLO. The quality gain behind this recommendation is an unverified scenario input of up to
~15% MAP [HYPOTHESIS], not quantified for this model pair — the same test applied to bge‑large
applies here: validate it on the target corpus. The 384‑dim option is viable only if storage or compute
budget is extremely constrained; the bge‑large‑en option is not justified at this scale: its quality gain
over all‑mpnet‑base‑v2 is not quantified for this model pair (the table gives use cases, not metrics),
and an unquantified gain would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar (≈43 vs ≈14 GFLOPs per 64‑token

[canonical scenario][DERIVED]: a 70B-class parameter model at FP16 occupies 70B × 2 bytes = ~140
GB (the 70B is the constructed canonical teaching geometry, Ch 4 Table 4-2; the 140 GB is derived
from it, not a vendor-published model card). [1P][FACT]: 8×H100 GPUs provide 8 × 80 GB = 640 GB
aggregate HBM memory (real hardware spec).
[canonical scenario][DERIVED] KV cache per token at FP16: for the canonical full‑MHA 70B
reference (80 layers, hidden 8192, no GQA — the constructed teaching geometry of Ch 4 Table 4‑2),
n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192, bytes per element = 2 (FP16). KV cache per token = n_layers × 2
× d_model × bytes = 80 ×2 × 8192 ×2 = 2,621,440 bytes ≈ 2.62 MB/token (FP16; = 2.5 MiB) (key +
value across all layers). A real Llama‑2/3 70B checkpoint is not this geometry: it uses grouped‑query
attention with 8 KV heads of head_dim 128 (n_kv_dim = 1024), giving 80 ×2×1024×2 = 327,680 bytes
≈ 0.33 MB/token at FP16 — ~8× less KV. The 2.62 MB/token full‑MHA value is the canonical reference
kept for cross‑chapter consistency. For the canonical 9.2K input: 9,200 ×2.62 MB ≈ 24.1 GB of KV
cache (initial residency).
[canonical scenario][DERIVED] per‑request memory budget: 640 GB total HBM − 140 GB weights
= 500 GB headroom (before the ~64 GB runtime reserve that the concurrency budget in Ch 7 subtracts
to reach the ~436 GB KV budget). 24.1 GB is ~5.5% of the ~436 GB KV budget, leaving ~411.9 GB
for other requests’ KV; the ~64 GB runtime reserve covers activations, intermediate buffers and OS
overhead. This is comfortably within a single 8×H100 node’s capacity.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]: a low-batch (single-stream) decode rate of ~50 tokens/s on
8×H100 with a 70B FP16 model and 9.2K context for 300‑token outputs. The prefill phase (9.2K
tokens) dominates TTFT: at ~1.08 s it leaves ~0.12 s against the 1.2 s budget — exactly the ~120 ms
retrieval allocation, i.e. zero true headroom. Adding retrieval (~120 ms) puts the retrieval+prefill
budget estimate (queueing, tokenization, network transit, scheduling and first-token sampling scoped
out) at ~1.20 s, i.e. at the 1.2 s design budget with no prefill-side margin; the real margin is the p95 ≤
2 s target.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: tokens/s per dollar for generation. On‑demand H100 list price
~$2.50/hour per GPU → 8×H100 = $20/hour. At ~50 tok/s aggregate throughput, the effective
cost is ~$0.40 per (tok/s) per hour, or equivalently ~2.5 (tok/s) per dollar-per-hour of budget. In
tokens‑per‑dollar terms: 50 tok/s × 3600 s/hr ÷ $20/hr = 9,000 tokens per dollar.
Economics unit note (reconciliation with Ch 4 and Ch 15). Both chapters use
the same on-demand price basis: ~$2.50/hr per H100 → ~$20/hr per 8×H100 host. Two
things must be kept straight. First, units: both chapters express tokens per dollar —
this chapter computes it as token-rate × 3600 s ÷ hourly cost (50 × 3600 ÷ 20 = 9,000
tokens per dollar), which is algebraically identical to token-rate ÷ per-second cost (50 ÷
(20/3600) = 9,000); no 3600 factor separates the two formulas. Second, throughput basis:
the ~50 tok/s used here is a deliberately low-batch (single-stream) generation rate —
conservative against batched serving rates, though above the canonical 40 tok/s batch-1

point (25 ms/token) — adopted to illustrate the per-dollar method, not a claim about the
host’s batched serving throughput. Chapter 15’s figures are two different quantities, and
neither is the low-batch generation rate used here: its ~8.5K tok/s is a prefill-side /
whole-request rate (Chapter 4’s ≈8.5K tokens/s prefill — 9,200 tokens ÷ ~1.08 s — not
batch-1 decode, which at the canonical 25 ms/token is ~40 tok/s, Chapter 2), while its
~35,000–56,000 tok/s is the multi-request serving throughput under FlashAttention
+ continuous batching. The ~50 tok/s here (this worked example’s low-batch decode

Chapter 15’s prefill-side rate are therefore different phases of the same host, not two
values for one quantity. The per-dollar figures therefore scale up substantially at batch,
and the 9,000 tokens-per-dollar figure should be read as a floor set by the single-stream
assumption, not as the host’s economic optimum. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

consumes ~97% of the tokens per request (9,200 ÷ 9,500) — and, because each prefill token runs the
full 2 × 70B forward FLOP, it is also ~97% of the linear forward-FLOP cost (before the quadratic
attention term). But it is only ~15% of the wall-clock time (1.08 s prefill vs 6.0 s decode), because
prefill is compute‑intensive and batchable across concurrent requests; decode has a per-request
sequential dependency but is also batched across requests (continuous batching) — batching raises
GPU utilization without removing per-token latency. So the honest picture is both: prefill dominates
the linear FLOP budget (~97% of tokens and linear FLOPs) while decode dominates single-stream
wall-clock (~85% of 1.08 s + 6.0 s); GPU-hour cost follows occupancy, batching and scheduling — it is
not proportional to either share without a stated utilization assumption. The per‑dollar economics
therefore favor models that reduce the prefill compute burden (smaller context, larger batch, lower
per‑token FLOP) more than models that optimize decode throughput alone — but a deployment
must balance both, since decode still sets the latency SLO.
