5.3.3. (c) Base‑model + RAG + guardrails vs fine‑tuned model
The architect must choose between two paradigms:
Paradigm 1 — Base model + RAG + guardrails:
• The base 70B model receives the retrieved 9.2K context via prompt injection.
• Guardrails (PII redaction, style enforcement, refusal filtering) are applied as post‑generation or
prefix‑check layers.
• No model weights are trained on domain data; the knowledge source is the vector database.
Paradigm 2 — Fine‑tuned model on domain‑specific Q‑A pairs:
• The base model is fine‑tuned (full-parameter, or low‑rank adaptation (LoRA)) on thousands of
question‑answer pairs reflecting the enterprise’s terminology and reasoning patterns.
• Inference uses the fine‑tuned weights without a retrieval step, or with a much shorter retrieved
context. Fine‑tuning is not a dependable substitute for retrieval when the requirement is
factual corpus access, freshness, attribution, or precise enterprise knowledge — fine‑tuning
distills behavior, style, task patterns, format, and tool‑use policy, not a guarantee that arbitrary
facts are recalled faithfully. Whether it reduces retrieval dependence for a particular task is an
empirical question to be measured on that task’s evaluation set.
• Additional costs: training compute, storage of fine‑tuned weights, and reduced flexibility for
new topics.
([ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — not a reference measurement): for the canonical workload,
a well‑designed RAG + guardrails pipeline may approach a fine‑tuned model’s answer quality on
in‑domain queries. This is task‑, model‑, data‑, and evaluation‑dependent — it is not derivable
from the architecture alone. The two mechanisms do different work: RAG supplies external, mutable
knowledge (grounding, provenance, freshness); fine‑tuning shapes behavior, style, domain reasoning
patterns, format, and tool‑use policy. Either or both can improve answer quality, and they can be
combined. Whether fine‑tuning reduces retrieval dependence for this workload must be established
by measuring answer quality on the actual evaluation set. The economic comparison should be framed
parametrically, not with a single number, because the break‑even depends on the quality uplift
(domain‑specific) and the query volume (workload‑specific). The decision variable is the break‑even
query volume Q∗ where the up‑front plus carry cost of fine‑tuning, divided by its quality advantage,
crosses the RAG baseline:
Q∗ =

Ctrain + Cweights-extra
∆Q · value per corrected query

where Ctrain is the one‑time training cost (monetary, compute included), Cweights-extra is the
incremental storage/carry cost, and ∆Q is the (domain‑specific, must‑be‑measured) quality uplift in
corrected answers per query, while value per corrected query is the monetary value of one additional
corrected answer, in the same currency as Ctrain .

89

From Workload to Model Selection

Note: this formula captures only the one‑time training and carry cost amortized against the
quality uplift; it omits the recurring per‑query prefill/retrieval saving that fine‑tuning’s shorter
context (§5.3(c)) would confer, so it yields an upper bound on the true break‑even volume — a
conservative (higher) estimate of the queries needed to justify fine‑tuning, in favour of RAG +
guardrails, because omitting fine‑tuning’s recurring saving understates its benefit.
Below Q∗ , RAG + guardrails is economically dominant because the fine‑tuning cost is spread
over too few queries to be repaid; above it, fine‑tuning may recover its upfront cost through quality
gain. (Scenario structure, not a single claimed break‑even volume; the exact Ctrain , Cweights-extra , and
∆Q are workload‑ and domain‑specific and should be measured, not assumed.)
Fine‑tuning does not make the model smaller — pruning is a separate operation. A full fine‑tune
keeps the ~140 GB 70B weight set (and adds a checkpoint), while a LoRA adapter is tiny but does
not change the live weight footprint. Consequently the latency effect of fine‑tuning is not “smaller
effective model” and cannot be assumed to cut TTFT; any TTFT change must be measured. The
monetary deltas are (a) one-time training cost and (b) incremental storage; separately, the latency
effect on TTFT must be measured — the RAG pipeline’s ~1.08 s prefill dominates any plausible
TTFT delta. Parametrically, fine‑tuning becomes worth it only when its total (one-time training +
storage/carry) cost spread over Q queries is repaid by ∆Q · value — this is exactly the Q∗ above.
Takeaway: For the canonical enterprise Q&A RAG workload, the base‑model + RAG + guardrails
paradigm is the default under this chapter’s stated assumptions — the break-even is parametric (Q* of
§5.3(c)) and not measured for this workload, so ‘economically preferred’ is conditional on lying below
Q*. Fine‑tuning is most compelling when the query distribution is highly concentrated, the domain
vocabulary is extremely specialized, and the workload volume sustains the training amortization
threshold. Style, format and tool-use-policy tuning can be compelling even without a concentrated
distribution or specialized vocabulary.

5.4. Measurement
How does an architect measure the workload dimensions that drive model selection? The tokencounting habits of Ch 1 §1.4 apply unchanged; the three things the selection view adds are:
1. Measure the token split on real employee queries, not the heuristic. Run the model’s
own tokenizer on representative prompts from the target domain — the “4 chars ≈ 1 token”
heuristic is for estimation only. For the canonical workload, measure the exact prompt+context
token count on real employee queries before fixing the model, because the ~30× input-to-output
ratio is the single biggest driver of this system’s cost structure (Ch 4).
2. Quantify the output size, since that drives decode cost and per-request latency. The
output token count determines total decode work and end-to-end decode latency; p95 TPOT
depends on per-token cost and scheduling; a large-output paradigm (e.g. long-form generation)
changes the model-selection calculus versus a short-output Q&A system.
3. Know the 95th-percentile context length, not just the average. Log the distribution of

From Workload to Model Selection

90

context lengths. A workload that averages 9.2K input but peaks at 32K (a variant flagged in Ch
4) requires a different KV budget and, with it, a different model-size or attention-hybridity
choice. Size against the tail.
These checks let model selection be made on measured workload dimensions rather than a
generic “bigger model is better” assumption.
5.4.1. Model identity includes the execution path
Backend identity completes the candidate: the relevant identity includes the checkpoint revision,
tokenizer, numerical representation, engine revision and device backend. A loader may recognize
the model while a fused attention operator, recurrent-state update or quantized expert kernel is
unavailable on the target device. A fallback can restore execution but change latency, memory use or
numerical behavior. We therefore separate model-quality acceptance from backend qualification. Both
must hold for the same configuration. A small successful completion does not validate long-context
state, concurrent-request isolation or the intended serving SLO.4

5.5. Common Mistakes
• Starting with “which model is best?” Instead of characterizing the workload first. The
workload’s token profile, latency budget, and economic constraints are what narrow the
model space; starting with a model short‑circuits the reasoning chain and leads to post hoc
justification.
• Ignoring the KV cache cost of long contexts. A 9.2K input on a 70B model costs ~24.1 GB
of KV cache (initial). An architect who does not account for this will either over‑provision
infrastructure or hit SLO violations when the cache spills to host memory or SSD.
• Quoting context window as free capacity. The 128K or 1M token window is an upper
bound, not a recommendation. Using even 9.2K of a 128K window still costs for the length
actually used. The cost is proportional to the used length, not the available length.
• Assuming embedding dimension is a free parameter. Increasing embedding dimension­
ality within a given model family or controlled configuration can improve retrieval fidelity,
but dimensionality alone does not predict quality across different embedding models. Higher

dimension also raises FLOP cost, index storage, and per‑query latency, so the architect must
balance these against the workload’s quality requirements rather than treat dimension as a
cost‑free or universally-better knob (see the caveat in §5.3(a); section references §N.M read as
chapter N, section M).
• Over‑engineering the fine‑tuning path. Fine‑tuning adds training compute and
model/checkpoint‑management cost; depending on the adaptation and serving method, it may
also add inference or operational overhead (e.g. a LoRA adapter applied dynamically at serve
time can introduce overhead, whereas a merged/fully‑fine‑tuned model of identical architecture
need not change the inference shape). The parametric Q∗ in §5.3 shows how to decide — RAG
+ guardrails dominates below the break‑even volume and fine‑tuning may dominate above it
— but the break‑even is workload‑ and domain‑specific and must be measured before either
paradigm is declared dominant for most workloads. Fine‑tuning should be a deliberate choice
triggered by a measured quality gap or domain/operational requirement plus sustained query
volume and economics, not a default.

5.6. Architecture Consequence
Whatever we learned here, file it under “can I size the workload before I pick a model?”
Concretely, the decision this chapter enables is:
• Estimate tokens‑per‑request (input and output separately), and therefore tokens‑per‑second
capacity and cost, before choosing a model or a serving configuration.
• Use the selection surfaces (quality, latency, KV cost, cost/token, retrieve‑vs‑generate) to narrow
the model space from the full vendor catalog to a handful of viable candidates.
• For RAG workloads, select the embedding model and generation model as a two‑part decision,
not a single choice. The embedding model is chosen at ingestion time (compute‑light, stor­
age‑bound) but also carries query‑time embedding cost and latency; the generation model is
chosen at serving time, with prefill often compute‑bound and decode often memory‑band­
width‑bound — the SLO makes it latency‑bound.
This consequence feeds directly into the fine-tuning-for-specific-workloads pattern and the RAG
pattern (both cataloged in Ch 26, Patterns Library): the architect first characterizes the workload,
then lets the characterization drive model selection, not the other way around.

5.7. What We Still Don’t Know
[HYPOTHESIS] : the interaction between embedding dimension and retrieval quality across
diverse enterprise domains is not yet characterized with reproducible benchmarks. Some inspected
embedding models use 768 dimensions; this is not a general quality optimum and must be validated
on the target corpus. The quality difference between 768 and 1024 dim varies by corpus genre (legal
vs. engineering vs. creative), and no public study quantifies this domain‑dependence.

From Workload to Model Selection

92

[HYPOTHESIS] : the break‑even point between RAG + guardrails and fine‑tuned models as a
function of query volume and domain specialization is model‑ and domain‑dependent: it is set
by the Q∗ equation above (training + storage cost over the quality uplift), not by a universal rule of
thumb. Any quoted break‑even volume is a derived scenario value; more data points and a measured
∆Q are needed before it can be stated as a general principle.
[HYPOTHESIS] : guardrail latency (PII redaction, refusal checking) on generated 300‑token
outputs, ~2–8 ms/request on CPU in the illustrative scenario; measure on the target stack (the figure
depends on the guardrail implementation and hardware).
Each of these flags is an open empirical question a team should resolve against its own target
workload — resolved by measurement into [1P][FACT] or [2°][FACT], promoted to [1P][DERIVED]
or [2°][DERIVED] where the resolution is arithmetic, or dropped — rather than left as an untested
assumption.

5.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Choosing the Model for the Enterprise Q&A
(Continuous scenario: the enterprise Q&A architect must now pick the model given the Ch 4 characteri­

An architect is assembled for a design review of the enterprise Q&A tool described in Chapter
4 — the canonical workload (Ch 4, Table 4-2). The team has agreed on the retrieval architecture:
vector search with embeddings, 768‑dim all‑mpnet‑base‑v2, single‑vector (cosine/dot‑product ANN)
retrieval over a 1 M‑chunk corpus.
From Ch 1’s unit-and-token work and Ch 5’s selection surfaces, the architect can immediately
check the consequences:
• 768‑dim embeddings are the agreed candidate; their retrieval quality is the gate still to validate
on the target corpus (§5.3(a), §7), and their cost is ~14 GFLOPs per embedding (64‑token query,
the Table 5‑1 embedding table’s own row: 2 × 110M × 64 ≈ 14.08 GFLOP), with ~3.1 GB index
storage for a 1 M‑chunk corpus (vs ~1.5 GB at 384‑dim) — a persistent footprint that scales
with corpus size, alongside the 70B base model.
• 9.2K input at ~2.62 MB/KV‑token costs ~24.1 GB of cache (initial) on the 70B generation model
— well within for a single request; the ~436 GB KV budget (640 − 140 − 64, §5.3(b)) supports
~436/24.9 ≈ 17.5, i.e. 17 whole‑slot concurrent 9,500‑token requests per host — a KV‑only upper
bound, computed at the end‑of‑generation ~24.9 GB footprint (9,500 × 2.62 MB); against the
initial 9.2K KV alone the quotient is 18.1 (Ch 7). The prefill TTFT of ~1.08 s plus retrieval (~120
ms) sits at the 1.2 s TTFT budget, with the p95 ≤ 2 s SLO giving the real margin.
• The 30× input‑vs‑output ratio means this system is prefill‑dominated in token/FLOP volume,
not in latency: at 300 output tokens and ~25 ms TPOT, decode alone is ~7.5 s versus ~1.08
s prefill, so end‑to‑end latency is decode‑dominated. Model selection must weigh KV cache
cost and prefill throughput for compute and capacity, and decode throughput for latency and
concurrency.

• The base‑model + RAG + guardrails paradigm is the chapter’s default; whether it has lower
TCO depends on where the workload falls relative to the parametric Q∗ break‑even above,
which is workload‑specific and unmeasured. A common industry claim is that RAG is 10×
cheaper — that ratio is not derivable from the architecture alone: the actual ratio depends on
the domain‑specific quality uplift and the query volume, and must be measured rather than
assumed.
The architect now has a concrete model shortlist: 768‑dim all‑mpnet‑base‑v2 for the retrieval
leg, and the 70B FP16 base model for the generation leg (dense — the ~47B‑total / 12.8B‑active

chapter 6.
Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to
Architecture Decisions

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to walk into a running inference system, read its metrics, and
answer a deceptively hard question: is this system meeting its obligations, and if not, which lever do
we pull? Teams commonly instrument the wrong thing — model capability and offline quality —
and then are blind when a real workload misbehaves. This chapter builds the metric hierarchy that
turns raw telemetry into architecture decisions: what to log, what each number means, how to read a
latency distribution instead of a mean, and how to tell bandwidth-bound from compute-bound purely
from the counters. After this chapter, “the system felt slow” becomes a falsifiable, diagnosable claim.

6.1. Concept
6.1.1. The Metric Hierarchy
Not all numbers are equal. We organize serving telemetry into three layers, each answering a different
question and each consumed by a different role:
1. Workload metrics — what the system is being asked to do. Requests per second (rps) and the
token profile (input length, output length, context length). These are the independent variables
— the offered load; we do not control them, we characterize them. Admitted concurrency is a
serving/scheduler state (Little’s law), not a workload input. For the canonical enterprise-Q&A
RAG workload these are fixed by canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average with
~40 rps peaks, ~9,200 input + ~300 output tokens per request.

95

Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions

96

2. Serving metrics — how well the system performs under that workload. Time-to-first-token
(TTFT), time-per-output-token (TPOT), inter-token latency, and goodput (tokens per second
that actually meet the SLO). These are the dependent variables; they are what the SLO is
written against — the canonical SLO targets are TTFT 1.2 s / TPOT ~25 ms. Queue depth is
not one of them: it is a scheduler state, a leading indicator that helps explain these serving
metrics.
3. Resource metrics — why performance is what it is. HBM bandwidth utilization, FLOP
utilization / model FLOPs utilization (MFU), KV cache occupancy, and memory pressure.
These reveal the binding constraint.
The discipline this chapter works toward: never jump from a workload metric straight to a
serving metric, or a serving metric straight to a hardware conclusion. The causal direction is
workload → resource demand → serving behavior (the workload’s token profile drives the resource
demand; the resource supply shapes how the model behaves). Diagnosis runs the other way: a slow
response (serving) is diagnosed by asking whether the kernel is bandwidth- or compute-bound
(resource), which is only meaningful given the token profile (workload). Skipping a layer produces
superstition — “it’s slow, let’s buy GPUs” — instead of a mechanism.
6.1.2. Why the Wrong Metric Persists
Teams default to measuring what they already have dashboards for: model quality (accuracy, ROUGE,
benchmark scores) and average latency. Both are dangerously incomplete. Quality is the goal and
a feasibility gate — a fast or cheap architecture that fails the quality bar is disqualified before
performance even matters — but it is not the bottleneck that explains a resource or latency failure
once quality is acceptable; that is the role of the serving metrics. Average latency is a single scalar
that hides the tail that actually violates SLAs. The entire thesis of this chapter is that the metric that
drives an architecture decision is usually not the metric the model card advertises.

6.2. Mental Model
The three metric layers form a diagnostic chain, like the layers of the OSI stack in miniature:
• Workload is the traffic — what we are asked to do.
• Serving is the service — how well we did it.
• Resource is the engine — how hard the machine is working, and on what.
(The listing order here is by role — independent inputs, dependent outputs, explanatory engine.
It is not the causal order: causation flows workload → resource → serving, which is how Fig 6.1
stacks them top to bottom. The two orderings are different and both intentional.)
When something breaks, we read upward: a p95 TTFT breach (serving) forces us to look at
the resource layer first (resource: is prefill queuing because we’re FLOP-bound?) and then the

token profile (workload: did context length grow?). The causal direction follows the system, not

behavior — so when numbers are healthy, the chain shows the system meets the SLO under the
observed workload.
The mental model also warns against one number standing in for many different things.
“Throughput” without a qualifier is meaningless: is it requests per second, tokens per second, or
goodput — tokens per second that arrived before the SLO deadline? We commit to always qualifying.

6.3. Worked Example
6.3.1. Latency Is a Distribution, Not a Mean
A very common measurement error is reporting (and SLO-ing) the average latency. Fig 6.2 shows a
synthetic request stream: the body of requests follows a log‑normal distribution centered near 0.8
s (99% of observations), with a 1% straggler cluster at 5.0 s. That combination is deliberately not a
two‑point “99% at 0.8, 1% at 5” distribution; it is a realistic spread, so the percentiles below are read
off the plotted histogram rather than guessed. The plotted stream is a synthetic sample of N = 10,000
requests — 99% drawn from a log‑normal with median 0.8 s, 1% a straggler cluster at 5.0 s — and the
percentiles are read by linear interpolation on the sorted sample. The two-point approximation of
the mean is
E[L] ≈ 0.99 × 0.8 + 0.01 × 5.0 ≈ 0.84 s
— looks fine. But the distribution actually has a long tail: p50 ≈ 0.80 s, p90 ≈ 0.94 s, p95 ≈ 0.99 s, and p99
≈ 1.33 s — a knife-edge property of this N = 10,000 sample, not of the distribution: linear interpolation
lands just past the largest non-straggler draw, between it and the first straggler (percentile position
1 + (N−1)×0.99 = 9,900.01; sorted-sample ranks: 9,900 → 1.30 s, 9,901 → 5.0 s; 1.30 + 0.01 × (5.0 −
1.30) ≈ 1.33 s; population p99 → 5.0 s), while the population p99 of the stated 99 % log-normal + 1
% straggler mixture is 5.0 s (one extra straggler, 101 of 10,000, moves the sample p99 to 5.0 s too).
The mean hides the tail; percentiles expose it — but notice how far one has to go to expose this tail.
Under the canonical p95 TTFT SLO of ≤ 2 s, even this sample’s p99 (≈ 1.33 s) still looks healthy
— the population p99 is 5.0 s, sitting on the straggler cluster. Request latency ≥ TTFT, so a
TTFT-budget line drawn on request latency flags a superset of TTFT violations. The 5 s stragglers
are the top 1% of the stream — in this sample they sit between the 99th and 100th percentile, so the
interpolated p99 line alone does not bring them into view. Only the p99.9 / maximum reading (or
the full distribution) surfaces them. This is the sharper lesson: a tail can hide not just behind the
mean but behind any single percentile, and the choice of which percentile to SLO against matters. It
is why we log the full distribution and also watch the outlier fraction (how much probability mass
sits beyond the SLO line), not just one percentile.
Why the mean is not a signal. The same request stream of 99% @ 0.8 s + 1% @ 5 s reported as a
single number looks healthy (mean ≈ 0.84 s; the figure’s exact simulated stream mean ≈ 0.85 s — the

Apply this to the canonical workload. We budget TTFT ≤ 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill ~1.08
s) with a p95 ≤ 2 s. Suppose a flash crowd (the ~40 rps peak) causes prefill requests to queue. If on
average the batch is well-behaved, p50 TTFT might sit at ~1.0 s. But the jobs that arrive behind
~1–2 same-time prefill requests each pay the full 1.08 s prefill of the job(s) ahead of them, so p95
TTFT drifts to ~2.5 s. The average says “fine”; the p95 says “we just violated our SLO.” We hence
log p50, p90, p95, and p99 independently and run the SLO against the percentile, never the mean.

Table 4-2); the arithmetic is the point, not a citation.
6.3.2. Goodput vs Raw Throughput
Deploying a higher-throughput configuration can reduce goodput: goodput = raw_rate × compliant_
fraction, so a throughput increase helps goodput only if the compliant fraction holds. Concretely:
suppose we enable larger dynamic batching to raise raw tokens/s from 50 tok/s to 70 tok/s, but the
batch window pushes p95 TTFT from 1.8 s to 2.3 s — above the 2 s SLO. Scenario A [ILLUSTRATIVE]:
the extra 20 tok/s are produced, but they land in the tail that misses the SLO, so goodput does not
grow. Raw throughput is up 40%; goodput (tokens that met the SLO) is effectively unchanged in this
case, because the batch of SLO-compliant tokens didn’t grow.
The “unchanged” claim holds only when the extra tokens all land in the SLO-missing tail, i.e. the
compliant fraction drops proportionally to the raw-rate gain. Scenario B [ILLUSTRATIVE]: if the
compliant fraction falls from 96% to 94%, goodput is 50×0.96 = 48 vs 70×0.94 = 65.8 — it rises despite
the p95 breach. A p95 breach is a configuration-level acceptance signal. Request-level SLO-goodput is
a separate measurement: compute it from the compliant fraction, not from the p95 alone.
Scope note: the 50→70 tok/s figures are low-batch decode operating points (Ch 5’s illustrative basis,
~14–20 ms/token across the 50–70 tok/s range; canonical batch-1 is 40 tok/s at 25 ms/token), not the
host’s aggregate serving rate (Ch 15: ~8.5K tok/s prefill-side, ~35,000–56,000 tok/s batched) — the goodput
argument holds at any consistent operating point.
Goodput is the metric the customer experiences; raw throughput is what the GPU achieves. The
architect optimizes goodput. This is why “faster” hardware or bigger batches do not trivially mean a
better system.

101

Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions

6.3.3. Detecting the Regime: Bandwidth-Bound vs Compute-Bound
The most decision-relevant resource question is: is this layer bandwidth-bound or compute-bound?
We recall the arithmetic from Chapter 2:
• Decode is HBM-bandwidth-bound at low batch. The shard-invariant reason comes first:
at batch 1 decode’s arithmetic intensity is ~1.0 FLOP/byte (140 GFLOP / 140 GB), far below the
~295 FLOP/byte roofline ridge — this low intensity, not any single device’s bandwidth total,
is why decode is starved for weights regardless of sharding. Generating one token needs a
full forward pass over the 70B weights of the canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA
70B reference = 140 GB (FP16) of reads per token — a batch-1-equivalent idealized weightstreaming read (one request’s full weight pass), not a measured bytes-physically-read figure.
As a concrete single-device illustration: within a ~25 ms TPOT budget, 140 GB / 0.025 s ≈ 5.6
TB/s (batch-1-equivalent) exceeds an H100’s ~3.35 TB/s peak [1P][FACT]. Scope warning:
this 5.6-vs-3.35 TB/s comparison is an illustrative single-device roofline argument, not
the canonical 8×H100 host’s actual deployment verdict. Two scope notes keep this honest.
First, 5.6 TB/s is the aggregate model-wide weight-read rate for a hypothetical single-device
implementation; under tensor parallelism (the canonical 8×H100 host) the 140 GB is sharded, so
each GPU only needs ~0.70 TB/s against its own 3.35 TB/s (~21–25% achieved HBM utilization:
the canonical 25 ms TPOT is a budget covering TP collectives, kernel inefficiency, sampling
and scheduling, not a bandwidth-saturated point) — the single-device 5.6>3.35 bound does
not itself show a per-GPU bandwidth shortfall. Second, the intensity reason stated first above
is what makes this a roofline classification rather than a device verdict (the roofline and its
ridge are developed in Ch 8). So the honest statement is: decode is memory-bound because
its intensity is low and batching raises it, not merely because an aggregate 5.6 TB/s exceeds
one GPU’s 3.35 [canonical scenario][DERIVED]. (This is an operating-point property, not an
identity, and it is a weight-only statement: at high batch decode climbs the intensity slope and
can become compute-bound. With the canonical 9.2K KV re-read included, intensity saturates
at ~6.8 FLOP/byte, so decode stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size — Ch 8.)
• Prefill is compute-bound at the canonical long-prompt operating point. The reason
prefill lands on the compute plateau of the roofline is its high arithmetic intensity: the FLOPs per
byte moved are far above the ~295 FLOP/byte ridge point (developed in Ch 8), so the compute
units — not the HBM weight stream — are the binding resource. Only after establishing that
regime do we check the deadline: the prefill pass for 9,200 input tokens costs ≈ 2 ×70e9 params
× 9.2e3 tokens ≈ 1.29 PFLOP of linear (2PL) FLOPs (the quadratic attention term adds
≈ 0.2 PFLOP at 9.2K — ≈ 1.5 PFLOP full-square total, Ch 22 Table 22-1), which against the
~1.08 s prefill budget implies a required rate of ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS — above a single H100’s ~0.989
PFLOPS dense BF16 peak (FP16/BF16: same H100 peak) (1.19 > 0.989). But that 1.19-vs-0.989
comparison is a single-device deadline/capacity illustration, not the evidence that prefill

Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions

102

is compute-bound: on the canonical 8×H100 host the aggregate peak is ~7.9 PFLOPS, so the
host comfortably satisfies the rate — the “single H100 can’t prefill a 9.2K prompt in 1.08 s”
conclusion is about whether one arbitrarily-chosen GPU can meet the deadline, not about the
kernel’s roofline regime. Prefill being compute-bound (rather than bandwidth-bound) follows
from its high arithmetic intensity, not from the 1.19-vs-0.989 comparison. [canonical scenario]
[DERIVED]
At the resource layer, the tell is utilization: a decode kernel pinned at ~95% of HBM bandwidth
but ~30% of FLOPs is bandwidth-bound; a prefill kernel with ~90% FLOP utilization is compute-bound.
The same hardware, the same model — the boundary flips between prefill and decode.
This is precisely why Splitwise/DistServe (and Mooncake’s KV-centric disaggregation) split prefill
from decode onto different pools: the bottleneck-regime difference is the primary motivation for
disaggregation — see §6 for the conditions under which it pays. [S4][1P][FACT] (source keys: each
[S#] names one entry in the References chapter, where [S3]–[S7] resolve; Ch 11 lists [S1]–[S6]

inline.) These percentages are hypothetical telemetry signatures used to illustrate how to read
utilization — not a measured benchmark find from any trace. They are representative operating-point
values (a low-intensity decode kernel at high HBM-utilization/low FLOP-utilization, a high-intensity
prefill kernel at high FLOP-utilization), useful to classify a kernel’s regime; an actual deployment’s
percentages come from its own counters, and a real utilization reading (observed vs. theoretical peak
vs. required minimum) must be distinguished from these example values. See Ch 8 for the underlying
intensity/roofline arithmetic that shows why these regimes occur.

6.3.4. Reading Telemetry Into a Decision
A concrete dashboard-read → decision trace. We see: p95 TTFT climbing (serving), KV cache hit ratio
low (resource: memory), and prefill queue depth growing (serving). Workload is unchanged. Reading
up the chain: low prefix-cache hit means many independent 9.2K prefixes are being prefill-processed
from scratch on the ~40 rps peak — each ~1.29 PFLOP (case (i), linear-only) — aggregate prefill
demand at the 40 rps peak is 40 × 1.29 ≈ 51.6 PFLOP/s against the 8×H100 sustained prefill capacity
of ~2.77 PFLOP/s (35% MFU, Ch 8 §3) — ~18.6× oversubscribed (the datasheet-peak ~7.9 PFLOPS
gives ~6.5×, the theoretical ceiling only), consistent with Ch 8’s 19-host screen at this peak, so the
prefill queue grows until backpressure or prefix caching intervenes. The decision: enable prefix /
RadixAttention-style caching (SGLang) or Automatic Prefix Caching (vLLM) so the byte-identical
shared prefix is reused instead of re-prefilled - in the canonical workload (1,200 prompt + 8,000
per-query retrieved, Ch 4 Table 4-2) that shared prefix is at most the ~1,200-token prompt (~13% of
prefill FLOPs), because the 8K retrieved block differs per query; prefix caching is therefore a partial
mitigation, not the fix for the 40 rps prefill queue (§7 keeps the actual reduction [UNRESOLVED]).
[S3][1P][FACT] Prefix caching is a compute-saving move — its TTFT benefit arrives through the
prefill work it removes, not through a latency knob of its own — and the telemetry told us that.

Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions

104

6.4. Measurement
Three practical habits anchor the architect:
1. Instrument the hierarchy, not just the app. Deploy counters at all three layers from day
one — rps and token profile (workload); TTFT/TPOT/goodput percentiles and queue depth
(serving — queue depth being the scheduler state that explains the others); HBM bandwidth,
FLOP/MFU, KV cache occupancy, memory pressure (resource). A system that only logs serving
metrics cannot tell why; one that only logs resource metrics cannot tell what it was asked.
2. Always qualify “throughput.” rps ≠ tokens/s ≠ goodput. The same number, three stories.
State the SLO window (p95 ≤ 2 s TTFT) before quoting any rate, or the rate is meaningless.
3. Log the distribution. Capture p50/p90/p95/p99 for every latency metric, and the full tokenlength distribution (a 32K-tail context is a different workload than a 9.2K average). The mean
is a summary, not a signal.
These habits answer the book’s recurring question — what would we actually measure here? —
with three layers of counters at the edge, before any architecture decision is committed.

6.5. Common Mistakes
• SLO-ing the average. A ~0.85 s mean (the figure’s simulated stream; the two-point analytic
approximation gives ~0.84 s — the figure’s displayed value is used here) hides a 5 s tail. SLO
against p95/p99, and watch the outlier fraction, not the mean.
• Optimizing raw throughput when the SLO windows it. Bigger batches raise raw tokens/s
but can push TTFT past its deadline, zeroing goodput. Optimize goodput.
• Jumping straight to “buy more GPUs.” A bandwidth-bound decode and a prefill-cost
problem need different fixes; without the resource layer we guess.
• Treating hardware peak as a ceiling we can hit. H100’s 3.35 TB/s is the theoretical HBM
peak; real memory-bound kernels realize a fraction of it. Design headroom against real utiliza­
tion, not the spec sheet.
• Conflating model-quality metrics with serving metrics. Accuracy is the goal; TTFT is
the constraint. A slow, accurate model fails its SLO just as surely as a fast, wrong one.

6.6. Architecture Consequence
The metric hierarchy directly dictates architecture. For the canonical workload:
• Bandwidth-bound decode + compute-bound prefill ⇒ P/D disaggregation (Split­
wise/DistServe/Mooncake) is a candidate remedy at scale when prefill/decode imbalance

105

Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions

is large, scale is sufficient, and KV-transfer + extra pool/scheduling costs stay below the inter­
ference savings — costs include KV migration, added failure domains, and pool sizing; compare
against colocated scheduling with chunked prefill. [S4][1P][FACT]
• Repeat-prefix RAG ⇒ enable prefix caching (RadixAttention/APC), which reuses the
shared prompt prefix of the 9.2K prefills (~13% of prefill work in the canonical workload; the
8K retrieved block is query-specific) and so partially defends the p95 TTFT against the 40 rps
peaks. [S3][1P][FACT]
• KV cache pressure ⇒ quantize or offload KV. FP8 KV = raw tensor byte-halving = 1.31
MB/token (exactly 50% of FP16) [canonical scenario][DERIVED]; any block-allocation/meta­
data overhead is NOT vendor-measured here and must be filled by a deployment benchmark.
(The vLLM FP8-KV blog’s ‘54%’ is a decode-ITL latency slope, not a memory ratio.) And
vLLM KV-offloading (its own 2026-01-08 blog [S7][1P][FACT]) cuts TTFT by 2–22× in a par­
ticular warm-cache-hit/reuse benchmark, not a generic cold-cache improvement — both are
memory-layer fixes the telemetry would call for when KV occupancy nears capacity.
• Speculative decoding where decode bandwidth is the wall — DFlash reports over 6×
lossless acceleration, up to 2.5× over EAGLE-3, in its paper’s evaluated configurations [S5]
[1P][FACT] — because it reduces weight reads per accepted token. These are paper-reported
results, not portable serving-speed figures: treat them as performance claims to re-measure on
the target workload, not as a guaranteed speedup.

6.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• Goodput in production is rarely published. The research corpus gives strong qualitative
and some quantitative anchors (Mooncake: a 525% throughput increase (simulated) and 75%
more requests [S4][1P][FACT], DFlash >6× [S5][1P][FACT]), but portable end-to-end goodput
figures across real enterprise RAG workloads remain [UNRESOLVED].
• Prefix-cache hit rates in mixed workloads are workload-dependent; the actual reduction
in prefill FLOPs from APC/RadixAttention for a given document-retrieval distribution is
[UNRESOLVED].
• Tail-latency drivers under batching interact: batch size, arrival burstiness, and KV frag­
mentation each affect p99 differently, and their joint effect is [UNRESOLVED].

6.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Post-Lunch Slowdown: Reading Telemetry
Up the Chain
An on-call architect is paged: “the internal Q&A tool got slow after lunch.” The dashboard shows
rps at the ~40 rps peak (workload, up from the 10 rps baseline), p95 TTFT at 2.4 s against a 2
s SLO (serving, breached), and KV cache occupancy at 85% with low prefix-hit ratio (resource,
memory/FLOP pressure). Following the chain rather than guessing, the architect reads: a concurrency

Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions

106

spike (workload) with repeated full 9.2K prefills (low prefix hit) drives prefill FLOP demand several
times past the host aggregate capacity (compute-bound). The architecture is memory- and computesane at the 10 rps design point but was never sized for the lunch peak. The diagnosis is the ~18.6×
prefill oversubscription at the 40 rps peak (40 × 1.29 ≈ 51.6 PFLOP/s vs the ~2.77 PFLOP/s host
capacity); prefix caching is a partial mitigation (~13% of prefill FLOPs), not the fix. The resolution
is capacity/scheduling — additional hosts, chunked prefill, admission control/backpressure, or P/D
disaggregation. The architect re-checks the dashboard an hour later: p95 TTFT is back under 2 s, and
the mechanism check confirms the capacity/scheduling change rather than the cache: a ~13% prefill
reduction alone cannot close an ~18.6× oversubscription (it still leaves ~44.9 PFLOP/s of demand
against ~2.77 PFLOP/s of sustained capacity, ~16.2×), so hosts were added to raise sustained prefill
capacity and admission control held the queue inside it, with the ~13% prefill reduction from prefix
caching contributing on top; goodput restored — because they measured the right thing at the right
layer.

The System

chapter 7.
Memory Is the First Constraint

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to answer the architect’s fundamental constraint question: does
the model and its context fit in the memory floor before we ask whether it can compute or communicate?
We will build the arithmetic for the KV cache from first principles, reconcile it with the canonical ~1.31
MB/token figure from Chapter 1, and contrast inference residency (weights + KV) with fine-tuning
residency (weights + gradients + optimizer states). The goal is to make “does it fit?” a concrete,
quantified check — not a back-of-the-envelope guess. Throughout, the arithmetic anchors to the
canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak traffic served
by a 70B FP16 model on an 8×H100 host. KV cache per-token figures are given at the referenced
precision throughout: ~1.31 MB/token at 8-bit (this is Chapter 1’s reference figure), ~2.62 MB/token
(exactly 2.5 MiB/token) at FP16 — and the canonical scenario’s KV constant is the FP16 2.62 MB/token
figure, not the 8-bit ~1.31 MB/token number. Color is not semantic anywhere in this chapter’s
figures (FIGS 7.1–7.8): the same concept (persistent KV/state storage) is rendered in different hues
across them, so read each figure’s own legend or note rather than carrying a color meaning from one
figure to the next. Every block is identified by a text label, never by hue alone, so the chapter also
reads correctly in grayscale.

7.1. Concept
Memory is the first constraint because every LLM workload begins with a residency check: can the
model and its active data structures be placed on the target hardware? The KV cache is the primary
expression of this constraint during inference: it grows linearly with context length, and its size

108

109

Memory Is the First Constraint

depends on the model’s layer count, KV-head count, head dimension (equivalently the KV width per
layer) and the precision chosen for key and value storage. Unlike FLOPs, which scale with operations
per token, the KV cache occupies memory continuously for the lifetime of a request — it is always
resident, always consuming HBM bandwidth for every re-read. The architect must therefore size
two distinct memory loads: the static weight footprint and the dynamic KV footprint that varies
with prompt length. Quantization (FP8, FP4, 2-bit asymmetric) reduces both, but the KV cache is
the one component whose reduction must be quoted per precision, not as a uniform factor: FP8 KV
realizes a 2× reduction vs FP16 (raw byte-halving), while 4-bit KV’s raw payload bound is 4× (2.62 →
0.66 MB/token at this chapter’s geometry); per-block scale/offset metadata and per-token variation
reduce the realized reduction below 4×, so no specific multiplier may be assumed without the actual
layout. Weight-only quantization carries the same raw-bound-versus-realized distinction — its 2×–4×
is a raw bit-width bound, not a realized saving (FP8 KV realizes exactly 2× before block metadata;
MXFP4 weights realize ~3.57× at 0.53125 B/value, §7.3). The residency floor is weights + KV for
inference; for fine-tuning it is weights + gradients + optimizer states (+ activations/workspace), and
the architect’s first question is whether this sum fits on the target GPUs. This is why “does it fit?” is
the architect’s primary gate: before we ask whether the model can compute or communicate, we
must first establish that the working set — weights plus the context-dependent KV state — resides
on-GPU. If it does not, every subsequent decision (offload, recompute, page) is a necessary trade-off
— acceptable only when it keeps the workload within its SLO.
Unit basis (locked): the H100’s quoted 80 GB is treated as decimal 80×10^9 B throughout, so the
canonical 8×H100 pool reads 640 GB. The vendor-binary reading is 81,559 MiB ≈ 85.5×10^9 B per part
(the first-party H100 80 GB specification’s binary-quoted capacity), which would give 2×H100 = 171.0
GB and an ~684 GB host pool. One conversion rule covers every capacity-dependent figure below:
on that basis the KV budget becomes ~480 GB (684 − 140 − 64) and the per-host concurrency ceiling
~19 (480 ÷ 24.9037 = 19.3; floor 19), against 436 GB and ~17.5 (floor 17) on the decimal basis. Re-run
this fit test on that basis before procurement. On the vendor-binary basis the aggregate test still
reads 164.1 < 171.0 GB, but per rank 70 + 12.05 + ~8 GB reserve = 90.05 GB > 85.5 GB, so the ≥3-GPU
conclusion is unchanged. The 2×H100 fit verdict, the 640 GB envelope, the 436 GB KV budget and
the ~17.5 concurrency all use this decimal basis.
The residency floor has two distinct regimes. For inference, the floor is weights + KV: the model’s
static parameters plus the context-dependent key/value tensors that grow with every token added to
the prompt. In fine-tuning, the floor rises further to weights + gradients + optimizer states, because
every parameter update requires its own momentum and velocity vectors (Adam) or per-parameter
scaling (LAMB/RMSProp). The contrast between these two floors — inference ~164.1 GB for a 70B
model at FP16 with 9.2K input (140 + 24.1; the 9.5K-max is 164.9 ≈ 165 GB) [canonical scenario]
[DERIVED], fine-tuning exceeding 1 TB [canonical scenario][DERIVED] — is the architect’s central
memory-takeaway.

Memory Is the First Constraint

110

We keep two terms rigidly distinct in this chapter, and the distinction is the antidote to “does it
fit?” mistakes:
• Residency floor = weights + KV. This is the minimum memory the model’s parameters and
active KV tensors must occupy for a single request. It is what the numbers in this chapter quote
(~140 GB weights + ~24.9 GB KV ≈ 165 GB at 9.5K max).
• Practical host requirement = weights + KV + runtime/workspace + safety margin. Deploying
a model on a GPU requires additional VRAM for CUDA kernels, activation buffers, NCCL
(NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) communication, a warmup/KV-allocation safety
pool, and (on a multi-GPU host) tensor-/pipeline-parallel communication and staging buffers
(plus any genuinely replicated components, e.g. embeddings or LM head where the engine
replicates them). On the canonical 8×H100 host this runtime/workspace term is ~64 GB,
turning the ~165 GB residency floor into a larger deployment footprint. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[ASSUMPTION] The ~64 GB is a planning reserve, not a measured constant; a representative
split is ~8 GB CUDA context/driver + ~16 GB activation buffers (batch + intermediate tensors) +
~8 GB NCCL communication buffers (tensor-parallel all-reduce staging) + ~32 GB warmup/KVallocation safety pool. The exact value must come from a deployment benchmark on the target
stack (Chapter 14); the 436 GB KV budget (640 − 140 − 64) shifts by the same amount if the
measured reserve differs.
When the text says a workload “fits” or “does not fit,” we are always talking about the residency
floor first; the practical host requirement is a superset that must be checked before committing
hardware. Conflating the two is exactly what produces a “165 GB fits in 160 GB” error.
7.1.1. Count state by lifetime, not by the model label
The residency floor is not a property of the model label; it is a property of the set of tensors alive at
peak.
The weights-plus-KV floor in this chapter describes the autoregressive baseline. For nonautoregressive generators, inventory state by lifetime before applying the KV arithmetic — the
formula prices K/V tensors, not all persistent state. The live sets are resident weights, reusable
context state, mutable canvas state, peak activations and logits, kernel workspace, and runtime
allocations. They must be disjoint at the instant being measured; two names for the same buffer do
not create two memory costs. [DERIVED]
The KV tensor byte formula remains valid for actual K/V tensors. What changes is the proof
that those tensors can be reused: Chapter 3’s dependency figure shows why unchanged token IDs
are insufficient under bidirectional refinement. A block-causal boundary can make an earlier prefix
immutable. Approximate cache policies instead trade refresh work against quality. Memory capacity
and cache validity are separate checks. [1P][FACT]
Repeated sequential evaluations need not multiply peak memory by the number of rounds when
inference releases temporary buffers after each round. Retained histories, previous-round logits for

111

Memory Is the First Constraint

self-conditioning, or simultaneous verification views change that lifetime calculation. A diffusion
runtime’s peak memory includes intermediate tensors (logits, attention scores, sampling buffers) that
have no analogue in the AR weights+KV formula. As a shape-only example, a 256-position canvas
over a 262,144-entry vocabulary needs 256 × 262,144 × 4 = 268,435,456 bytes, or 256 MiB, for one
FP32 logits tensor at batch one. This excludes probabilities, sampling workspace, retained logits,
attention buffers and the rest of the model. It is not a measured model footprint. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[ASSUMPTION][DERIVED]
This distinction affects admission control. A runtime may have enough capacity for prefix state
yet fail when many requests enter a high-workspace refinement phase together. Weight precision
alone cannot certify fit: the deployed sampler’s live tensor shapes and lifetimes decide the practical
requirement. [DERIVED]
None of this changes the canonical autoregressive budget above — it changes what must be
inventoried before that budget’s arithmetic is reused for a different generation mechanism.

7.2. Mental Model
The KV cache is per-request state that persists across autoregressive decode steps for
the lifetime of the active sequence — unlike weights, which are loaded once and reused across
requests, the KV cache is allocated per request and grows with every token added to the context. A
9.2K prompt on a 70B model at FP16 carries ~24 GB of KV state that must remain on-GPU for the
entire prefill + decode sequence. If it does not fit, the serving stack must page, offload, or recompute
— each option degrades latency or throughput. The durable mental model is: every token we add to the
context exacts a fixed memory toll, and that toll is paid in HBM every time the GPU re-reads the cache
during decode. This is why context length is the single most powerful lever on inference memory
pressure, and why “does it fit?” is the architect’s primary gate.
7.2.1. Persistent state is architecture-specific
The KV formula in this chapter describes keys and values retained across autoregressive steps. A
whole-clip denoiser has a different lifetime model. Its latent video changes after each scheduler
update, so video keys and values cannot simply be retained as immutable prefix entries for every
later step. Static prompt embeddings can remain reusable, but that is not the growing autoregressive
cache. [1P][FACT]
The canonical KV table below is untouched: it prices the autoregressive text path this chapter
sizes. The boundary changes which state function we plug into “does it fit?” for a different generator
— the same decision, a different inventory.

Note on “does it fit?”: this residency check answers a single-request question — does ONE request’s
weights + KV fit in the pool? It says nothing yet about how many such requests fit concurrently. For that,
an architect must subtract the runtime/activation/workspace floor (~64 GB on the 8×H100 host) from
the 640 GB pool before sizing KV. We compute that concurrent capacity here — the ~436 GB KV budget
and ~17.5 requests/host (byte-accurate 17.51; conservative integer floor 17; arithmetic in this section)
— and carry it into Chapter 17’s fleet sizing. Keep the two numbers separate: the ~500 GB headroom
(Ch. 4/7, single-request) and the ~436 GB KV budget (Ch. 17, concurrency) answer different questions.
“Passes aggregate bytes” is NOT an execution result. A fit verdict needs three distinct gates: (1)
aggregate bytes (pool ≥ residency), (2) per-rank allocation/shard compatibility (a hidden dim of 8192
does not shard evenly into 3 ranks; attention-head partition, runtime/workspace and topology must be
supported), and (3) a working engine/kernel/topology benchmark. 8×H100 (no sharding ambiguity at
8 shards) passes gates 1–2 for the 9.2K and 32K rows. The 3×H100 row passes gate 1 only (8192 does
not shard into 3 ranks) and carries the label “passes aggregate bytes only — placement not established.”
The 128K row — also 8×H100, so TP=8 sharding is integral — clears gate 1 and the shard check, and its
per-rank budget fits at the stated reserve (17.5 + 41.94 + 8 = 67.4 GB of 80 GB); what it does not carry is a

115

Memory Is the First Constraint

measured context-scaled activation/workspace reserve at 128K, so its label reads “passes aggregate bytes
+ shard; long-context reserve unmeasured” — a different label for a different reason.
Attention-family sensitivity note. The ~2.62 MB/token (2.5 MiB) figure is the full-MHA (multihead attention) upper bound: n_KV-heads = n_query-heads, and n_KV-heads × head_dim = hidden_
dim, i.e.
KVMHA per-token = 2 × nlayers × dhidden × B
Real 70B-class dense models commonly use grouped-query attention (GQA): LLaMA-2 70B,
for instance, has 64 query heads but only 8 KV-heads, so per-token KV shrinks by the head ratio to

KVGQA per-token = 2 × nlayers × nKV-heads × dhead × B = 2 × 80 × (8 × 128) × 2 B ≈ 0.33 MB/token
— about 8× smaller. For the canonical 9.2K context that is ~3 GB of KV instead of ~24 GB, and
the fleet-sizing arithmetic of Chapter 17 changes accordingly (many more concurrent requests fit for
KV). We keep the full-MHA bound as the canonical conservative teaching bound, not the chosen
model’s worst case — the honest move is to read the model card’s KV-head count and substitute it
into the GQA formula above. The framework is unchanged; only the constant changes. (the GQA
variant’s per-token constant is tracked alongside the canonical workload’s other constants.)
The figure shows one group’s geometry: 8 query heads funnel into a single shared K/V
head. Because GQA caches only one K/V per group — 8 K/V heads per layer (2,048 K/V elements per
token per layer) instead of 64 (16,384 elements per layer) — the per-token KV falls ~8× — from ~2.62
MB/token (full MHA) to ~0.33 MB/token. That is the takeaway: many query heads can share a few
K/V heads, and the cache shrinks by exactly the 8:1 head ratio. Head count is the real dial: substitute
the model’s KV-head count into 2 × layers × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes.
7.3.1. A smaller-model counterexample: fit is a gate, not a prediction
An illustrative 8-billion-parameter model stored entirely in FP16 has raw weights of 16 GB. Assume
32 attention layers, eight KV-heads per layer, a head dimension of 128 and two bytes per KV element.
This is a separate GQA example, not the handbook’s canonical 70B attention layout, and none of its
constants feed the canonical tables in this chapter. The KV storage per resident token is 2 × 32 × 8 ×
128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes.
At 9,500 resident tokens, one sequence needs 1.245184 GB of raw KV. With an explicitly assumed
4 GB reserve for runtime state and workspace, the analytical budget is 21.245184 GB. A nominal 24
GB device passes this preliminary capacity gate. It does not yet pass an allocation or serving test. The
reserve is an assumption, and the calculation excludes unmodeled conversion peaks, fragmentation
and additional sequences. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

byte-transfer floors, not measured token latencies. They ignore attention, KV traffic, launch overhead
and communication, and they assume the nominal bandwidth is achieved. Batching or reuse can also
change the bytes moved per output token. Passing the capacity gate therefore justifies a measurement,
not a throughput or cost claim. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
7.3.2. A dense model with a mixed history-state budget
The history budget has two terms, and the second one is not a KV cache. Each recurrent update
replaces a fixed-shape summary of previous tokens, while a separate attention layer retains tokenindexed keys and values. The states below are shown at successive times; the recurrent snapshots
are not all retained together. The schematic does not claim that every operation within the model
has constant memory or constant execution time.
The full-attention component of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B illustrates the transfer from a configuration
to a memory estimate. Its language configuration has 16 full-attention layers, four KV-heads per
layer, and a head dimension of 256 (released configuration, retrieved 2026-10-28). With BF16 KV
storage, the raw component is:
2 × 16 × 4 × 256 × 2 = 65,536 bytes per cached token.

At 262,144 cached tokens, this component occupies 16 GiB. This analytical result assumes one
sequence and unsharded raw tensors. It excludes the recurrent and convolution states of the other
48 language layers, visual processing, runtime buffers, and allocation overhead. It is neither the
complete request footprint nor a measured concurrency limit. [1P][FACT] for the configuration;
[DERIVED] for the storage.
At 131,072 tokens the same component is 8 GiB. Doubling history therefore adds 8 GiB to
this component under the stated assumptions; it does not double every memory object in the
request. In notation, the simplified history budget is M_history(L) = L × 65,536 bytes + M_
recurrent, where M_recurrent covers fixed-shape recurrent and convolution state for this decode

path. Temporary prefill workspaces remain outside that expression. These are derived storage
estimates, not measured allocations. [DERIVED]

The serving consequence follows from the state lifetimes. Capacity planning needs both terms,
including any replication or sharding imposed by the engine. A prefix checkpoint for an intermediate
position must preserve the time-recurrent state corresponding to that position, not merely a list of
attention pages. A preempted or branched request can require additional snapshots, and speculative
rollback needs the correct pre-draft state. Bounded live decode state therefore does not imply free
checkpointing or unrestricted prefix sharing; the implementation determines which extra copies are
retained. [DERIVED]
Less history traffic can relax one memory bottleneck without removing the weight-read or
compute bottleneck. A recurrent token mixer and a full-attention layer also expose different prefill
execution opportunities. Their kernel mix and sequence-length dependence must be measured
separately before transferring a decode-state estimate into a throughput forecast. The architectural
decision is which state representation the engine can maintain correctly at the required concurrency,
not which family label sounds smaller.

Inference residency = weights + KV cache; the KV footprint scales with context length. Fine-tuning
residency adds optimizer states (Adam m, v, and master weights), which for 70B at ~16 bytes/param
totals ~1,120 GB — roughly 1.75× the 640 GB of 8×H100. This contrast is the architect’s central takeaway:
inference is memory-limited by weights + KV, while fine-tuning is memory-limited by weights + gradients
+ optimizer, a substantially higher floor. Note the ~1,120 GB is the parameter/optimizer floor (weights
+ gradients + Adam m/v/master), which is fixed by model size and precision. The actual training peak
is higher and is not inferable from that floor alone: it also includes activation memory (scales with batch
size × sequence length × hidden dim, and is the dominant term for long-context or large-batch runs),
temporary kernel workspace, allocator fragmentation, and checkpointing buffers. A host that fits the
1,120 GB floor can still fail to fit a given training run if its activation peak exceeds the remaining HBM —
so the fit verdict for training must be checked against the measured peak for the specific batch/sequence
configuration, not the parameter floor. (QLoRA’s ~36 GB figure is likewise a floor: it holds the 4-bit base
(~35 GB) + adapters + a small optimizer (~1 GB); a training step holds no inference KV cache, so no KV
term enters a fine-tuning floor, and activation memory is not in the floor — the activation/workspace
peak is additional and must be measured for the run’s batch and sequence length. Any inference residency
after* fine-tuning is a separate weights+KV question, priced by Table 7-1.)*

7.3.3. Quantization describes several different choices
“Four-bit model” leaves several architectural questions open. Which tensors use four-bit values? How
are those values chosen? What do the four bits represent? Where are scales stored? Which kernel
consumes the resulting tensors? The figure below separates these questions. A calibration method, a
tensor encoding and a checkpoint container can participate in the same deployment; they are not
competing answers to one question.
AWQ and GPTQ primarily address error control during post-training weight quantization. AWQ
uses representative activations to identify important channels and chooses equivalent channel
scaling that reduces the error introduced by quantizing weights. “Activation-aware” describes the
information used by the method; it does not mean that activations are also stored in four bits. The
paper’s exploratory observation about protecting a small fraction of salient weights is not a definition
requiring those weights to remain FP16. Its scaling method seeks protection without that irregular
mixed-precision storage. [1P][FACT] (AWQ, §3).
GPTQ instead uses approximate second-order information to compensate for quantization error
in the remaining weights as quantization proceeds. Its original implementation targets weight
quantization, not activation quantization. Neither method name uniquely specifies a group size, scale
dtype, zero-point layout, permutation or checkpoint packing. Those fields are needed to reproduce
both accuracy and memory use. Calibration data must represent the intended workload; a method’s
reported behavior on one evaluation does not establish behavior on another distribution. [1P][FACT]
(GPTQ, §2–4).
A container answers a different question. GGUF stores model metadata, tensor descriptions,
tensor types and aligned tensor payloads. It is not a single numerical precision. Its tensor-type field
permits different encodings within one model. Consequently, a comparison labeled “AWQ versus
GGUF” confounds an error-control method with a file format unless both sides are expanded into
complete deployment configurations. The useful comparison specifies the method, tensor encodings,
mixed-precision exceptions and execution backend. The same caution applies to safetensors: storing
tensors in a recognized container does not establish that a loader understands their quantized schema.
[1P][DERIVED] (GGUF specification, pinned revision, retrieved 2026-10-28).

The record is more durable than a list of product names. It also exposes a missing assumption
before a memory estimate becomes a hardware recommendation.
Shared scales change the storage calculation
OCP MXFP4 1.0 uses E2M1 four-bit values, with one eight-bit E8M0 scale shared by a block of
32 values. E8M0 represents a power-of-two scale. The common one-dimensional NVFP4 scheme
also uses E2M1 values, but shares an E4M3 local scale over 16 values and uses an additional FP32
tensor-global scale. Neither scheme uses an affine integer zero point in this comparison. The local
scale’s encoding and granularity change the set of representable values and its adaptation to a
block’s dynamic range; smaller groups also require more scale bytes. This is a mechanism difference,
not an automatic accuracy ranking. [1P][FACT] (OCP MX 1.0, §4–6; NVIDIA NVFP4 explanation,
2025-06-24).
The next figure holds the number of logical values constant. The same 32 four-bit values require
16 payload bytes in either scheme. MXFP4 adds one local-scale byte, producing 17 bytes per 32 values,
or 0.53125 B/value. Common 1D NVFP4 adds two local-scale bytes, producing 18 bytes per 32 values,
or 0.5625 B/value, before the tensor-global scale. For a tensor with N values in complete blocks, this
example’s compact NVFP4 storage is 0.5625N + 4 bytes. The four global-scale bytes are shared across
the tensor, not repeated for each block. [1P][DERIVED]
These rates are not the total footprint of a model. A mixed-precision model retains some tensors
at higher precision. A file adds metadata and alignment gaps. A runtime may pad dimensions,
reorder scales, create extra representations or reserve workspace. The memory ledger therefore
separates checkpoint bytes, resident tensors, load/repack peak, activations, KV cache and workspace.
A checkpoint that fits on disk may still fail during loading, and a successfully loaded checkpoint
may not leave enough memory for the intended context and concurrency. The exact runtime layouts
remain implementation-dependent. [1P][DERIVED]

Worked example: scale overhead is small but not zero
A 4096 × 4096 weight matrix holds 16,777,216 values. The shape is illustrative; the byte results
follow the stated layouts. BF16 payload occupies 33,554,432 bytes. MXFP4 with complete 32-value
blocks occupies 8,912,896 bytes. Common 1D NVFP4 with complete 16-value blocks and one FP32
global scale occupies 9,437,188 bytes. The difference comes from the chosen scale representation
and grouping, not a different number of four-bit payload values. Both calculations exclude padding,
additional scale copies and non-weight tensors. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
An integer scheme can produce a different bill again. With groups of 128, an illustrative INT4
layout containing an FP16 scale and a packed four-bit zero point per group uses 8,716,288 bytes
for the same matrix. Replacing the packed zero with an FP16 scaled-zero increases that layout to
8,912,896 bytes. Equal total bytes do not make this integer scheme numerically equivalent to MXFP4.
The example explains why an estimate needs the actual scale and zero layout rather than “four bits
plus a little overhead.” It does not choose an accuracy or speed winner. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
For a separate resource sensitivity, a 70B-parameter teaching model that stores 98% of parameters
in MXFP4 and 2% in BF16 — fractions deliberately chosen, not a real checkpoint inventory — needs
39.24375 GB of compact weight storage rather than 140 GB. Retaining this chapter’s full-MHA, BF16
KV assumptions (80 layers, KV width 8192, 9,500 tokens per sequence) leaves raw KV at 24.90368 GB
per sequence. In a 640 GB aggregate pool with a fixed 64 GB reserve, the storage-only integer ceiling
rises from 17 sequences to 21, not in proportion to the weight compression. The added KV budget
does not prove that the ranks can place it or that 21 requests meet the latency SLO. Workspace,
fragmentation and per-rank balance still need measurement, and the reserve itself may change.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
The causal consequence is narrower than “quantization solves memory.” Weight compression
frees one term in the memory ledger. If KV dominates the remaining footprint, context length
and concurrency can still bind. Weight precision and KV precision remain separate decisions, with
separate scale calibration, attention-kernel support and quality validation. KIVI’s separate treatment
of key and value statistics is one example of a KV-specific method, not a consequence of choosing an
AWQ weight checkpoint. [1P][FACT] (KIVI).

7.4. Measurement
Four practical measurement habits follow from the arithmetic above:
1. Compute KV cache per-token cost for the model. The per-token KV footprint of a fullycached (MHA) model is

KVper-token = 2 × nlayers × dhidden × bytes-per-value
(one key and one value per layer, each dhidden wide), evaluated at the chosen precision. For a
70B model at FP16 the answer is 2 × 80 × 8192 × 2 B = 2,621,440 B ≈ 2.62 MB/token (exactly 2.5
MiB/token; 2,621,440 bytes is 2.62144 decimal MB). At 8-bit the per-token value halves to ~1.31
MB/token (~1.25 MiB; the Ch.1 reference). Do not assume the 1.3 MB/token figure applies at FP16 — it
does not; it is an 8-bit number. When evaluating a model whose geometry differs from this chapter’s
80-layer / 8192-hidden full-MHA reference geometry, recompute the constant factor from the general

127

Memory Is the First Constraint

form (2 × layers × n_KV-heads × head_dim × bytes) — a real LLaMA-2 70B is GQA-8 (8 KV heads) at
~0.33 MB/token, not 2.62 (see the sensitivity note) — a model with 64 layers and 8192 dim will have
~2.1 MB/token at FP16 (2 × 64 × 8192 × 2 B = 2,097,152 B), while a model with 100 layers and 12288
dim will have ~4.9 MB/token (2 × 100 × 12288 × 2 B = 4,915,200 B).
2. Log peak context length, not just average. A workload that averages 9.2K input tokens
but has a long tail toward 32K or 128K will have a very different KV cache profile. Log the
95th-percentile context length and re-run the KV arithmetic; the memory floor may shift from
already exceeding 2×H100 at the 9.2K average (164.1 GB > 160 GB) toward needing most of
the 8×H100 host at a 128K tail. This is especially important for RAG workloads, where the
retrieved context may average 8K but occasionally peak at 32K+ for technical documents.
3. Measure inference residency as weights + KV, not weights alone. It is common to see the
140 GB weight footprint (70B FP16) fit across two 80-GB accelerators and conclude that 160
GB is sufficient. But 140 GB of weights leaves only ~20 GB before runtime/workspace and KV
are added; at 9.2K input the KV cache adds ~24.1 GB, pushing the total to ~164.1 GB — already
over the 160 GB aggregate, so the model does not fit on two accelerators once KV is counted
(decimal 80×10^9 B basis, §1; on the vendor-binary basis the pool is 171.0 GB, where the same
per-rank reserve test still fails — §1). Always include KV when we state the memory floor for
inference.
4. Account for KV quantization when reporting residency. If the serving stack uses FP8
KV, the per-token KV cost drops from ~2.62 MB to ~1.31 MB (raw tensor byte-halving, exactly
50% of FP16 = 2,621,440/2 = 1,310,720 B = 1.25 MiB), and the 9.5K max residency falls from
~165 GB to ~152 GB (weights 140 GB + KV 12.45 GB). State both the BF16 and FP8 residency
numbers, because the choice of KV dtype changes the hardware requirement decisively. Note
the accounting basis: the ~1.31 MB/token figure is the raw tensor byte-halving of the same
MHA tensors (one byte per K/V element, exactly half of a 16-bit (FP16/BF16) element’s two
bytes); it is NOT a vendor-measured serving footprint, and any block-layout or per-token
scale/offset metadata overhead is not included. Do not generalize a fixed ratio to all FP8-KV
deployments: the realized per-token footprint depends on the engine version, cache-block
layout, scale/offset metadata, allocator rounding, and the accounting boundary (logical payload
vs allocated cache vs observed resident memory), so re-derive it for the target serving stack
rather than inheriting a multiplier. (For reference, the 9.5K total at this byte-halving basis is
~152 GB — still above a single H100, but now within 2×H100, 160 GB.)

7.5. Common Mistakes
• Assuming KV cache size scales sub-linearly. The KV cache grows linearly with context
length. Doubling the context from 9.2K to 18.4K doubles the KV memory, all else equal. There
is no automatic compression unless the attention mechanism itself is hybrid or sparse.

Memory Is the First Constraint

128

• Using the 8-bit KV figure (~1.31 MB/token) at FP16. Chapter 1’s ~1.31 MB/token is explicitly
at 8-bit precision. At FP16, the per-token KV cost is ~2× that, ≈2.62 MB/token (2.5 MiB — §7.4).
Mixing the two figures produces wrong residency calls.
• Ignoring the weight + KV residency contrast. Quoting only the weight footprint (140 GB
for 70B FP16) and claiming it fits on one H100 (80 GB) is a category error. Weights alone exceed
one H100; KV must be added.
• Quoting one KV-quant reduction for every precision. KV cache quantization must be
read per bit width: FP8 KV ≈50% of FP16 (raw byte-halving) is the first-order raw figure
before block/scale metadata (§4 point 4), while 4-bit KV’s raw bound is a full 4× (2.62 → 0.66
MB/token here; 0.52 → 0.13 for a 7B, §12.3) — the realized saving falls below that 4× bound
once block/scale metadata is counted, and no fixed multiplier may be assumed without the
actual layout. Weight-only quantization’s 2×–4× is the same raw bit-width bound applied to
weights; do not transfer an expectation across precisions or across tensors without naming the
bit width.
• Overlooking the fine-tuning residency floor. Full fine-tuning of 70B requires ~1.12 TB with
Adam optimizer states — roughly 1.75× the 8×H100 host. This is not a temporary overhead; it
is the permanent memory floor for the training duration.

7.6. Architecture Consequence
The memory floor is the first constraint every architecture decision respects, because unlike
compute or bandwidth it cannot be moved by better kernels or scheduling — it is set by the model’s
weights, its KV state and (for training) optimizer state, and moves only with precision, architecture,
or where the state lives. Several concrete consequences follow for the canonical enterprise-Q&A
workload:
• Model residency decides host count. A 70B FP16 model (140 GB weights) at the 9.5K
max context (9.2K in + 300 out) needs ~24.9 GB of KV cache (FP16), so the max end-ofgeneration residency ≈ 165 GB — it does not fit on a single 80 GB H100, nor within the 160
GB aggregate of 2×H100 (160 GB < 165 GB; decimal 80×10^9 B basis — on the vendor-binary
basis, 165 GB < 171.0 GB in aggregate but the per-rank test fails, §1). By aggregate memory
capacity it needs ≥ 3×80 GB (240 GB) — but note this is an aggregate-HBM lower bound
on card count, NOT a validated 3-way tensor-parallel configuration: whether three
80-GB cards actually admit a 70B model depends on head/layer shard divisibility, KV-head
routing, TP=3 support, workspace/communication layout, and per-rank fragmentation, none
of which the aggregate sum establishes. A practical TP topology (e.g. TP=4 or TP=8) must
be checked against the serving engine and model geometry before three cards are treated as
deployable. The canonical single host of 8×H100 (640 GB) is not justified by basic capacity

129

Memory Is the First Constraint

alone — three 80 GB GPUs already clear the 165 GB residency floor; the 8×H100 host is chosen
for compute, bandwidth, topology, concurrency, implementation constraints, and headroom.
[canonical scenario][DERIVED]
• KV cache quantization buys back memory, not compute. FP8 KV ≈ 50% of FP16 (raw
byte-halving), dropping the 9.5K max residency from ~165 GB toward ~152 GB. KV quantization
is primarily a capacity lever; it also reduces the K/V bytes read during decode, so it can relieve
KV-bandwidth pressure, but it does not reduce attention FLOPs. Pull it when KV capacity
binds, and benchmark it when decode bandwidth may also be limiting.
• Fine-tuning is a different memory regime than inference. The same model that serves in
~165 GB demands ~1,120 GB under full Adam fine-tuning (weights 140 GB + gradients 140 GB
+ Adam m/v/master states 840 GB) — roughly 1.75× the 8×H100 host. This is why the architect
separates the serving fleet from the training fleet: the memory floors differ by roughly 7×
(~164 GB at 9.2K vs ~1,120 GB). [canonical scenario][DERIVED]
• Context length is the largest controllable KV lever. Doubling context from 9.2K to 18.4K
doubles KV (~24.1 GB → ~48 GB); 128K context drives KV to ~335 GB — on a single 80 GB GPU
that forces quantization, offloading or model parallelism; on the canonical 8×H100 host ~475 GB
total residency fits in 640 GB but leaves little headroom for concurrency. The architecture must
set a context-length ceiling to keep the served model within host memory. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[DERIVED]
In short: the architect sizes the host by weights + KV at the longest supported context, treats KV
quantization as a spare memory dial, and keeps inference and training on separate memory-planning
tracks.

7.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• Per-model KV state beyond K/V — the additional per-head state and per-layer scale/offset
metadata some attention implementations store alongside keys and values. The 2 × layers
× n_KV-heads × head_dim × bytes formula prices the K/V entries themselves (§7.3 covers

GQA/MQA exactly by substituting the model card’s KV-head count), but the extra per-token
bytes an implementation adds on top of K/V are not derived in this chapter and must be
established per architecture and serving stack.
• Quality loss from aggressive KV quantization (2-bit KIVI, or sub-4-bit schemes) at very long
context lengths (128K+) and in MoE models. The primary sources anchor FP8 KV ≈50% of
FP16 (raw byte-halving) with only a small loss in the cited benchmarks, but 2-bit asymmetric
patterns and their interaction with RoPE and sliding-window layers are not fully mapped.

Memory Is the First Constraint

130

(a) decode-time KV offload to CPU DRAM trades TPOT/ITL and KV capacity, not TTFT
(TTFT is already complete when decode starts); (b) prefix/KV reuse loaded from CPU can
reduce TTFT for cache-hit requests — the vLLM KV Offloading Connector’s 2–22× figure
is defined in Ch 6 (TTFT metric, warm-cache-hit/reuse benchmark) [S7][1P][FACT] and
is highly prompt-size-dependent. The community is converging on tiered KV storage
(GPU resident hot set + CPU/DRAM cold set), but the latency trade-offs at concurrency >
1 are not yet primary-anchored.

• Whether each frontier model’s re-engineered KV constant reproduces on a serving
stack. Frontier 2026 has begun re-engineering the KV constant factor, not just quantizing
it. All four 2026-class open architectures modify attention for long-context cost; DeepSeek
and GLM report first-party KV-cache ratios, while Kimi and Qwen describe mechanisms with
no stated KV metric (Table 7-3). These are first-party figures, not independently reprofiled.
Whether these constants reproduce on serving stacks, and what they imply for concurrency
and fleet sizing, is unresolved. Size the host against the specific model’s KV scheme, not a
universal constant.
• Whether a given MoE model’s governing KV constants have been validated per model (routing
itself is settled): The total-vs-active and MoE-vs-dense facts of Ch 3 (total parameters ≠ active
parameters per token; MoE gives compute sparsity, not weight-residency sparsity) confirm
that attention layers process every token densely and emit key/value per token — under the
standard-MoE assumption (sparse MLP experts with dense attention; hybrid-attention models
must be checked separately) — so MoE sparsity does not reduce KV — and the constants
that do govern KV (attention geometry: layers, KV-heads, head dimension, cache dtype) need
per-model validation; expert count belongs to weight-residency and dispatch validation, not
KV sizing.

Technical note — per-rank fit (moved out of the caption). Whether a given allocation
actually fits depends on tensor-parallel sharding, KV partitioning, replication, runtime layout, perrank fragmentation, workspace requirements and communication topology, so “total bytes < total
HBM” is necessary but not sufficient. Worked TP=8 example: with a KV budget per rank of 436 ÷ 8 =
54.5 GB and 17.5 concurrent requests, a rank holds 17.5 + 8 + 54.48 = 79.98 GB = 99.97% of an 80 GB
rank, so the aggregate 17.5 is a hard ceiling — exactly full, with zero per-rank headroom — not a
comfortable operating point. The per-rank quantities:
• weights per rank: 140 ÷ 8 = ~17.5 GB
• runtime/NCCL per rank: ~8 GB — the ~64 GB reserve is a host aggregate of these per-rank
overheads
• KV budget per rank: 436 ÷ 8 = ~54.5 GB
• per-request KV per rank: 24.9 ÷ 8 = ~3.1 GB (tensor-parallel attention shards each request’s
KV across the 8 ranks)
Per-rank budget: 17.5 + 54.5 + 8 = 80 GB — exactly the rank’s capacity. At 17.5 concurrent requests
the rank actually consumes 17.5 × 3.11296 = 54.48 GB of KV (budget 54.5 GB, consumption 54.48 GB),
so occupancy is 17.5 + 54.48 + 8 = 79.98 GB = 99.97% of 80 GB. A rank can be the binding constraint
even when the aggregate fits, so per-rank fit and sharding must be validated separately (Chapters
9–10). Byte-accurate, 436 ÷ 24.9037 = 17.51, so the conservative integer “requests that fit” floor is 17,
not 18.
