chapter 8.

Compute

The Architect’s Question
After chapters on tokens, workloads, and memory, the architect naturally asks: how much compute
does this actually require, and at what point does the hardware cease to be the limiting factor? This
chapter gives us the FLOP-scale arithmetic, the arithmetic-intensity roofline, and the utilization
framework that lets us answer that question without guessing. We will move from per-token FLOPs
to prefill PFLOP counts to sustained MFU on real hardware, and then to the roofline that tells us
whether a given layer is compute-bound or memory-bound — the difference that decides whether
we should reach for batching, quantization, or a different hardware generation. Throughout, the
arithmetic anchors to the canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average
/ ~40 rps peak traffic, with 70B FP16 weights and an 8×H100 host. KV cache per-token figures are
referenced at FP16 (~2.62 MB/token, i.e. 2.5 MiB) unless an 8-bit (~1.31 MB/token, 1.25 MiB) variant is
explicitly stated.

8.1. Concept
Compute in a language model is priced in floating-point operations, or FLOPs. Every matrix multi­
plication, every attention-score computation, every activation function evaluation contributes to the
total. The architect’s first principle is that FLOPs scale linearly with parameter count and token count
for projection-dominated work (~2N per token), while attention adds a term quadratic in context
length (~4·n_layers·L²·d, where d is the model hidden dimension, d = n_heads × d_head = 8192 here;
the term counts both the QK^T and AV matmuls for full dense attention and excludes projections

137

Compute

138

and softmax; derived in §8.3 (Table 8-1) and Ch 22) — the hardware ridge point and the kernel’s
arithmetic intensity decide the efficiency of both.
For a dense transformer layer, the dominant cost is the matrix multiplication — the attention-score
and value-aggregation matmuls, and the MLP projections. A single multiply-add counts as two FLOPs
(FP16 affects throughput, not this count). The per-token cost is therefore approximately 2 ×N FLOPs
where N is the number of active parameters. This is the arithmetic baseline: every token processed
costs roughly two floating-point operations per parameter.

The trace also needs attention pair counts, output-head work, routing, sampling, refresh and

with L. For K active queries over a cached prefix of length C, the attention main term grows with
K(C + K), before the architecture’s head and layer factors. Reducing the number of recomputed
query positions does not eliminate reads of a long prefix. The 2N rule therefore applies to processed
positions, not just output tokens: a diffusion-style generator that evaluates 8× positions per step has
8× the projection work even with ¼ the sequential steps — fewer rounds ≠ less total work. Profile the
actual position count before quoting FLOPs. [DERIVED]1
Why might the higher-work path still finish earlier? Processing more positions together can reuse
loaded weights across more matrix rows and improve low-batch utilization. Why might it lose under
load? Optimized AR request batching can already supply those rows, while refinement continues to
repeat work. Distributed execution also repeats tensor-parallel collectives and any expert dispatch
required by each evaluation. The number of sequential rounds and the total communicated bytes
can move in opposite directions. [DERIVED] The low-concurrency case is vendor-reported rather

8.1.2. The roofline diagnostic
But FLOPs alone do not tell the full story. The hardware can only execute FLOPs if data is available
— weights, activations, and KV cache all compete for the same HBM bandwidth. The arithmetic
intensity (FLOP/byte) determines whether a kernel is compute-bound (intensity above the ridge
point) or memory-bound (intensity below). This roofline model is the central diagnostic tool of this
chapter: it tells us, for any given layer and precision, whether adding compute throughput/resources
reduces latency or whether we are already starved for bytes.
Three different “bounds” — keep them apart. Throughout this book, three words
that all contain “bound” mean three different things, and conflating them is a real error.
Compute-bound means performance is limited primarily by arithmetic throughput (the
kernel sits above the ridge; the compute units are the bottleneck). Memory-bandwidthbound (what the roofline calls “memory-bound”) means performance is limited by
memory-transfer bandwidth (the kernel sits below the ridge; it is starved for bytes
moving per second). Memory-capacity-constrained (often KV-capacity-constrained
in long-context inference) means feasible concurrency or context is limited by how
much data fits in HBM — not by how fast it moves. The canonical RAG workload
illustrates all three as distinct constraints: prefill is compute-bound (high intensity),
decode is bandwidth-bound (low intensity), and long input raises KV residency, which
capacity-constrains how many requests can be resident at once. These regime labels are
operating-point properties: they shift with batch size and precision, and in a serving
system prefill and decode from different requests overlap on the same devices, so the
regimes coexist rather than partition the timeline. “Input-heavy” does not by itself mean
“memory-bound” — it tends to raise prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure, two
distinct effects. When the book says “memory-bound” without qualification, it means
bandwidth-bound in the roofline sense; capacity pressure is stated explicitly.

Compute

140

8.1.3. A resource model survives a backend change; an implementation may not
Backend-documentation observations: 2026-10-28. They do not establish feature availability at the
edition’s 2026-08-30 cutoff.
The compute and memory equations apply across accelerator vendors; their constants belong
to a specific device and execution path. A peak INT8 dense TOPS figure does not describe BF16
throughput, a sparse peak does not describe a dense workload, and aggregate device memory is not
one allocation pool — so the useful comparison starts with the model’s operators, resident bytes
and communication pattern, then asks which kernels implement those operations on the candidate
hardware. [1P] One example: in PyTorch, torch.xpu names the Intel GPU device backend, while
Intel Gaudi uses a separate hpu path, a client NPU can use the OpenVINO NPU plugin, and an
engine-native SYCL path can bypass PyTorch — the API name alone does not establish operator
support. [1P][FACT] for the stack boundaries; the portability consequence is [DERIVED].2
This distinction changes a portability decision. A device API can be available while a required
model operator or cache layout is not. Source-level portability therefore reduces one part of mi­
gration work. It does not establish feature parity, numerical equivalence or sustained performance.
[DERIVED]
The chapter unfolds by section: §8.1–§8.3 build the core arithmetic (FLOPs per token, prefill
PFLOP counts, H100 sustained utilization) and the roofline that explains why prefill is computebound while decode is memory-bound, worked through the canonical scenario (70B on 8×H100,
TTFT 1.2 s, TPOT ~25 ms); §8.4 turns to measurement, §8.5 to common mistakes, §8.6 to architecture
consequences, §8.7 to open questions, and §8.8 closes with a mini-case that threads the prefill/decode
divide.

8.2. Mental Model
FLOPs are like the total distance of a trip: they tell us how much work the request requires, not
how fast the system can cover it. The ridge point picks which ceiling binds the trip: if the arithmetic
intensity is below the ridge, adding more compute throughput (FLOP/s) won’t help because we
are waiting for data. If we are above the ridge, we are limited by how fast the compute can chew
through operations. The roofline chart — attainable performance on the vertical axis (bounded by
the hardware’s peak TFLOPS), FLOP/byte on the horizontal — is the map that resolves this. Where
our kernel lands on that chart decides whether we should profile memory bandwidth or compute
throughput.
Read this figure together with the roofline: the roofline’s vertical axis (peak TFLOPS) is set by the

figure 8.1: Where inference computation and data movement actually live. The figure groups the
resources three ways: compute units (tensor cores/ALU); the memory hierarchy, whose levels run from
the smallest/fastest/closest (registers, shared memory, L2) to the largest/slower/farther (HBM); and
interconnect (GPU interconnect, other GPUs/remote). Inference work maps onto these groups: matrix
multiply runs on the tensor cores; model weights and the KV cache are predominantly HBM-resident;
FlashAttention restructures attention to tile through on-chip memory and cut HBM traffic; tensorparallel (TP) communication crosses the GPU interconnect; pipeline-parallel (PP) communication
moves activations between pipeline stages. The gradient of speed↔capacity↔distance is why
compute, memory bandwidth, memory capacity and interconnect bandwidth are distinct architectural
constraints — compute, memory and interconnect are separate groups in this figure, not levels of one
ladder. Color key: blue = compute, orange = memory (registers to HBM), green = interconnect — the
colors mark the groups, and only the memory hierarchy is a smallest-to-largest ladder. Schematic
note: the vertical ordering is a relative speed/capacity/distance ranking, not a measured timing scale
— the gaps between levels are not to scale. [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]

Compute

142

hardware ceiling, while a kernel’s horizontal position (FLOP/byte) is set by its arithmetic intensity,
which depends on the kernel’s data reuse and tiling — including how much data it keeps on-chip —
not merely on the nominal memory level. A kernel is compute-bound when its arithmetic intensity
sits above the ridge point (keeping data on-chip raises that intensity); it is bandwidth-bound when
its intensity sits below the ridge, so it must stream large tensors from HBM faster than the bytes
can move. So the “bound” classification of Ch. 8 is not a property of the model alone — it follows
from where the model’s weights and the KV cache happen to be resident, and how much of the
computation a kernel can keep on-chip. Ch. 15’s FlashAttention discussion is exactly this ladder in
action: keep more of the tile on-chip, move fewer bytes between HBM and the compute units.

8.3. Worked Example: Canonical Scenario Arithmetic
The canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2) is an enterprise Q&A system: the canonical 80-layer,
hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference (a 70B-class dense model), FP16 weights (~140 GB), 1 host with
8×H100-class GPUs (80 GB each), average prompt 1,200 tokens + 8K retrieved context (~9.2K input),
300-token output, TTFT budget 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill), TPOT budget ~25 ms/token.
Scope. “1 host with 8×H100” here is a per-host / per-request feasibility container (does one
host meet one request’s latency and memory SLO). It is not a claim that one host absorbs the 40
rps peak arrival rate — as Ch 17 derives, that peak puts in-flight concurrency λ·W ≈ 344 at the ~8.6
s service time, far above one host’s KV-residency ceiling (C ≈ 17.5, conservative integer floor 17),
so the full-utilization KV-residency floor is ~21 hosts (Ch 17’s floor-17 screen), while at the 70%
× 95% policy the fleet is 31 working / 32 total — Table 17-1). The compute/roofline arithmetic of
this chapter answers the per-request and per-host-shard question; the fleet question is a separate
multiplication that Ch 17 performs (with the cost basis in Ch 16). We keep them distinct because
each requires measuring against a different quantity (a latency budget vs an arrival rate).
8.3.1. FLOPs per token
For a 70B-parameter dense model in FP16, the per-token forward FLOP count is approximately:
FLOP/token ≈ 2 × N = 2 × 70 × 109 ≈ 140 GFLOP/token
[DERIVED: 2 FLOPs/parameter × 70 ×10⁹ params; standard dense-forward arithmetic, which is
the same 2×N rule that gives, e.g., a 175B dense model 2 × 175 × 10⁹ ≈ 0.35 TFLOP/token]
This applies to both prefill and decode: each token that enters the forward pass costs ~140
GFLOP. The distinction between prefill and decode is not in the per-token FLOP count but in the data
movement pattern — prefill reads the full context once, while decode re-reads weights per decode
step (a batch-1-equivalent read per sequence, amortized across the batch at batch > 1).
The cited implementation reports were inspected on 2026-10-28. The 2N estimate (two FLOPs per
parameter — the 2 ×N rule above) applies to the parameterized matrix work in a specified execution
path. It does not account for all history-dependent attention, indexing, routing, or repeated-depth

143

Compute

computation. A shared core executed several times reuses weights but repeats arithmetic. A phasedependent architecture can also activate different paths during prefill and decode. The parameter
estimate therefore needs a phase and an execution count before it enters the roofline analysis.
(DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash technical report; Huginn model card and Geiping et al., arXiv:2502.05171 for
recurrence-aware cache and per-token adaptive compute). [1P][FACT] for the phase-dependent
mechanisms; the execution-count qualification is [DERIVED].
8.3.2. A small execution-budget example
An illustrative work model makes the distinction precise. Let C be fixed work outside a repeated core,
F the work of one core pass, and r the executed pass count. Ignore decision overhead for this first

estimate. Total work is C + rF; the unique core weight inventory remains unchanged as r changes.
If C = 1 work unit and F = 2 work units, four passes cost 9 units and three passes cost 7. Omitting
one of four passes removes 25% of core work but only 2/9, approximately 22.2%, of total work. The
units are illustrative operation-budget units, not milliseconds, FLOPs measured on a device, or a
model benchmark. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
Selecting pass 3 after executing pass 4 still costs 9 units in this model. A real stopping check
adds overhead, and lower work does not guarantee proportionally lower wall time. Small batches
can underfill kernels. State movement, synchronization and memory stalls can dominate. A qualitypreserving reduction in actual core executions is necessary evidence for a compute saving; a selected
exit index alone is insufficient. [DERIVED]
Communication follows the executed path as well. If each core pass uses tensor-parallel collectives,
repeating the core repeats those collectives unless a specific implementation changes the schedule.
Weight sharing does not share their results across different hidden inputs. If MoE routing is also
present, expert dispatch adds a separate traffic term; it cannot be inferred from the number of depth
passes alone. Neither a shared parameter count nor a lower active-parameter count establishes the
communication time. The deployment record must identify placement, parallel strategy, tensor sizes
and the actual overlap achieved. [DERIVED]
8.3.3. Prefill PFLOP for 9.2K input
For a single request with 9.2K input tokens, the prefill FLOP cost is:
prefill FLOPs ≈ 2 × N × L = 2 × 70 × 109 × 9.2 × 103 ≈ 1.29 PFLOP
[DERIVED: 2 × N × L where N=70B, L=9,200; the figure is large because every input token is
processed through the model’s parameterized layers (2NL); attention adds a separate quadratic term;
this is the linear term only — attention adds ~17% at 9.2K (case (ii), below); it is a one-time cost per
request, not a sustained rate]
Accuracy of the 2 ×N × L approximation. This linear prefill count omits the quadratic attention

Compute

144

term, ≈ 4 × nlayers × L2 × d. At the canonical 9.2K context that correction is small — roughly +17%
of the 1.29 PFLOP — so the 2NL roofline is a sound teaching baseline there.
The ONE prefill-FLOP accounting convention used in this book. Chapters 8, 15, 16, 17, 20
and 22 name the same three cases, and every prefill FLOP figure and every prefill host count states
which case it uses:
• (i) linear-only lower bound — 2N·L = 1.288 PFLOP per 9.2K request (excludes attention);
• (ii) full-square attention upper/conservative model — 2N·L + 4·n_layers·L²·d = 1.5099
PFLOP, +17.23% over (i); a full-square (un-masked) attention-work approximation;
• (iii) causal-triangle kernel sensitivity — 2N·L + 2·n_layers·L²·d = 1.3989 PFLOP, +8.61%
over (i): a causal mask performs half the attention-pair work of (ii).
But the omission grows with context: at 32K the attention term is ~+60% of the linear term (case
(ii); ~+30% under case (iii)) and at 128K it dominates (~2.4× the linear term, ≈+240%; ~1.2× under
case (iii)). An architect sizing long-context prefill must add the quadratic term or measure it; the
Unknowns section returns to this.
At 10 requests/s, the sustained prefill throughput demand is:
prefill demand = 1.29 × 1015 FLOP × 10 rps ≈ 12.9 PFLOP/s

account for TP communication, per-rank load imbalance, kernel inefficiency under a given batch, or
scheduling/system overhead. It is an upper-bound analysis value, not a servable goodput. Actual
reachable prefill throughput must come from benchmark goodput under the target workload (Chapter

host count they produce (listed in the preceding paragraph) as an illustrative planning screen

under its stated FLOP-counting case and the 35% MFU assumption, not measured SLOgoodput.
The 1.08 s budget versus the 35% planning rate. The canonical prefill takes about 1.08 s for
9.2K input tokens (Ch 4) — a rate of 9,200 ÷ 1.08 ≈ 8,519 input tokens/s on the request leg, which is
1.288 PFLOP ÷ 1.08 s ÷ 8 GPUs ≈ 149 TFLOPS/GPU ≈ 15% MFU, not the 35% used above. The two
numbers measure different things and must not be mixed: 1.08 s is the end-to-end prefill budget inside
the 1.2 s TTFT (it absorbs queueing, scheduling, tokenization and admission overhead), while ~19,800
tokens/s/host is the sustained planning rate for capacity arithmetic. Size the host screens against
the planning rate; if a deployment sustained only the 1.08 s-implied rate, the peak prefill demand of
~51.6 PFLOP/s (1.288 PFLOP × 40 rps) would need 51.6 ÷ 1.19 = 43.4 → ⌈43.4⌉ = 44 hosts, not 19 —
the gap a benchmark (Ch 14) has to close before either number is quoted as capacity. [DERIVED]
This rough sizing illustrates that prefill is FLOP-bound at this scale — its arithmetic intensity
sits far above the ridge, so memory bandwidth (HBM at 3.35 TB/s per H100) is sufficient to keep
the compute fed if the kernel is efficient. Whether prefill compute or KV residency is the binding
fleet constraint depends on the FLOP-counting case: KV residency binds under case (i); case (iii) is a
21/21 tie; compute binds under case (ii). The screens are within one host for cases (ii) and (iii); case
(i) is two hosts apart. The ridge point for dense FP16 on H100 is ~295 FLOP/byte (989 ÷ 3.35); the
arithmetic intensity of a mature attention kernel sits near or above this ridge, meaning the kernel
is compute-saturated rather than bandwidth-starved once the sequence is long enough (attention
intensity scales with L; at the canonical 9.2K it sits far above the ridge).
8.3.5. Decode: bandwidth-bound
Reading the roofline (summary of Fig 8.2): the dense-FP16 ridge at ~295 FLOP/byte (H100: 989 TFLOPS ÷
3.35 TB/s) separates the compute-bound region (right) from the memory-bound region (left). Prefill sits
far above the ridge — its arithmetic intensity is set by the sequence length (weights read once, reused
across all tokens), so it is compute-bound; decode at batch=1 sits at the far left of the chart (~1 FLOP/byte,
~295× below the ridge) and is memory-bound. Batching and quantization shift kernels rightward toward
the ridge; the distinction between the two phases is the single most important reading of this chart.
For decode, the parameterized linear FLOP cost is the same ~140 GFLOP; decode attention
adds a context-dependent term (~24 GFLOP/token at 9.2K), about 164 GFLOP/token in total — but
the arithmetic intensity drops sharply. Each decoded token re-reads all 70B weights from HBM
(a batch-1-equivalent weight-streaming read). A 70B FP16 weight matrix is 70 ×10⁹ × 2 B = 140
GB — one full pass reads 140 GB (batch-1-equivalent), not 280 GB. (The naïve “2 ×70 ×10⁹ × 2 B ≈
280 GB” double-counts the FP16 footprint: the leading “2” is the FLOPs-per-parameter factor (2N
FLOPs/token), which has no place in a byte expression — multiplying it into N × 2 B doubles the
FP16 footprint, so writing 2 ×70 ×10⁹ × 2 B counts the weight bytes twice. Any KV-cache reads are a
separate term on top; the output projection is already included in the 140 GB weight footprint.) The
effective arithmetic intensity is therefore:

[DERIVED; a minimum-bytes model, hence an upper bound on intensity — real kernels also read

This is well below the H100 dense-FP16 ridge of ~295 FLOP/byte, meaning single-stream decode
is overwhelmingly memory-bandwidth-bound. Throughput improves with batching because the
weight-reread amortizes across tokens — decode intensity ≈ batch size (weight-only), so at batch=32
the effective intensity is ~32 FLOP/byte, still ~9× below the 295 ridge (compute-bound decode needs
batch ≈ 295 at FP16 — weight-only first-order estimate; FP8 weights halve the bytes but also double
the peak, so the ridge doubles to ≈591 FLOP/byte and the required batch is unchanged — quantization
raises achieved bandwidth utilization, it does not move the classification), and TFLOP/s utilization
increases accordingly. KV-read caveat: the weight-only intensity above omits the per-sequence KV
re-read (~24 GB at the canonical 9.2K context, FP16 full-MHA). Including it, the decode intensity is
(164·b)/(140 + 24·b) FLOP/byte — (164 GFLOP × b) ÷ (140 GB + 24 GB × b) for batch b, where 164 =
140 linear + 24 attention — which saturates at ~6.8 FLOP/byte as b→∞ — far below the 295 ridge.
So with the KV term, decode stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size; the “batch ≈ 295” figure
is the weight-only first-order estimate (valid when the KV re-read is small relative to the weight
stream, e.g. short contexts or KV quantization). This is why continuous-batching systems (Orca,
vLLM) prioritize batch growth: it is the primary lever for pushing decode arithmetic intensity toward
the ridge (on the weight-only term).
Scope note on the single-device roofline here: the 140 GB weight-read and the per-GPU ~3.35
TB/s HBM bandwidth are single-GPU quantities, so the ~1.0 FLOP/byte intensity and the “memorybandwidth-bound” label above are a per-kernel / single-device roofline argument. It is not a verdict
on the canonical 8×H100 host’s actual bandwidth adequacy — under tensor parallelism the 140
GB weight matrix is sharded across GPUs, so each GPU streams only its own shard (~0.70 TB/s
against its own ~3.35 TB/s, Ch 6). The classification (low-batch decode is bandwidth-bound) is shardinvariant because it follows from the low arithmetic intensity, not from the aggregate weight-read
rate exceeding one GPU’s bandwidth.
8.3.6. The execution path determines the applicable roofline
Quantizing stored weights reduces one source of memory traffic, but the selected kernel determines
the arithmetic. In a fused weight-dequantization path, a kernel reads compressed weights and converts
them for higher-precision multiplication. A native block-scaled path instead requires compatible
low-bit operands, scale layouts and device instructions. An emulation path may reconstruct higherprecision weights before GEMM. These paths can load related checkpoint representations while
having different traffic, compute and workspace costs. Their operation counts and supported peak
rates cannot be mixed in one roofline. Fig 7.3 makes this execution gate explicit. [1P][DERIVED]

151

Compute

In the Chapter 7 mixed-weight sensitivity — a teaching model storing 98% of parameters in
MXFP4 and 2% in BF16 — a dense 2N useful-operation convention and one complete weight stream
give about 3.567 FLOP/B at batch one, compared with 1 FLOP/B for BF16 weights. This is a weightonly analytical intensity, not a 3.567× throughput prediction. It excludes activation and KV traffic,
conversion, additional scale traffic and communication. At large batch or during prefill, a GEMM
may already be compute-bound; during long-context decode, attention and KV access can dominate.
A lower weight-byte count therefore changes a candidate bottleneck, not the measured end-to-end
bottleneck by definition. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
Communication needs a separate ledger. Compressed checkpoint loading can reduce distribution
bytes if compressed files are transferred. It does not automatically compress activation all-reduces,
expert all-to-all traffic or optimizer communication. Fewer devices might become feasible after a
memory reduction, but that is a new parallelism configuration with different compute, memory
and interconnect limits. Communication savings cannot be credited before the transmitted tensor
types, placement and collective schedule are known. [1P][DERIVED] (The distinction follows the
weight-only scope of GPTQ.)

8.4. Measurement
Three measurable quantities anchor compute sizing:
1. Per-token FLOP count. Measure by flops profiling (e.g. NVIDIA Nsight Compute) on the
target model and precision. The 2×N rule is a useful prior, but actual count varies by layer
depth, activation choice (SiLU vs. ReLU), and whether kernel fusion combines matmuls.
2. Sustained MFU. Profile TFLOP/s achieved divided by peak TFLOP/s for the target hardware
and precision. A well-tuned transformer on H100 FP16 typically lands in the 30–40% range;
below 20% suggests a memory or communication bottleneck that should be diagnosed before
scaling.
3. Arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte). Compute as achieved FLOPs divided by bytes transferred
(weights + activations + KV read/write). Compare to the hardware ridge point (H100 dense
FP16: ~295 FLOP/byte; H200: ~989 TFLOPS ÷ 4.8 TB/s ≈ 206 FLOP/byte — H200 keeps H100’s
GH100 die and its dense FP16 peak, trading a bigger/faster HBM3e for bandwidth — more
bandwidth at the same dense peak (FP16 and BF16 dense peaks are identical on GH100: 989
TFLOPS), so its ridge is lower; GB200 superchip (2 GPUs): higher on both terms (dense BF16
peak 4,500 TFLOPS = 2× B200’s 2,250 per GPU, over 16 TB/s HBM3e = 2× 8 TB/s per GPU →
4,500 ÷ 16 ≈ 281 FLOP/byte, granularity-invariant, just below H100’s ~295 — as superchip-vssingle-GPU its 4.8× bandwidth advantage slightly outpaces its 4.5× compute advantage; per
GPU the factors are 2.28× compute and 2.39× bandwidth), while its NVFP4 ridge is far higher
again). If intensity is below the ridge, the kernel is memory-bound; above, compute-bound.

Compute

152

A compute roofline does not include every exposed distributed stall. A communication kernel can
consume SM and HBM resources while appearing to overlap a matrix multiplication. The joint trace
must therefore distinguish model computation, collective work, exposed waiting and computation
slowed by contention. Peak interconnect bandwidth cannot be added to peak compute to predict the
combined schedule; Chapter 9 separates their mechanisms and measurement boundaries. [DERIVED]

8.5. Common Mistakes
• Assuming 2×N FLOPs/token is exact. It is a baseline derivation; actual per-token FLOPs
vary with layer depth, activation fusion, and kernel fusion. Profile before quoting.
• Treating prefill and decode as having the same FLOP/byte profile. At the canonical
operating point, prefill reads the full context once and is FLOP-bound (weight-only intensity
~9,200 FLOP/byte — an upper bound that omits the ~24 GB KV write; including it, ~7,850
FLOP/byte — both far above the ~295 ridge); low-batch decode re-reads weights per token and
is memory-bound (~1 FLOP/byte) - both are operating-point properties: decode’s intensity rises
with batch, and prefill’s falls as context shortens. The arithmetic-intensity roofline distinguishes
them.
• Using peak TFLOP/s as sustained throughput. Peak includes sparsity or BF16/FP8 variants
that may not be available in the chosen precision. Use the FP16 number without sparsity (≈989
TFLOPS on H100) as the baseline for dense compute sizing.
• Ignoring the batch-size dependence of arithmetic intensity. A single-token decode batch
has very low intensity; batching raises it. Always state the batch assumption when reporting
TFLOP/s or tokens/s.
• Confusing H100 sparsity-inclusive peak (1,979 TFLOPS) with dense peak (989 TFLOPS).
The 2× sparsity figure appears in vendor data sheets but most transformer workloads do not
activate sparsity. Quote the dense figure unless the kernel is specifically sparsity-enabled.

8.6. Architecture Consequence
The compute arithmetic and roofline have direct consequences for system design:
• If prefill is FLOP-bound (as it is for 70B+ models with long contexts), the primary opti­
mization is batching — larger prefill batches do not remove the per-request attention work
(each sequence still has its own attention computation); they improve accelerator utilization by
forming larger matrix operations, amortizing weight and execution overhead across requests,
and raising achieved FLOP/s. The relevant lever is the achieved efficiency (MFU) of the prefill
kernel, not a change to the per-request FLOP count. System design should therefore provision

153

Compute

for batchable prefill (continuous batching, Orca, vLLM continuous batching) as the first-order
throughput lever.
• If decode is memory-bound (single-stream, low batch), the primary optimization is batching
— decode arithmetic intensity ≈ batch size, so even modest batch sizes (8–16) raise it to ~8–16
FLOP/byte (batch 16 → ~16, still ~18× below the 295 ridge), improving TFLOP/s utilization
without reaching compute-bound; compute-bound decode needs batch ≈ 295 at FP16 (weightonly first-order estimate) — FP8 weights halve the bytes but also double the peak, so the
ridge doubles to ≈591 FLOP/byte and the required batch is unchanged, i.e. quantization raises
achieved bandwidth utilization, it does not move the classification. KV cache quantization (FP8,
int8) also reduces bytes per token, raising effective intensity. P/D disaggregation (prefill on
GPUs, decode on a separate pool) can rebalance: prefill’s FLOP demand is served by computeoptimized GPUs, while decode’s bandwidth demand is served by wide-memory GPUs, or by
CPU offload only for latency-tolerant, low-throughput paths.
• If the workload’s intensity crosses the hardware ridge (e.g. a workload at ~250 FLOP/byte
is memory-bound on H100’s ~295 ridge but compute-bound on H200, whose FP16 ridge is ~206
FLOP/byte — 989 TFLOPS ÷ 4.8 TB/s — from its higher HBM3e bandwidth), the same workload
may shift from memory-bound to compute-bound, changing the optimal hardware choice.
The shift comes from the lower ridge, not from precision: a higher ridge moves the boundary
right and makes compute-bound harder (H200’s ~412 FLOP/byte ridge in dense FP8 — ~1.98
PFLOPS ÷ 4.8 TB/s, never the sparsity-inclusive ~4 PFLOPS (§8.5) — would do the opposite),
and precision scaling moves intensity and ridge together (bytes halve → intensity doubles;
peak doubles → ridge doubles), so FP8 alone does not change the classification. H200’s lower
ridge means workloads that are memory-bound on H100 can land on H200’s compute plateau —
the ridge is a hardware property, not a workload property [1P: NVIDIA H200 SXM datasheet].
In practice, the architect measures arithmetic intensity for the target workload and precision,
locates the kernel on the roofline chart, and then selects hardware and batching strategy accordingly.
The roofline is the diagnostic; the architecture decision follows.
8.6.1. From video dimensions to repeated attention work
The same derive-then-decide move applies to a workload that evaluates all of its token positions
together rather than one per step: the budget is derived from counted dimensions, not from a duration
label, and it applies the §8.1 principle (fewer sequential evaluations ≠ less total work) to a whole-clip
denoiser.
Take Wan2.2 TI2V-5B’s text-to-video path — a dense transformer, hidden width 3,072, 30 layers,
24 attention heads. Its “720P” example yields a 31×44×80×48 latent tensor (121 frames at the stated
strides), patchified into 27,280 video tokens per evaluation (= 31 × 22 × 40, i.e. a 2×2 spatial patch
over the 31×44×80 latent with the 48 input channels folded into the patch embedding); full noncausal

Compute

154

attention (causal=False, no window) then costs about 4N 2 d ≈ 9.145 TFLOP per layer, ≈ 274 TFLOP
per branch evaluation, and ≈ 27.4 PFLOP over the inspected 50 scheduler steps × 2 CFG branches.
[1P][DERIVED]
The architectural consequence is the scaling, not the absolute figure: extend 121 to 241 frames
and tokens rise ~1.97× while the dense pairwise term rises ~3.87×; double both spatial dimensions
and tokens quadruple while the pairwise work rises sixteenfold. Count dimensions, derive FLOPs,
observe the exponent, then decide. The full geometry, memory-boundary and timing-convention
derivation, with its citations, is in Appendix A’s video-attention note.

8.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• Arithmetic intensity of fused kernels. Most roofline estimates treat attention or MLP as
separate matmuls, but in practice frameworks fuse multiple operations into a single kernel.
The effective FLOP/byte of a fused attention+MLP kernel is not well cataloged in primary
sources and would require profiling on the target hardware to anchor.
• MFU across precisions and sparsity. The 30–40% H100 FP16 figure is a rule of thumb; actual
utilization depends on architecture, kernel quality, and batch config. A systematic MFU atlas
across H100/H200/GB200, FP16/BF16/FP8, dense/MOE would be a valuable reference.
• Arithmetic intensity of emerging attention mechanisms. Linear attention (DeltaNet),
low-rank/compressed attention (MLA, CSA, HCA), and hybrid sparse patterns have different
FLOP profiles and data movement. Their roofline position is not yet established in primary
sources.
• Frontier 2026 has begun to answer this. DeepSeek-V4’s hybrid CSA+HCA attention reports
that, at 1M-token context, single-token inference drops to ~27% of the FLOPs (Pro) / ~10%
(Flash) and KV cache to ~10% / ~7% of DeepSeek-V3.2 [1P: arXiv 2606.19348]. In its 2026-0826 release article, Z.ai compares GLM-5.3-Flash with GLM-5.3: it reports 3× less attention
compute per head per layer and a 4.4× smaller average BF16 KV cache per layer. These
are normalized attention metrics, not whole-model FLOP or total-cache ratios. These are [1P]
first-party vendor figures, not yet independently reprofiled on our own hardware — which
is exactly the arithmetic-intensity measurement an architect should still do before trusting a
vendor’s roofline claim for their own workload.
• How quantization shifts the ridge. Moving from FP16 to FP8/int8 changes peak TFLOP/s
and bytes-per-operand, shifting the ridge point. The net effect depends on the quantization
scheme (element-wise vs. per-tensor, dynamic vs. static) and whether the kernel is re-tuned
for the lower precision. At first order the two shifts cancel: FP8 halves bytes-per-operand
(doubling intensity) and roughly doubles dense peak (doubling the ridge), so the classification
does not move (§8.6, third bullet). What does move the effective ridge is a scheme whose

8.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Continuous Deployment Scenario
An architect is brought into an ongoing deployment of a 70B-class Q&A system on a fleet of 8×H100
GPU nodes (tensor-parallel 8 per node; at ~10 rps the prefill leg alone demands ~12.9 PFLOP/s, so
the fleet spans several nodes — Ch 24’s prefill screen: 1.63 nodes at 100% MFU, ~5 at 35% MFU). The
system is serving ~10 requests/s average with ~9.2K input + 300 output tokens per request, and the
TTFT budget is being missed: p95 TTFT is 2.8 s, exceeding the 2 s p95 TTFT SLO (the 1.2 s figure is
the internal design budget). The TPOT of 28 ms/token is within the 35 ms p95 TPOT SLO (though
above the 25 ms design budget), but the prefill delay is the bottleneck.
The temptation is to reach for a roofline and “prove” prefill is memory-bound. That reasoning is
wrong here, and the error is worth naming: it is spread by treating prefill like token-by-token decode.
In decode, each new token re-reads the weight matrix from HBM, so the arithmetic intensity is ~1
FLOP/byte — genuinely memory-bound. In prefill, the weight matrix is read once and reused across
the whole sequence; the sequence dimension supplies the matrix-matrix reuse. Prefill’s weightonly effective intensity is (2 × N × L) / (N × 2 bytes/param) = L = 9,200 FLOP/byte at the
canonical 9.2K context; including the ~24 GB KV write it is ~7,850 FLOP/byte — both far above
the ~295 FLOP/byte dense-FP16 ridge, ~1.5 orders of magnitude. At that operating point prefill is
compute-bound, exactly as the rest of this chapter teaches.
So a high TTFT is not evidence of a bandwidth problem. The architect does the correct thing:
profile the prefill kernel and determine which of several distinct causes is actually limiting it, rather
than assuming memory. The profile separates four candidates:
• Compute-bound — the GEMMs are saturated at high MFU; more FLOPs/ops per token would
not help, but better kernel efficiency (flash-attention, fused MLP) would.
• Communication-bound — tensor/pipeline parallelism crosses the NVLink/Host fabric; data
movement, not math, is the ceiling. The fix is a different parallelization or a smaller cross-GPU
footprint.
• Launch / occupancy-limited — the kernel is too small or the grid under-fills the SMs;
increasing batch or improving occupancy raises utilization without adding hardware.
• Attention-term (compute) constrained within prefill — the quadratic attention term, not
the linear weights, grows with context; at 128K+ contexts this FLOP term dominates prefill
cost (at 32K it is already ~+60% — the 4·n_layers·L²·d term, Fig 22.1; case (ii) convention), so
the fix is to reduce the attention FLOP term (sparse/linear attention) or, where the attention
kernel is memory-bound, cut its HBM traffic (FlashAttention) — not to batch harder. A distinct
sub-case exists where score-matrix and KV HBM traffic, rather than attention FLOPs, is the
binding term; that one is a bandwidth constraint and should be diagnosed separately.

157

Compute

The architect measures MFU to choose among these. If the prefill kernel is running at 12% MFU,
the problem is occupancy or launch — grow the batch or fuse kernels. If MFU is already near ~40%
and the kernel is compute-saturated, then prefill is compute-bound and more batch just queues
more work without reducing per-request TTFT; the lever instead is kernel efficiency, attention-term
control, or P/D disaggregation so prefill’s FLOP profile is served by compute-optimized GPUs while
decode’s bandwidth profile runs on wide-memory GPUs.
The recommendation is therefore: profile first (MEASURE, do not assume), and only then pick the
intervention. Batching helps when prefill is occupancy-limited; kernel fusion helps when GEMMs are
under-saturated; attention-term control and disaggregation help when the bottleneck is the quadratic
attention term or the compute/bandwidth mismatch between phases. The workload’s true roofline
position, not an assumed “memory-bound prefill,” dictates the fix.

Prefill PFLOP also grows with context: 2 ×70B × L tokens scales linearly — ~0.28 PFLOP at 2K →
~4.5 PFLOP at 32K (K = 1,000, the book’s convention: 9.2K = 9,200) — so the longer the window, the larger
the one-time compute cost of loading it. Sustained throughput (tokens/s) is what matters for continuous
serving, and at the canonical 9.2K point the prefill is ~1.29 PFLOP (Table 8-1).

chapter 9.
Communication

The Architect’s Question
Before we can place a model across multiple GPUs or across a cluster, we need to know what the
interconnect can — and cannot — move. This chapter asks: given a model size, a parallelism strategy,
and a traffic pattern (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter), what is the communication time, and
does it dominate the compute budget? We will size the hidden bottleneck that often goes unnoticed
until the job stalls.

9.1. Concept
Implementation citations in this chapter were inspected on 28 October 2026 for the separately dated
addendum, outside the 30 August snapshot. They identify documented or source-inspected paths, not a
tested combined environment or a refresh of the August hardware comparisons.
Communication in a distributed LLM system follows the deployed topology, not a universal
vendor hierarchy. A server may connect its accelerators through PCIe, a dedicated scale-up fabric,
integrated Ethernet links, or a combination of paths; NVLink and NVSwitch are NVIDIA’s examples
of such a path, while Gaudi organizes a different integrated-network topology (Gaudi 3 white paper,
retrieved 2026-10-28). Across hosts, Ethernet/RoCE or InfiniBand may carry the traffic, subject to
the actual adapter, routing and transport support. Each layer still has a distinct bandwidth ceiling, a
distinct latency profile, and a distinct cost per gigabyte, so the architect must match the collective
operation to the layer where the bandwidth is sufficient: moving the same data over a slower
layer adds minutes to training time or inference latency for no computational benefit. The relevant

158

159

Communication

quantities are directional bandwidth, latency, contention, and the physical traffic of the chosen
collective — a product name alone supplies none of those measurements for a deployment.
A collective operation describes how data from a group of ranks becomes a result; it does not
specify a network, an algorithm, or a hardware vendor. A rank is an index within a communication
group, not a synonym for a server — one server can host several ranks, and several independent
groups can occupy the same devices. The communicator identifies the participants and the context
in which their operations match (MPI 5.0 standard; NCCL communicator API, retrieved 2026-10-28).
The collective operations that dominate multi-node training and inference are:
• all-reduce: each rank contributes an equal-shaped tensor; a reduction such as the elementwise
sum is returned to every rank. Averaging additionally requires division by the rank count;
the collective does not imply that division. Data-parallel training commonly uses gradient
reductions, while tensor-parallel inference uses activation reductions.
• all-gather: every GPU contributes a tensor; every GPU receives the concatenation of all
fragments. Used when a consumer needs the concatenation of distributed fragments locally —
e.g. FSDP-style materialization of a full weight tensor; KV cache normally stays sharded rather
than all-gathered.
• reduce-scatter: ranks contribute equal-shaped tensors, reduce corresponding elements, and
receive distinct partitions of the reduced result. Each output partition has 1/N of the input
tensor’s elements. Unlike all-gather, this operation also performs a reduction; it is not its
mathematical inverse.
• all-to-all: each rank sends a destination-specific block — the dominant collective for MoE
expert routing (Table 9-2, Ch 9).
The bandwidth each collective consumes depends on three factors: the data volume (bytes), the
number of participating ranks (N), and the interconnect’s effective bandwidth in the presence of
contention. A 70B FP16 model is 140 GB, and its FP16 gradient is the same size — the §9.3 worked
example all-reduces that 140 GB gradient tensor. The 140 GB is a logical input size, not the physical
traffic of the collective. For an eight-rank point-to-point ring, each rank sends 245 GB and receives
another 245 GB (§9.3). A one-way transfer of the logical 140 GB alone would take 56 s at an assumed
effective 2.5 GB/s; the ring’s send volume instead gives 98 s. The bandwidth denominator must use
the same direction convention as the counted bytes.

9.2. Mental Model
The concentric-ring model represents increasing communication distance in the actual topology,
not a mandatory sequence of fabrics. An accelerator accesses its local HBM first. Inside a server,
PCIe or a dedicated scale-up fabric connects devices; NVLink and NVSwitch are examples for the
NVIDIA configuration in Table 9-1, not universal server components. Across servers and racks,
Ethernet/RoCE or InfiniBand can carry traffic according to the deployed links, adapters, and routing.
A useful placement keeps frequent exchanges within a measured low-latency group where possible
and budgets any traffic that crosses its boundary. Physical distance alone does not establish a
bandwidth ranking: rail count, topology, contention, and transport support remain part of the
measurement.
Directionality comes before division. H100’s advertised NVLink bandwidth is 900 GB/s bidirec­
tional per GPU, or 450 GB/s per direction (NVIDIA H100 datasheet). This per-GPU port aggregate is
not a measurement of a particular topology’s bisection. A one-way 140 GB transfer at the directional
peak takes about 0.31 s [1P][DERIVED]. A collective also incurs reduction, synchronization and
routing work:
Tcollective ≈ α × nsteps +

bytes
β

where α is the per-step latency, β is the achieved bandwidth under an explicit directional con­
vention, and nsteps is the number of communication steps. The byte term must count that algorithm’s
physical traffic rather than substitute the logical tensor size. This expression is a simplified model;
overlap, reduction work and collective offload can change the critical path. For a flat one-way 140 GB
transfer, the nominal 25 GB/s of one HDR port gives a best-case 5.6 s; an assumed practical-effective
2.5 GB/s Ethernet path gives 56 s. The eight-rank ring in §9.3 instead sends 245 GB per rank: about
0.54 s at the H100 directional peak, 6.1 s at an assumed effective two-rail 40 GB/s, and 98 s at 2.5
GB/s. These are analytical comparisons, not measured NCCL results; deployment choices require
§9.4 measurements.
The reduce-scatter and all-gather rows of Table 9-2 become concrete in Fig 9.2, which follows
one SUM through a balanced four-rank ring. Reduce-scatter leaves a different reduced fragment at
each rank, and all-gather then replicates those already-reduced fragments — gathering the original
inputs instead would not produce the same result. The two phases are also the traffic §9.3 counts:
each phase sends (N − 1)/N of the tensor per rank, which is where 122.5 GB per phase, and 245 GB
per rank, comes from at eight ranks and 140 GB (MPI 5.0 standard; nccl-tests performance definition,
pinned, retrieved 2026-10-28).
Floating-point SUM adds another constraint. Its mathematical expression is unchanged when
an implementation changes the reduction tree, but finite-precision addition can produce different
bits, and the MPI standard explicitly recognizes this effect (MPI 5.0 standard). A reproducibility
claim therefore needs a scope: inputs, dtype, rank count and mapping, algorithm, kernels, and

hardware/software versions. A fixed random seed does not by itself establish bitwise collective
reproducibility.
The software path above those physical rings has several distinct decisions, and Fig 9.3 separates
them from the setup path. The framework chooses a communication group and operation; its backend
connects that request to a collective implementation; the implementation chooses an algorithm and
uses device execution and transport facilities; those facilities share HBM, device links, PCIe, NICs, and
switches — the layers of Table 9-1. Changing a transport can leave the collective semantics unchanged
while changing which resource limits the operation (NCCL API header, pinned to v2.32.3-1; NCCL
transport selection, pinned; oneCCL MPI transport, pinned to 2022.1.0; oneCCL OFI transport, pinned,
retrieved 2026-10-28).
MPI is a standard, not one library and not a CPU-only transport: Open MPI, MPICH, and Intel MPI
are implementations, and GPU-aware implementations can accept supported device buffers, so eligible
configurations can move their payload without staging it through host memory. Device-pointer
recognition, direct RDMA, operation support, and stream integration are separate capabilities — none
follows automatically from the phrase “GPU-aware.” The fair comparison is specific: Open MPI’s
v5.0.x CUDA documentation supports device buffers for several blocking collectives yet explicitly
restricts nonblocking reduction collectives on the documented CUDA-aware UCX path (Open MPI
CUDA-aware support), while MPICH v5.0.2 documents CUDA, HIP, and Level Zero build support —
a build statement, not a guarantee for every datatype, provider, or persistent device-buffer operation
(MPICH v5.0.2 README, retrieved 2026-10-28). A nonblocking MPI request allows overlap; it does
not guarantee independent background progress, and a correct MPI program must tolerate weak
progress (MPI 5.0 standard).
A typical NCCL call instead submits work to a CUDA stream: stream order connects the collective
to preceding producers and later consumers, a consumer on another stream needs an explicit
dependency, and network paths can use CPU proxy threads, so GPU-oriented communication does
not imply zero host resource use (NCCL stream semantics; NCCL proxy source, pinned to v2.32.3-1).
The submission-versus-completion contract itself is measurement business, taken up in §9.4.
MPI and NCCL can coexist: NVIDIA’s own example uses MPI to launch and coordinate ranks and
distribute the NCCL unique ID, then calls NCCL for the tensor reduction (NCCL MPI example). The
presence of mpirun or MPI_Bcast in an application therefore does not identify the collective payload
path; conversely, an MPI implementation may itself carry GPU payload, and oneCCL’s transport
layer includes MPI as well as OFI paths (oneCCL MPI transport, pinned; oneCCL OFI transport,
pinned). Bootstrap, collective algorithm, and transport require separate labels.
A ring is one execution strategy, not the meaning of all-reduce. A balanced point-to-point
ring pipelines fragments through reduce-scatter and all-gather — the structure Fig 9.2 shows —
while trees can reduce synchronization depth, hierarchical algorithms can keep much of the traffic
inside a fast local group, and pairwise exchanges serve a different redistribution pattern in all-to-all
(NCCL ring implementation, pinned to v2.32.3-1; NCCL cost model, pinned). Channels add parallel

communication paths, and protocols such as NCCL’s LL, LL128, and Simple govern lower-level

The useful choice depends on message size and topology. For small messages, launch and per-step
latency can dominate — the per-step latency term of the model above; for large messages, sustained
directional bandwidth and load balance matter more — its byte term. Communication kernels may
compete with model kernels for SMs, HBM, and cache, while network progress consumes host
and NIC resources, so more overlap can reduce exposed waiting yet slow the computation being
overlapped. The architecture decision follows the combined critical path, not a library name or an
isolated bandwidth score.

9.3. Worked Example
For a communication-only illustration, a 70B model has 140 GB of FP16 weights. We separately
assume an FP16 gradient tensor of logical size M = 140 GB at each rank. Chapter 10 instead
assumes FP32 gradients, so its logical tensor is 280 GB. Neither a 140 GB weight tensor nor this
gradient buffer fits on one 80 GB GPU. Even two 80 GB GPUs fitting the weights would not establish
training-state fit: gradients, optimizer state, activations and workspace also require memory. A real
deployment must specify partitioning and chunking before applying this model. For the arithmetic
below, eight logical ranks perform a point-to-point ring without collective offload. Each phase sends
(N − 1)M /N = 122.5 GB per rank; reduce-scatter followed by all-gather therefore sends 245 GB
and receives another 245 GB per rank. These are endpoint traffic counts, not a claim that the full
buffer can be allocated on an H100. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
Option A — H100 NVLink directional-peak model. The advertised 900 GB/s is the sum of
both directions at each GPU endpoint. The corresponding peak in one direction is 450 GB/s. We use
that directional peak to obtain an ideal ring time, not an achieved bandwidth or a memory-feasible
eight-replica training deployment. A flat one-way transfer alone would take
Tflat =

its ideal time is Tring ≈ 245/450 ≈ 0.54 s. Equivalently, 490 GB of sent-plus-received traffic divided
by 900 GB/s gives the same time. Reduction, synchronization, contention and staging can increase
the elapsed time. The ring accounting follows the NVIDIA nccl-tests performance definition. [1P]
[DERIVED]

link (≈ 25 GB/s before link coding; NDR doubles this to 400 Gb/s). InfiniBand uses a 64b/66b line
code, so the useful payload sits a bit below the line rate. A ring-all-reduce or tree-all-reduce across 8
nodes will see lower effective bandwidth due to multi-hop forwarding and congestion. A realistic

overlap and computation; they do not predict a real training iteration without its collective schedule.

The worked example also highlights why tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism exist: when
a single GPU cannot hold the model, splitting it across nodes moves the communication from the
inner rings to the outer rings, and the architect must budget the extra seconds per collective against
the benefit of enabling a model that fits.

9.4. Measurement
Measuring communication in situ is harder than counting tokens, because the bandwidth numbers
above are peaks; real systems see lower effective bandwidth due to congestion, operating-system
interference, and protocol overhead. Three practical measurements an architect can make:
1. Correctness and completion. A known-input test establishes the operation, dtype, element
count, communicator, reduction, root, rank order and output partition. Floating-point compar­
isons use a documented tolerance; bitwise repeatability is a separate result. Device producers
must finish before the collective reads their buffers, and consumers must observe completion
rather than host submission. A CUDA-stream submission returning successfully does not by
itself establish that its result is ready on another stream (NCCL stream semantics).
2. Collective performance on feasible buffers. A microbenchmark uses resident per-rank
allocations that fit after runtime reserves, including any separate input/output buffers and
scratch space. The logical 140 GB example in §9.3 is not a request to allocate 140 GB on one 80
GB GPU. The test matrix spans small activation messages and larger gradient buckets, group
sizes and node mappings. Each result records the stack, topology, transport, selected algorithm,
warmup, sample count, repeated trials and timing boundary. Host enqueue time differs from
device-completed latency. The original elapsed time stays beside algbw and busbw; the latter is

169

Communication

an algorithm-specific normalization, not a physical-link byte counter (nccl-tests performance
definitions). A point-to-point link test answers a different question from a collective test.
3. Service impact under contention. The same shapes run in the actual compute and arrival
schedule, first in isolation and then with concurrent traffic. Profiler traces separate exposed
communication stalls, hidden communication and compute slowed by shared-resource con­
tention. Summing all collective durations can overstate the exposed cost, while subtracting
all overlap can understate it. TTFT, ITL, errors and SLO-goodput establish the serving con­
sequence; training uses device-completed iteration time and its critical path. A large-buffer
bandwidth result alone does not establish either outcome (Chapter 14).
Collective tests must also exercise the backend the workload actually uses. NCCL tests describe
an NCCL path; they do not certify XCCL or HCCL. The examined vLLM XPU configuration selects
the XCCL backend with recent PyTorch (vLLM XPU platform source, pinned to revision 5df63a7),
while Gaudi exposes HCCL (Habana HCCL API reference, retrieved 2026-10-28). The test record
therefore needs rank placement, data type, message size, transport, and a sent/received bandwidth
convention. For Gaudi’s documented 24 × 200 Gb/s port total (Gaudi 3 white paper), the nominal
arithmetic is 600 GB/s per direction or 1,200 GB/s bidirectional aggregate — derived nominal figures,
and neither is an achieved all-reduce bandwidth. [1P][DERIVED]
The key invariant: always measure on the same hardware and software stack that the production
job will use. A benchmark run on a clean VM with no other traffic will overstate the achievable
bandwidth compared to a crowded cluster.
Failure tests complete this contract. Missing ranks, mismatched counts or collective order, network
faults and process exits can block a group. Framework watchdogs, asynchronous library errors and
request deadlines need one recovery policy. An asynchronous success code does not establish
correctness after communicator failure; recovery must be exercised at the framework and service
boundary (NCCL communicator errors and abort).

9.5. Common Mistakes
• Assuming peak bandwidth is sustained. PCIe Gen5 x16 peaks at ~64 GB/s per direction
(~128 GB/s bidirectional aggregate), but measured effective bandwidth falls short of the peak
because of protocol overhead, latency, message size and contention — not because traffic splits
across links; each link of a ring carries a large fraction of the tensor. (A two‑rank collective
over one path is the exception — per phase each link carries (N−1)/N of the tensor; over the
full reduce-scatter plus all-gather each link carries 2(N−1)/N — for N=2 that totals one full
tensor per link, which is why a two-rank collective can saturate the link.) For PCIe Gen5 x16
and small-to-medium collectives, measured effective bandwidth is often in the 40–60% range
[ILLUSTRATIVE]; NVLink and InfiniBand large-message collectives can achieve 80–90%+;
design against the measured number, not the spec sheet peak.

Communication

170

• Placing all-reduce on Ethernet without a bandwidth budget. A 70B model gradient allreduce (FP16, §9.3) at 25 Gb/s Ethernet (≈ 2.5 GB/s practical-effective): a flat one-way transfer
of the 140 GB gradient takes ~56 s (the §9.3 flat-transfer lower bound), while the ring all-reduce
takes ~98 s per step. If the training runs 1,000 iterations, that is ~56,000 s (15.6 hours) at the
flat-transfer lower bound — ~98,000 s (~27.2 hours) under the ring factor — spent exclusively in
communication, a no-overlap total: with gradient-bucketing overlap the exposed critical-path
cost is lower and must be measured. Always compute the per-iteration communication cost
before committing to a lower-bandwidth fabric.
• Ignoring contention from other traffic. NVSwitch can carry many concurrent channels,
but if other collectives (e.g., all-gather for parameter shards (FSDP) or reduce-scatter for
gradients) are running simultaneously, the bisection bandwidth is shared. Measure with the
full production workload pattern, not an isolated micro‑benchmark.
• Using InfiniBand as a default without checking the cost–performance ratio. InfiniBand
HDR 200 Gb/s gives ~25 GB/s unidirectional, which is sufficient for many workloads, but the
price per port (or per Gb/s) of optics and cables is 5–10× that of Ethernet [ILLUSTRATIVE].
If the communication time is acceptable on RoCEv2, the cheaper fabric may be the better
architectural choice.
• Overlooking protocol overhead. At the speeds discussed here Ethernet and InfiniBand use
different physical-layer coding and framing (Ethernet line coding is named per rate: 200GbE
and 400GbE (802.3ck) use 256b/257b block coding before FEC, while InfiniBand HDR and NDR
both use 64b/66b) — use the specific standard’s payload-efficiency figure. An NDR 400 Gb/s
InfiniBand link delivers a ~380 Gb/s class useful payload [DERIVED: 64b/66b line code plus
framing/FEC overhead]; a 200 Gb/s RoCEv2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s [DERIVED: 256b/257b
block coding plus RS(544,514) FEC and Ethernet framing overhead]. The difference matters
when we are computing per-second throughput for a fixed data volume. [ILLUSTRATIVE]

9.6. Architecture Consequence
The interconnect choice is not a detail to be decided after the model, the parallelism strategy, and
the hardware are selected — it is a first-class design variable that shapes all three. If the architecture
calls for data-parallel training of a 70B FP16 model across 8 nodes (an eight-rank DP group, e.g. one
rank per node), the all-reduce bandwidth dictates whether the nodes are connected by InfiniBand,
200 GbE, or even 100 GbE. If the budget can accommodate NVLink‑equipped hosts (GPUs connected
on‑node), the ratios are: an ideal ring time about 1/11th the assumed InfiniBand case and about
1/180th the assumed RoCE case (§9.3), for a single-host eight-rank collective against a cross-host one
(NVLink figure is a directional peak; fabric figures are effective — the ratios are peak-vs-effective
upper bounds). For the eight-node DP job the all-reduce is necessarily inter-node, so compare

171

Communication

InfiniBand with Ethernet only for that portion. These ratios apply to this communication-only model,
not to end-to-end throughput. An eight-node data-parallel job uses NVLink/NVSwitch for intra-node
exchanges and InfiniBand/RoCE for inter-node exchanges; compare InfiniBand vs Ethernet only for
the inter-node portion. The 1/11 and 1/180 ratios compare an eight-rank single-host collective with
an eight-rank cross-host collective (communication-only, peak-vs-effective), not two fabrics for the
same job.
The architecture consequence also flows in the other direction: a tighter communication budget
(e.g., target <0.5 s per all-reduce) may force a particular parallelism strategy. We might choose model
parallelism (pipeline parallelism, tensor parallelism) to keep the per-collective data volume smaller, or
we might accept a slower fabric and reduce the frequency of collectives (e.g., gradient accumulation
steps between all-reduce calls). The interconnect bandwidth number is the anchor that makes these
trade-offs quantifiable.
Finally, the architecture consequence extends to cost. A cluster of 8‑GPU H100 servers (NVSwitch
inside each node) is the highest upfront capital expenditure, but it delivers the lowest per-iteration
communication time, which can translate to higher throughput per dollar over the life of the cluster
when communication is a significant fraction of iteration time and the switch-fabric premium is
repaid by the time saved. A cluster connected by 200 GbE RoCE has lower capital cost but higher
per-iteration communication time, which may increase the total cost of ownership if the training
job runs for many weeks. NVSwitch inside each node and a 200 GbE RoCE or InfiniBand inter-node
fabric are not exclusive alternatives — they are different layers of the same cluster and are normally
both present, so the capex comparison must name which layer it prices. The architect must balance
capex vs. opex by way of the communication arithmetic shown in this chapter.

9.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• Contention patterns under mixed workloads. The analytical estimates above assume a
dedicated collective on a quiet fabric. In a production fleet, other traffic (user requests, other
training jobs, KV cache movement) shares the same links. The effective bandwidth under
realistic multi‑job congestion is not yet characterized with a standard suite, and the interaction
between all-reduce and RoCE/Ethernet best‑effort traffic can cause tail latency spikes that are
difficult to predict.
• Adaptive collective algorithms. New compression and approximation techniques (e.g.,
gradient compression, sparse all‑reduce, error‑bounded approximations) applied to collectives
claim to reduce the data volume at the cost of a small accuracy loss. The bandwidth arithmetic
changes when the data volume is 30 GB instead of 140 GB, but the compression/decompression
compute may offset the bandwidth savings. The net effect on iteration time is workload‑specific
and not yet settled.
• Optical interconnects and the next generation. NVLink‑Switch and the next‑generation
switch fabrics are pushing intra‑node bandwidth higher (NVLink 5 provides 1.8 TB/s per GPU

Communication

172

bidirectional aggregate, i.e. 900 GB/s per direction), and optical intra‑rack fabrics are entering
data centers: 400–800 Gb/s aggregate module rates ship today, with per‑lane (per‑wavelength)
rates of 100–200 Gb/s deployed and 400 Gb/s per lane in development [1P: vendor datasheet].
The arithmetic base — the relative magnitudes of PCIe, NVLink, Ethernet, InfiniBand — is stable
in the near term, but the absolute numbers will shift as new silicon and cable technologies
ship. Keep the framework; update the constants.
• Cross‑domain generalization. Most published bandwidth measurements use standard dense
buffers (e.g., an all‑reduce of a gradient tensor). Sparse gradients and structured compression
may exhibit different effective bandwidths because the reduced or irregular data volume
changes how the transfer fills the links. The arithmetic framework applies, but the constants
need re‑measurement for the specific tensor shape.

(ccl.h, pinned to 2022.1.0); its legacy plugin connects to the existing C++ collective implementation,
and its tree contains MPI and OFI transports (legacy plugin, MPI transport, and OFI transport, all
pinned to that tag, retrieved 2026-10-28). SYCL/Level Zero describe the device execution and memory
path; MPI/OFI describe transport choices at another layer, and actual device-buffer support still
depends on the selected plugin, transport, build, and system configuration.
Queue semantics are part of that contract. The inspected 2022.1.0 legacy plugin expects an
in-order SYCL queue for its queue path; its CPU branch with a null stream waits on an event,
and other branches contain queue waits or host tasks (legacy plugin source, pinned). The broad
description “asynchronous GPU collective” cannot replace those path-specific completion rules, and
similar-looking function names do not establish matching error, lifetime, or recovery semantics. The

173

C API has a concrete plugin error boundary: in the inspected tag its wrapper converts caught C++
exceptions into onecclPluginException, and a communicator without a finalize or abort callback
causes the corresponding API to return onecclNotImplemented — a conditional code path, not a
claim that every plugin lacks recovery callbacks (oneCCL API source, pinned). A synchronous return
code also does not establish completion of previously queued device work; runtime failures and the
selected plugin’s recovery behavior remain separate obligations.

standalone successor called Intel XCCL has been verified; proposals in a PyTorch RFC are not release
evidence (PyTorch RFC discussion).

9.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Naming the Parallelism Before the Arithmetic
An architect is asked to design a 70B inference service for a population of 10,000 users. The request
frequency and arrival trace have not yet been supplied. The team considers replicating an eight-GPU
tensor-parallel engine or partitioning one engine across 32 hosts. The communication scheme can be
assessed before the fleet count is known, but a user population alone cannot determine that count.
The per-request all-reduce is not the right model for inference, and neither is a blanket “allgather the full weights every decode step.” It matters which parallelism is in play: ordinary tensor
parallelism (TP) shards each weight matrix across the GPUs, and every decode step exchanges only
the activations (not the weights) via collective ops like all-reduce/all-gather of the small activation
tensors — weight matrices stay resident and are read in place, they are not re-fetched each step. A
different scheme, FSDP-style weight gathering (used in training, and in some sharded-inference
arrangements) does all-gather weight shards before the forward pass. So the architect must name
the scheme before doing the arithmetic. Concretely, for the canonical 8×H100 host the meaningful
per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (each per-layer all-reduce
operates on a ~256 KiB logical tensor — batch × hidden × bytes — so an 8-rank ring sends 1.75 × that
≈ 0.45 MB per rank; across all 80 layers the per-step total is ~36 MB of per-rank send traffic, against
~20 MB of logical volume, sub-MB to tens of MB and not GBs at the canonical batch and hidden size).

175

Communication

In disaggregated serving a separate, one-time movement — not a per-step one — moves the KV cache
fragment: e.g. ~35 GB of KV moved over NVLink (~0.08 s at 450 GB/s per direction, §9.2) when a P/D
sequence transfers a ~13K-token context (35 GB ÷ 2.62 MB/token ≈ 13.3K) between prefill and decode
pools. The distinction changes the answer by orders of magnitude: re-fetching 140 GB of weights
each step is pathological (that is a design smell, an anti-pattern to flag, not a baseline); exchanging
activations or KV fragments is the normal case — bandwidth-feasible within NVLink (~0.08 s for the
35 GB KV move), with acceptability judged against the TTFT/SLO budget.
The architect proposes keeping each tensor-parallel engine within an eight-GPU host where
memory and operator support permit. Additional independent replicas can then absorb greater traffic
without extending tensor parallelism across hosts. Activation exchange still consumes bandwidth
and synchronization time; it is not free. Cross-host partitioning becomes a separate candidate when
a model or its required request state cannot fit within the chosen host, or when measurements
demonstrate another benefit. A prefill/decode split also needs a measured KV-transfer path; NVLink
timing only applies when that path is actually available.
Scope note. People, request arrivals and resident requests are different populations. The 10,000user setup needs a request-frequency assumption or trace before Chapter 17 can determine occupancy
and fleet capacity. The separate canonical 10/40 req/s workload can use the established Chapter
17 planning analysis. If a deliberately different storage scenario specifies 10,000 simultaneous fullcontext resident requests, the ideal whole-context limit of 17 slots per host (Ch. 7, Fig 7.7: C ≈ 17.5,
floor 17) gives ⌈10,000/17⌉ = 589 hosts before throughput, runtime overhead, placement, SLO
headroom and failure reserve. That is a request-storage lower bound, not a user-derived deploy­
ment recommendation. More replicas do not by themselves require cross-host model partitioning.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

chapter 10.
Parallelism: Splitting Work Across Machines

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to answer the inevitable scaling question: a single GPU cannot
hold this model or keep up with this workload — how do we split the work across many GPUs, and which
split is right? We will build the arithmetic for why a model outgrows one GPU, then study the five
parallelization strategies — tensor (a layer’s weights), pipeline (the layer stack), data (replicates the
model, splits the batch), expert (MoE experts), and sequence parallelism (the sequence) — plus a
serving-only sixth, P/D disaggregation, which splits request phases rather than model parameters
and has no training counterpart, and develop a rule for choosing among them based on the model’s
weight-residency, the workload’s batch shape, and the interconnect speed. After this chapter, “we
scaled it out” becomes a precise claim about what was split and why.

10.1. Concept
The central idea: parallelism is splitting one of the three things a model occupies — its weights,
its layers, or its data — across multiple devices. Before reading on, one framing note that
prevents a common source of confusion: the parallelism toolkit differs between training and
inference, and “data parallelism” means different things in each mode. In training, DP means
replicated weights plus gradient all-reduce every step (plus FSDP, which shards and re-gathers
weights/optimizer state); for plain DP the communication load is at the gradient-sync point, while
FSDP also communicates during the forward pass when it all-gathers parameter shards and during
backward when it reduce-scatters gradients. In inference, DP simply means running independent
model replicas to raise throughput — there is no gradient sync at all, because each request is

176

177

Parallelism: Splitting Work Across Machines

served by one replica. There is also a serving-relevant family — context/pipeline partitioning, expert
parallelism, and P/D disaggregation (splitting the prefill stage from the decode stage into separate
pools) — repurposed here for serving; of the three, only P/D disaggregation has no training analogue
(context/pipeline partitioning and expert parallelism both appear in training too). The rest of this
section defines the strategies, and §10.3 applies them to inference (the book’s canonical serving
context) unless a strategy is explicitly training-only.
The strategy names tell us what gets split:
1. Tensor parallelism (TP) splits a single layer’s weights across GPUs. Each GPU holds a slice
of the weight matrix and exchanges partial results through the TP group’s interconnect. These
layer-level dependencies require sufficient measured bandwidth and low latency; NVLink
is one implementation, not an algorithmic requirement. TP is intra-layer. (Inference: shards
weights; per-step exchange is activations, not weights — see Ch. 9.)
2. Pipeline parallelism (PP) splits the model’s layers (stages) across GPUs. GPU 0 runs layers
1–8, GPU 1 runs 9–16, GPU 2 runs 17–24, and so on; activations flow forward, gradients flow
backward. PP is inter-layer, communication-light, but idle bubbles appear at stage boundaries.
(Inference: can split decode stages; bubbles hurt latency-sensitive serving more than training.)
3. Data parallelism (DP) — different in the two modes. Training: replicates all weights on every
GPU, feeds each a different batch, all-reduces gradients after each step; communication-heavy
only at the gradient-sync point, but each GPU must hold the full model. Inference: independent
replicas each serve a disjoint set of requests; no gradient sync; throughput scales linearly until
KV or memory binds (Ch. 17).
4. Expert parallelism (EP) shards the experts of a Mixture-of-Experts model across GPUs and
routes each token to the GPU holding its experts — an all-to-all exchange per token. EP is
MoE-specific. (Used in both training and inference for MoE models.)
5. Sequence/context parallelism (CP) splits the sequence dimension across GPUs, useful for
very long contexts where the KV cache or attention activations exceed one GPU. (Applies in
both modes: training shards the sequence for long-context forward/backward; the inferencespecific variant here shards the KV cache and attention activations — the serving analogue of
training sequence parallelism.)
6. P/D disaggregation (inference) — separates the prefill stage (compute-dominated at the
canonical operating point) from the decode stage (bandwidth-dominated there) onto different
GPU pools so each can be sized and scaled independently (Ch. 11). This has no training
counterpart and is a serving-only strategy.
These are not alternatives; production systems compose them (e.g. DP across nodes × TP within
a node × PP across a few nodes; or TP+CP within a decode pool + a separate prefill pool). The

Parallelism: Splitting Work Across Machines

the parallelism is being applied.

panels. Tensor parallel shards one layer’s weight matrix across GPUs — activations are replicated,

179

Parallelism: Splitting Work Across Machines

and each GPU’s partial sums are all-reduced every layer in the illustrated layout. Those frequent
exchanges make measured collective latency and throughput margin important. Pipeline parallel
cuts the layer stack into stages on different GPUs — hidden states cross stage boundaries point-topoint, an idle bubble appears as the pipeline fills and drains, and the communication can span nodes
if the stage-boundary transfer meets its budget. Data parallel replicates the whole model and splits
the batch — in training every replica all-reduces its gradient each step; in inference the replicas
are independent, each serving a disjoint slice of requests with no sync at all. Expert and sequence
parallelism (EP/CP) are additional axes that reuse the same machinery. Communication-specificity
note: the TP collective is algorithm-dependent — a plain all-reduce of partial sums is one option,
but fused kernels often use reduce-scatter + all-gather (or a single all-reduce) depending on the
framework; the PP bubble size depends on micro-batch scheduling (more micro-batches shrink the
bubble but add memory). The panels show the canonical configuration (TP all-reduce per layer; PP
with a small fixed micro-batch count; GPU counts and layer ranges schematic); substitute the actual
collective and schedule for the target stack. Which dimension binds determines which to split first.

10.2. Mental Model
Each strategy is best distinguished by what it trades bandwidth for. Tensor parallelism exchanges
layer results to distribute weight residency but adds synchronization dependencies. Pipeline paral­
lelism transfers stage-boundary activations and accepts bubbles as the price of not holding all layers
on one GPU. Training data parallelism trades gradient bandwidth for replicated weights; inference
replicas have no gradient synchronization. In either mode, each replica’s assigned devices must fit
its state.
The useful mental model is a resource triangle: we have weights (memory), activations (work),
and data (batch). Each strategy moves one corner off a single GPU at the cost of communication.
When a GPU runs out of memory, we reach for TP/PP (weight splitting). When aggregate throughput,
not memory, is the limit — the data corner is what is starved — we reach for DP (more replicas, each
with its own batch); CP addresses long-sequence/KV capacity, not idle-fill. DP does not create work
for an idle GPU, and if the device is idle for lack of arrivals, DP makes it idler. When the model is too
big to replicate, TP wins over DP. The binding constraint chooses the strategy.
