10.3. Worked Example
10.3.1. Why the Canonical 70B Doesn’t Fit One H100
The canonical model is 70B FP16 dense = 140 GB of weights [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] (reality
check: 70 ×10⁹ params × 2 bytes). A single H100 has 80 GB of HBM [1P][FACT]. The arithmetic is
immediate:
• The weights alone don’t fit on one H100:

140 GB weights > 80 GB HBM
We need at least 140/80 ≈ 1.75 → ≥ 2 GPUs just to hold the weights (and that’s before KV
cache, which adds ~2.62 MB/token at FP16 (2.5 MiB) — the 9.2K-token canonical prompt needs ~24.1
GB more (initial KV)). [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
1
2

In the Replicates column, an entry names an object held in multiple copies on multiple devices.
The canonical 70B (140 GB) exceeds one H100 (80 GB), so DP is not its baseline; see §10.3.

181

Parallelism: Splitting Work Across Machines

The canonical 8×H100 host (640 GB total) fits the weights + KV comfortably, which is why the
single-host baseline in earlier chapters works. But if the model grows (say to 400B) or its context/state
grows, the split becomes mandatory. The next three subsections take that split in turn: tensor, pipeline,
and data parallelism.
10.3.2. Tensor Parallelism: Splitting Weights Across GPUs
With tensor parallelism, the 140 GB weight tensor is partitioned across GPUs. Two H100 GPUs
would hold 70 GB of weights each, before KV state, activations and runtime overhead. A simplified
tensor-parallel forward pass exchanges partial activations rather than gathering the full weights.
For an eight-rank ring, one equal-sized all-reduce per layer and no overlap, the bandwidth term
is Ttp ≈ nlayers × 2(N − 1)/N × Mact /Bdir . Here Mact is the full logical activation tensor in bytes
contributed by each rank to one collective; for a dense activation it is token count times hidden
dimension times bytes per element. The actual number and shapes of collectives depend on the
partitioning and kernels. Bdir is directional effective bandwidth, not the sum of send and receive
peaks. H100 advertises 900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU, corresponding to a 450 GB/s peak in each
direction; achieved bandwidth requires measurement. Step latency, contention and reduction work
are additional costs. [1P][DERIVED]
Tensor parallelism keeps weight shards resident and exchanges layer results. In a row-parallel
linear layer, ranks compute partial outputs from their local weight shards; a reduction combines
those partial outputs. Other layouts can use reduce-scatter and all-gather instead.3 The buffer shape,
communication precision, group size and number of collective calls determine the byte budget.
Ordinary TP decode does not fetch the full model weights over the network again for every token.
Consider a small illustrative decode step with 16 active sequences, one new token per sequence,
hidden width 8,192, two-byte BF16 communication and eight TP ranks. Assume two output allreduces per transformer block — attention output and MLP — 80 blocks, no sequence parallelism,
and a balanced point-to-point ring. (The bandwidth term above counts one collective per layer;
this budget’s two-per-block assumption is why the call count below is 160 rather than 80.) These
are explicit teaching inputs, not a measured model configuration. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]
[ANALYTICAL]

10.3.4. Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients
Plain data parallelism is infeasible here: it would replicate the 140 GB model on every GPU, and at 80
GB HBM per H100 the replica does not fit on one device (which is why sharded variants such as
FSDP exist) — the gradient arithmetic below is a communication model, not a feasible allocation. For
the gradient all-reduce: if the model has 140 GB of weights and we sync gradients after each step
across G GPUs, each GPU sends its gradient tensor once per step. The gradient bytes are
grad bytes = Nparams × bytes/param = 70 × 109 × 4 B ≈ 280 GB
per step (FP32 gradients are used here as a conservative communication model; mixed-precision
implementations that sync FP16/BF16 gradients with loss scaling or FP32 master weights would
halve these bytes; the all-reduce moves the gradient once, not weights+gradients). As in Chapter 9, a
ring all-reduce moves 2 NN−1 times the per-rank gradient through each rank, so for N = 8 each of
the two phases sends NN−1 × 280 ≈ 245 GB per rank, and the per-rank send volume is 2 × 245 ≈ 490
GB (490 GB received as well, so 980 GB of send-plus-receive traffic); here and in Chapter 9, per-rank
traffic means send volume unless stated otherwise, and the sync time is Tring = send volume/Bdir
with Bdir the directional bandwidth. At 25 GB/s (single 200Gb/s link) that is 490 / 25 ≈ 19.6 s
per step — far too slow if the step takes ~1 s. At the H100 NVLink directional peak of 450 GB/s, the
same ideal ring estimate is 490/450 ≈ 1.09 s (equivalently, 980 GB of send-plus-receive traffic
divided by the 900 GB/s bidirectional sum gives the same time). The 900 GB/s bidirectional sum
divides only that send-plus-receive total, never a send-only count; this remains a communication
model, not proof of training-state fit. The sync cost, not compute, often caps DP at small scale unless
the interconnect is fast. [1P][DERIVED]
The 280 GB is the logical FP32 gradient for a full model replica, not a feasible single-H100
allocation. In hybrid DP×TP training, a DP communicator can join matching parameter shards from
different replicas. Its per-device buffer size and participating ranks replace the full-replica logical
inputs above; the TP group within each replica is a different communicator (NCCL communicator
definition). Chapter 9’s separate 140 GB example assumes FP16 gradients, so the two examples must
retain their different precision bases.
Two more communication objects complete the picture. For expert parallelism, the population
is routed token copies rather than TP partial outputs. With eight EP ranks, 256 local tokens per
rank, top-2 routing, hidden width 8,192 and BF16, an illustrative uniform routing model produces 8
MiB of route rows per rank. Seven eighths go remote: dispatch sends and receives 7 MiB per rank.
An equal-sized combine doubles those totals to 14 MiB sent and 14 MiB received. This excludes
metadata, padding, compression, route deduplication and load skew. A hot destination can dominate
completion even when the average byte budget fits. Specialized dispatch/combine implementations

Parallelism: Splitting Work Across Machines

184

may exploit structure that a fixed-count all-to-all does not expose.5 [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
[ANALYTICAL]
FSDP changes the object again. Its communication can gather a module’s parameter shards before
computation and reduce-scatter that module’s gradients afterward. An illustrative 64 MiB unit split
eight ways requires 56 MiB sent and 56 MiB received per rank for a balanced ring all-gather; the same
full-size gradient gives the same per-rank reduce-scatter volumes. This is a unit-sized calculation,
not a claim that every forward gathers the whole model or every optimizer state.6 [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[DERIVED][ANALYTICAL]

10.4. Measurement
Four habits anchor the architect:
1. Measure weight residency before choosing a split. bytes = params × bytes_per_
param lands first; it decides whether TP/PP (memory) or DP (replication) is even possible.

2. Measure the actual collective path. For the H100 example, 900 GB/s is the bidirectional peak
sum, not a directional or sustained rate. Compare measured collective completion times at the
deployed message shapes, rank placement and contention. A cluster’s bandwidth depends on
its links, rail count and topology; the fabric name alone does not determine the gap.
3. Measure the bubble and the step time. For PP, log the fraction of idle GPU time (bubble) vs
compute. For DP, time the gradient all-reduce as a fraction of step time — if it exceeds ~20%
[ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic], it caps scaling.
4. Measure communication overlap. The best systems overlap all-reduce with the next for­
ward/backward compute. Log the non-overlapped comm time — that is the true cost, not the
raw bytes.

10.5. Common Mistakes
• Splitting with DP when the model doesn’t fit. DP replicates weights; if 140 GB > 80 GB,
one DP replica doesn’t even fit one GPU. Reach for TP/PP first.
• Using TP without budgeting its exchanges. The same byte term is larger at 25 GB/s than
at 450 GB/s, but whether it binds depends on message shape, call count and exposed latency.
Tensor parallelism requires a communication path fast enough for its per-layer exchanges:

NVLink is one implementation, not a requirement of the algorithm.7 PCIe or another fabric is
viable only when measured collective cost leaves sufficient latency and throughput margin —
a measurement requirement, not a claim of universal performance for any fabric. The feasible
split also depends on each rank’s memory and supported kernels; a slower link can erase a
capacity gain even when the weights fit.
• Ignoring the pipeline bubble. PP’s idle stages waste real utilization; the bubble grows with
stage count. It is not free.
• Quoting peak interconnect spec as sustained. NVLink 900 GB/s is aggregate peak; real
all-reduce achieves a fraction. Budget headroom.
• Treating parallelism as an either/or. Real systems compose DP×TP×PP; the question is
which dimension binds, not which one to use.

10.6. Architecture Consequence
The parallelism strategy is forced by the binding constraint, and that constraint is usually
memory for large models:
• A model that exceeds one GPU’s memory must split weights → TP (within a node, over
the fabric that actually connects its GPUs — the requirement is measured collective latency
and throughput margin, not a vendor fabric name) or PP (across nodes, low comm). Which
one depends on whether the model fits a node: fits one node → TP among its GPUs; spans
nodes → PP across them, with TP inside each node.
• A workload with high throughput demand (like the canonical ~10 rps / 40 rps) → inde­
pendent inference replicas after the state fits each replica’s assigned devices. The canonical 70B
fits across an 8×H100 node through intra-host model parallelism; additional replicas address
fleet capacity. Gradient synchronization applies only to training or fine-tuning.
• MoE models (if chosen per Ch3) push toward EP, because the full expert set must be resident
(the active count sets compute per token, not residency) and EP shards the experts across
GPUs.
• The canonical answer: the book’s canonical host uses intra-host TP=8 to distribute the model
weights and serving state. It requires model parallelism within the host, but not cross-host

model parallelism. Eight ranks are the chosen baseline, not a minimum derived from weight

10.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• Optimal split for very large MoE or long-context models is workload- and interconnectdependent; the exact NVLink-vs-fabric crossover for a given model is unmeasured
[UNRESOLVED] — measure on the target cluster.
• How should EP sizing and all-to-all communication be budgeted for frontier MoE
models at extreme sparsity? 2026 MoE scaling has moved the specialist/EP frontier: Kimi
K3 activates just 16 of 896 routed experts per token (2.8T total / 104B active) via its Stable
LatentMoE [1P: arXiv 2607.24653]; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next routes 10+1 of 512 experts (125B total
/ 6B active) [1P: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next]. This combination — extreme sparsity (16/896
≈ 1.8% expert activation), the total expert residency that must be sharded if the deployment
keeps all experts resident in HBM (expert offloading or caching otherwise changes the capacity
calculus), and the all-to-all routing EP can require when experts are distributed across devices
(replicated or cached expert placements avoid it) — is why expert-parallel and fused crossexpert comm kernels (e.g. MoE expert parallelism with fused compute/communication, as
in DeepSeek’s DeepEP/TileLang infra) are increasingly central to serving large MoE fleets
[1P: arXiv 2606.19348]. For the architect this changes the serving calculus: a frontier MoE’s
activated footprint (Kimi 104B, Qwen 6B) can be dramatically smaller than its total size, so
the compute decision is made against active parameters — but the memory-bound EP decision
(how many experts must be resident) is made against total parameters when the full expert
set must occupy HBM even when only a fraction is routed per token. The activated-vs-total
residency crossover at current interconnect bandwidths is unmeasured [UNRESOLVED].
• Communication-overlap efficiency in real kernels is hard to predict from spec; sustained
all-reduce throughput is a [HYPOTHESIS] until measured on the target cluster.

187

Parallelism: Splitting Work Across Machines

• The right parallelism for mixed prefill/decode (P/D disaggregated) serving — where
the prefill pool and decode pool may want different splits — is an active research area and a
[HYPOTHESIS] for this book.

10.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Diagnosing Why the Grown 400B MoE Is Slow
An architect inherits a deployment where the internal Q&A model (from Ch1’s mini-case) has
been fine-tuned and grown to a 400B-parameter MoE. The team reports “parallelism is killing us
— everything is slow”: TPOT is measured at 80 ms against a 25 ms target [ILLUSTRATIVE]. The
architect applies this chapter’s lens. First, weight residency: a 400B model needs ~400e9 ×2 bytes
= 800 GB even before KV — that is ~10×H100 for weights alone (~11 once KV/workspace is included),

far beyond one node. The model necessarily spans nodes; the architect must choose an
inter-node decomposition — often PP and/or EP for MoE — while avoiding expensive cross-node
TP where possible (TP benefits from a tightly coupled NVLink-style interconnect; across a slower
network its per-layer all-reduce cost grows fast). Within each node, the MoE active weights are
small (~40B active of the 400B total [ASSUMPTION]) — active parameters set compute per token,
not residency — so the team uses EP to shard the total expert set (EP shards total residency, not the
active count) + TP inside the node, and checks the sharded total resident bytes per node against the
node’s 640 GB HBM. The architect measures the interconnect: profiling the inherited configuration
attributes 45 ms of the 80 ms TPOT to its cross-node per-layer all-reduce [ILLUSTRATIVE]; the
cross-node PP boundary runs over the cluster fabric (not NVLink), so they choose the stage count P
and micro-batch count m jointly to shrink the bubble (utilization u = m/(m+P−1); each stage also
carries its own activation memory, so per-stage memory cost bounds P from below), and they verify
the DP gradient-sync (if fine-tuning) stays under ~20% [ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic] of step time. The
result: a composed PP × EP × TP configuration whose binding constraints (memory across nodes
+ expert routing) are each addressed by the strategy that trades the right bandwidth. Moving the
cross-node decomposition from TP to PP cuts TPOT from 80 ms to 38 ms [ILLUSTRATIVE], with
~3 ms of the residual being PP stage-boundary and bubble cost under the chosen P and m, and the
team’s “parallelism is slow” becomes a precise, diagnosed, and fixed split.

chapter 11.
Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in
Flight

Serving is a small set of composable mechanisms — continuous batching, paged/blocked KV cache,
prefix caching, and prefill/decode disaggregation — that turn a static in-memory model into a live
multi-request system. The architecture choices that matter are which of these are adopted and how
they share the node’s HBM KV budget, because the latency SLO is met by the batch and cache
strategy rather than by the model alone.

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to answer the operational half of deployment: the model is
in memory and the requests are arriving at ~10 per second — how do we actually serve them without
violating our latency SLO? We will develop the serving mechanisms that turn a static model into
a live, multi-request system: how requests are batched, how KV cache memory is managed, how
repeated prefixes are reused, and when to split prefill from decode onto separate pools. After this
chapter, serving is not a black box — it is a sequence of explicit architectural choices, each with a
measurable consequence.

11.1. Concept
Serving is a small set of mechanisms, invented roughly in order:
1. Batching — running multiple requests through the model together to amortize the weight
reads. The key modern advance is continuous (iteration-level) batching introduced by

188

189

Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight

Orca (OSDI 2022): instead of waiting for an entire batch to finish, the scheduler admits and
evicts requests at every decoding step, filling the GPU’s idle slots as soon as they free up. [S1]
[1P]
2. PagedAttention / vLLM (SOSP 2023) — managing the KV cache in fixed-size blocks (like a
virtual-memory page table) so that different requests’ KV caches no longer need contiguous
memory, slashing fragmentation and letting the serving engine pack far more concurrent
requests. [S2][1P]
3. Prefix caching — recognizing that many requests share context (e.g. the same retrieved
documents), and caching the KV of the common prefix so a new request does not re-prefill it.
RadixAttention (SGLang) and Automatic Prefix Caching (vLLM APC) are the canonical
implementations. [S3][1P]
4. P/D disaggregation — splitting the prefill stage (compute-dominated at the canonical operat­
ing point) from the decode stage (bandwidth-dominated there) onto separate pools, because
they bottleneck on different resources. Pioneered by Splitwise (ISCA 2024) and DistServe
(OSDI 2024); Mooncake takes the KV-centric view, transferring KV caches from the pre­
fill pool to the decode pool (with CPU/DRAM/SSD offload) and reports up to 525% higher
throughput (6.25× the paper’s own baseline) in long-context simulation and 75% more
requests than the paper’s baseline method on a real Kimi workload. [S4][1P]
These mechanisms compose: continuous batching is the baseline, PagedAttention makes it
memory-efficient, prefix caching makes it cheaper, and P/D disaggregation can improve goodput at
scale when measured phase interference and KV-transfer cost justify it.
Source keys [S1]–[S6]. The bracketed keys used throughout this book (and in the evidence
taxonomy of the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility chapter) point to the primary sources below.
Each is a [1P] first-party or peer-reviewed source; the book’s derived numbers cite the key plus a
[DERIVED] tag.
• [S1] Orca — Yu et al., “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative
Models,” OSDI 2022. Continuous (iteration-level) batching.
• [S2] PagedAttention / vLLM — Kwon et al., “Efficient Memory Management for Large
Language Model Serving with PagedAttention,” SOSP 2023. Block-based KV cache.
• [S3] Prefix caching — “Fast Inference from Transformers via Radix Attention” (SGLang, 2023)
and vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching (APC). Caching shared-prefix KV.
• [S4] P/D disaggregation — “Splitwise: Efficient Generative LLM Inference Using Phase
Splitting” (ISCA 2024), “DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized
Large Language Model Serving” (OSDI 2024), and Mooncake (KV-centric disaggregation, 2024).
• [S5] DFlash — Chen et al., “DFlash: Block Diffusion for Flash Speculative Decoding,” ICML
2026 (PMLR v306; arXiv:2602.06036). Speculative-decoding system reporting >6× lossless

Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight

190

acceleration over autoregressive decoding (up to 6.1× on Qwen3-8B) and up to 2.5× faster than
the prior state of the art, EAGLE-3.
• [S6] vLLM FP8-KV blog — The State of FP8 KV-Cache and Attention Quantization in vLLM,
vLLM blog, 2026-04-22 (retrieved 2026-11-15). The post’s ‘54%’ figure is a decode inter-tokenlatency (ITL) slope, a LATENCY metric, not a memory/residency ratio. Any reference to it
(Chapters 1, 3, 6, 7, 15, 22, Appendix A and the glossary) is a latency reference only. The KV
memory footprint this book uses is the raw tensor byte-halving of ~1.31 MB/token (exactly
50% of FP16) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]; any block-allocation/metadata overhead is NOT
vendor-measured here and must be filled by a deployment benchmark.

11.2. Mental Model
Serving is managing three precious resources against a stream of arrivals: GPU compute
(FLOPs — the binding resource for prefill at the canonical operating point), GPU memory bandwidth
(HBM — the binding resource for decode at the canonical operating point), and GPU memory capacity
(HBM bytes, bound by KV cache). Both bindings are regime statements, not laws (Ch 2): they depend
on model architecture, batch size, precision, kernels and hardware, and §3 re-derives them at the
canonical operating point. Each mechanism trades one of these:
• Batching improves compute and bandwidth utilization by amortizing the fixed per-step weight
reads across more requests.
• PagedAttention reduces external fragmentation and over-reservation, improving effective
KV capacity; block-level internal fragmentation and metadata overhead remain.
• Prefix caching trades cache memory for reduced prefill compute and, when prefixes are
shared, reduced duplicate KV residency; it can also reduce effective capacity if hit rate is low.
• P/D disaggregation lets the prefill pool run at high compute utilization and the decode pool
at high bandwidth utilization simultaneously, instead of one pool being starved.
The mental model is a resource budget: a request arrives, consumes some FLOPs (prefill), some
bandwidth (decode), and some memory (its KV cache) for its lifetime. Serving architecture is about
sizing and scheduling those three budgets so the SLO holds across the burst.

11.3. Worked Example

191

Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight

11.3.1. The Canonical Workload in a Serving System
Recall the canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average, ~40 rps peak;
each request carries ~9,200 input tokens and ~300 output tokens; TTFT budget 1.2 s, TPOT ~25
ms/token. [ASSUMPTION]
11.3.2. Discrete Batching Wastes the GPU
Naive discrete (static) batching accumulates requests until a batch fills, then runs them to comple­
tion, then starts the next batch. Problems compound at this workload’s 9.2K-input shape:
• Requests arrive in bursts (recall the ~40 rps peak). Discrete batching forces early-arriving
requests to wait for the batch to fill, inflating TTFT toward the 2 s SLO breach (budget 1.2 s,
p95 ≤ 2 s).
• The batch is locked until its slowest member finishes (the batch runs to completion), so a
short 100-token output tails behind the longest while the GPU finishes the whole batch — idle
bubbles at the end of every batch.
• Batch boundaries create periods where the GPU drains (no work) then floods — utilization is
spiky around the mean. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
11.3.3. Continuous Batching Fills the Bubbles
Continuous batching (Orca [S1][1P]) eliminates the batch boundary: at every decode step the
scheduler accepts any new prefill-ready request and evicts any finished one, so decode slots can be
kept busier by refilling freed slots when requests are available; idle can still occur from insufficient
arrivals, KV capacity, prefill, or scheduling policy. In the canonical stream, a 300-token decode at ~25
ms/token occupies a slot for ~7.5 s; while a long decode runs, the freed decode slots and memorybandwidth capacity are continuously refilled by new short requests, amortizing the per-step weight
reads. The utilization gain is the difference between spiky discrete batches and a continuously-fed
pipeline. Rather than stipulate a single percent, the mechanism shifts the bottleneck from batchboundary idle time toward GPU resources when arrivals and KV capacity permit — scheduler policy,
KV capacity and arrival rate can still bind. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
11.3.4. PagedAttention: Killing the Fragmentation Tax
In re-packaged (naive) serving, each request’s KV cache for 9.2K input is ~24.1 GB (FP16, ~2.62
MB/token × 9,200, initial KV) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. If served contiguously, variable-length
completions leave fragmented, unusable holes — exactly like a fragmented heap. PagedAtten­
tion/vLLM [S2][1P] allocates KV in fixed-size blocks mapped through a per-request block table
and evicted like page frames; blocks are shared across requests only when the engine implements
copy-on-write or prefix reuse, so the ~24.1 GB per request is packed densely and more concurrent

requests fit in the same 640 GB node [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. The win is more concurrency
under the same SLO, not faster single-request math.
11.3.5. Prefix Caching: Don’t Re-Prefill the Same Documents
The RAG request’s 8K retrieved-context tokens are largely shared across queries (same documents;
the book’s K = 1,000). Without caching, every request re-runs the ~1.12 PFLOP prefill for those 8K
tokens (2 × 70 × 10⁹ × 8,000 ≈ 1.12 PFLOP, since 1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200; the full 9.2K canonical input
is ~1.29 PFLOP) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. RadixAttention / APC [S3][1P] caches the KV of
common prefixes, so a new request reuses the shared-document KV and prefills only the unique query
tail — cutting the dominant prefill FLOPs and TTFT for repeated-context traffic [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[DERIVED]. Layout caveat: this reuse requires the shared documents to sit at a fixed prefix position
in the prompt (e.g. system prompt → retrieved documents → unique query tail). If the unique query
precedes the documents, the causal K/V of the document span differs per query and no prefix is
reusable — the savings above assume the documents-then-query layout, which the architect must
verify in the actual prompt template.
Prefix reuse is also only one of the state-preservation requirements a serving system must meet:
preemption, speculative rollback, and adaptive-depth execution all constrain what a cache may evict
or reuse — see the serving qualification in §6.
11.3.6. When to Disaggregate: Prefill and Decode Want Different Pools
Recall from Ch2/Ch6, at the canonical operating point (9.2K/300, FP16, the stated batch on 8×H100),
the two phases sit in different regimes: prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound
— regime statements, not laws (Ch 2). Prefill needs ~1.29 PFLOP, or ~1.19 PFLOPS over the ~1.08 s
prefill budget, against a 0.989 PFLOPS peak on a single H100; under the canonical 8×H100 TP=8 host
the same prefill is ~0.16 PFLOP per GPU and takes ~0.47 s at 35% MFU (Ch 12), so the single-device
figure describes a one-GPU deployment, not the canonical host. Decode’s arithmetic intensity is B
FLOP/byte for FP16 weights: ~1.0 at batch 1 and ~17.5 at the canonical ~17.5-concurrent operating
point (Ch 4 §6 / Ch 7 / Ch 17; 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB = KV budget ÷ per-request KV). Both are far below
the H100 ridge of ~295 FLOP/byte, so bandwidth binds: the whole-model weight-read rate is ~5.6
TB/s if served by one device, 3.35 TB/s per GPU, and ~0.70 TB/s per GPU when sharded across the
canonical 8×H100 host (Ch 6). [1P][DERIVED] Serving both from one pool forces a compromise:
batch for prefill and it slows decode; optimize for decode and prefill starves. P/D disaggregation
(Splitwise/DistServe/Mooncake [S4][1P]) runs prefill nodes at high FLOP-utilization and decode
nodes at high bandwidth-utilization, transferring KV across via the fabric (Fig 11.3 shows the twopool topology and what moves between them). Mooncake’s reported up to 525% higher long-context
throughput (6.25× the paper’s own baseline, from its long-context simulation results) and +75%
request count (vs the paper’s baseline method on a real Kimi workload) are the quantitative anchor
[S4][1P] — paper-specific scope, not a portable serving figure. Before the canonical 10 rps aggregate

Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight

194

is scaled to a fleet (per-host ≈1.3–2 req/s), this disaggregation is premature; it pays off when measured
prefill/decode interference binds — evaluate it against measured phase conflict, not topology alone
(e.g. when the workload outgrows a node).
The state crossing between prefill and decode pools is a different communication object from
a TP activation reduction. Its endpoints, ownership, block layout, and transfer frequency must be
stated independently. A KV-transfer path may use point-to-point or specialized transfer facilities
rather than a group collective. The service budget includes transfer and orchestration on the request’s
critical path; it does not count a whole KV cache again on every ordinary decode step. Ch 9 provides
the directional byte convention; this chapter determines when moving ownership is worthwhile.

11.4. Measurement
Good serving telemetry answers “are we meeting the SLO while keeping the GPU busy?”:
1. Measure goodput, not raw throughput — tokens/s that arrive before their SLO deadline
(Ch6). Continuous batching is only a win if it raises goodput.

195

Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight

2. Measure KV utilization — live/allocated KV blocks ÷ total KV block capacity (weights,
activations, and workspace reported separately). PagedAttention raises effective KV packing
(block utilization); prefix caching instead dedupes shared prefixes (prefix-hit rate) — track the
two separately.
3. Measure prefill-vs-decode utilization separately — a FLOP-bound prefill core and a
bandwidth-bound decode core running on one pool tells us when to disaggregate.
4. Measure the scheduler’s real occupancy — idle decode slots, queue wait, and the tail of
TTFT under load, not the average.
5. Record the model revision and the execution path in use — so a fallback is visible in
telemetry.

11.5. Common Mistakes
• Assuming bigger batches always help. Bigger discrete batches raise raw tokens/s but push
TTFT past the SLO, zeroing goodput (Ch6). Continuous batching exists precisely to uncouple
batch size from wait.
• Serving KV contiguous and watching fragmentation. PagedAttention removes the frag­
mentation tax; skipping it wastes memory under concurrency.
• Re-prefilling shared context. Without prefix caching, repeated RAG documents are recom­
puted per request — one of the most wasteful failures for this workload.
• Choosing P/D disaggregation too early. Splitting pools adds fabric + orchestration; for a
single host it is overhead without the resource conflict that motivates it.
• Believing speculative decoding (DFlash reports >6× lossless acceleration, up to 2.5×
faster than EAGLE-3 [S5][1P]) is a serving baseline. These are paper-reported results
under the paper’s evaluation setup, not portable serving-speed figures. Speculative decoding
is an optimization for bandwidth-bound decode, not a requirement, and must be validated on
the workload.

11.6. Architecture Consequence
The serving mechanisms dictate the deployment choices:
• Baseline (canonical single-host): continuous batching (vLLM/Orca) is near-mandatory to
hold TTFT under the SLO (1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s) at the replica’s admitted load (≈1.3–2 req/s per
Ch 14 Step 3); at the canonical 10 rps average the host class must be replicated ~5-6x (Ch
12/17); PagedAttention packs the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV densely (fixed-size pages, minimal

Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight

196

fragmentation) so more concurrent requests fit in the 640 GB node; prefix caching is the
highest-leverage optimization because the workload is repeated-context RAG. This matches
the memory and compute conclusions of Ch4/Ch7 for the ~10 rps average baseline; at the ~40
rps peak the KV budget forces replication, which Chapter 17 sizes. [S1][S2][S3][1P]
• Scaling up: those three carry the workload far before disaggregation is justified. FP8 KV (raw
tensor byte-halving = 1.31 MB/token, exactly 50% of FP16) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] and
KV offloading are memory levers available without restructuring.
• Beyond a node: when prefill FLOPs and decode bandwidth fight on one pool, P/D disaggrega­
tion (Splitwise/DistServe/Mooncake) is the architecture of choice, with Mooncake’s KV-transfer
engine moving caches between pools. [S4][1P]
Note 11.3-1 (Fig 11.3) — transfer-time derivation, both links. The ~35 GB is ≈13.3K tokens ×
2.62 MB/token (§9.8; 13.3K = 35 GB ÷ 2.62 MB, the count ch 9 quotes). (A) within-NVLink-domain,
on-node: at NVLink’s 450 GB/s per direction (§9.2) that transfer is 35 ÷ 450 ≈ 0.08 s. That is the
whole 35 GB over one unsharded link — a conservative bound; the panel’s 4-way shard would be 35
÷ (4 × 450) ≈ 0.02 s. The transfer is still small against the ~1.08 s canonical 9.2K prefill budget (the
13.3K prefill would be ~1.86 PFLOP, longer still), so the inequality holds. (B) cross-host, over the
fabric: at 40 GB/s the same transfer is 35 ÷ 40 ≈ 0.9 s, which can erase the benefit — the transfer cost
is the term that decides whether P/D disaggregation pays. The 1.4 TB/s caveat is the aggregate check
(35 GB/request × 40 req/s against the shared fabric), not a per-request time; the per-request times
above assume the link is not shared. Per case: (A) 4 decode GPUs × 450 GB/s = 1.8 TB/s aggregate
ingress absorbs the 1.4 TB/s (~78% — feasible but tight); (B) the 40 GB/s NIC cannot (≈35× over) —
so the transfer link, not topology alone, decides whether P/D disaggregation pays. Canonical 9.2K
request: 24.1 GB → 24.1 ÷ 450 ≈ 0.054 s on NVLink, 24.1 × 40 rps ≈ 0.96 TB/s aggregate; the 0.08 s
and 1.4 TB/s figures above are the §9.8 13.3K-context scenario. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
11.6.1. The Mechanisms, Not the Product Catalog
The mechanisms above are what matter; the engines are just implementations of them. This compar­
ison is organized by architectural capability so it transfers across specific products and versions. It is
explicitly time-sensitive — capabilities, supported models, and features change fast, and these rows
must be re-verified against each engine’s current first-party documentation before any deployment
decision. The table is a map of which mechanism to look for, not a ranking.

197

Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight

figure 11.2: Serving is four separable concerns, not a stack (they interact — batching pressure feeds
KV residency — but each is addressable in any order) (request scheduling, state management, reuse,
resource specialization). A concrete serving design that chooses one mechanism per concern: request
scheduling = continuous (Orca-style) batching; state management = PagedAttention (fixed-size
KV pages); reuse = prefix caching of shared context; resource specialization = P/D disaggregation
(separate prefill and decode pools). The four are separable dials — mechanisms can be combined in
principle, subject to implementation support and resource interactions (e.g. prefix caching under
aggressive continuous batching: cached prefixes and the live batch’s pages draw on the same 640
GB KV pool, so reuse needs headroom) — and the canonical baseline uses the first three; resource
specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (dashed border = not in the canonical
baseline; see “When to Disaggregate”, §11.3). [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]
The design lever is what each concern trades: request scheduling exchanges latency for utilization,
state management exchanges memory capacity for concurrency, reuse avoids re-prefill FLOPs, and
resource specialization matches two compute/memory regimes to two pools.

The columns read as knobs on a common set of mechanisms, not as “which engine is best.” An
engine’s real value is which mechanisms it implements well for the deployed workload’s shape — e.g. a
repeated-context RAG workload cares most about the prefix-caching row (RadixAttention in SGLang
is a strong implementation), while a latency-critical single-stream deployment might care more about
the scheduler and structured-generation rows. Never conclude “X is the go-to engine” — that is
workload-independent and will be wrong. The only defensible statement is workload-specific: for
this request shape, this precision, and this hardware, engine Y implements the mechanism Z we need;
benchmark it against the alternative (Ch. 14).
11.6.2. What the capability table does not promise
A recognized quantization name is not an end-to-end support claim. A deployment needs
a chain of compatible choices: checkpoint schema, model graph, tensor layout, operator coverage,
runtime dependencies, and device instructions. “Supports four-bit weights” does not establish support
for a model’s grouped expert GEMMs, attention variant, modal branches, or KV format. A backend
may accept a checkpoint and select a different arithmetic path, reject a particular shape, or need
a temporary higher-precision representation; the serialized tensor layout and the kernel-required
runtime layout are different objects. A missing compatible path is a deployment failure, not a
guaranteed fallback. [1P][DERIVED] Implementation-specific examples are dated separately.
The deployment record therefore includes the exact model and engine revision, device architec­
ture, driver/toolkit and library versions, quantized tensor inventory, selected kernels, and fallback
logs. It also records cold-load peak and steady HBM separately. This record determines whether the
configuration can be reproduced; a single support-table checkmark does not. Allocator or scheduling
limits then determine how much of the remaining memory can become usable KV capacity without
violating latency targets. Smaller weights do not justify increasing admitted concurrency until the
new operating point is measured. [DERIVED]
A serving feature belongs to an algorithm path. The capability table is a map of mechanisms,
not a guarantee that every supported model can combine every row. Diffusion language models
make this qualification especially important. A paged allocator can manage buffers without proving
that their contents remain valid across refinement. A prefix-cache key must describe finalized
token content and compatible state, not an unresolved mask canvas. Grammar constraints, quantized
loading, graph capture, and distributed parallelism also depend on the selected model implementation
and sampler. [DERIVED]
Requests can require different numbers of refinement rounds. A lockstep batch waits for its
slowest active member unless the scheduler can preserve unfinished state and admit or complete
requests independently. The SGLang diffusion scheduler inspected on 2026-10-28 (revision a1966e1)
implements a first-done-first-out path that retains partial block state.1 This is explicit iteration-aware

The complete backend path. A serving engine needs more than a visible accelerator. It needs

kernel set, runtime and driver. Distributed execution adds a collective backend and a supported
transport. Fig 11.4 separates these dependencies from the final qualification decision. Its columns are

11.6.3. Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability
Before choosing a serving engine, verify that it supports the model’s state requirements — a point
that becomes critical for the model classes below. Model support is not a complete serving capability.
A hybrid model (a transformer interleaved with a recurrent/state-space block) can require both
paged history and bounded recurrent state. A looped-depth model (one that re-runs a block stack for
multiple iterations per token) can require iteration-specific caches. Prefix reuse, preemption, and
speculative rollback must preserve the state that the next execution actually consumes. An early-exit
interface (a trained head that lets a token leave before the final layer) also needs a runtime path that
avoids the skipped work, rather than selecting logits after all work has already run. A capability
record can therefore identify the exact model revision, engine revision, state representation, cache
policy, precision, and supported execution paths; kernel or module speedups remain separate from
end-to-end goodput at the service SLO. [DERIVED]
Adaptive depth (per-token early exit — the same early-exit interface above) changes the sched­
uler’s unit of work. Tokens that exit at different iterations can leave an initially uniform batch with
different amounts of remaining computation. A single request can contain a mix of exit depths, so its
remaining computation differs from that of other requests in the batch. A runtime may compact active
requests or group them by depth, but compaction, cache indexing, and synchronization consume
resources. Padding every request to the deepest active iteration can preserve batching convenience
while eliminating the hoped-for arithmetic saving. These are alternative implementation choices,
not measured features. [DERIVED]
Latency evaluation must retain the depth distribution. Average passes per token does not deter­
mine p95 token latency: difficult tokens, long histories, and queueing can coincide. A comparison
therefore fixes the prompt population, output length, quality criterion, and SLO, then records actual
pass counts, state allocation, and elapsed time by phase. When prefill and decode use different cache
policies, one aggregate cache-reduction factor hides the capacity bottleneck. [DERIVED]
The economic denominator is completed, quality-compliant work within the service target. A
reduced core-work budget is useful only if it increases that useful output or lowers the resources
required to produce it. Routing a difficult request to more depth can be rational even when its
per-token cost rises. Conversely, premature exits that can require retries can raise task cost despite
shorter first attempts. A training-time self-improvement loop and an inference-time depth loop
are different mechanisms; sharing the word “iteration” assigns no inference-time saving to either.
[DERIVED]
A compact qualification record can contain seven gates:
1. The model class’s runtime requirements are met (paged history and bounded recurrent state
for a hybrid model, iteration-specific caches for a looped-depth model, a real early-exit path),
and the exact device, checkpoint, tokenizer, engine, and dependency identities are fixed.
2. Each rank fits weights, KV, workspace, and temporary conversion state.
3. Required operators, weight/activation/KV formats, and attention layouts execute correctly.

Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight

204

4. Scheduling, cache reuse, graph behavior, and any fallback are observable.
5. Required collectives work on the deployed topology and message sizes.
6. Long-context quality, concurrent-request isolation, and failure recovery pass.
7. Measured tail latency and quality-qualified goodput satisfy the workload contract.
A failure closes the proposed configuration. A different configuration can be evaluated, but a
reduced context, changed quality threshold, or disabled feature is a changed deployment — not an
unnoticed repair to the original result.
The four serving concerns — request scheduling, state management, reuse, and resource spe­
cialization — hold for any workload, not only autoregressive text. The mechanisms that implement
them do not transfer automatically: a video or diffusion service raises the same four concerns with
different mechanisms. The serving side is treated in the appendix, “Beyond autoregressive text: video
and diffusion serving”; Ch 14 keeps the video measurement protocol.

11.7. What We Still Don’t Know
As of 2026-08, several questions remain open, each flagged [HYPOTHESIS] or
[UNRESOLVED] (measure on the target cluster):
• Portable end-to-end goodput across real enterprise RAG — Mooncake’s up to 525% higher
throughput (6.25× the paper’s own baseline) and 75% more requests [S4][1P], and DFlash’s
>6× [S5][1P], are strong anchors but are workload-specific; general rules remain an open
hypothesis [HYPOTHESIS].
• Prefix-cache hit rates in mixed traffic — the real reduction in prefill FLOPs from RadixAt­
tention/APC for a given document-distribution remains a hypothesis [HYPOTHESIS].
• KV-transfer cost at scale — Mooncake’s engine moves KV to CPU/DRAM/SSD [S4]
[1P], but the exact latency/bandwidth crossover where disaggregation wins is unmeasured
[UNRESOLVED] — measure on the target cluster.

11.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Which Serving Mechanism to Reach For
This is an illustrative scenario, not a measured result. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] An architect
examines one 8×H100 replica in the canonical internal Q&A service, whose aggregate service peak
is 40 rps. Suppose that replica’s assigned load produces p95 TTFT of 2.2 s against a 2 s SLO. The
first checks are whether continuous batching and PagedAttention are active: the baseline KV at
the request’s final 9.5K-token context (9.2K input + 300 output) is about 24.9 GB per request (initial
9.2K input KV is ~24.1 GB, §3), so allocation behavior matters. Repeated RAG documents then make
prefix caching a candidate because valid shared-prefix KV can avoid repeated prefill work. Suppose a
controlled test at the same assigned load and request mix brings p95 TTFT below 1.8 s. That assumed
result would support the cache change for this replica; it would not establish service capacity at 40

205

Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight

rps. P/D disaggregation and speculative decoding remain separate candidates, not required steps in
this diagnosis.
Scope note: with the baseline mean service-time assumption of 8.6 s, the aggregate 40 rps peak
implies approximately 344 in-flight requests. The baseline unshared-KV capacity quotient is about
17.5 complete requests per host, conservatively floored to 17 integer slots. [canonical scenario]
[DERIVED] That baseline requires multiple replicas; a per-request TTFT result does not size the fleet.
Any capacity credit for sharing must follow measured prefix-cache occupancy, hit rates, service time,
and tail latency under the admitted workload. Chapter 17 applies joint residency and throughput
constraints, headroom, and failure reserve. The replica’s latency result and the service’s capacity
decision remain distinct.

11.9. Appendix — Beyond autoregressive text: video and diffusion serving
11.9.1. The serving concerns transfer; the text mechanisms do not transfer automatically
A video service still schedules requests, manages live state, reuses valid work, and chooses resourcespecialized pools. The mechanisms implementing those concerns differ. The inspected full-clip
Wan path does not emit a completed next frame at each denoising step.4 A step boundary can be a
scheduling or cancellation point if the runtime exposes it, but it is not automatically a text continuousbatching boundary. Jobs with different shapes, samplers, guidance branches, and timestep sched­
ules may be difficult or wasteful to batch together. [1P][FACT] model execution; [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[HYPOTHESIS] scheduling consequence.
A useful admission record therefore includes the checkpoint revision, task type, exact height
and width, frame count, audio/reference inputs, schedule, guidance method, precision, and parallel
layout. Shape-aware buckets limit padding and kernel recompilation. A deadline-aware dispatcher
can separate interactive previews from full-quality completion. It must include queue age and avoid
starving long jobs. A low-step preview is a separate quality contract unless the implementation
proves that its state can continue into the final recipe. A preview image, first decoded frame, and
finalized downloadable clip are three different completion events.
Per-request memory limits follow measured peaks for each admitted configuration. The largest
VAE reconstruction, full-clip attention workspace, compiler workspace, and overlapping transfers
can bind even when the weight set fits. Offload and quantization change those peaks only where
the actual kernels support the chosen representation. A quantized checkpoint file alone does not
establish faster execution, adequate reconstruction quality, or a supported attention backend. [1P]
[FACT] documented offload paths; [ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS] deployment consequences.
Parallelism also changes the cost of a step. Sequence or context parallelism partitions video

part IV.
The Architecture

207

chapter 12.
Designing the AI System: From Constraints to
Candidates

Designing an AI system is constraint-driven generation, not menu-picking: the architect extracts
the hard constraints from a characterized workload — the three gates this chapter fixes: memory fit,
throughput at the SLO, and quality — then synthesizes candidate architectures that must clear them.
The payoff is a bounded set of two to three candidates, each designed to probe a different aspect of
the constraint set — single-host throughput, phase-split throughput, or quality-vs-size (memory fit is
screened for all three) — which the measuring chapters then adjudicate.

The Architect’s Question
Designing an AI system means producing candidate architectures from the substrate — memory,
compute, communication, and parallelism — rather than selecting a canned stack. This chapter works
through a synthesis method: given a characterized workload from the six-dimension framework
(Ch. 4), generate two or three candidate architectures that each satisfy the hard constraints — the
three gates fixed here: memory fit, throughput at the SLO, and quality — then carry them forward
for evaluation in Chs. 14–16. The core thesis is that design is constraint-driven generation, not
menu-picking. This distinguishes our approach from the abstract meta-method presented in Ch. 22,
which operates at a level of generality that does not instantiate against concrete substrate constraints.
In the language of the book’s spine — the decision loop constrain → synthesize → measure → decide
→ refine — this chapter is the synthesize step: we turn a constraint-characterized workload into a
bounded set of candidate architectures that then enter the measure/decide stages in Chs. 14–16.

208

209

Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates

12.1. Concept
The architect’s first step is to reverse-engineer the workload into its constituent constraints. From
the six dimensions — quality requirements, traffic profile, token profile, latency budget, economic
ceiling, and operational constraints — we extract the three hard constraints — the three gates used
throughout this chapter — that any candidate must satisfy: (1) memory fit — the weight memory
plus the KV cache footprint must fit the target host’s aggregate memory; (2) throughput at the
SLO — sustained prefill and decode tokens-per-second, delivered within the latency budget (prefill +
decode), must meet the workload’s demand; and (3) quality — answer quality on the true evaluation
set must meet the quality requirement. Any architecture that violates any one of these is eliminated
before evaluation — candidates that fail a gate are not finalists (a finalist is a candidate advanced to
evaluation; a conditional finalist is one advanced with its gate still open): they return to synthesis
or are carried forward only as labeled sensitivity cases. A layout whose memory fits but whose
throughput falls short of demand — as a single host falls against the canonical ~92K input tokens/s — is
not carried forward as-is; it returns to synthesis for a larger layout or is dropped, and a smaller-model
candidate whose quality is unmeasured is gated, not promoted. (The economic ceiling is recorded
but is not one of the three gates; §12.8 states its consequence at fleet scale.) This constraint-first
posture inverts the typical practice of browsing vendor offerings and then hoping they fit; instead, we
generate architectures that we know can physically reside and operate within the specified substrate.

12.2. Mental Model
The substrate is a set of bounded resources, and the architecture design problem is essentially a
packing exercise. The resources are: GPU memory (weight residency + KV cache), compute (prefill
throughput — prefill is compute-bound, Ch 11, scoped to the canonical architecture × batch ×
precision × kernel operating point), memory bandwidth (decode throughput — decode is bandwidthbound, scoped to the canonical architecture × batch × precision × kernel operating point), inter-GPU
communication volume (for parallelism schemes), and the latency budget split between prefill and
decode. A candidate architecture is a valid packing of the workload’s weight memory and KV cache
into the available GPU memory, paired with a parallelism and caching strategy that delivers the
required tokens-per-second throughput within the latency budget. The architect alternates between
squeezing the residency footprint (e.g., via KV quantization or precision reduction) and adjusting the
parallelism layout (e.g., tensor vs. data vs. pipeline, TP/DP/PP) until all three hard constraints are
simultaneously satisfiable. This mental model — substrate as packing problem — is what enables
systematic candidate generation rather than ad hoc selection.

Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates

210

12.3. Worked Example
We generate three candidate architectures for the canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload: ~10
requests/s average, peak 40 rps, 70B FP16 model, 9.2K token input (1,200 prompt + 8K retrieved
context), 300-token output. The canonical weight memory is 140 GB (70B × 2 bytes FP16). The KV
cache for 9.2K context at FP16 precision ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2)) is approximately
24 GB (2 × num_layers × hidden_dim × 9,200 × 2 bytes per FP16 element), giving a total residency
of 164 GB. A single 8×H100 host provides 640 GB aggregate memory (8 ×80 GB), leaving ample
headroom. Each candidate satisfies the three gates to a different degree.
Candidate (a): single 8×H100 host with prefix caching (Ch. 11). This is the per-requestlatency baseline — the single 8×H100 host that the early book (Ch 2, 4, 7, 8) establishes as meeting one
request’s latency SLO. It is not a capacity baseline: a lone host cannot carry the arrival rate (~6 hosts
are needed for the canonical average, and ~21 at peak — see Ch 11, 13, 17), so its throughput-gate
failure below is expected and is not a reason to dismiss the host class itself. All 70B weights and the full
24 GB KV cache reside on the 8-GPU host. Prefix caching from Ch. 11 amortizes prefill computation
for shared prefixes (attention and MLP work) over repeated requests with the same prompt prefix,
reducing effective prefill FLOPs by ~30% at 10 rps average and ~50% at peak 40 rps when many
requests share common document roots. (That 30–50% amortization range is a reasoned expectation,
not a measured figure — it rests on the untested premise about traffic overlap flagged in §12.7, so it
is labeled [HYPOTHESIS] and should be confirmed by measuring the actual prefix-hit rate before
it is relied on.) The 8×H100 host fits the full 164 GB residency easily, but on throughput we must be
honest with the Chapter 8 arithmetic: a single 8×H100 host sustains only ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s at
the idealized 35%-MFU operating point under TP=8: each GPU carries ~19,780 tok/s of the shared
token stream (989 TFLOP/s × 35% ÷ 17.5 GFLOP/token per GPU), so the host aggregate is the same
~19,800 — not 8× a per-GPU rate (Ch. 8 scope note); the ~2,472 figure is one GPU’s share of the 70B’s
full-model FLOPs, i.e. a full-model-equivalent rate, never a per-GPU capability. That is far below the
~92K input tokens/s the workload needs on average. Even if prefix caching (~30% at average load)
lifts effective prefill throughput toward ~28K tokens/s [HYPOTHESIS], that is still well below 92K,
so a single host fails the throughput gate too — prefill is compute-bound at this operating point, and
meeting it is exactly the scaling problem Chapters 15–17 take up. Memory fit and throughput fit are
different gates: the memory gate passes with one host; the throughput gate does not. Memory fit:
140 GB weights + 24 GB KV = 164 GB < 640 GB aggregate ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table
4-2)). Throughput at the SLO: per-request prefill + decode are expected to stay within the latency
budget at the admitted load thanks to prefix caching and the high bandwidth of 8×H100 — this is the
SLO gate that Ch 14 must close — but the sustained rate fails at one host, as shown above — the gate
closes only when the host class is replicated to ~5 hosts on the average prefill screen (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈
4.65 → 5), ~6 on the average KV/service-time screen (10 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 5.06 → 6), and ~21 at peak (40 ×
8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 20.2 → 21) (Chs. 15–17). Quality: the 70B is the workload’s quality reference, so candidate
(a) inherits the reference quality by definition rather than by measurement — the gate is satisfied

211

Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates

relative to the reference, and the absolute requirement still needs the Ch 14 capability screen on the
true evaluation set. Economics (recorded, not one of the three gates — §12.8): one host purchase, one
software license tier.
Candidate (b): P/D-disaggregated two-pool.
We keep the full 70B model in both pools and split by phase — which is what prefill/decode (P/D)
disaggregation actually means (Chapter 11): a compute-bound prefill pool and a bandwidth-bound
decode pool, each holding the complete 140 GB weights plus the in-flight KV, with the KV cache (K/V
tensors) handed between them (Splitwise / DistServe / Mooncake [S4][1P]). Each pool therefore needs
its own 8×H100 host (residency = 140 GB weights plus the pool’s in-flight KV population — at the
canonical per-host KV budget (640 − 140 weights − ~64 runtime ≈ 436 GB, Ch 7/17), 140 GB weights +
436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB — exactly the pool, zero headroom; co-residency beyond the
canonical KV budget requires reducing the KV allocation or adding memory; one request’s 24 GB is
not the pool’s population). The win is that prefill and decode no longer fight over the same host’s
resources: the prefill pool runs compute-bound at the same 35% MFU basis as (a) on the 9.2K input,
the decode pool runs bandwidth-saturated on the 300 output tokens, and KV crosses between them.
Crucially, P/D disaggregation does not raise the per-host prefill ceiling (it may raise achieved prefill
by removing interference): one 8×H100 prefill host still sustains only ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s (the
same Chapter 8 arithmetic as Candidate (a)), far short of the ~92K input tokens/s the workload needs
on average. So Candidate (b) passes the memory gate per pool but still fails the throughput gate at a
single prefill host — its real advantage is that the prefill pool can be scaled independently of the
decode pool, so meeting the ~92K demand means scaling the prefill pool to ~5 hosts (92K ÷ 19.8K
≈ 4.65) plus the decode pool, rather than forcing every host to serve both phases. Disaggregation
buys the ability to scale each phase separately, not the throughput itself. Economics: two hosts and
added fabric as a baseline, more as each pool scales; it is the right architecture at scale, not a two-host
answer to the canonical case.
Candidate (c): KV-quantized smaller host.
We downgrade to a 7B-class model (7B × 2 bytes = 14 GB weights) with KV cache quantized to 4-bit.
The per-token KV depends on the model’s own attention shape (layers × KV-heads × head dim ×
bytes, Chapter 7), NOT the 70B’s constant: a typical 32-layer, 4096-hidden, full-MHA 7B carries ~0.52
MB/token FP16, so ~0.13 MB/token at 4-bit → ~1.2 GB for the 9.2K context (vs the ~6 GB that comes
from naively reusing the 70B’s 2.62 MB/token ÷ 4). Total residency: 14 GB + ~1.2 GB ≈ ~15 GB, which
fits on a single H100 (80 GB) with large headroom. The trade-off is a quality question, and here we
must be careful not to assert an architectural theorem where one does not exist. Whether a 7B-class
model can match the 70B model’s answer quality on this workload is not derivable from parameter
count — a newer or task-specialized 7B can beat an older or general 70B on some tasks. It is an
empirical question answered only by running the actual evaluation set. The correct architectural
lesson is the quality gate: the smaller candidate must pass the capability/quality gate on the true
evaluation set; if it fails there, no amount of infrastructure optimization fixes that failure. So candidate

Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates

212

(c) is flagged for measurement against the quality gate, not dismissed by parameter counting. The
4-bit KV cache is a memory optimization, not a quality one; aggressive KV quantization can add its
own quality penalty that must also be validated on the target workload. Throughput is genuinely
much higher on the smaller model — a 7B prefill costs only ~14 GFLOP/token, so a single card sustains
~24,700 prefill tokens/s (~24,725 from the stated inputs: 989 TFLOP/s × 35% MFU ÷ 14 GFLOP/token;
vs ~19,780 per GPU for the 70B under TP=8, Chapter 8) — but that throughput advantage is only
useful if the quality gate is first satisfied. The candidate is therefore provisional: its fate depends
on the measured quality gate, which Chapter 14 (the capability screen) administers. This candidate
illustrates the extreme end of the KV-quantization space: the memory footprint is trivially small
and its throughput is a genuine strength (24,725 prefill tok/s per H100 vs the 70B’s ~19,780 per GPU
under TP=8 — ~1.25× per GPU, ~10× per host-equivalent; ~4 cards at average load, ~15 at peak, Table
12-2); what keeps it from being competitive is quality, the still-open Ch 14 gate.
Memory/residency arithmetic summary. The canonical weights (140 GB) + KV (24 GB FP16 at the
9.2K input context) = 164 GB fits 640 GB (8×H100). Candidate (a) uses the full host with room to
spare. Candidate (b) keeps the full model in each pool, so each 8×H100 host holds the same ~164 GB
single-request fit and — at the canonical per-host KV budget — up to 140 + 436 + ~64 = 640 GB (§12.3)
— exactly the pool, zero headroom. Candidate (c) fits ~15 GB on one H100 and its throughput is high,
but it is provisional — its fate turns on the Ch 14 quality-gate measurement, not on parameter
counting.

12.4. Measurement
To validate a candidate architecture, the architect must derive three numbers from first principles
and verify them against the substrate: 1. Weight memory.
W = N × bytes-per-param
where N is the parameter count and bytes-per-param is 2 for FP16 (replace 2 with bit-width/8 for
quantization). Derived fact [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] on the canonical inputs [ASSUMPTION]
canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2): 70 × 109 × 2 B = 140 GB. 2. KV cache footprint.
KV = 2 × nlayers × nKV-heads × dkv × L × bytes-per-activation
where L is the context length (full-MHA assumption: nKV-heads ×dkv = dhidden ; for GQA/MQA use
the reduced KV-head count). For a 70B model with 8-bit KV caching, this is approximately 12.06 GB
for 9.2K context (the raw tensor byte-halving bound: 2.62 MB/token FP16 ÷ 2 = 1.31 MB/token, exactly
50% of FP16; 9,200 × 1.31 MB ≈ 12.06 GB, Ch 7); at FP16 precision it is ~24.1 GB [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[DERIVED] on the canonical 9.2K context [ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2). The architect
should compute this for the exact context length of the workload, not assume a fixed value. 3.
Throughput per device [ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2). Tokens-per-second that a

213

Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates

single device can sustain for prefill and decode, measured on the target hardware. This is the number
that, multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, must exceed the workload’s
tokens-per-second demand (92K input tokens/s average, 3K output tokens/s average, 368K input
tokens/s peak, 12K output tokens/s peak). Vendors publish peak numbers; the architect should treat
these as benchmarks to be verified by measuring on equivalent hardware.
All three numbers must be confirmed before a candidate is carried forward. If any one fails, the
candidate is returned to the synthesis step.

12.5. Common Mistakes
• Menu-picking without constraint validation. Browsing vendor offerings and selecting the
one that “feels right” rather than generating candidates against quantified hard constraints.
This is the opposite of the constraint-driven method described here.
• Ignoring the KV cache residency arithmetic. Assuming that the weight memory is the only
memory budget item. In input-heavy workloads ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2):
9.2K average context, 30× more input than output), per request the KV is ≈15% of residency at
the canonical 9.2K context (24.1/164.1), but at the canonical host concurrency the KV budget is
436 GB of 640 GB (~68%) — which is why KV is often the binding constraint.
• Over-optimizing prefix caching. Assuming that prefix caching can amortize prefill across
all requests. In practice, cache effectiveness depends on the overlap of prompt prefixes across
the traffic workload; sparse prefix sharing reduces the realized savings.
• Using KV-quantization as a free lunch. Quantizing the KV cache reduces memory footprint
but introduces quality degradation that may be unacceptable for the target workload. The
architect must measure the quality impact before committing to a quantized KV layout.
• Forgetting the latency split. Treating the latency budget as a single number rather than a
prefill/decode split. A candidate may meet the total latency budget by trading prefill for decode
or vice versa, which may not satisfy the service-level objectives for either leg.

12.6. Architecture Consequence
Candidates (a) and (b) carry forward as conditional finalists (a finalist is a candidate advanced to
evaluation; a conditional finalist still has an open gate) into the evaluation chapters (Chs. 14–16) with
distinct test plans (Candidate (c) is gated, not a finalist: carried into the Ch 14 quality gate; if it passes
it becomes a finalist, otherwise it is retained only as a labeled sensitivity case), all written against the
same three gates — memory fit, throughput at the SLO, and quality. Candidate (a), the single 8×H100
host with prefix caching, is the baseline: we evaluate throughput at the SLO (TTFT/TPOT compliance
under load) on a single hardware configuration, with cost-per-token recorded as an economic byproduct rather than a gate. Candidate (b), the P/D-disaggregated two-pool, is evaluated on the added
complexity of inter-group communication and the pipeline overlap efficacy; we measure whether
the latency budget is maintained under the partitioned layout. Candidate (c), the KV-quantized 7B

Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates

214

model, is evaluated on the quality-degradation trade-off; we compare answer quality against the 70B
baseline and compute the economic break-even point (number of hosts required) against the quality
loss. The synthesis method produces these candidates as a set from which the evaluation chapter
selects based on quantitative results, not on gut feeling.

12.7. What We Still Don’t Know
As of 2026-08, several questions remain open, each flagged [HYPOTHESIS]:
• KV-quantization quality impact at 4-bit for enterprise Q&A. The quality loss from 4-bit
KV quantization has not been systematically characterized across the diversity of enterprise
prompts in the canonical workload [HYPOTHESIS].
• Prefix-caching effectiveness under realistic traffic overlap. The assumed 30–50% prefill
amortization rests on the premise that many requests share document-level prefixes. Empirical
measurement of prefix overlap across a production enterprise traffic trace is needed to confirm
these numbers [HYPOTHESIS].
• P/D-disaggregation communication overhead in multi-host settings. The KV-transfer
volume and latency between prefill and decode pools — as a function of context length,
request rate, and fabric bandwidth — is relatively unexplored at the 70B scale; the actual
communication volume and its latency impact depend on the routing library and network
topology [HYPOTHESIS].
• Whether 8-bit KV caching is sufficient for 9.2K context at FP16-equivalent quality.
The arithmetic in §12.4 assumes only the 2× memory reduction; whether 8-bit KV preserves
acceptable quality is the open question — the interaction between 8-bit quantization and the
retrieval-augmented generation pipeline has not been verified [HYPOTHESIS].
These flags exist because home-lab measurements do not count as reference evidence per the
evidence taxonomy; each is an open empirical question a team should validate against its own target
workload, not a claim the handbook has settled.

12.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: From Vague Ask to Candidate Architectures
An architect is brought into a design conversation for a company-wide internal Q&A system. The
stakeholder states: “We need an AI system that can answer employee questions over our internal
documentation, with acceptable quality and within budget.” Before any architecture can be defended,
the architect applies the constraint-driven method from this chapter.
First, the workload is characterized across the six dimensions. Quality requirements fix the model
class: the system must achieve ~70B-model answer quality on enterprise prompts. The traffic profile
is the canonical one (Ch. 4/5, canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2)): ~2,000 registered users, ~5%
concurrent (~100), ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak. The token profile is the canonical 1,200-token

215

Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates

prompt plus 8K retrieved context (~9.2K input) plus 300-token answers, with TTFT ≤ 1.2 s (p95 ≤
2 s) and TPOT ~25 ms/token. The stakeholder’s $15,000 is a total monthly system budget — the
chapter notes it equals one host’s cloud-equivalent (one 8×H100 at ~$20/hr × 730 hr ≈ $14.6K/mo; an
on-premise host has no $/hr, so this is a budget cap, not a metered cost, and the cloud-equivalent
is a proxy at those assumptions). Total fleet cost $155.8K/mo (21 hosts) ÷ $15K = ~10.4× the total
budget — the economic constraint fails at fleet scale (Ch 16). The consequence must be stated, not
dissolved: the 21-host full-utilization screen fleet (Ch 16 case (i)/KV-screen line) costs ~$155.8K/mo
— and the Ch 17 Table 17-1 provisioning policy (70% × 95% + N−1) yields 32 hosts at the same 40
rps peak (Ch 13), i.e. ~$232.2K self-host (32 × [per-host capex/60 + energy] + $10K/mo staff) and
~$467.2K cloud-equivalent (32 × 730 h × $20/h rental only, staff excluded), so the self-host totals
do not scale purely per-host ($155,816.93, ≈$24.97/1K on the 6.24M‑req/mo business‑hours basis,
Ch 16 — the cloud legs are $87,600 ≈ $14.04/1K at the default paid-occupancy input and $306,600
≈ $49.13/1K at 21 hosts always-on) — ~10.4× the stakeholder’s stated $15,000 total monthly budget
for the 21-host screen (~15.5× self-host and ~31× cloud-equivalent for the 32-host policy fleet) —
so the economic constraint, as stated, fails at fleet scale. Economics is therefore recorded as
failing at fleet scale — the economic ceiling is not one of the three gates and is deferred to Ch 16 and
the budget renegotiation; the architect’s first return-to-synthesis move is to renegotiate the budget,
shape peak demand, or revisit the model class. The operational constraint is that the system must
run on existing on-premise GPU infrastructure (no cloud add-ons).
From the token profile, the architect computes: 9.2K input tokens + 300 output tokens ≈ 9.5K
tokens per request. At 10 rps average and 40 rps peak, the system must sustain ~92K input tokens/s
average and ~368K input tokens/s peak. Three hard constraints follow — the chapter’s three gates,
verbatim: memory fit (weight memory plus KV cache must fit within the on-premise GPU inventory),
throughput at the SLO (total tokens-per-second across the installed devices, delivered within the
TTFT/TPOT budget, must exceed the traffic demand), and quality (answer quality on the evaluation
set must meet the ~70B requirement).
The architect generates three candidates using the method from §12.3. Candidate (a): a single
8×H100 host with 70B FP16 weights + 24 GB KV cache and prefix caching, which fits the memory
budget (164 GB < 640 GB aggregate ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2))) — but as Chapter
8 shows, one 8×H100 host sustains only ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s at the idealized 35%-MFU TP=8
operating point (~19,780 tok/s per GPU; the host aggregate is the same rate, since each GPU carries
1/8 of the shared token stream — the ~2,472 figure is a full-model-equivalent FLOP rate, not a per-GPU
capability), far short of the ~92K input tokens/s the 10 rps average demands, so the memory gate
passes while the throughput gate already fails. Candidate (b): a P/D-disaggregated two-pool design
keeping the full 70B in each pool (prefill and decode pools, each ~164 GB single-request residency —
up to ~640 GB (140 weights + 436 KV + ~64 runtime) at the canonical per-host KV budget (§12.3) —
zero headroom — on its own 8×H100 host), which buys phase-splitting at the cost of a second host
plus the KV-transfer fabric. Candidate (c): a KV-quantized 7B model on a single H100, which fits the

Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates

216

memory budget (~15 GB total residency: 14 GB FP16 weights + ~1.2 GB 4-bit KV), but its quality is
provisional — whether a 7B-class model can reach the required answer quality is a hypothesis to be
measured against the quality gate (Chapter 14), not a settled fact.
The architect does not discard Candidate (c) by parameter counting alone: it is provisionally
moved to the quality-gate evaluation (Chapter 14) to measure whether a 7B-class model actually
meets the workload’s capability/quality threshold on its evaluation set. Its memory and economics
are trivially favorable; its fate turns on that measured gate. Because candidate (c)’s quality gate is
still open [HYPOTHESIS], it is not a finalist — and it stays in the gate evaluation (Ch 14) rather
than being excluded pre-measurement; the finalists are Candidates (a) and (b), and the near-term
decision falls between them. The decision between Candidates (a) and (b) hinges on whether the
doubled hardware cost of Candidate (b) is justified by its operational flexibility (e.g., independent
scaling of prefill and decode pools, fault isolation). The architect presents both candidates, together
with the honest throughput arithmetic of Chapter 8 (no canonical single host meets the full prefill
demand alone), to the stakeholder as the decision foundation.

chapter 13.
Reference Architectures: From Local to
Hyperscale

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to look at a characterized workload and place it on the right
archetype — the canonical deployment shapes that recur across the industry — without reinventing
a design from scratch. We will map the four tiers (local/edge, server, cluster, hyperscale), state what
each can serve in model size, and develop the decision rule — traffic against host goodput — for when
a workload outgrows a tier and must escalate. After this chapter, “we run on a server” or “we need a
cluster” is a defensible, quantified statement tied to the workload’s numbers — not a guess.

13.1. Concept
Architectures recur not because engineers lack imagination but because the constraints recur. Four
archetypes cover the vast majority of AI deployments, distinguished by how many GPUs are involved
and over what interconnect:
1. Local / edge — a single GPU (or a laptop-class accelerator). Serves small models (up to ~7-13B
at tight context, assuming 8-bit/4-bit weight quantization — 13B FP16 = 26 GB exceeds many
edge GPUs) that must run on-device for privacy, latency, or connectivity reasons. Interconnect
is not the question; memory capacity is.
2. Server — one host with 1-8 GPUs, typically H100/H200 — multi-GPU servers joined by
NVLink/NVSwitch (a 1-GPU host uses PCIe; no intra-host fabric is needed). Serves dense
models up to ~70B-180B with real concurrency. This is the canonical enterprise-Q&A tier and

222

223

Reference Architectures: From Local to Hyperscale

the book’s 8×H100 baseline. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] (the tier’s model-size range is
a book-defined characterization; the H100/H200 and NVLink/NVSwitch specs it cites are [1P]
vendor datasheets)
3. Cluster — multiple hosts (tens to hundreds of GPUs) joined by InfiniBand or high-speed
Ethernet. Required when a model exceeds a node’s memory (so it must be split per Ch10) or
when traffic outgrows one host (requiring multi-host scaling: data-parallel replication, P/D
disaggregation, or both — Ch 11).
4. Hyperscale / data-center fleet — dedicated fleets of specialized inference/training clusters,
often MoE or KV-centric (Mooncake-style disaggregation [S4][1P]), serving many tenants at
enormous scale. The economics favor extreme specialization.
These are a continuum, not hard categories; the useful question is always which tier does OUR
workload’s bounds demand?

13.2. Mental Model
Each tier is a box with a fixed memory budget and a fixed cross-node bandwidth. A
workload fits a tier if (a) the model’s weight + KV residency fits the tier’s total GPU memory
(Ch7), and (b) the tier’s interconnect can carry the communication the chosen parallelism requires
(Ch9/Ch10), and (c) the resulting throughput + latency meets the SLO (Ch11).
The mental model is a ladder with explicit rungs: we climb a rung when a binding constraint
can no longer be met. The classic triggers for climbing:
• Memory: model + KV no longer fits one node → cluster (split weights) — the Single host →
Multi-host climb in Fig 13.1.
• KV residency per GPU: model + KV no longer fits one GPU → single host — the within-tier
step Fig 13.1 shows between Single GPU and Single host.
• Traffic: one host’s throughput ceiling (goodput) below demand → more replicas (DP across
nodes) or P/D disaggregation → cluster.
• Contention / phase interference: SLO can’t be met because prefill and decode contend for
the same resources → split prefill/decode (a within-tier move).
• Distance / geography: SLO can’t be met because the users are too far from the serving site
→ move the serving edge closer or add regional replicas (a placement move, not a climb — it
belongs with the de-escalation moves in Fig 13.1).
We do not climb for fashion; we climb when a measured number crosses a threshold.
