13.3. Worked Example
13.3.1. Placing the Canonical Workload
The canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload’s model residency is server-class, and at the 40 rps
peak its deployment is a cluster of ~21 server-class hosts (Ch 16/17) — placed there by Table 13-1’s
traffic > host goodput trigger, not by weight-splitting. We verify each bound:
• Memory: 70B FP16 weights = 140 GB; KV for the 9.5K max context at FP16 ≈ 24.9 GB; inference
residency ≈ 165 GB [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. An 8×H100 host (640 GB) fits this with ample
headroom for concurrency (Ch11 showed ~24 GB per request × concurrent requests still fits).
✓ [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
• Throughput/latency: ~10 rps average / 40 rps peak, input-heavy (9.2K in / 300 out). On the
per-request latency axis, Ch11’s serving analysis indicates that continuous batching + prefix
caching keeps p95 TTFT under the 2 s SLO on a single 8×H100 host below capacity — at
the 40 rps peak the queueing delay breaches it (the host does not carry the full arrival rate,
as the capacity axis below shows). But on the capacity axis the single host does not
carry the full arrival rate: with the canonical ~8.6 s service time, Little’s Law puts ≈40
× 8.6 ≈ 344 requests in flight at the peak, against ~17.5 KV-resident requests per host (an
analytical continuous-occupancy figure; the conservative integer floor 17 is what hard host
provisioning uses) — so a single host is a latency-feasible but not capacity-sufficient server
(Ch16/17 size the fleet to ~21 hosts at the 40 rps peak on the full-utilization screen — ⌈344/17⌉
= 21; under the 70% × 95% policy (u = 0.70 utilization target, ρ = 0.95 load-balancer efficiency,
per Table 17-1) — applied to the unrounded 344/17 ≈ 20.2, not the rounded 21 — that becomes
31 working + 1 spare = 32 total, Table 17-1). On the compute axis a single host also serves only
~19.8K of the ~92K input tokens/s the 10 rps average needs (~5 hosts, Ch 12/8), so the peak
failure is a compute shortfall, not merely queueing delay. The tier choice here is about model
residency and per-request latency, not about whether one host serves the entire peak arrival.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
• Interconnect: no cross-host model parallelism is required (one node; intra-host TP=8 fits the
140 GB model) — the interconnect question doesn’t bind. ✓
So the server tier is the right model-residency archetype for the canonical workload — the model
and its KV fit a single 8×H100 node and the per-request TTFT SLO is met on one host. It does not
mean one host serves the whole arrival rate; a single host is latency-bound and the peak capacity is
a fleet-computing question (Ch17). [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

225

Reference Architectures: From Local to Hyperscale

13.3.2. Escalating: When 10×Traffic Forces the Cluster Tier
Now suppose the workload’s demand grows to ~100 rps average (a 10×) — assuming the canonical
4× peak/average shape persists, 100 rps average implies ~400 rps peak; the screen below is run at the
average — at peak it reads ⌈400 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = 203 hosts at full utilization. Recompute the ceiling:
• Throughput ceiling of one host: continuous batching on 8×H100 at ~9.5K tokens/request
sustained roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s; goodput against the SLO is the binding
number. At ~920K input tokens/s (100 rps × 9.2K input; ~950K total tokens including the 300
output tokens), far above one host’s ~19.8K prefill ceiling, one host’s goodput is exceeded; the
host count that follows comes from the KV/service-time screen below, not from a tokens/s
comparison. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
• Response: replicate the model across multiple servers (data parallelism at the serving layer —
run N identical 8×H100 hosts behind a load balancer). At ~100 rps average, the book’s wholeslot KV/service-time screen (Ch 16/17; floor the KV-residency quotient to 17 whole-context
slots, then divide by the 8.6 s service time — a KV/service-time screen, not an independently
measured compute or goodput benchmark) gives ⌈100 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = ⌈50.59⌉ = 51 hosts at full
utilization, and Ch17’s 70% utilization target plus the N−1 spare gives 73 working + 1 spare =
74 hosts on the u-only screen (ρ = 1) — 77 working + 1 spare = 78 hosts at the Table 17-1
policy (u × ρ = 0.70 × 0.95 = 0.665; ⌈860/(17 × 0.665)⌉ = ⌈76.07⌉ = 77) — not a handful. (The
naive screen is one host short — 50 vs ⌈50.59⌉ = 51 — because it uses the unfloored 17.5-slot
quotient: 50 × (17.5 ÷ 8.6 ≈ 2.03) ≈ 101.7 rps, exactly at the 100 rps demand with zero utilization
headroom; on the conservative floored 17 whole-context slots, 50 hosts deliver only 50 × 17/8.6
≈ 98.8 rps. The larger 50 → 74/78 gap comes from the 70% × 95% headroom and the N−1
spare, not from slot flooring.) The escalation is still the cluster tier: the model fits one node
(no weight-splitting), but the fleet is a real cluster sized by the per-host goodput ceiling. The
escalation is driven by traffic, not memory. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
13.3.3. Dropping a Tier: When On-Device Execution Forces Local
Two distinct constraints are often filed under “privacy,” and they have different tier consequences.
Data residency / sovereignty — data must not leave the facility or the jurisdiction — forces the
on-prem server (or cluster) tier: data stays in the facility, and the canonical 70B still runs on server
hardware. On-device execution — offline/connectivity, or a tight on-device latency — is what forces
the local/edge tier, and it applies only when the model can be distilled to a 7-13B capable of the
Q&A task: a single GPU then runs the distilled model at reduced (but acceptable — verified against
Ch 14’s quality gate) accuracy. That second move trades capability for the operational constraint; the
first trades only deployment location. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

13.4. Measurement
The tier decision is only as good as the numbers that trigger it. We measure three things:
1. Residency vs tier memory (Ch7): does weight + KV fit? If not, the floor is a cluster.
2. Host goodput ceiling vs demand (Ch6/Ch11): measure the max rps/tokens/s the host delivers
at the SLO, and compare to demand. When demand > ceiling, escalate.

227

Reference Architectures: From Local to Hyperscale

3. Communication fraction (Ch9/Ch10): if the parallelism the cluster requires spends >~20%
[ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic] of step time on collectives, the interconnect (not the GPU) is the
binding tier constraint.
These three numbers support a defensible first-order placement on the ladder — validate it by
measurement.

13.5. Common Mistakes
• Choosing hyperscale before measuring goodput. Most workloads never exceed one host’s
capacity/goodput ceiling; the mistake is building a fleet before measuring whether traffic
actually outgrows one host’s capacity. (Note: the book’s own canonical workload does outgrow
one host’s capacity at its 40 rps peak — ~21 hosts per Ch17 — so for that workload the fleet is
warranted, not premature.)
• Using model size as the only tier driver. A 70B model fits a server; traffic, not size, usually
forces the cluster — an architect who only watches parameters escalates too early or too late.
• Ignoring the operational constraint. Data-residency/sovereignty or on-device requirements
can force a different — often lower — tier regardless of what compute wants; the ladder is
bounded by operations, not just performance.
• Assuming a smaller model can’t serve the tier. Distilled small models on local GPUs can
meet the goal when the capability suffices — don’t over-provision the tier.
• Treating tiers as walls. They are a continuum; the correct answer can be a hybrid (edge
cache + server generation) the measured numbers justify.

13.6. Architecture Consequence
The archetype sets the entire downstream design vocabulary. On the server tier (canonical),
the consequences are already established: continuous batching + PagedAttention + prefix caching
(Ch11), KV quantization when residency binds (Ch7), no cross-host model parallelism (Ch10; intrahost TP=8 fits the 140 GB model). Moving up to cluster introduces: DP/PP/TP replicas (Ch10), P/D
disaggregation (Ch11), and interconnect budgeting (Ch9). Moving down to local forces distillation
and on-device KV limits. The tier is the top-level decision; every other choice in the book slots
beneath it.

13.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• Exact host goodput ceilings depend on the specific server, model, degree of parallelism and
batching; the representative numbers here are [UNRESOLVED] per deployment.
• When P/D disaggregation’s benefit crosses its cost for mid-tier workloads is
[HYPOTHESIS]; the breakpoint is workload- and fabric-specific.
• Fleet-level economics (Ch16 TCO across a cluster) interact with the tier choice in ways that
are [HYPOTHESIS — workload-dependent; requires the architect’s own cost model].

13.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Escalating Through the Reference-Architecture
Tiers
An architect returns to the canonical internal Q&A service a year later. The company has grown
from ~2,000 to ~20,000 users; traffic is now ~10× (≈100 rps average). The on-prem service is saturated:
p95 TTFT has drifted to 3 s against the 2 s SLO [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO INPUT]. Applying this
chapter’s ladder, the architect measures the three triggers. Memory: the 70B model still fits one
8×H100 node (165 GB max residency), so the model does not force a cluster. Traffic: host goodput is
exceeded at ~100 rps — the binding trigger. Operational: the data privacy requirement still forbids a
public hyperscale cloud. The architect’s decision: escalate to the cluster tier but keep it on-prem —
run a fleet of 8×H100 replicas behind a load balancer. With the canonical whole-slot KV/service-time
screen (Ch 16/17), the fleet is ⌈100 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = 51 hosts at full utilization — 73 working + 1 spare
= 74 hosts at Ch17’s 70% target and N−1 rule on the u-only screen (ρ = 1), or 77 working + 1 spare =
78 hosts at the Table 17-1 policy (u × ρ = 0.70 × 0.95 = 0.665) — a real cluster rather than a handful;
at 51 hosts each replica sits right at its per-host ceiling (100 ÷ 51 ≈ 1.96 rps vs the 17 ÷ 8.6 ≈ 1.98 rps
ceiling), which is exactly why the sizing rule adds the 70% × 95% headroom and the spare host. The
result, with the 74-host headroom fleet (78 hosts at the Table 17-1 policy): p95 TTFT back under
1.8 s at 100 rps [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO RESULT], on site, without hyperscale — because the
architect moved from single-host to multi-host deployment — one step up the ladder, taken because
the measured traffic trigger said so, not because of fashion or model size.

chapter 14.
Benchmarking: Predicting Real Experience, Not
a Leaderboard

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to look at a benchmark result and judge whether it predicts
what our users will actually experience. We will draw the crucial distinction between capability
benchmarks (what a model can do on standardized tasks) and deployment benchmarks (what
a system will do on OUR workload), then build a workload benchmark from the six-dimensional
characterization (Ch4) that measures the numbers that actually decide architecture. After this chapter,
“the model scores well on MMLU” is recognized as a weak claim — and “it meets our p95-TTFT SLO
at 40 rps on our token profile” is a strong one.

14.1. Concept
Benchmarking fails most often because the wrong benchmark is used for the wrong decision. The fix
is to separate two very different instruments:
1. Capability benchmarks — measure the model’s output quality on standardized tasks (MMLU,
GSM8K, HumanEval, MT-Bench, retrieval-QA suites). They answer: is this model good enough at
the skill our workload needs? They do NOT tell us how fast, how cheap, or how it behaves under
our traffic. Model capability is the goal (Ch4’s Quality dimension) and forms the quality gate;
deployment benchmarks measure the constraints (latency, throughput, cost) that capability
benchmarks do not. If capability fails its quality gate (Ch 12’s candidate (c)), it becomes the
binding constraint before any serving optimization.

230

231

Benchmarking: Predicting Real Experience, Not a Leaderboard

2. Deployment benchmarks — measure the system’s behavior on a representative workload:
TTFT, TPOT, throughput, goodput, KV cache utilization, cost per request. They answer: does
this model-on-this-hardware meet the SLO at our traffic and token profile? These are the numbers
that actually pick the architecture.
The core insight: a capability leaderboard is a poor proxy for serving performance. Two
models with identical MMLU can differ wildly in TTFT under the same batching, because serving
depends on tokenizer, context length, KV layout, scheduler, model size, architecture, and hardware
— none of which a leaderboard scores. Benchmarks select models only after capability filters and
deployment measurement both pass.

14.2. Mental Model
Capability benchmarks serve as screening and deployment benchmarks as selection. Screening
answers “which models are even in the running?” cheaply and broadly. Selection answers “among
the screened-in models, which system actually works for our workload?” expensively and precisely.
The two-stage mental model prevents two classic errors:
• Picking a serving stack with capability metrics — e.g. benchmarking a model’s MMLU to
choose serving hardware. (Wrong tool: MMLU is a capability benchmark, §1, not a deployment
metric.)
• Selecting with leaderboards — e.g. taking the top-scoring MMLU model and assuming it will
meet our SLO. (Wrong tool, again.)
Just as important, we benchmark the workload, not the model in the abstract. A deployment
benchmark that doesn’t reproduce our token profile (input/output ratio, context length), our traffic
(rps, concurrency, burst), and our SLO (percentiles) is measuring someone else’s problem.

14.3. Worked Example
14.3.1. Designing a Deployment Benchmark for the Canonical Workload
We build a deployment benchmark for the canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload (canonical
scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2)): ~10 rps average / 40 rps peak, ~9,200 input tokens (1,200 query + 8K
retrieved) + ~300 output, TTFT budget (median ≤ 1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s), TPOT ~25 ms/token. [canonical
scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2)]
Step 1 — representative queries. We sample real user questions and run them through the
RAG pipeline to produce the actual prompt shapes, matching the ~9.2K-in / ~300-out token profile
with the model’s own tokenizer (not a heuristic). [2°]
Step 2 — sweep the offered load, not a single point. The analytical KV quotient C ≈ 17.5
FP16-KV request-equivalents (436 GB FP16 KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9,500-token maximum sequence;
9,500 = 9,200 input + 300 output, the conservative whole-context basis, not the input-only 9,200;

Benchmarking: Predicting Real Experience, Not a Leaderboard

232

9,500 × 2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB) gives at most 17 whole-context slots, not a deployable concurrency of 17.5.
At the assumed 8.6-second execution time, 17/8.6 ≈ 1.98 req/s is a single-host residency ceiling before
headroom and competing resource limits (the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient gives ~2.03 req/s on the
analytical planning screens; the ~3% gap is the fractional-slot rounding — floor 17 for provisioning,
17.5 for analysis). We sweep offered load and measure the tail rather than treating that ceiling as
achieved capacity. An illustrative single-host sweep can cover 2, 4, 8, 12 and 16 active requests. Higher
offered concurrency tests queueing or rejection; it does not imply that all requests are simultaneously
resident. At each level we record:
• TTFT p50/p95/p99 (must be median ≤ 1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s).
• TPOT p50/p95 (SLO: p50 ≤ ~25 ms/token; record p95 for tail diagnosis, not SLO-bound).
• Goodput — tokens/s that meet the SLO (Ch6), not raw throughput.
• KV cache utilization and prefix-cache hit ratio (to validate the serving choices of Ch11).
• Admission / rejection — the offered-load level at which the server starts queueing or rejecting
(the saturation knee).
The analytical ceiling sets the range of the sweep. The scenario’s 40 req/s peak and assumed
8.6-second execution time imply about 344 executing requests fleet-wide, not resident requests on
one host. Chapter 17 distinguishes the integer-slot planning minimum, occupancy headroom and
spare capacity; those are not measured fleet capacity. The benchmark supplies the highest offered
load that still meets the SLO. That measured SLO-goodput, not the analytical C/W, becomes the
provisioning input.

14.4. Measurement
Four habits make benchmarks trustworthy:
1. Use the model’s own tokenizer on representative real prompts. The “4 chars ≈ 1 token”
heuristic can be materially wrong for code/JSON/technical text — the often-quoted ~1.5–3×
shortfall is [ILLUSTRATIVE], not a measured range — so measure chars/token with the model’s
own tokenizer rather than assuming a fixed ratio.
2. Measure distributions, not means — log p50/p90/p95/p99 for every latency metric and the
full token-length distribution. A 32K-tail context is a different workload than a 9.2K average.
3. Reproduce the concurrency and burst — a benchmark must hit the model at our peak
concurrency, not a single request, or it won’t show the queuing and KV contention that break
SLOs.
4. Include goodput and cost, not just latency — the SLO-windowed throughput and $/request
complete the picture for the economics (Ch16).
These four habits are the standard. The guidance below applies them to each candidate change a
deployment benchmark actually has to judge — a precision recipe, an iterative or media generation
path, a serving backend, and a communication library. Each needs an explicit boundary: what is held
constant on both sides, what counts as a completed result, and what counts as acceptable quality.

235

Benchmarking: Predicting Real Experience, Not a Leaderboard

14.4.1. Acceptance test for a quantized deployment
The comparison is paired: one base-model revision, fixed tokenizer and prompt template, fixed
decoding/reasoning budget, the same workload and the same hardware. The candidate differs by a
documented precision recipe and its required kernel path. Calibration data are separate from test
data. If a high-precision baseline was never published, that absence remains explicit; the experiment
cannot establish loss relative to unavailable original weights. [DERIVED]
Accuracy is checked on the actual exported implementation. Reasoning tasks need verifiable
answers under a fixed effort budget. Code tasks need execution and tests, not only syntactic validity.
Tool tasks need correct tool selection, valid arguments, completed outcomes and a record of retries
or unsafe actions. Multimodal tasks fix preprocessing and evaluate every affected modal branch.
Long-context tests cover both retrieval and dependencies over position and generation length; weight
precision and KV precision are varied separately. A favorable perplexity result does not establish all
of these capabilities. These are acceptance criteria for the proposed experiment, not claims that a
particular format passes them. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION][UNMEASURED]
The load test keeps arrival traces, prompt/output distributions, parallelism and cache state fixed.
It measures load peak, steady/reserved HBM, kernel selection, TTFT, inter-token latency, completion
time, errors and task quality. A bounded first screen might use 200 paired examples per critical task
and three repetitions per load point as a smoke test; this is not sufficient for p99 or rare-failure
claims. Final sample sizes follow the predeclared degradation bound and statistical power. Only
candidates that pass the quality gate enter a comparison of SLO-goodput and cost per successful
task. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION][UNMEASURED]
14.4.2. Measure drafts, commitments and valid results separately
Iterative generation introduces more than one plausible “first token.” A service can expose a pro­
visional draft, commit an irreversible prefix or block, and later finish a valid response. Those are
different events. A first-draft timestamp measures early visibility. A first-commit timestamp measures
when a downstream consumer can safely act on text that will not be overwritten. Time to a validated
answer includes any required schema checks, unit tests or task acceptance. Comparisons need the
same boundary on both sides. [DERIVED]
Burst streaming also changes the meaning of inter-token latency. A runtime may deliver an
entire block in one event and pause while refining the next block. Splitting that event into individual
client tokens creates near-zero within-block gaps without shortening the pause between blocks. We
therefore retain final-token throughput but add block size, block-arrival gaps, first-commit latency
and end-to-end p95/p99 latency. [DERIVED]
The existing token SLO-goodput definition still counts only service-compliant final output.
Provisional text that is overwritten is not extra useful output. A separate successful-request metric
can count requests that pass all three gates — task validity, required quality and the service SLO —
per unit wall time. This is an additional metric, not a silent redefinition of token goodput. If retries,

Benchmarking: Predicting Real Experience, Not a Leaderboard

236

fallback or tool execution belong to the service, their time and cost remain inside the boundary.
[DERIVED]
A reproducible comparison freezes model and tokenizer revisions, sampler, thresholds, block size,
cache policy, quantization and runtime commit. It uses a calibration set to choose operating points
and a separate holdout set to evaluate them. Both sides receive reasonable optimizations: optimized
AR KV/batching and, where available, a speculative baseline; the applicable diffusion cache, refresh
and verification paths. Speed is compared only after the quality gate is met. [DERIVED]
We measure a warmed single request, a concurrency sweep and an open-loop offered-load
sweep. The workload includes long prompts, code infilling, fixed-region editing and structured
tool calls. The execution trace records evaluations, recomputed positions, verification and final
committed tokens; the service trace records queueing, drafts, commitment, completion, failures and
cancellation. Hardware-matched experiments can support resource-efficiency claims. A closed API
whose hardware and internal schedule are unknown belongs in a separate service-level comparison,
not a GPU-FLOP ranking. [DERIVED]
14.4.3. A video benchmark is a workload tuple
A reproducible video result identifies the exact model and revision; task and conditioning; hardware
model, count, and topology; precision and quantization; pixel dimensions; frames and frames/s;
scheduler and timestep sequence; guidance; branch evaluations; engine commit and attention back­
end; cache and offload settings; and output-quality criteria. It also identifies the timing boundary.
Seconds per denoising step, seconds for all sampling steps, and seconds to a finalized clip are not
interchangeable. [DERIVED]
This section keeps the video measurement protocol; the serving side — request scheduling, live
state, reuse, and resource-specialized pools for a video workload — is treated in the Ch 11 appendix,
“Beyond autoregressive text: video and diffusion serving”.
A primary report can still leave that tuple incomplete. HunyuanVideo-1.5 reports 5.5070 versus
2.9475 seconds per diffusion step for dense versus sparse attention at 720 × 1,280 pixels and 241
frames. Those measurements use eight H800 GPUs with context parallelism and a CFG-distilled
model. Its separate 50-step table adds SageAttention, compilation, and feature caching, and reports
96.78 versus 58.39 seconds for the same shape. Neither table establishes a single-GPU service rate or
a complete request-to-media latency.1 [1P][FACT]
LTX-2’s report compares 22.30 seconds/step for Wan2.2-14B with 1.22 seconds/step for LTX-2.
The stated context is an H100 GPU, 121 frames, a 720p label, single-step Euler, and CFG=1. It is
not a matched-quality completed-clip comparison. Missing precision, exact pixel shape, engine

The deployment experiment pairs fixed prompts and reference assets across explicitly declared

14.4.4. Two fair comparisons answer different questions
A hardware-isolation comparison holds the model revision, numerical representation, KV format,
request distribution and functional features constant. This limits the claim to the tested common
path. A deployment comparison can instead use each backend’s best available implementation, but
all candidates must first satisfy the same quality and service constraints. If one candidate uses a
different representation or disables a feature, the result concerns a different complete configuration
— not hardware alone. [DERIVED]
Both comparisons need cold and warm runs, separate prefill and decode observations, a load
sweep, and per-request timing. Request goodput counts successful requests that satisfy quality and
every request-level SLO. Token goodput counts the output tokens of those compliant requests over
the same wall-clock interval. Timeouts, failed attempts and fallback work still consume resources. A
p95 threshold is a configuration-level statistic; it is not itself a count of compliant work. A p95 SLO is
evaluated over a defined population and window, while goodput counts the requests that individually
meet their SLOs within that window. An increase in raw tokens per second can therefore coexist
with unchanged or lower goodput. [DERIVED]
Graph startup, cache warmth, host-side conversion and request isolation belong in the record.
Reasoning workloads also need total generated-token counts and a fixed quality test. Fewer generated
tokens can mean less work, not a faster implementation. These controls preserve the interpretation of
Chapter 15’s optimization map when the backend changes. This section states a comparison protocol
and introduces no new measured performance claim. [DERIVED]

14.4.5. A collective microbenchmark is not a serving-capacity claim
Collective microbenchmarks isolate one communication mechanism; they do not establish serving
capacity. A deployment comparison preserves the layer shapes, precision, group mapping and arrival
process, then measures device-completed work and SLO-goodput under contention. Cross-vendor
tests compare complete systems unless hardware is controlled; they cannot isolate a library-only
speedup. Chapter 9 supplies the correctness and traffic-accounting contract. [DERIVED]

14.5. Common Mistakes
• Citing a capability leaderboard as proof of serving fitness. MMLU does not predict TTFT;
it screens capability only.
• Benchmarking a single request. Real SLOs break under concurrency; a single-request
benchmark hides the tail.
• Mean-only latency reporting. A 0.84 s mean hides a 5 s tail that breaches the p95 SLO (Ch6).
• Using the wrong tokenizer estimate. Under-counting context via the 4-char heuristic
mis-sizes KV cache and prefill.
• Optimizing raw throughput past the SLO window. Bigger batch sizes raise tokens/s but
push TTFT over the deadline for the affected requests and can reduce goodput — to zero only
if no request in the measurement window meets the SLO (Ch6, Ch11).

14.6. Architecture Consequence
The benchmark is the bridge from candidate architectures (Ch12) to selection and then to TCO
(Ch16):
• Capability screen narrows the candidate models (from Ch3/Ch5 model-selection) to those
that meet the accuracy/quality threshold.
• Deployment benchmark then measures each surviving candidate under the canonical
workload, producing the TTFT/goodput/cost numbers that drive the choice.
• The chosen system becomes the basis for the TCO and performance-engineering work of
Ch15-16.
The benchmark is not a one-time event; it is the recurring production validation that catches
drift (model updates, traffic shape changes, memory pressure) before they breach the SLO.

14.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• How closely capability benchmarks predict enterprise Q&A quality for a given domain
is [UNRESOLVED]; a custom retrieval-QA screen on real documents is stronger but costly.
• Portable goodput ceilings across serving stacks are [HYPOTHESIS] until measured on the
target host with the target model.

14.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Capability Screen vs. Deployment Benchmark
In this hypothetical mini-case, a team proposes a model because it tops MMLU. It also passes the
task-specific retrieval-QA capability screen. The remaining question is deployment fitness. The
comparison fixes prompt texts, output requirements, hardware, arrival trace and timing boundaries;
each model uses its own tokenizer. A single-host load sweep establishes each replica’s accepted
operating point before the fleet is tested at the scenario’s 40 req/s peak. The SLO remains median
TTFT ≤ 1.2 s, p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s and median TPOT about 25 ms. Suppose the candidate generates more
input tokens for the same prompt texts and the paired deployment test yields p95 TTFT 2.6 s, versus
the incumbent’s 1.9 s at that same offered load. Those are illustrative results, not book measurements.
The candidate fails the latency gate despite passing the capability screen; diagnosis must separate
token-count effects from implementation and queueing costs before a revised deployment is accepted.

The Architect’s Question
We are tasked with engineering performance for a serving layer that must absorb the day-to-day
traffic of a growing user base while delivering acceptable latency. The core question: how do we
configure an 8×H100 host to serve a 70B parameter model at 40 requests-per-second peak while
keeping per-request latency within a target budget, and what architectural knobs—batch size, KV
cache design, kernel choice—most affect that outcome? Scope of the one-host framing (stated
up front, matching Chapter 8’s Scope note): the 8×H100 host here is the per-request feasibility
container — a per-host SLO claim (does one host meet one request’s latency and memory SLO?).
No single host absorbs the 40 rps peak, so the framing carries a fleet implication; the host-count
arithmetic is collected in the Fleet implication note below, and the fleet sizing itself is Chapters
16/17’s job. This chapter’s worked example and mini-case are single-/dual-host micro-benchmarks,
not the fleet configuration. This chapter walks through the performance-engineering lifecycle: from
concept, to mental model, to worked arithmetic, to measurement, to common pitfalls, to architectural
consequences, to open questions, and finally a mini-case that ties the thread.
Fleet implication (host-count arithmetic): At the canonical peak, Little’s Law puts
λ·W ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344 requests in flight against ~17.5 KV-resident slots per host (wholeslot floor 17), so the fleet is ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts on the FP16 KV reference (Chapters
16/17/20; with the §6 FP8-KV decision, ⌈344/35⌉ = 10 hosts at 40 rps, bounded below by
the ~7-host prefill requirement at theoretical peak (100% MFU); at the 35% MFU planning
assumption the prefill screen is 19 hosts and binds above the 10-host FP8-KV screen)

— an illustrative planning screen under the stated FLOP-counting case and the

15.1. Concept
Performance engineering in LLM serving is the discipline of matching compute, memory, and I/O
throughput to the stochastic workload of token generation and prompt processing. Unlike traditional
web serving, where request‑cycle overhead dominates the tail, the dominant cost in LLM inference
is the FLOPs plus the bytes moved — the FLOP count of transformer matrix multiplications and
the memory traffic of KV cache reads and writes on every token step — with arithmetic intensity
(a FLOP/byte ratio, not a cost) deciding which of the two dominates. The serving system must
therefore optimize three inter‑dependent quantities: SLO‑goodput, per‑token latency, and GPU
memory utilization. Goodput = SLO‑meeting requests (or tokens) per second — distinct from
raw throughput, which counts work that may miss the SLO. The canonical SLO this chapter
measures against: TTFT median ≤ 1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s, TPOT median ≤ 25 ms, p95 ≤ 35 ms (Ch 4,
Table 4-2). These are governed by the model FLOP count, the chosen kernel (e.g. FlashAttention
vs. scaled‑dot‑product), and the batching strategy (static vs. dynamic, continuous vs. chunked). The
architect’s first move is to identify which resource—compute, bandwidth, or latency—is the primary
constraint for the canonical scenario, then apply the appropriate optimization to shift the bottleneck.
A secondary concept is the trade-off between batch size and tail latency: larger batches amortize
kernel launch overhead and increase arithmetic intensity, but they increase the wait time for straggler
requests, raising p99 latency. The designer must therefore balance arithmetic gain against tail‑latency
penalty, a tension that shapes every later architectural decision.

15.2. Mental Model
We model the serving request lifecycle as a pipeline of computational phases with a cross‑cutting
state‑management plane. The compute phases run in order: (1) request preprocessing / tokenization,
(2) prefill, (3) iterative model decode, (4) token sampling / selection, (5) detokenization / streaming.
KV management is not a temporal stage after generation — allocation, growth, paging, reuse,
eviction, and (in a disaggregated deployment) transfer occur throughout the whole request lifetime,
so we draw it as a state‑management plane that spans prefill and decode rather than a step that
follows them. Each compute phase has a resource ceiling: compute‑bound phases are limited by
TFLOPS, memory‑bound phases by GB/s of GPU HBM bandwidth. The architecture designer must
identify which phase is bottlenecked for the canonical scenario and then apply the appropriate
optimization—kernel fusion, cache reuse, or batching—to shift the bottleneck. The mental model
also emphasizes the role of token reuse: when many users share similar prompt prefixes, the shared
prefix’s KV need not be recomputed or re-allocated — removing prefill FLOPs and KV capacity —
while the KV bytes for that prefix are still read from HBM during decode, so the saving is in compute
and capacity, not in decode-time traffic. This reuse effect is difficult to quantify without workload

243

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

profiling, but it is a first‑order consideration in multi‑tenant serving. The model also captures the
interaction between sequence length and memory cost: attention quadraticities (O(L²) FLOPs and
O(L²) memory per head once the QK T /softmax score matrix is materialized) mean that long contexts
(9,000+ tokens) disproportionately strain both compute and HBM bandwidth, making kernel choice
(FlashAttention vs. SDPA) one of the first kernel‑level optimizations to validate for long‑context
prefill — not a demonstrated global ranking, since prefix reuse, KV precision, batching policy, P/D
scheduling, weight precision, admission control, and simply provisioning more prefill capacity can
each dominate depending on the measured workload.

15.3. Worked Example
Canonical scenario: ~2,000 registered users, ~5% concurrent (100 users), ~10 rps average / ~40
rps peak, prompt ~9,200 input tokens + ~300 output, the canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA
70B reference model (a 70B-class dense FP16 model), 8×H100 SXM host (3.35 TB/s HBM per GPU,
NVLink/NVSwitch intra-host — the Chapter 8 canonical H100 specification) with 640 GB GPU
memory.
Derived quantity 1 – concurrent users: 2,000 ×0.05 = 100 users.
Derived quantity 2 – peak token throughput demand: At 40 rps the workload mixes prefill
(input) and decode (output) tokens, and they hit the hardware differently. Prefill demand = 40 rps ×
9,200 = 368,000 input tokens/s; decode demand = 40 rps × 300 = 12,000 output tokens/s. These two
regimes must not be collapsed into one “380,000 tokens/s” when reasoning about compute, because
long-prompt prefill commonly occupies a higher-arithmetic-intensity regime and low-batch decode
commonly occupies a lower-arithmetic-intensity regime; whether either phase is actually computeor bandwidth-bound is a property of the model × workload × kernel × hardware operating point
(Chapter 8).
A hard terminology distinction the rest of this book relies on. Do not conflate two separate
statements:
• Kernel regime — the arithmetic intensity of the kernel relative to the roofline ridge (is this
one kernel compute-bound or bandwidth-bound?).
• Workload capacity deficit — the aggregate offered demand relative to the achievable service
capacity (does the deployment have enough compute/bandwidth/concurrency to absorb this
arrival rate?).
A workload can exceed a deployment’s capacity even when the underlying kernel is not computebound; conversely, a compute-bound kernel does not imply the deployed fleet lacks compute. In
the canonical scenario at peak, prefill exerts a large aggregate compute demand (a capacity-deficit
signal), while the prefill kernel’s high arithmetic intensity is what makes it land on the compute
plateau of the roofline — two different facts that happen to co-occur. Keep them separate.
Compute demand versus peak — and why this is not an MFU: A 70B FP16 transformer needs ≈2
×70×10⁹ FLOPs per generated token. The instantaneous prefill compute demand is 368,000 ×2 ×
70×10⁹ ≈ 5.15 ×10¹⁶ FLOPs/s — case (i), the linear-only lower bound of the Ch 8/15/16/17/20/22

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

244

prefill-FLOP convention; case (ii) (full-square conservative) gives 40 × 1.5099 PFLOP ≈ 6.04 ×10¹⁶
FLOPs/s and case (iii) (causal-triangle) 40 × 1.3989 PFLOP ≈ 5.60 ×10¹⁶ FLOPs/s — against a theoretical
FP16-dense peak of 8 ×989 TFLOPS = 7.91 ×10¹⁵ FLOPs/s for the 8×H100 host (989 TFLOPS per GPU,
Chapter 8 canonical). Taken naively this ratio is ~6.5× under case (i) (~7.6× under (ii), ~7.1× under (iii))
— a demand that exceeds a single host’s peak. That is a legitimate and important architectural signal:
a single 8×H100 host cannot prefill the peak arrival rate on the naive dense-FLOP model, so prefill
either needs to be spread across burst headroom, handled by prompt/prefix caching, disaggregated
(P/D separation), or absorbed by queueing headroom at off-peak. What it must not be called is
“MFU = 6.5”: MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is by definition achieved realities divided by peak —
a utilization ratio that cannot exceed 1.0. Presenting a ratio above 1 for a utilization metric is a
unit/modeling error. The honest formulation separates the two quantities. The first is a congestion
check: is the arrival-rate FLOP demand above or below peak? Here it is ~6.5× above for prefill, so the
host is short of prefill capacity at peak and must lean on caching/batching/queueing. The second
is an achieved MFU : measured device FLOPs ÷ peak, which we only report from a real benchmark.
For illustration we suppose it lands in the 30–40 % range for FlashAttention-based inference. The
decode FLOP demand at 12,000 tokens/s is ≈ 1.68 ×10¹⁵ ÷ 7.91 ×10¹⁵ ≈ 0.21, i.e. ~21 % of the host
FP16 peak — a demand ratio on the compute axis, not an achieved MFU and not evidence of decode
headroom, because decode is limited by bytes/token and KV residency; the actual achieved value
must come from the target serving benchmark. On the bandwidth axis the same 12,000 tokens/s
at a 17-request decode batch streams the 140 GB of weights once per step — 140 GB × (12,000/17)
≈ 98.8 TB/s of demand against the host’s 8 × 3.35 = 26.8 TB/s HBM peak, a ~3.7× ratio — which
is the axis on which decode actually binds. The architectural conclusion, that there is no single
bottleneck for the whole request, stands — and it must be argued phase by phase. At the canonical
peak, prefill shows a workload capacity deficit — aggregate compute demand above the host’s peak (it
needs more FLOPs/s than the host can supply, and leans on caching/queueing). Decode is primarily
memory-bandwidth constrained, and maximum concurrency is constrained by KV residency. Each
phase is established from arithmetic intensity and the roofline (Chapter 8), never from an impossible
“MFU > 1.” None of them is the same statement as “the prefill kernel is compute-bound.” The ~6.5×
figure is a lower-bound impossibility check (the host cannot meet peak on the naive dense model),
not a fleet-sizing estimate: the real fleet count comes from the achieved prefill tokens/s under the
actual latency SLO and representative traffic mix (Ch 17/20), and it is sensitive to cache-hit rate,
input-length distribution, batch schedule, and sustainable efficiency — the 6.5× only says “more than
one host is required,” not “how many.” The bridge to the fleet screens: 6.5 hosts at 100% MFU → 6.5
÷ 0.35 = 18.6 → 19 hosts at the 35% MFU planning screen (case (i)) — the same fact at two efficiency
assumptions. The equivalent decode-side check, which the 19/21-host screen does not include:
decode reads the weights once per step, so bytes/token = 140 GB/B + 24.9 GB of KV per request (at
the KV-resident B = 17: 140/17 ≈ 8.24 GB + 24.9 GB ≈ 33.1 GB), and at 12,000 decode tokens/s the
demand is ≈ 12,000 × 33.1 GB ≈ 398 TB/s against the host’s 8 × 3.35 = 26.8 TB/s HBM peak — ≈15×

245

over. The resulting per-host decode ceiling is ≈ 26.8 TB/s ÷ 33.1 GB ≈ 809 tok/s/host, i.e. ⌈12,000/809⌉
≈ 15 hosts to hold the peak decode rate at that batch. The 19/21-host prefill-and-KV screen above is
therefore not a host count on its own: it is prefill-and-KV derived and must be combined with this
decode-bandwidth screen (and both with measured SLO-goodput), because whichever axis binds
sets the fleet.
KV cache memory footprint: The KV cache grows linearly with cached context and layers; it
must never be computed per-layer and then treated as the whole-model total. For the canonical
full-MHA reference geometry (80 layers, hidden dimension 8,192 — the 70B-class teaching model,
not a universal 70B property), the per-token footprint across ALL layers is 2 × layers × hidden ×
bytes = 2 ×80 ×8,192 ×2 = 2,621,440 B ≈ 2.62 MB/token (2.5 MiB; canonical value from Chapter 7) —
not the 32 KiB (32,768 B) that a single-layer calculation would suggest. For a 9,500-token context,
one user’s KV cache is therefore ≈9,500 ×2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB, not ~311 MB (9,500 × 32,768 B). For
the canonical workload’s ~86 average in-flight requests at 10 rps (Lexec = λ × Wexec ≈ 10 × 8.6; see
Ch 4 — note ~86 is the request occupancy, distinct from the ~100 active-user population), the total
KV cache would be ≈86 × 24.9 GB ≈ 2,140 GB — which does not fit the 640 GB GPU pool; using
the canonical practical KV budget (640 GB − 140 GB weights − ~64 GB runtime/workspace ≈ 436
GB), only ≈17.5 concurrent requests (9,500-token KV each) fit on-host for KV (436 GB ÷ 24.9037
GB; conservative integer floor 17 (aggregate bound; per-rank and fragmentation must be checked
separately)) — the 436 GB is already net of the 140 GB weights and ~64 GB runtime. This is a
decisive, order-of-magnitude correction to the intuitive picture: long-context KV is a first-order
memory constraint, and the architect sizes concurrency by KV capacity, not by the small per-layer
number. Doubling context to 19,000 tokens pushes per-user KV to ~49.8 GB (19,000 × 2.62 MB) and
halves on-host concurrency to ~8.75 (436 GB ÷ 49.8 GB; conservative integer floor 8). The canonical
unit-check rule (quantity/unit/formula/substitution/result/sanity) catches this class of error: if 9,500
tokens × 2,621,440 B/token ≈ 24.9 GB does not reconcile with the intended ~311 MB single-layer
counterexample, the unit layer-count has been dropped.
Attention FLOP comparison: Scaled‑dot‑product attention (SDPA) for 9,200‑token prompts. Note
the 2P/token figure above approximates the parameterized dense‑matmul work per token (2 ×
parameters); it does not capture all sequence‑length‑dependent attention work, which is accounted
for separately here. Attention is two matmuls per head over the full L-token prefill — Q·K T then ·V
— each a multiply‑accumulate of L²·d, so in FLOPs (2 per MAC) the per‑layer cost is ≈ 4 × L² × d_
model, where L=9,200 and d_model=8,192. That is 4 × 9,200² × 8,192 ≈ 2.8 × 10¹² FLOPs per layer (the
full 64 heads; the per‑head figure 4 × 9,200² × 128 ≈ 4.3 × 10¹⁰ must be multiplied by the number of
heads, not quoted alone). Across 80 layers that is ≈ 2.2 × 10¹⁴ FLOPs — the quadratic attention term
that grows dominant at long context, matching Chapter 8’s 4·n_layers·L²·d formula: the attention
term is ≈17% of the parameter-matmul FLOPs (≈15% of total forward FLOPs) at 9.2K (Fig 22.1) — that
is the full-square case (ii) of the Ch 8 convention; under a causal mask (case (iii)) the triangle halves
to ≈8.6% of 2NL (≈8% of total).

figure 15.1: FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic. Before (naive materialized attention),
the intermediate attention matrix is materialized to HBM and re-read, so every query block re-streams
the full K/V row-block — many HBM round-trips (arrow legend is panel-specific: in the BEFORE panel
arrows are double-headed — up = K/V tile read, down = the L×L intermediate write; in the AFTER
panel they are single-headed upward — K/V tile reads only, because the per-tile result is accumulated
on-chip and no L×L intermediate is written to HBM). After (FlashAttention-class fused kernel), the
computation is tiled and fused so each K/V tile is read into on-chip memory once for that tile and the
result is accumulated in place — far fewer HBM round-trips. Scope of the “read once” claim: the
tile-level on-chip reuse is per-tile; it is not a guarantee that every K/V element is read exactly once
globally across all query blocks (the exact number of K/V re-reads depends on the tile scheduling,
sequence length, and SRAM size — see the original I/O analysis in the FlashAttention papers). The
attention result is the same mathematical target; the gain is fewer HBM round-trips, not a change to
the attention mathematics. In matched units, the fused kernel’s HBM traffic is Θ(L²d²/M) against
Θ(L²) for the materialized path — a reduction factor of M/d² (≈6× at d = 128, M ≈ 192 KB of fp16), not
a lower order in L. (Floating-point caveat: the tiled accumulation order differs from the naive path,
so results are equivalent in exact arithmetic but can differ in the last bits under finite precision — a

247

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

FlashAttention is not “faster attention” in the sense that it does less arithmetic. It computes the
exact same Q·K T , softmax, ·V sequence. What changes is where the intermediate lives: a naive kernel
writes the L×L attention matrix to HBM and reads it back, so the materialized intermediate itself
is O(L²) in memory; FlashAttention avoids materializing that full L×L matrix in HBM and instead
tiles the computation so each tile stays in on-chip registers/shared memory with the softmax done
online — substantially reducing HBM reads/writes through tiled on-chip computation (the precise I/O
complexity is more nuanced than a clean quadratic-to-linear swap, but the materialized-intermediate
traffic is what drops — baseline: the naive materialized-L×L path; reframe the gain as bytes/request to
measure on the target stack). Because the arithmetic intensity — FLOP/byte — rises (same FLOPs, far
fewer bytes moved), the kernel moves up the hardware ladder of Fig 8.1 toward the compute-bound
region, even though the model and the math are unchanged. That is the whole reason the speed-up
is workload-dependent: it is largest for long contexts where the O(L²) intermediate dominates, and
negligible for short ones where HBM traffic is already small. It is also why the improvement should
be measured (Ch. 14) rather than quoted from a published “2–3×” figure that was never portable.

15.4. Measurement
To validate the mental model we instrument the serving stack with three metric families: (a)
token latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) per request type, (b) GPU utilization (SM active, memory
bandwidth via Nsight), and (c) KV cache size over time; plus queue depth (prefill and decode),
prefix-cache hit rate, SLO-compliance rate, effective bytes/token, and KV fragmentation/activesequence count — the evidence column of the Optimization Decision Map is produced from these
families. A minimal benchmark runs 40 rps — a saturation run on one host (6.5× the ~56,500 tok/s
prefill ceiling at 100% MFU — theoretical peak), whose queue is expected to grow — with warm‑up,
recording offered load alongside p95 TTFT and p95 TPOT/ITL separately (report p95 only at offered
loads ≤ the host’s admission capacity, ~2 rps per host: 17 slots ÷ 8.6 s), and measuring the GPU
memory fraction consumed by KV cache. Repeating with different batch sizes (1, 4, 16, 32) reveals
the throughput‑latency knee. The illustrative numbers below are scenario values to be measured
on the target stack, not vendor or published figures: beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises
(implying a knee near batch 4) because kernel launch overhead is amortized but inter‑request
token interleaving increases per‑step HBM traffic and scheduler fairness/queueing delay (the KV
working set exceeds L2 at any batch ≥ 1, so L2 eviction cannot be the batch-specific cause). On
the FlashAttention “traffic reduction” claim, be precise about the units: one often sees (the
figures below are hypothetical, not a cited measurement) a FlashAttention‑class kernel reported at a
different achieved HBM bandwidth than a naive SDPA kernel (illustratively FlashAttention‑class ~400
GB/s achieved vs naive SDPA ~150 GB/s achieved for 9,200‑token contexts). That is a rate, not a byte
count (bytes = rate × time), so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run does not by itself establish
fewer bytes; the reduction follows from the mechanism (the L×L intermediate is never materialized)
and must be confirmed as bytes/request under a matched workload. A bandwidth figure alone does

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

248

not establish that fewer bytes/request were transferred — it only shows the kernel’s achieved memory
throughput. To claim a traffic reduction, compare the bytes transferred per request (or read/write
transaction counters) under a matched workload; the FlashAttention advantage shows up there as
fewer materialized/intermediate bytes, not as a low raw bandwidth. And separate the two cache
concepts: “cold‑start KV warm‑up” (populating the KV cache blocks for a new context) is different
from “model‑weight loading” (streaming the 140 GB weights into HBM) and from CUDA/JIT kernel
warm‑up. A 70B cold‑start that reuses cached weights is far faster than one that must load them
from scratch — but these are distinct effects, not one number. Set these illustrative figures from the
target host’s profiler before quoting them as fact. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
The evidence families above also cover multi-GPU communication measurements: when timing
collectives, summing all collective durations can overstate exposed cost when operations overlap.
Subtracting every overlapped duration can understate cost when communication slows concurrent
compute. The measured quantity is the change in the end-to-end critical path, supported by compute
and communication traces. CPU progress threads, HBM, device links and NICs remain shared
resources even when their work appears in separate profiler lanes.1
Goodput vs. Batch Size: Two Levers — Prefix Reuse and Batching
The capacity response to batch size under peak load. Two distinct levers act on different phases:
batching raises decode goodput (right plot) until bandwidth saturates, while prefix caching lowers
the prefill work per repeated prompt (left plot) so more prefill‑recompute headroom remains under
the same host. They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck itself is unaffected
by caching, but the two levers couple through KV capacity — prefix reuse frees KV blocks, which
raises achievable concurrency and hence the decode batch, so the right-hand curve can shift; the
coupling is a capacity effect, not a compute effect.

The Optimization Decision Map
The measurement section tells us what is slow; this map tells us which lever to try next. It is organized
as a symptom → bottleneck → evidence → candidate mechanism chain, so the architect diagnoses
before acting rather than applying a known technique because it is fashionable. Every mechanism
below is a hypothesis to benchmark, not a guaranteed win — each trades one resource for
another, and whether it helps depends on the measured workload and hardware (Ch. 14).

Two cautions. First, do not read the table as “technique X fixes symptom Y”: the same symptom
can come from two bottlenecks (high TPOT with a bandwidth-saturated GPU is different from high
TPOT with a capacity-capped GPU), so the evidence column matters as much as the symptom. Second,
the P/D-disaggregation row and the interconnect/parallelism row are the expensive, structural levers
— they are worth testing only after the cheaper in-kernel and in-scheduler mechanisms have been
measured and shown insufficient, because they change capacity, orchestration, and cost, not just a
kernel constant.
Weight quantization is a candidate intervention when weight capacity or weight traffic is limiting.
After the change, the bottleneck may move to KV access, attention, collective communication,
conversion kernels or queueing. The next measurement therefore repeats the workload and SLO test
rather than inferring a gain from checkpoint size. More KV headroom can permit a larger batch, but

253

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

a larger batch can also increase waiting time or decode-step duration. The useful operating point is
the one that preserves task quality and request-level SLOs, not the one that fills the most memory.
Chapter 7’s storage sensitivity and Fig 7.4 describe an input to this decision, not its performance
result.

Two Mechanisms, Read as Mechanisms
Two entries in the map deserve their mechanism spelled out, because they are frequently cited by
reported speed-up numbers rather than by how they work.
Speculative decoding. The idea is to turn one slow serial step into a draft-then-verify pair. A
small, cheap draft model proposes a candidate sequence of tokens; the larger target model then
verifies all of them in a single batched forward pass, accepting the ones that match its own distribution
(the exact acceptance rule — not mere token agreement — is stated in the next paragraph). The loop is:
draft → propose candidates → target verifies → accept a prefix → continue from the last accepted
token. Why this can be faster: the expensive part of decode is not the arithmetic per token but the
serialization — each target-model step streams the weights from HBM. If the draft can propose k
tokens that the target accepts in one verification pass, the target’s expensive weight-stream is spent
once on k tokens instead of k times on one — a genuine reduction in HBM round-trips (the same
resource the FlashAttention discussion is about, but at the whole-model scale). Why it is not free: the
draft costs extra compute, the verification pass itself has cost, and the acceptance rate (how many
of the proposed tokens the target actually accepts) decides the win — a low acceptance rate means
the draft and verification are spent for almost nothing. It is therefore workload/model/hardware
dependent: a draft that closely matches the target (or a workload that is highly predictable) accepts
more. No published speed-up is portable: a “6×” from one model/paper is a statement about
that evaluation, not a guarantee for a different model or serving stack — measure it on the target
workload or treat it as a hypothesis.
One subtlety about “matching its own distribution”: the target does not simply accept the draft
tokens that happen to agree. Under stochastic sampling, accepting a proposed token outright (rather
than by the exact-speculative-sampling correction that re-weighs each accepted and rejected token by
the target’s posterior) can bias the output distribution away from the target model’s true distribution.
The distribution-preserving result holds only when each proposed token is accepted or rejected by the
exact acceptance/sampling procedure (the modified-rejection-sampling step of Leviathan et al., “Fast
Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding,” arXiv:2211.17192; see the Sources chapter),
which re-normalizes the continuation at each step. For greedy/argmax decoding the agreement test
is exact; for temperature/prompt-driven sampling it is not, and the acceptance criterion must be the
correction procedure, not mere token equality.
Chunked prefill. A very long prompt produces a large prefill operation that can monopolize the
compute for hundreds of milliseconds, stalling concurrent latency-sensitive decode work. Chunked
prefill splits that prefill into smaller pieces and interleaves them with decode steps in the scheduler,

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

254

so the GPU keeps serving decode between prefill chunks instead of blocking on one burst. The causal
chain: long prompt → large prefill → scheduler/resource monopolization → decode interference →
TTFT degrades for the queued prompt while TPOT degrades for in-flight decode requests (a trade-off
across request classes) → chunked prefill as a scheduling mechanism to bound the per-phase burst.
The trade-off is not “smaller is better”: a smaller chunk reduces the decode stall but adds scheduler
overhead (more per-chunk bookkeeping, potentially lower prefill throughput from less parallelism
within a chunk), so chunk size is an empirically-chosen middle — measure the goodput/latency knee
rather than assume.

15.5. Common Mistakes
Over‑provisioning batch size to chase throughput: Increasing batch size improves TFLOPS utiliza­
tion but degrades p99 latency: under continuous batching a larger decode batch lengthens each decode
step, so every in-flight request sees a higher ITL/TPOT, and arriving requests also queue behind
fuller steps (static batching is worse still — requests wait for a larger batch to fill before they start).
The designer must balance batch‑size‑driven arithmetic gain against tail‑latency penalty. A practical
illustrative rule of thumb: choose the smallest batch size that keeps MFU above ~25 % while keeping
p95 latency under the SLO target (the 25 % threshold and the knee are scenario values — measure them
on the target workload). Ignoring KV cache growth: A 70B model with 9,500‑token contexts consumes
≈24.9 GB of KV per in-flight request (≈2.62 MB/token × 9,500, max end-of-generation). Without cache
eviction, compression, or a concurrency cap, even ~17.5 concurrent requests would exhaust the host’s
canonical practical KV budget (~436 GB after weights + runtime), so ~86 concurrent in-flight requests
(§3: 10 rps × 8.6 s — request occupancy, not the ~100 active-user population) require either multiple
hosts, much shorter contexts, or KV compression (FP8/8-bit). But be precise about what “evicting”
a context means, because it is not one action. Three distinct mechanisms exist. (a) Evicting an
idle/inactive prefix-cache entry — a cached prefix not currently in service — is safe, because no active
request depends on it and it can be recomputed on reuse. (b) Offloading or recomputing the KV of an
active request whose context is still being generated changes nothing about semantics, but it costs a
recompute or a transfer when the request resumes. (c) Deliberate sliding-window or context-truncation
strategies drop older tokens of an active request’s context. This changes the model’s effective
context: it alters what the attention can attend to, and it is a semantics change, not merely a memory
optimization. LRU of inactive cached prefixes is different from truncating active KV. Do not conflate
them. KV quantization is a separate, orthogonal lever that cuts the per-token footprint without
changing context length or the attention window; it introduces a numerical approximation (FP8
rounding) that must be quality-validated (Ch 14) before it is relied on (FP8 ≈2.62 → ~1.31 MB/token
— exactly 50% of FP16 by raw tensor byte-halving, the same FP8 constant defined in Ch 7; vLLM’s
cited 54% [S6] is a decode inter-token-latency slope, a latency metric, not a memory ratio, and
any allocator block/metadata overhead is not vendor-measured). Using scaled‑dot‑product attention
without FlashAttention: For long contexts (9,200+ tokens) the O(L²) intermediate makes the naive

255

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

kernel memory-traffic-bound (it dominates the attention kernel’s HBM traffic). FlashAttention fuses
read‑write‑compute and reduces HBM traffic by ~3–5× ([ILLUSTRATIVE] — kernel- and lengthdependent; measure bytes/request on the target stack), raising effective arithmetic intensity. This is
one of the highest-impact kernel-level choices (it sits among prefix caching, KV-precision, batching,
and P/D disaggregation as a major lever, not the single deciding one), and it pays off specifically
when memory-bound; for moderate lengths (2,000–4,000 tokens) the HBM bandwidth reduction can
translate to a ~1.3–1.8× attention-kernel throughput gain on H100 (illustrative — bench the specific
kernel on the target hardware) — attention-kernel throughput, not end-to-end request throughput:
attention is only ~4–8% of forward FLOPs at 2–4K tokens, so the end-to-end gain is bounded near
4–8% even for a perfect attention kernel. Neglecting kernel launch overhead: In dynamic‑batching
setups, each new token generation can trigger a kernel launch. Without continuous batching or
token‑level fusion, the kernel-launch overhead (illustratively ~10–20 % of GPU time on H100-class
parts at this traffic) can artificially depress measured MFU.

15.6. Architecture Consequence
The measurement and mistake analysis drive three architecture decisions for the canonical
deployment: (1) FlashAttention‑2 for the attention computation (attention-I/O fusion: tiled, online
softmax, no materialized L×L score matrix); separately, fuse the three QKV projections into a single
GEMM and fuse RoPE into the attention prologue where the serving engine supports them, to
minimize HBM transactions — each a distinct lever with its own validation; (2) continuous batching,
with the maximum decode-step batch granularity chosen empirically from the measured good­
put/latency knee (distinct from the Two Mechanisms subsection’s prefill token-budget chunking)
(a maximum decode-step batch of 4–8, set by the measured knee — an [ILLUSTRATIVE] starting
point, not the recommendation; extend the §4 sweep grid (1, 4, 16, 32) to include the chosen value);
(3) KV cache management via FP8 KV quantization (≈2.62 → ~1.31 MB/token — exactly 50% of FP16
by raw tensor byte-halving, cutting a 9,500‑token per‑user KV to ~12.45 GB; vLLM’s 54% [S6] is a
decode inter-token-latency slope, a latency metric, not a memory ratio, and any block/metadata
overhead is not vendor-measured) plus length‑based eviction of inactive prefix-cache entries (never
truncation of an active request’s context — active KV is offloaded or recomputed, per §5), so that
under the same ~436 GB practical KV budget on‑host concurrency rises from ~17.5 to ~35.0 concurrent
full‑context requests (436 GB ÷ 12.45 GB). FP8 KV quantization is adopted only after the Ch 14 quality
test passes; the 17.5 → 35.0 concurrency and 10-host FP8 figures assume that gate is met. These
choices together would change the basis of the throughput figure, not raise it like-for-like: ~8.5K
tokens/s (raw, no flash — a prefill-dominated, single-request rate, 9,200 ÷ ~1.08 s ≈ 8.5K tok/s per
Chapter 4, not a batch‑1 decode rate: batch‑1 decode is ~40–50 tok/s, Chapters 2/5/6) and ~35,000
tok/s [ILLUSTRATIVE, mini-case per-host outcome] at the canonical context (with flash, continuous
batch) are different bases, not a like-for-like gain — compare phase-resolved rates after measurement,
per Chapter 17’s reconciliation box. Three per-host quantities must be kept apart rather than merged
into one “achievable range”: (a) bounds — the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul-only ceiling 7.91×10¹⁵

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

256

FLOP/s ÷ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOP/token ≈ 56,500 tok/s under the linear-only case (i) (a 2N-only figure), lowered
to ≈48,000 tok/s by the case-(ii) attention term at the canonical 9,200-token context (≈52,000 under
causal case (iii)); (b) the planning screen — at the 35% MFU assumption, ~19,800 tok/s/host (7.91×10¹⁵ ×
0.35 ÷ 1.4×10¹¹), i.e. ~2.15 rps of the canonical request; (c) the mini-case outcome — ~35,000 tok/s/host
at ≈62% MFU under case (i) (§8), an illustrative measured-style result with its own basis, not the top
of an achievable range. 70,000 tok/s on one host would be ~124% MFU (a 2N-only check), so that
figure is the two-host aggregate of the mini-case below (≈35,000 tok/s/host at its ~2× second-host
factor) — the exact figure must come from the target benchmark — while keeping the host’s 640 GB
for weights plus KV. A fourth decision, raised by the mini‑case (Ch11 §11.8) and not yet validated, is
to design the request‑routing layer for KV cache affinity: when a user re‑submits a request, routing
to the same host avoids cache warm‑up penalties and keeps p99 latency under the target SLO.

15.7. What We Still Don’t Know
How does token‑level sparsity in user prompts affect the actual FLOP/token cost, and how does
prefix/KV reuse interact with it? Two separate open questions: (a) token‑level sparsity in prompts
(skipping computation for selected tokens) could reduce the effective FLOP count, and (b) prefix/KV
reuse (few‑shot prefixes, cached query prefixes) removes prefill work and KV capacity — different
mechanisms with different resource effects; the savings depend on the sparsity pattern and the
attention implementation. What is the optimal continuous‑batching admission and scheduling policy —
maximum decode‑step batch, fairness, and prefill/decode interleaving — for the canonical workload? The
policy trades decode throughput against tail latency, so its knee must be measured on the target stack.
What is the optimal chunked‑prefill chunk size as a function of request arrival distribution (Poisson
vs. bursty) and tail‑latency targets? Analytical models assume Poisson arrivals, but real user traffic
exhibits bursts (e.g. social‑media events) that may require larger chunks or alternative back‑pressure
mechanisms. Can in‑flight KV eviction/pruning (attention-score-based retention — H2O-, SnapKV- or
TinK-style) reduce memory pressure without increasing p99 latency? Keeping only the highest-attentionweight key/value tokens (heavy-hitter retention; the H2O line, Zhang et al., arXiv:2306.14048, and
the KV-cache-eviction family built on it) is promising, but the accuracy‑latency trade‑off needs
empirical validation across model families. How does multi‑tenant isolation—guarding one user’s cache
from another’s—translate to multi‑GPU scaling when the model exceeds a single GPU’s 80 GB? Model
parallelism (pipeline or tensor) adds communication overhead; the performance cost of moving KV
cache between GPUs during tenant rotation is an open question.

15.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Second Host: a Kernel/Batching Gain, Not a
Capacity Win
A new deployment adds 500 registered users (traffic rises to ~12.5/50 rps at the same 5 % concurrency
profile). Scope: this mini-case is a single-/dual-host micro-benchmark, not the fleet configuration
— at 50 rps the canonical fleet is ⌈430/17⌉ = 26 hosts at full utilization (~37 at the 70% target on the ρ
= 1 u-only screen, or 39 working hosts (40 with the N−1 spare) under the book’s provisioning

257

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

policy that also multiplies the independent ρ = 0.95 — ⌈430/(17 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈38.04⌉, Chapter
4), just as the 40 rps peak needs ~21 on the FP16 KV reference (Scope note above; with §6’s FP8
KV, ⌈344/35⌉ = 10, bounded below by the 35%-MFU prefill screen of 19 hosts under case (i) (21
under case (iii), 22 under case (ii)) — the FP8-KV screen of 10 lies below it, so prefill compute binds).
The team provisions a second 8×H100 host and (in this worked example) runs the benchmark with
continuous batching and FlashAttention‑2. The p95 queueing/scheduling delay ahead of prefill —
not TTFT, which at this profile is dominated by the canonical ~1.08 s prefill (Chapters 4/8; Chapter
14’s illustrative case assumes p95 TTFT 1.9 s — explicitly “hypothetical, not a measurement made
for this book” — and at a different, far lighter load of 1.3 req/s, not this ~12.5/50 rps profile) — drops
from 320 ms (single host, batch‑1) to 140 ms (dual host, continuous batch) — both latencies quoted
at the same sub‑capacity offered load used for the latency measurement (the ~12.5 rps average,
below a host’s admission capacity; the 50 rps peak is a saturation run, where the single-host queue
grows without bound rather than draining) — while the saturated capacity rates rise from ~8.5K to
70,000 tokens/s (~8.5K = the same prefill-dominated raw single-host rate labeled in §6, a saturated
capacity rate, not a batch‑1 decode rate; 70,000 = the two-host aggregate with continuous batching +
FlashAttention‑2, ≈35,000 tok/s/host). The MFU stabilizes at ~62 % under the linear-only convention
(case (i)) — 70,000 tok/s × 2 × 70×10⁹ FLOP/token = 9.8 ×10¹⁵ FLOP/s against the two-host 15.82
×10¹⁵ FLOP/s peak (half of the ~124 % one-host figure in §6); including the attention term at 9.2K
context (case (ii)) it is ≈73 % of peak — the aggregate mixes prefill and decode, and the attention
share depends on the phase mix (§3); the 38 in Table 15-1’s illustrative load pressure note is that
table’s congestion label, not an MFU. These are [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO RESULT] values — an
illustrative benchmark outcome, not a home-lab measurement; the exact figures must come from
a deployment benchmark on the target hardware/stack (Chapter 14). The remaining question is
whether the cross‑host request routing layer can maintain affinity KV cache residency, avoiding cache
warm‑up penalties on re‑requests. The ∼20 % affinity throughput gain and the ∼2.1 s cold-start KV
warm-up cost are themselves [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO RESULT] values, not measured results.
Do not read the 8.2× throughput jump as a capacity-side win. It is dominated by the kernel/batch­
ing change (batch‑1 no‑flash → continuous batching with FlashAttention‑2), which is worth most of
the multiplicative gain, plus ~2× from adding the second host — the two are not separable from
this single outcome number. This is a per‑host kernel/batching improvement story, not a claim that
“more GPUs = 8.2×.” Were we adding a second host with no kernel/batching change, the expected
throughput gain would be roughly the host-pool ratio (≈2×), and the fleet-sizing consequence is
computed separately in Ch 16–17 from the service-time model, not from this mini-case’s aggregate
number.

Concurrency here is in‑flight requests, computed as λ·W with the canonical per‑request service
time W ≈ 8.6 s (the Little’s‑law discipline of Chapter 17 — never equate in‑flight concurrency with a
number of registered or simultaneously‑online users). The three rps values are the canonical average
(~10 rps) and peak (~40 rps) plus an illustrative light case (~2 rps) — a low‑traffic shape illustration, not
a third canonical rate; the resulting in‑flight concurrency (17/86/344) is what must be compared against
a host’s concurrent‑request ceiling. KV per request uses the canonical ~2.62 MB/token × 9,500 ≈ 24.9 GB
— a per-request* (per in-flight request) figure, not a per-user one: a user with several requests in

Performance Engineering: From “It Works” to “It Meets the SLO”

260

flight holds several times that, and the per-user figure depends on that user’s in-flight count. Context
tokens/req is the 9,500‑token canonical context (9,200 input + 300 output), identical across the three
regimes. Illustrative load pressure — kept in prose here, not as a table column — is a dimensionless
labeled score (0–100), not MFU: the 12/38/52 values (light/typical/peak) are a demand-side/congestion
label for teaching shape [ILLUSTRATIVE], on a stated scale in which the light regime sits near 12,
the typical regime near 38 and the peak regime near 52 as the offered load presses harder on the
regime’s dominant bottleneck (compute → KV memory → KV + inter‑GPU bandwidth). The scale
is ordinal and scenario-chosen — it has no FLOP numerator or denominator behind it (for
computed ratios, use the table’s prefill-demand ÷ ceiling and KV-demand ÷ budget columns), so it
is not a percentage of anything hardware-achieved and must not be read as one. It is deliberately
not called MFU: achieved MFU requires a measured (or explicitly modeled) achieved FLOP/s ÷ peak
FLOP/s (Chapter 8’s definition), and the peak score of 52 exceeds the ~30–40 % sustained H100 FP16
MFU of Chapter 8 precisely because it is a load-pressure label, not a utilization measurement — it
is not a claim that a real kernel reaches 52 % utilization. To report a real MFU here, add a defined
numerator/denominator pair from a Chapter 14 benchmark. The two bottleneck columns split the §3
axes: kernel regime (a kernel property — it does not change across these three load regimes, so only
the row that states one carries a label) and binding workload constraint (the row’s tighter computed
ratio; in the Light row KV binds first at 0.97× versus prefill’s 0.33×). Both reflect the roofline logic of
Chapter 8.*

chapter 16.
TCO: The Total Cost Reality Check

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to answer the question every stakeholder actually asks —
what does this really cost? — with a defensible number, not a guess. We will build a total-cost-ofownership model that separates capital, operating, and opportunity costs, then price the canonical
workload across three delivery modes: self-hosted on our own cards, cloud GPU instances, and a
managed inference API. After this chapter, “we save money by self-hosting” is supported or refuted
by arithmetic under the stated assumptions, with sensitivity analysis, and the break-even point
between modes is explicit.

16.1. Concept
Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) is the sum of everything required to deliver a capability over its
lifetime, not just the price tag of the hardware or the per-token rate. It has three cost families:
1. Capital (capex) — the one-time cost of the cards, servers, networking, racks, and cooling that
make up the system. For self-hosted inference this dominates up front: an 8×H100 server with
networking and infrastructure carries a large price. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
2. Operating (opex) — the recurring cost of running it: electricity and cooling, staff, soft­
ware/licenses, cloud instance rental, and replacement/amortization of hardware. For cloud and
managed API this is the whole cost; for self-hosted it compounds on capex.
3. Opportunity — the cost of the alternative not taken: the team time spent operating vs building,

261

TCO: The Total Cost Reality Check

262

the delay to market, and the engineering hours that do not scale with either card or token
counts. This is the most omitted term and can be the largest in engineering-heavy orgs.
The architect’s job is not to minimize capex, nor opex, nor provider bill — it is to minimize the
number that matters for the organization’s decision, which usually means total cost per useful
request at the required quality and SLO.

16.2. Mental Model
TCO is a utilization-weighted average over the whole system, not a sticker price. Three
mental moves keep the arithmetic honest:
• Amortize, don’t stare at the price tag. A $350K server is an asset consumed over ~5 years;
spread it into dollars-per-month, then into dollars-per-request, before comparing to a per-token
API rate. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
• Follow the token, not the GPU. The thing being bought is completed, SLO-meeting requests.
Two systems with the same card count can differ ~10× in cost per request through two
independent levers: 3× from higher per-card capacity (kernels, quantization) × 3.4× from
higher effective utilization (batching, SLO-goodput per slot) ≈ 10×. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
• Include what does not scale. Staff, power, networking engineering, and the latency of
procurement are sunk or recurring whether utilization is 20% or 80%. A low-cost-per-card
system that burns engineers can be the most expensive.
The decision shape is a break-even graph: at low volume, managed/cloud-and-shut-down wins
(no idle capex); at high volume, self-hosted cards amortize below the per-token rate. The crossover
point is what we compute.

16.3. Worked Example
16.3.1. Size the fleet first, then price it
TCO is meaningless until we know how many hosts the workload actually requires. A common
sizing mistake is to start from a single host: a single 8×H100 host can only clear ~2.0 req/s under
the KV-slot-based analytical UPPER bound on admitted request completion rate, conditional on
an assumed mean KV residency time (Chapter 17/20), so it cannot serve even the canonical 10 rps
average, let alone the 40 rps peak. We therefore size the fleet first (Ch 17) and price it second.

Two things about that table are load-bearing. First, the ~2.0 rps per-host figure (C/W = 17/8.6 =

conditional on an assumed mean KV residency time — a capacity screen inside the KV screen,
defined in full below (“What kind of number is ~2.0 req/s?’ ’) and in the Evidence boundary panel
(Preface); and the lower bound on host count derives FROM it (⌈40 ÷ 1.9767⌉ = ⌈20.24⌉ = 21 hosts
— a per-host ceiling becomes a fleet floor at that one division); the “throughput ⌈40/2.0⌉ row” and
the KV row are algebraically the same bound. Second, the prefill rows are a genuinely independent
compute screen — the scope ledger’s 5 avg / 19 peak, ⌈368,000 ÷ 19,780⌉ = 19 at peak under case
(i), linear-only — and they are deliberately NOT forced to equal the KV row; the same screen
