×1.1723) gives 6 / 22, so which FLOP-counting case is stated decides whether the compute
screen (19), the KV screen (21), or the compute screen again (22) governs the peak. Every
host count in this table is an illustrative planning screen — NOT measured SLO-goodput: the
prefill/compute rows depend on their stated FLOP-counting case and the 35% MFU assumption,
while the KV-residency row depends on the slot budget and the assumed KV-residency time, not on
35% MFU. The third scope, N_SLO (queueing / goodput under concurrency), has no number here
because it is unmeasured: it is a named scope, not a row.
So the canonical workload’s peak KV screen is 21 hosts (⌈344/17⌉, zero spare — the headline
policy is a minimum integer count, no reserve; 21 × 17/8.6 = 41.51 rps is ~3.8% headroom above the 40
rps peak), and the average needs 6 — a fleet, not one box. Ch 17’s whole-slot convention floors C to
17 first and gives 21; equivalently the floored whole-slot rule gives 21 — this TCO prices that 21-host
scenario, and a one-host difference changes no mode comparison. FP8 KV quantization changes only
the KV arithmetic in this screen: the raw FP8 byte factor 0.5 gives a hard floor of 35 slots BEFORE
efficiency and the host ceil, so the FP8 KV screen is ⌈344/35.0⌉ = 10 at peak (11 at the 95% scheduling
factor) — KV-residency arithmetic on a screen, not an assertion that real deployments halve in
size; FP8 weights or FP8 compute would change other screens and are not modeled here; measured
allocation, compute and goodput are absent, and the independent prefill and unmeasured SLO scopes
do not shrink with it. Every self-hosted TCO figure below is scaled to a named peak fleet — 21
hosts (KV screen / case (i) compute screen) or 22 hosts (case (ii) full-square compute screen),
both priced in §16.3; pricing a single host would understate the cost by roughly 21–22×.
Mode 2 (cloud) is instead priced on a paid-occupancy input (host-hours) and Mode 3 (managed API)
on served volume, so neither is scaled to a host count.
What kind of number is ~2.0 req/s? The per-host rate C_KV / E[W_KV-resident] ≈ 17 /
8.6 ≈ 2.0 req/s is a KV-slot-based analytical UPPER bound on admitted request comple­

tion rate, conditional on an assumed mean KV residency time — an average-in-system relation
under a particular concurrency, timing, and cache geometry, not an observed service rate, not a
measured goodput, not a lower guaranteed rate, and not an SLO goodput. It is derived from the KV
bound, so it does not add an independent constraint; the host-count lower bound (21) is what derives
from it. The scopes behind fleet sizing must be derived and measured separately, and the formula is
only as strong as the weakest one:
• N_KV (KV-memory occupancy ceiling) — how many requests reside in KV cache given the
host’s usable HBM and the per-token KV footprint. This is an arithmetic allocation bound (the
floor-17 figure).
• C/W (KV-slot upper bound on admitted rate inside the KV screen) — the ~8.6 s E[W_
KV-resident] proxy is an uncontended request-level estimate; C/W inherits both the KV bound
and the service-time assumption, so it is not an independent compute bound and not an
independently measured throughput.
• Independent prefill screen — a separate compute bound (5 avg / 19 peak from ⌈368,000 ÷

265

TCO: The Total Cost Reality Check

19,780⌉ under case (i), linear-only; 6 / 21 under case (iii) causal-triangle; 6 / 22 under case
(ii) full-square conservative), legitimately independent of KV size.
• N_SLO (queueing / goodput) — the number of hosts needed to hold p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT, and
success rate under concurrent arrival. This scope is unmeasured here. Little’s law relates
average in-system work to elapsed time under stability; it does not independently
prove a throughput ceiling or a p99 latency. At concurrency ~17, TTFT and TPOT can differ
substantially from the isolated ~8.6 s used to obtain C/W, because batch efficiency, per-request
duration, and interference are all coupled to load.
So the 21-host figure is a scenario-specific KV/service-time screen contingent on the
8.6-second assumed mean KV residency time remaining valid under concurrent execution,
not a deployment-validated estimate — and it is only the capacity requirement: the deployable host
count is max(capacity requirement, tail-latency requirement N_SLO), with N_SLO the p95/p99
TTFT/TPOT/success-rate count that is unmeasured here (Little’s Law is a mean relation — E[L]
= λ·E[W] — so a p95 or p99 W must never be substituted for E[W] inside it; tail percentiles are
a separate stochastic constraint). Before budgeting against it, measure λ_goodput per host at the
target p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT, and success rate on the actual workload, and re-derive N_hosts. (See the
falsification protocol in Ch 17.)
Treat both provisioning policies explicitly. The headline $ figures below use the 21-host
ideal-active fleet (zero spare, provisioned exactly at the 40 rps peak). The capacity-planning rule (Ch
17’s authoritative provisioning-policy table, Table 17-1) is N = ⌈λ·W/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare with u = 0.70
and ρ = 0.95 independent (u × ρ = 0.665, not nested; u and ρ derate slot occupancy and LB/scheduling
efficiency for the KV screen — applied to the compute screen they are the same numerical headroom
derate against the 35% MFU assumption, identical arithmetic, different quantity), which gives 31
working hosts at the peak ⌈40×8.6/(17×0.70×0.95)⌉ = ⌈344/11.305⌉ = 31 and 32 total with N−1;
because one host must be able to drain (failover/maintenance) while the fleet still clears the peak,
the N−1 policy requires 32 hosts total (31 working + 1 reserve — 31 surviving × 1.9767 × 0.70 ×
0.95 ≈ 40.7 ≥ 40 rps). That spare is a reserve host, not serving capacity. (A ρ-omitted variant (ρ = 1)
would read 29 working / 30 total — Table 17-1 states why ρ is not nested inside the 70%.) A third,
separate model row is the 95% scheduling factor alone: 22 hosts, also zero spare — NOT a reserve,
an efficiency derate of the same KV screen ($162,760.59/mo, $26.08/1K). A fourth row comes from
a different screen entirely: the full-square case (ii) independent prefill compute screen also
lands on 22 hosts (⌈21.81⌉, zero spare) and therefore on the same $162,760.59/mo ≈ $26.08/1K — cost
depends only on N, not on which screen produced it — while at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy case (ii)
gives ⌈21.81/0.665⌉ + 1 = 34 hosts (using the unrounded 21.81, not the displayed 22) against 32 for
KV-only. All four outcomes belong in the decision:

Mode 2 — cloud GPU instances (rent, occupancy-input priced). An 8×H100 on-demand
instance ~$20/hr (canonical $2.50/GPU-hr × 8). Because the workload’s peak is 40 rps, the fleet must
be able to burst to 21 instances, but what the bill actually depends on is paid host-hours — an
INPUT this chapter does not derive:
Hpaid = 4,380 host-hours [input];

Cost = phost × Hpaid

The 4,380 is the default assumed Hpaid for the 6-host example.
The honest cloud bill would be the integral of required capacity over time, plus the warm-pool
and capacity-reservation terms:
∫︂ T
Nburst (t) dt + Nwarm · Twarm + Rreserved ;

0

TCO: The Total Cost Reality Check

Here T is the billing month, Nwarm · Twarm is the warm-pool host-hours, and Rreserved is the
reserved host-hours — each term in host-hours. Hrequired already includes the warm-pool and reser­
vation terms, so the closure is Hpaid ≥ Hrequired and every term is counted exactly once. Nburst (t)
is the number of load-following hosts above the warm/reserved baseline at time t — the hosts the
load curve requires, excluding the warm pool and reserved capacity, which enter as the next two
terms (a step function that rises with the load curve at that hour of the day/week). This depends
on the actual temporal load profile — the burst duration and frequency, the scale-up latency
(how many seconds/minutes to attach and load a fresh instance), the model-loading/warmup time
(loading a 140 GB model into a new host is not instant), the minimum warm pool to serve the base
load without cold-starting, provider capacity/availability, and billing granularity. Only if the
provider can attach instances faster than the load curve demands, with a warm pool already holding
the model, can the cloud bill approach a pure average-load figure.
Default paid-occupancy ASSUMPTION. The canonical default bills 6 × 730 = 4,380 hosthours → $87,600/month → $14.04 per 1,000 requests (14.038461538461538 exact). This is an
explicit illustrative occupancy INPUT: it is not a measured duty cycle, not a load-duration
integral, not a guaranteed lower bound, not a complete warm-plus-burst forecast, and not
a proven feasible serving schedule — and it must never be inferred from the 6/21 host-count
ratio (a ratio of selected host counts, not an occupancy). 6 hosts × 1.9767 req/s ≈ 11.9 rps < the
canonical 40 rps peak — this configuration cannot serve the canonical peak; it is priced only as a
lower-bound warm-pool occupancy illustration (burst term excluded, see the mid-case). The alwayson-at-peak alternative bills 21 × 730 = 15,330 host-hours → $306,600/month → $49.13 per 1,000
(49.13461538461539 exact). [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
The cloud case is a family, not a single line. $87.6K and $306.6K are the two named endpoints
(default occupancy input vs always-on at the 21-host peak). Anything between them requires
the customer’s own trace or occupancy input (render/tco_calc.py --paid-host-hours). For
example, a mid-case with ~6 reserved warm hosts + ~15 burst hosts held for ~4 peak hours/day, at
$20/hr (burst) and the warm pool at a reserved rate, lands between the two endpoints; the exact
number depends on the provider’s reserved/discount and billing-granularity terms, which are scenario
inputs, not market facts. The durable lesson — fleet size first, price second — does not depend on this
occupancy assumption, but the specific $14.04/1K number does and should be read as the default
occupancy INPUT , not a decision line.
• Per request: 6.24M/month (active business-hours window, Ch 4). Cost = $87,600 / 6.24M ≈
$0.014038/request ≈ $14.04 per 1,000 requests. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] (The 4,380
host-hours are an illustrative paid-occupancy input — six continuously rented hosts for 730 hours
— not a measured duty cycle, not a 6/21 utilization ratio, and not a feasible peak-serving schedule;
a 10-rps-arriving workload still needs warm capacity for its 40-rps peak. Staff & integration add
on top.)

($232,197.23/mo). None of these three numbers is an unconditional ranking. The $87.6K cloud
line is a paid-occupancy INPUT assumption (not a measured duty cycle or a proven feasible serving
schedule), the $155.8K self-host line is an always-provisioned 21-host fleet carrying a fixed staff
alloc, and the scopes are not equalized — the not-apples-to-apples caveat preceding Table 16-1 names
the specific mismatches. Any “cheaper” reading is conditional on those named inputs, not
demonstrated.
Apples-to-apples caveat. The $87.6K cloud figure is an occupancy input; it does not include an
N−1 failover reserve, capacity held for failures/maintenance, warm-capacity cost during idle periods,
model-startup time, or provider availability variance, and the self-host figure does not charge for
the same availability target’s redundancy. So the two are not compared on equal reliability or
load-serving assumptions. Before treating any mode as cheaper, add: the same served-load trace,
p95 SLO, peak duration, availability target, failover coverage, warm capacity, model startup time,
occupancy evidence, and price period to both sides. Under a nonideal elastic case (a reserved warm
pool sized for N−1 plus slower scale-up), the cloud cost rises toward the always-on-at-peak figure
and any “cloud is cheapest” result may not hold. As above: the $14.04/1K figure is an assumptionbounded input — frame the decision as “cloud is cheaper if the occupancy input holds and a warm
pool can be held cheaply,” not as an unconditional ranking. The decisive caveat remains the staff/ops
term and whether it is sunk, and now also the fleet requirement — a single-host TCO understates
the real cost by about 21× against the 21-host peak fleet and about 6× against the 6-host average —

TCO: The Total Cost Reality Check

270

the multiplier depends on whether the comparison is against peak- or average-provisioned capacity
(Table 16-2, this section).
Included-cost scope and exclusions. The priced scope covers the fully built host only; rack,
external network, site preparation and colocation are excluded and unpriced — no separate price line is
invented for them here. Fully-built-host capex covers only its stated scope; unpriced external items are
exclusions/unknowns. Staffing, startup, reservation and availability costs are NOT equalized across
delivery modes. This model totals included illustrative lines only; it is not procurement-complete.
Multi-region active-active availability is NOT priced in this TCO. The canonical workload’s
stated SLA (Ch 4) is multi-region active-active at 99.9% availability, but every $/1K figure in this
chapter (and the host counts in Ch 17) prices a single-region deployment — the 21-host headline
rows are the ideal zero-spare fleet with no N−1 reserve priced, and only the 32-host policy row
carries the 31 working + 1 reserve N−1 single-host failover — not multi-region active-active. Multiregion active-active is a different provisioning problem from N−1 single-host failover: it requires
cross-region capacity duplication (no single region’s loss may take the service down), region-failure
tolerance, data locality and traffic routing (geo/health-based routing, per-region caches and indices),
and consistent state/data replication. Mandatory vs optional in that replication: each region
must be able to load the model weights and serve its retrieval index — weight/index availability is
mandatory, because a region that cannot load the model or answer retrieval cannot serve traffic —
whereas replicating live KV across regions is an optional policy, not a requirement: clients
may instead replay or recompute the context in the surviving region, trading cross-region KV transfer
for recovery time inside the SLA’s recovery objectives. None of that is priced or validated here, and
none of it is implied by the N−1 reserve host above (the 32-host policy row). Accordingly the canonical
cost figures understate the cost of the canonical workload’s own stated 99.9% availability
requirement — read the $/1K and monthly totals as single-region numbers — zero-spare at the
21-host headline, N−1-reserve only at the 32-host policy — and add a separate multi-region capacity
+ replication cost line (on the order of ≥2× the single-region fleet on the capacity-duplication term
alone) before the availability SLA can be considered met.

result). No row below is sized, priced or tested; each names the input the book would have to fix
before its own 99.9% requirement could be closed, using the same provisioning formula as Table 17-1:

Parametric sensitivity is the durable form. All the fixed inputs above — GPU price, electricity,
staffing, capacity, API price, occupancy, and the fleet size itself — are [ILLUSTRATIVE] scenario
values; the structure of the model is what generalizes. The architect computes N_hosts from the
workload first (Ch 17/20), then re-runs this TCO with the customer’s real numbers (Chapter 23). A
runnable, parameterised version ships with the book as render/tco_calc.py (its pure model is
render/tco_model.py, reading design/canonical-workload.yaml).

Crucially, these are independent sensitivity dimensions, and each pushes the break-even in a
different direction; do not collapse them into one “the assumptions vary” disclaimer:
• Fleet size (N_hosts) — driven by the KV/prefill/SLO scopes (Ch 17-20), not by TCO. A larger
fleet raises the flat self-host line (more capex+opex) and shifts break-even right.
• Paid occupancy — the cloud bill is an occupancy INPUT (host-hours), while self-hosted
reserved cards bill flat regardless of utilization. Separating these two is what makes the selfhost (high fixed, low variable) vs cloud (low fixed, high variable) comparison meaningful —
and it is exactly why the two scopes are not comparable until the occupancy is evidenced.
• Utilization — the provisioning utilization target (70% vs 100%, Ch 17) sets how many hosts are
needed, not how much they cost per unit; it is a separate line from the price-per-host.
• Reserved / on-demand mix — whether capacity is committed (cheaper, flat) or burst (pricier,
on-demand) is a distinct lever; a mixed fleet has both a flat and a variable term.
• Failover reserve — N-1/headroom hosts (Ch 17) add cost but are not production-serving
capacity; they must be counted as a separate reserve line, not folded into the served-load hosts.
• Staffing — the dominant human term for self-hosting; it is frequently the decider at low
volume (Ch 16 §16.8 mini-case) and should be its own sensitivity dimension, not absorbed into
opex.
Because these dimensions are independent, the break-even is a region, not a point: Fig 16.1 marks
the [ILLUSTRATIVE] price band, and the honest output is a range (here ~6.2–10.4M req/mo) rather
than a single “the break-even is 7.5M” claim. The headline range varies the API price against the 21host self-host cost ($155,816.93/mo): the low end is 6,232,677.2 = 155,816.93 ÷ 0.025 (the $0.025/request
top of the band) and the high end is 10,387,795.33 = 155,816.93 ÷ 0.015 (the $0.015/request bottom of
the band) — the same ~6.2–10.4M range reported with Fig 16.1 and in §16.6; the canonical-price point
at $0.0208/request is 7,491,198.56 ≈ 7.5M. The 22-host case (ii) line gives the same method at N =
22: 6,510,423.6 = 162,760.59 ÷ 0.025 to 10,850,706 = 162,760.59 ÷ 0.015, canonical-price point 7,825,028
≈ 7.8M at $0.0208/request — a ~0.3M shift from the one extra host. The 70% × 95% provisioning
case is a separate dimension and is named separately: the $232,197.23/mo 32-host cost against the
canonical $0.0208/request API rate gives 232,197.23 ÷ 0.0208 ≈ 11.2M req/mo. Report the range and
name which dimension is being varied. Note also that these are parameterized fixed-resource cost

279

TCO: The Total Cost Reality Check

curves, not capacity forecasts: the self-host line is flat because the 21 hosts are paid for regardless
of volume, so nothing here predicts what volume the fleet can serve as requests grow.
Which dimension the x-axis varies — stated explicitly. Fig 16.1 varies (A) served volume
through duration / duty-cycle at a FIXED 40 rps peak and a FIXED fleet: the 21-host idealactive line is held constant — a case (i)/KV-screen line; the 32-host = 31 working + 1 reserve policy
line and the 22-host case (ii) line are both priced in §16.3 but neither is plotted (see the Fig 16.1 note)
— and only how long the peak-shaped load runs inside the active window moves along x. It does
not do (B) — scaling average and peak together and re-running N_hosts(volume) with the integer
slot floor — which would stair-step the self-host line upward (⌈λ·8.6/17⌉ hosts per step) instead of
leaving it flat. Because the fleet and its cost are frozen, $155,816.93 ÷ $0.0208 = 7,491,198.56 ≈
7.5M is a frozen-fleet crossover, not a generalized scalable crossover: it holds only while those
21 hosts and that $155,816.93/month are held fixed, and it must not be read as “the volume at which
a growing deployment becomes cheaper.”
Feasible served-volume bound (Fig 16.1 marks it). Under (A) the fixed 21-host fleet is sized
for the 40 rps peak over the canonical active window of 624,000 active seconds/month (6,240,000
requests ÷ 10 rps), so the most it can serve is 40 × 624,000 = 24,960,000 ≈ 24.96M requests/month.
Everything to the right of 24.96M on the x-axis — the plot runs to 10^8 — is infeasible for this
frozen fleet under the canonical 624,000-active-s/mo duty cycle and is drawn only to show the
shape of the cost functions; Fig 16.1 shades and labels that region. A 24×7 shape raises the envelope
to 40 rps × 2,592,000 s ≈ 103.7M req/mo on the same fleet. The break-even region (~6.2–10.4M) and
the canonical 6.24M both sit inside the feasible region, so the crossover itself is reachable without
re-sizing; only the far right of the plot is not. The break-even stays a region, not a point, and the
dimension varied to produce that region is the API price ($15–25 per 1,000 requests (≈$0.015–0.025
per request) band) against the frozen self-host cost — not volume, and not fleet size. The figure is
illustrative, not apples-to-apples.

16.4. Measurement
Four metrics keep the TCO model honest:
1. Cost per useful (SLO-meeting) request — the decision number; divide total cost by goodputmeeting requests (Ch 6), not raw tokens.
2. Effective utilization — SLO-qualified goodput ÷ sustained SLO-qualified capacity (both
measured at the same SLO); low utilization is the hidden tax in both capex and rented instances.
Raw utilization = served ÷ provisioned — cost per useful request uses the effective
definition above.
3. Break-even volume — the requests/month where self-host cost-per-request crosses managed
API; below it, don’t buy cards.
4. Staff/occupancy adjusters — the engineering-hours and paid-occupancy assumptions that
dominate the comparisons; measure them, don’t assume.

TCO: The Total Cost Reality Check

280

16.4.1. Support lifecycle belongs in service cost
A lower accelerator price does not establish a lower service cost. Migration work, pinned-runtime
maintenance, security updates, failed attempts, spare capacity, and fallback execution belong in
the numerator. The denominator remains quality-qualified, SLO-compliant work. If a candidate
needs more replicas because of worse tail latency or lower usable KV capacity, that requirement
can reverse an apparent device-price advantage. This extends the cost model; it does not supply a
backend ranking. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
Software-lifecycle observation, 28 October 2026 — outside the 30 August evidence snap­
shot. Intel’s IPEX retirement guidance recommends upstream PyTorch and states that active devel­
opment and official quarterly releases stopped after release 2.8. The inspected IPEX-LLM README
separately declares that the project is archived, disclaims ongoing support, and warns of known
security issues.1 An archived optimization may remain executable without being an appropriate
default for a maintained service. An existing deployment therefore needs a documented migration or
support decision. Current prices and measured service capacity are still required before either IPEX
or IPEX-LLM receives a TCO recommendation; this is not a new price or capacity measurement.

16.5. Common Mistakes
• Comparing sticker price to per-token rate. A $/1K-token API quote already includes
amortization; a card price tag does not. Amortize both.
• Ignoring the staff/ops term. Self-host “saves money” on paper and loses the moment two
engineers are consumed full-time.
• Assuming 100% utilization. Idle cards are still burning electricity and depreciation; bake
duty cycle in.
• Forgetting opportunity cost. A 6-month procurement cycle versus a same-week API inte­
gration is a real cost measured in time-to-value.
• Using peak capacity for cost-per-request. Peak sizing (40 rps) overstates cost if average
(10 rps) utilization is what governs. (The headline $24.97/1K above does divide the peak-sized
21-host fleet by average volume — deliberately: this workload must clear the 40 rps peak, so
peak capacity is real cost here; the mistake applies when peak sizing is avoidable, e.g. batch or
queueable traffic.)
• Treating an occupancy input as a measurement. The cloud default (4,380 paid host-hours)
is an assumption, not a trace; never promote it to a measured duty cycle or a guaranteed lower
bound.

16.6. Architecture Consequence
TCO is the final gate in the design loop (Ch 12 candidates → Ch 14 benchmark → Ch 16 cost). It
settles which candidate survives: the 70B 8×H100 self-host passes the capability screen and is
analytically screened for feasibility — it would need a representative hardware benchmark
to establish SLO-goodput (the C/W and roofline estimates of Chs. 7–8 are planning bounds, not a
measured p95 TTFT/TPOT pass at the target offered load), and on TCO it sits above the managed
API at the canonical 6.24M volume ($155,816.93/mo vs $129,792/mo — the ~7.5M API break-even
sits above the canonical volume) and above the cloud default-occupancy input ($87,600/mo) on that
input’s assumptions — so the surviving recommendation is conditional (self-host wins only once
volume passes the ~7.5M break-even — lower if the staff/ops term is sunk — with the fleet running
~12 rps of its 40 rps peak (30%) at the crossover, i.e. a frozen-fleet crossover won with substantial
idle capacity, plus a benchmark confirming the SLO; the cloud alternative is lower-cost only if its
paid-occupancy input holds and the scopes are equalized; neither is an unconditional ranking).
DECISION STATE — CANDIDATE SCREENED; NOT COMMITTABLE — regional
availability, failover, SLO-goodput and matched-scope costs pending.
This candidate clears the capability screen and the single-region cost screen only; it must
not be recorded as passing the spine loop’s Validate & Defend → Commit stages
(Fig 1 — the Preface’s decision-loop figure) or as a committed ADR (Ch 22 → Ch 25).
Four items are outstanding: regional availability — the canonical 99.9% multi-region
active-active SLA (Ch 4) is UNSIZED and NOT PRICED here (§16.3, Table 16-2); failover
— only N−1 single-host failover is modeled (the 32-host policy row), with no regionfailure test; SLO-goodput — the p95 TTFT/TPOT pass is provisional until measured
at the target offered load (Ch 14); matched-scope costs — the A/B/C modes are not
compared on equal availability, failover, warm-capacity, occupancy-evidence or p95-SLO
assumptions (§16.3, Table 16-1). Until all four are in hand the honest status is screened, not
committed: no least-cost selection, no procurement recommendation. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[ASSUMPTION]
This completes the chain from vague requirement to a screened, costed candidate, while being
honest that the TCO gate is not an unconditional win and that the SLO pass is provisional until
benchmarked.
It also feeds fleet decisions (Chs. 17–18): the same break-even logic — fixed cost amortized against
a per-unit rate — feeds the fleet decision, while the marginal buy-versus-burst call needs its own
capacity-expansion analysis; the staff term is what pushes toward consolidation (Ch 18).

16.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: TCO Discipline and the Staff Term
A startup’s CTO shows the architect a warrant to buy two 8×H100 servers for the new internal RAG
assistant, citing “we’ll save on token fees.” Same 70B FP16 as the canonical case, 2 GPUs per replica
→ 8 replicas across the two hosts; 2 rps average is 1 rps per host, well inside the 40/21 ≈ 1.9 rps per
host the canonical 21-host fleet sustains at its 40 rps peak (host-level comparison: the canonical fleet
runs TP=8, one model instance per host, so it has no per-replica rate to quote). The rate comparison
hides the memory geometry: 4 replicas per host × 140 GB = 560 GB of the 640 GB per-host pool. After
the ~64 GB runtime reserve, ~16 GB of KV remains per host — 0.64 of a 9,500-token request (24.9
GB) — against 1 rps × 8.6 s ≈ 8.6 requests in flight per host (~32 GB of KV across both hosts against
~17 in flight). The two hosts clear the rate comparison, not the full-context KV budget. Capability
gate before any TCO comparison: ~16 GB of KV holds 0.64 of one 9,500-token request, so this

two-host configuration cannot serve the canonical full-context workload at all; the $64K/mo figure
below therefore compares an infeasible option with a feasible one and is not a realizable saving. The
TCO arithmetic that follows is still the arithmetic a feasible self-host configuration would face —
a conditional comparison, not a procurement case for two servers. Applying TCO discipline, the
architect does not dispute the raw token math. Instead they price it: at this startup’s actual early
volume — ~2 rps average, ~5M requests/month, and only a 0.5 FTE engineer fully available for GPU

part V.
The Fleet

chapter 17.
From Server to Fleet

The Architect’s Question
Having established the single-host serving model — a 70B FP16 model on 8×H100 serving the
canonical workload (Ch 4, Table 4-2) at ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak — the natural next question
is: when does one host cease to suffice, and how do we scale to a fleet? This chapter answers the
architect’s question: at what point must we move from a lone server to a coordinated fleet, and what
are the quantitative trade-offs of that transition?

17.1. Concept
The transition from a single-server deployment to a fleet is not a qualitative leap but a quantitative
threshold crossing. In the single-server model, all request routing, load balancing, and health moni­
toring occur within one process on one machine. The architect thinks in terms of request-per-second
capacity, GPU memory utilization, and inference latency on that one host. As traffic grows, the single
host hits limits in three domains: computational throughput (tokens/sec), GPU memory capacity, and
inter-request interference (contention for shared resources such as NVMe I/O, PCIe bandwidth, and
CPU). When any of these limits is breached, the fleet model introduces multiple identical hosts behind
a load balancer, each independently serving a slice of the total traffic. The fleet model adds three
new architectural ingredients: (a) a load balancer that distributes requests across hosts, (b) cross-host
communication patterns when a request spans multiple machines, and (c) capacity planning that
accounts for redundancy, failover, and the diminishing returns of horizontal scaling. The key insight
is that horizontal scaling transforms per-host limits into system-wide capacities, but at the cost of
added coordination overhead, state synchronization, and network budgeting.

288

289

From Server to Fleet

17.2. Mental Model
We visualize the fleet as a two-level hierarchy. At the top level, a load balancer — either hardware
(L7 switch) or software (NGINX, HAProxy, Cloud Load Balancer) — accepts inbound requests and
routes them to one of N backend hosts. Each backend host runs an identical copy of the model and
serves requests independently. At the bottom level, each host operates exactly as the single-server
model does: a model engine accepting prompts, producing completions, and returning tokens to the
load balancer, which forwards the response to the client.
The mental model introduces two new invariants. First, the throughput invariant: total system
throughput ≈ N × throughput_per_host, reduced by a factor ρ that captures load‑balancer overhead,
health‑check traffic, and imperfect distribution (typically ρ ∈ [0.95, 0.98] depending on LB sophisti­
cation) [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] (scope and labels: §17.4). Second, the memory invariant:
total GPU memory across the fleet is N × memory_per_host, but the per-host memory available for
model weights and KV cache remains the same as the single-host case. The fleet does not increase
the per-host model size; it increases the aggregate number of concurrent requests the system can
serve by parallelizing across hosts.
A critical detail is the session-affinity decision. If user sessions must maintain conversation
state (KV cache, accumulated tool outputs, retrieval context), the load balancer must route subsequent
requests from the same user to the same host (sticky sessions). This reduces cross-host communication
but limits the effective parallelism, because a popular user can pin a single host to capacity while other
hosts stand underutilized. If sessions are stateless (each request starts with fresh context — no carriedover KV, tool output, or retrieval context), any host can serve any request, and load distribution
becomes even. The architect must choose between density (sticky sessions, higher per-host utilization)
and evenness (stateless routing, lower per-host utilization but better load balance).

17.3. Worked Example
We continue from the canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak, prompt
~9,200 input tokens + ~300 output, 70B-class dense FP16 model, 8×H100 host with 640 GB GPU
memory. A single 8×H100 host’s capacity is set by the binding constraint among GPU compute,
HBM bandwidth, and KV cache memory. Let us verify with arithmetic, keeping the two quantities
distinct: aggregate HBM (640 GB) is not the same as KV-available memory (640 − 140 GB weights
− runtime/workspace reserve).
Single-host concurrency capacity (KV-bound). The per-token KV footprint for the canonical
full-MHA reference geometry is 2 × layers × hidden × bytes = 2 ×80 ×8,192 ×2 = 2,621,440 B ≈ 2.62
MB/token (Chapter 7 canonical). Subtract the 140 GB FP16 weights and ~64 GB runtime/activa­
tions/workspace from the 640 GB pool, leaving ≈436 GB available for KV. Each request at 9,200 input
+ 300 output reserves a 9,500-token max KV of 9,500 ×2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB (the initial 9.2K residency
is 24.1 GB). A single host therefore holds C = 436 GB ÷ 24.9037 GB ≈ 17.5 concurrent requests

Viability at peak. Peak traffic is 40 rps; with the canonical ~8.6 s per-request service time (1.08

the 70% × 95% provisioning policy, 32 total with N−1 — Table 17-1), and more for growth to 100 rps.
This flips the original conclusion: the fleet is not a distant luxury but a necessity at the canonical
peak, driven by the product of service time (8.6 s) and arrival rate.
KV compression is the first lever. Switching KV to FP8 (κ ≈ 1.31 MB/token, raw byte-halving

roughly doubling headroom before buying hardware. This is why the architect treats KV precision
as a first-class capacity dial, not a cosmetic detail.
Threshold for fleet expansion. One host ceases to suffice above λ ≈ C/W ≈ 17/8.6 ≈ 2.0 req/s
of admitted traffic (KV screen); the canonical 40 rps peak is ~20× that. Suppose the agentic layer

in T=1, 25% in T=2, 5% in T=3, and 2% exceeding the turn limit (falling back to single-shot). That
makes the median turn count T=1 (68% of requests finish on the first turn) and the 95th percentile
T=3 (cumulative 68+25+5 = 98% by T=3). Each turn adds ~800 tokens of retrieved context (delta) and
~65 tokens of model-generated reasoning (gamma), so the effective per-request token count is
I(T ) = I0 + T (δ + γ) + Ofinal = 9,200 + T × 865 + 300
• Median (T=1): I(1) = 9,200 + 1 × 800 + 1 × 65 + 300 = 10,365 tokens
• 95th percentile (T=3): I(3) = 9,200 + 3 × 800 + 3 × 65 + 300 = 12,095 tokens
• Hypothetical extension (T=4, if the turn limit were not enforced — per Ch 19 the >2% that exceed
the limit fall back to single-shot, so no request actually reaches T=4): I(4) = 9,200 + 4 × 800 +
4 × 65 + 300 = 12,960 tokens
The KV cache per request rises proportionally with context length, so per-host concurrency
capacity falls in inverse proportion to context length — C = Mkv /(I(T )κ):
• at T=1 (median): 10,365 × 2.62 MB ≈ 27.2 GB/request ⇒ C ≈ 16 concurrent (floor 16)

Scaling forecast (service-time-aware). The 344 in-flight / 21–31–32 host result is derived once,

per-host KV usage must stay comfortably under its C. This is the fleet point: hosts are added because
concurrency in flight × KV-per-request exceeds a single host’s residency — and concurrency in flight
must be computed from the full service time, not a target latency.
Cross-host communication. In the canonical scenario, requests are independent — no user
session spans multiple hosts. If an agentic loop required retrieving results from a prior host (e.g.,
distributed retrieval), the system would need a coordination layer (Redis, gRPC, or message queue)
with added latency. We quantify this below in the measurement section.

17.4. Measurement
We derive three planning quantities from the worked example and Chapter 19’s illustrative
turn-count distribution. These are not measurements from production traffic. A deployment must
measure its own traffic distribution before using these quantities for provisioning.
17.4.1. Per-host throughput and KV cache budget
Let N be the number of hosts, λ the incoming rps peak, T the random variable for agent turn count
with distribution P(T), δ = 800 tokens per turn of retrieved context, γ = 65 tokens of model-generated
reasoning per turn, and O_final = 300 final output tokens. The per-request token count is
I(T ) = I0 + T · δ + T · γ + Ofinal
where I₀ = 9,200 is the baseline input tokens. The per-host concurrent‑request capacity in terms
of KV cache is
C=

Mkv
I(T ) · κ

where M_kv is the KV‑available memory — the portion of on‑host HBM left for KV after weights
and runtime — and κ = 2 × nlayers × dhidden × bytes ≈ 2.62 MB/token (2.5 MiB) is the per‑token
KV footprint (Chapter 7 canonical; κ includes all layers — omitting the layer factor understates KV
memory by orders of magnitude). For the canonical host, M_kv = 640 GB − 140 GB (FP16 weights)
− ~64 GB (runtime/activations/workspace/NCCL) ≈ 436 GB. Dividing memory by bytes (not the
byte‑divided‑by‑bytes collapse that trips unit analysis): Byte-accurate κ = 2.62144 MB/token (2.62

• For T = 0 (baseline, I = 9,500): C = 436 GB / (9,500 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/24.9037 ≈ 17.5 concurrent
requests per host (byte-accurate; floor 17 — rounding rule in §17.3).
• For T = 1 (median, per the Chapter 19 distribution; 68% terminate on turn 1): C = 436 GB /
(10,365 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/27.17 ≈ 16 concurrent requests per host.
• For T = 3 (95th percentile; cumulative 98% by T=3): C = 436 GB / (12,095 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/31.71
≈ 13.8 concurrent requests per host (floor 13).
• For T = 4 (hypothetical extension beyond the enforced turn limit — Ch 19’s >2% tail falls back
to single-shot, so no request reaches T=4): C = 436 GB / (12,960 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/33.97 ≈ 12.8
concurrent requests per host (floor 12).
These numbers are the KV-residency ceiling; measured concurrency may be lower if GPU
throughput or bandwidth binds first, so the architect takes the min of the KV, compute, and bandwidth
capacities.
Reconciliation box — the four throughput rates in this book are different quan­
tities, not a contradiction. (1) ~50 tok/s (Ch. 5) is a deliberately conservative singlestream, low-batch generation rate used to illustrate the tokens-per-dollar method; it is a
floor, not the host’s serving throughput. (2) ~19,800 tok/s (Ch. 8) is the idealized prefill
aggregate (8 × 2,472 at 35% MFU) before TP/system loss — an analytical upper bound on
prefill, not a servable goodput. (3) ~35,000–48,000 tok/s (Ch. 15) is the batched serving
decode+prefill range under FlashAttention + continuous batching — the multi-request
serving throughput of the same host. (4) ~2.0 req/s (Ch. 17/20) is the KV-slot-based
analytical UPPER bound on admitted request completion rate, conditional on an assumed
mean KV residency time (C ÷ E[W_KV-resident]) — the quantity that sizes the fleet, and
the source of the lower bound on host count. The first three are token-rates at different
batch/phase assumptions; the fourth is a request-rate bound. They reconcile only phaseby-phase, never as one fungible “total” rate. Do not set a summed 19K tok/s against
any single-phase capacity. At ~2.0 req/s the request workload decomposes into two
components that hit the hardware differently: 18,400 input tokens/s (2.0 × 9,200 — the
prefill phase, compute-bound) and 600 output tokens/s (2.0 × 300 — the decode
phase, bandwidth-bound) — both first-order regime labels; see Ch 15/Ch 8 for the
scope conditions. Compare the prefill component only against the prefill-only capacities
(~19,800 tok/s, item 2; ~35–48K only if those figures are themselves phase-resolved) and
the decode component only against decode-scale capacity — never the summed ~19,000
tok/s against a single-phase figure. The apparent near-equality of ~19,000 tok/s and
~19,800 tok/s is a numerical coincidence of units, not a physical equivalence: the
two sit in different phases with different arithmetic intensity and different cost (computebound prefill vs. bandwidth-bound decode), so they cannot be added into one rate and

From Server to Fleet

294

compared to any single-phase number. Aggregate prefill + decode into a single “total”
rate only after stating an explicit cost/phase-equivalence model (e.g., a weighted-FLOP
or weighted-dollar basis). Use the token-rates for kernel and cost reasoning (keeping
prefill and decode separate), and the request-rate for fleet sizing. [DERIVED]

The KV population is its own derivation — E[L_KV] = λ_admitted × E[W_KV-resident].
The quantity that must fit in the KV pool is
E[LKV ] = λadmitted × E[WKV -resident ]
where λadmitted is the rate the host actually admits (equal to the arrival rate only while nothing
is being shed or queued) and E[WKV -resident ] is the mean KV-holding time — a mean, never a
percentile (tail rule below). Memory is then sized from that population by cache geometry and policy:
slots per host = ⌊usable KV pool ÷ per-request KV at the sizing context⌋ (436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5 →
whole-context floor 17 at T=0), then adjusted for the rank/replication layout (tensor-parallel rank
count, and whether KV is sharded across ranks or replicated) and the admission policy (wholecontext admission with no fractional slots; a prefix-cache hit or a pre-reserved block changes the
effective holding time, not the byte geometry). The deployable host count is the maximum of two
requirements — (i) the capacity requirement ⌈λ·E[W_KV-resident]/(C·u·ρ)⌉ and (ii) the tail-latency
requirement N_SLO that holds p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT and success rate under concurrent arrival
(unmeasured here; Chapter 14) — never the capacity screen alone. (The ρ = 0.95 scheduling/efficiency
factor is the independent multiplier defined in Table 17-1; the ρ-omitted ⌈λ·E[W_KV-resident]/(C·u)⌉
is the ρ = 1 u-only comparison screen.)
Which one drives KV residency? Only the KV-resident population E[LKV ] = λadmitted ×
E[WKV -resident ] holds KV slots — a queued request (λ·W_queue) is “in flight” from the user’s view but
does not yet reserve a KV block, and the orchestration/planning portion of We2e has not reached the
host at all. The KV-residency ceiling C therefore bounds E[LKV ] (the resident sequences), not λ·W_

From Server to Fleet

296

e2e or λ·W_queue. The end-to-end time (We2e ≈ 10 s planning round) is the workload-level Little’s-law
basis used to derive the arrival rate from the population (Chapter 4); the mean KV-residency time
(E[WKV -resident ] ≈ 8.6 s under the stated assumption) is the capacity-level Little’s-law basis used to
size the fleet (this chapter). The C/W shortcut is thus a KV-residency screen, valid only when the
serving system is the bottleneck and no queue/planning backlog or released-KV tool gap changes
the resident count — state that scope, and never quote C/W as a measured end-to-end goodput.
Two transplant errors to refuse explicitly. (i) Do not put λ × W_e2e into KV slots. End-to-end
time includes queue, tool and inter-turn gaps that — under the stated assumption — hold no KV, so
λ·W_e2e overstates the cache population and over-sizes the fleet; the KV formula takes λ_admitted
× E[W_KV-resident] and nothing else. (ii) Do not substitute a p95/p99 for E[W] in Little’s Law.
Little’s Law is a mean relation, E[L] = λ·E[W]; pairing a mean λ with a p95 W mixes moments
and yields a number that is neither a mean population nor a percentile one. Tail percentiles enter
as a separate stochastic constraint — the N_SLO tail-latency requirement above, and the p95/p99
measurement gates of Chapter 14 — never as the W inside λ·W.
If the peak traffic λ_peak = 40 rps, Little’s Law gives the number of requests in flight as λ_peak
× W, where W must be the mean time the resource in question is actually held — for the
KV-slot screen that is E[WKV -resident ], which for this canonical workload is ~8.6 s (1.08 s prefill +
~7.5 s decode of 300 output tokens at ~25 ms/token, Chapter 8) under the explicit assumption
that KV is held only during GPU execution — NOT a sub-second TTFT-type latency, and NOT
We2e (which adds the tool/orchestration time that, under that assumption, holds no KV). Using a ~1 s
“latency” here is the classic fleet-sizing error: it undercounts in-flight concurrency by roughly the
ratio of service time to target latency (here ~8.6×). The minimum number of hosts is

Why u and ρ are independent here — and the nested variant, stated so it cannot be
confused with it. The 70% is an operational utilization ceiling on the host; the 95% is a separate
load-balancer/scheduling efficiency loss on top of it (§17.4: health checks, affinity skew, LB CPU).
They are therefore applied as two factors. If the 70% had instead been measured after LB losses —
i.e. ρ already inside the net derate — the formula would set ρ = 1 and the same screen would read
⌈344/(17 × 0.70)⌉ + 1 = 30 hosts; this book makes no such claim, so ρ = 0.95 stays in the formula.
A ρ-omitted (ρ = 1) variant would read 29 working / 30 total — a figure this book does not claim.
Recomputed at the canonical peak under this policy (each an analytical lower-bound screen, not
measured SLO-goodput): ideal-active, zero derate, zero spare = 21 (KV screen); ρ-only, zero spare =

→ 29); policy u × ρ working = 31, + Nspare = 32 (KV-only, case (i)); the independent full-square
case (ii) prefill screen at the same policy = ⌈21.81/0.665⌉ + 1 = 34 (33 working + 1); case (i) = 29
(case-(i) prefill screen at u × ρ + spare: ⌈18.606/0.665⌉ + 1 = 28 + 1 = 29) and case (iii) = 32 (case-(iii)
prefill screen at u × ρ + spare) at the same policy. Two coincidences to keep straight: the u-only
KV screen and the case-(i) prefill screen both give 29, and the KV-only policy total and the
case-(iii) prefill screen both give 32 — same numbers, different screens. FP8 KV is unchanged
by the policy debate at the working level — ⌈344/(35 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈14.78⌉ = 15 working, 16
with the spare.
At the canonical peak:
• KV-residency ceiling (C) is a per-host concurrency limit, not a fleet-size answer by
itself. A host holds C ≈ 17.5 concurrent full-context requests (computed above; conservative
integer floor 17). The fleet size is governed by how many requests are KV-resident at the
peak, which is λ_admitted × E[W_KV-resident] — equal to λ_peak × 8.6 s here only because
admission is assumed to match the arrival rate and 8.6 s is the assumed mean KV-holding time.
• At λ_peak = 40 rps and W ≈ 8.6 s, in-flight concurrency ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344 requests. With
C ≈ 17.5 per host (FP16 KV) at full utilization, the minimum N = ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts (31
working at the 70% × 95% policy, 32 total with N−1 — Table 17-1) — the KV screen alone —
case-independent (case (i) labels only the prefill screen). The independent prefill compute
screen (Ch. 8, 35% MFU) is a separate named screen: 19 hosts under case (i) (⌈18.60⌉, linearonly), 21 under case (iii) (⌈20.21⌉, causal-triangle), 22 under case (ii) (⌈21.81⌉, full-square
conservative). Under case (ii) the compute screen binds above the KV screen, so the capacity
floor is max(KV, compute) = 22 hosts — and at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy ⌈21.81/0.665⌉ +
1 = 34 hosts under case (ii) versus 32 for KV-only (⌈344/11.305⌉ + 1). 19 / 21 / 22 / 32 / 34
are all illustrative planning screens under their stated FLOP-counting case and the
35% MFU assumption — NOT measured SLO-goodput. This is the honest fleet size and
matches the throughput/latency analysis in Chapter 20.
• The 25 ms/token in W is the TPOT budget, not a measured per-step time. The weightsonly decode-bandwidth floor for the canonical 8×H100 host is 140 GB ÷ (8 × 3.35 TB/s) ≈ 5.2

299

From Server to Fleet

ms/step, but that floor omits the KV read. A decode step must re-read every resident sequence’s
KV: bytes/step = 140 GB + B × 24.9 GB, so at the canonical B = 17 a step reads ≈ 563 GB and
takes ≈ 563 GB ÷ 26.8 TB/s ≈ 21 ms/step — about 4× the weights-only floor. At ~21 ms/step an
ideal, well-tuned decode sits at ~84% of the 25 ms budget, not well under it; any inefficiency
pushes the step past the budget. Decode-leg feasibility at the canonical peak load: serving all
12,000 output tok/s on one host needs 12,000 × (140/17 + 24.1) GB/token ≈ 388 TB/s — weights
per token at B = 17 plus the ≈24.1 GB KV re-read each output token costs — which is ≈14×
the host’s 26.8 TB/s of HBM, so the peak decode demand cannot land on one host; it spreads
across the fleet’s KV-resident slots. The fleet number above therefore uses the 25 ms budget
pole of the service time — a tighter internal sizing target, not the least-favourable pole: the
canonical SLO pole is 40 ms/token (Ch 15 §1), and it is in the band below. The sensitivity
band, holding prefill at 1.08 s and 300 output tokens: at the weights-only floor 5.2 ms/step
(B → 0, no KV reads) W ≈ 2.6 s (in-flight ≈ 106, ~7 hosts at full util); at the KV-inclusive
floor ~21 ms/step (B = 17) W ≈ 7.4 s (in-flight ≈ 295, ~18 hosts); at the 25 ms budget W ≈ 8.6 s
(in-flight ≈ 344, ~21 hosts); at the 40 ms TPOT SLO pole W ≈ 13.1 s (in-flight ≈ 523, ~31 hosts
on the KV screen). Sizing at the 25 ms budget is a tighter internal target than the 40 ms SLO
pole, so name the sizing pole once and state it once: sizing at the SLO pole gives ~31 hosts,
and a measured per-step time from a Chapter 14 benchmark should replace the model before
committing hardware.
• Switching to FP8 KV (κ ≈ 1.31 MB/token, raw byte-halving — 50% of FP16, C ≈ 35.0 at T=0;
conservative integer floor 35) raises per-host concurrency, cutting the fleet to a minimum N ≈
⌈344/35.0⌉ = 10 at full utilization → 15 working hosts at the 70% × 95% policy (⌈344/(35 ×
0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈14.78⌉ = 15 — the same 15 the u-only screen gave, because the ceil absorbs the
extra derate here) and 16 total with N−1.
Separate the two questions explicitly — they are not interchangeable, and mixing them is the
source of the under-sizing error:
1. KV-only concurrency sizing (does one host’s KV budget hold the in-flight requests?):
NKV = ⌈λW /(C · u · ρ)⌉. This uses C (KV-residency ceiling) and the mean KV-holding time
E[WKV -resident ] (the ~8.6 s proxy) — not We2e — with u and ρ exactly as Table 17-1 defines
them.
2. Full service-capacity sizing (does the fleet’s aggregate request rate clear the peak?): the
same quantity when C/W is the per-host service rate — i.e. N = ⌈λ/((C/W ) · u · ρ)⌉.
Because Little’s Law ties concurrency, service time and arrival rate, these two views coincide:
λW /(C · u · ρ) = λ/((C/W ) · u · ρ) — provided the same W (E[W_KV-resident]) is used
on both sides; mixing W_e2e on one side and the 8.6 s residency proxy on the other breaks
the identity.
KV residency provides one capacity ceiling, but it is not a fleet-size answer by itself. When the
canonical 300-token decode duration is included, Little’s Law raises in-flight concurrency from the

From Server to Fleet

300

misleading “40 requests at 1 second” approximation to roughly 344 requests at 40 rps, and the fleet
must be sized to that.
The fleet is governed by the minimum of several independent ceilings, not by KV alone.
C/W — and the KV-residency ceiling C that feeds it — is a necessary condition, not sufficient under

mixed prefill/decode scheduling. An architect must convert each ceiling to a common unit — requests
per second — and then take the min: (a) KV-residency concurrency C → C/W req/s, (b) prefill
compute capacity → ÷ 9,200 tokens per request (the ~19,800 tok/s/host prefill screen of Ch. 8
— case (i), linear-only; ≈16,870 linear-equivalent tok/s under case (ii), full-square), (c) decode
bandwidth/compute capacity → ÷ 300 tokens per response (the HBM-bound decode roofline),
and (d) the observed p95-TTFT/TPOT SLO goodput under a load test (already a request rate). A
host may hold 17.5 KV-resident requests but never serve 17.5 at the quoted service time, because
batch scheduling, prefill/decode interleaving, and tail latency couple the two.
Small queueing counterexample. Suppose a KV ceiling C = 17.5 and W = 8.6 s, so C/W ≈ 2.0
req/s. That is an average occupancy bound. If a burst of arrivals is shorter than the service-time

spread, or if the prefill of some requests monopolizes the GPU and stalls decode, the achieved goodput
can be well below 2.0 req/s even though the host holds 17.5 slots. Conversely, prefix caching or batchfriendly load changes the effective C or W, so the bound must be recomputed on those effective values
— under fixed C and W, achieved goodput cannot exceed C/W. The upshot: C/W is a KV-slot-based
analytical UPPER bound on admitted request completion rate, conditional on an assumed
mean KV residency time — a capacity screen only; its standing qualifiers (not a lower guaranteed
rate, not a measured throughput, not an SLO goodput) are stated once in the Evidence boundary
panel (Preface). The lower bound on host count derives FROM this upper bound on the per-host
rate: a ceiling per host becomes a floor per fleet at exactly one step, N ≥ ⌈λ/(C/W)⌉ = ⌈λ·W/C⌉
(⌈40/(17/8.6)⌉ = ⌈20.24⌉ = 21). The fleet SLO-passing count comes from the measured goodput at the
target p95 — not from C/W. State the line’s assumptions (time-in-KV occupancy, overlap of phases,
admission policy) explicitly in the sizing summary rather than presenting C/W as the achieved rate.
17.4.2. Simultaneous feasibility check (prefill + decode coexistence)
The ~2.0 req/s/host ceiling assumes prefill and decode run on the same host at the same time. We
check the prefill leg against the hardware.
• (a) Prefill demand at 2 req/s. 2.0 req/s × 9,200 input tokens = 18,400 input tokens/s per
host (2.0 × 9,200; the prefill leg of the ~2.0 req/s decomposition in the reconciliation box above).
• (b) Idealized prefill ceiling. 8 × 0.989 PF/s × 35% / (2 × 70e9) ≈ 19,780 tokens/s (Chapter 8,
35% MFU, prefill-only — case (i), linear-only FLOP convention).
• (c) The ratio. 18,400 ÷ 19,780 ≈ 93% under case (i). Prefill must run at ~93% of the idealized
prefill ceiling.
• (d) FLOP-counting sensitivity (same 35% MFU). The ceiling is quoted in linear-equivalent
tokens/s, so case (ii) (full-square, ×1.1723) lowers it to ≈16,870 tok/s and the ratio becomes

301

From Server to Fleet

18,400 ÷ 16,870 ≈ 109% — the same demand ÷ ceiling written in PFLOP/s, 2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692,
where 2.7692 PFLOP/s is the Chapter 8 35%-MFU host peak; case (iii) (causal-triangle, ×1.0861)
gives ≈18,210 tok/s and 18,400 ÷ 18,210 ≈ 101%. Under the conservative case the prefill leg
alone exceeds the idealized ceiling at 2 req/s — so the headroom the ~93% implies is a property
of the linear-only convention, not of the hardware.
This result is [ANALYTICAL]. It is a prefill-load check, not a measured rate. The ~93% (case
(i)) leaves very little headroom. The host must also run decode. Prefill and decode coexist on the
same hardware. Batch scheduling, prefill/decode interleaving, and interference consume the same
compute. The idealized ceiling assumes no decode interference. The achieved MFU is below the 35%
ideal. Under case (i) the available headroom is only ~7%; under cases (ii) and (iii) the prefill leg alone
exceeds the idealized ceiling, so headroom is negative — the real headroom is smaller than ~7% and
may be negative.
Therefore the ~2.0 req/s/host figure is a KV-slot-based analytical UPPER bound on admitted
request completion rate, conditional on an assumed mean KV residency time — the same
single phrase used in Chapters 16 and 20, one phrase with one meaning. It is a necessary capacity
screen: NOT a lower guaranteed rate, NOT a measured throughput, NOT an SLO goodput, and NOT
a claim that a host serves 2 req/s at SLO. The lower bound on host count (21) derives from this upper
bound on the per-host rate — ⌈40 ÷ (17/8.6)⌉ = ⌈20.24⌉ = 21 — and never the other way around.
Before treating 2 req/s/host as deployable, measure the p95 TTFT, p95 TPOT, and SLO-goodput
on a representative host (Chapter 14). Until then, the sizing in this chapter is a planning bound.
Effect on the headline counts. At the KV-screen rate the prefill leg alone consumes ~93% of
the idealized prefill ceiling under case (i) and more than 100% (≈109% / ≈101%) under cases (ii)/(iii), so
2.0 req/s/host is not simultaneously sustainable with decode. The 21/31/32 host counts derived from
that rate are the KV screen’s counts, unchanged. Under case (i) the prefill leg leaves ~7% headroom
and does not bind against the 21-host KV screen — only cases (ii)/(iii) bind, and there the policy
screens already reported in Table 17-1 carry the extra hosts (29 under case (i), 32 under case (iii), 34
under case (ii)).
17.4.3. Load‑balancer overhead factor
Let ρ be the effective throughput fraction after load‑balancer effects. These LB-efficiency val­
ues are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] engineering thresholds, not universal vendorindependent constants — a well‑configured software LB (NGINX) typically achieves ρ ≈ 0.95,
and a hardware L7 switch may achieve ρ ≈ 0.98, but both must be measured on the target topology,
workload, and sample duration before being trusted. The overhead comes from: health‑check traffic
(~1% of requests), session‑affinity hashing skew, and LB process CPU limits. The per-host throughput
itself must come from a benchmark on the actual workload (tokens/context/batch) — it is an ILLUS­
TRATIVE proxy until measured. What is derivable is the KV‑residency ceiling C from §17.3; the LB
overhead multiplies the schedulable fraction of that ceiling, and the ρ value should be replaced by

From Server to Fleet

302

a measured figure from a load test before it is used as a capacity coefficient. In the provisioning
formula (Table 17-1) ρ enters as that schedulable-fraction multiplier, independently of the
70% utilization target u — it is not folded into u and it is not a spare host. In the worked
example, the fleet is currently sized by KV capacity (§17.3), not by a fabricated tokens/s number: at
T=3 (the §17.8 agentic T=3 stress point; effective slots C × u × ρ = 8.645), FP16-KV C ≈ 13.8/host (436
GB ÷ (12,095 × 2.62 MB ≈ 31.7 GB) ≈ 13.8; conservative integer floor 13) sets the continuous ceiling.
The product 13.8 × 0.95 ≈ 13.1 is a continuous relaxation only, not usable additional-host capacity.
The host can admit at most 13 whole contexts. The provisioning formula’s effective slot count is C ×
u × ρ = 13 × 0.70 × 0.95 = 8.645. The ρ-only product 13 × 0.95 = 12.35 (no u) is not that slot count: it is
shown here only to be rejected, and it is not an integer admission count. Converting the formula’s
8.645 coefficient to a request rate still requires the stated service time and workload assumptions.
17.4.4. Cross-host interconnect budget
If a fraction φ of requests require cross-host data (e.g., distributed retrieval, shared vector index), each
such request incurs an additional network round-trip and moves data volume D over the host-to-host
network. Four time terms must be separated before any D is divided by anything:
tnet ≈ tRTT + tprotocol-fixed +

D
Beffective

+ tqueue

• tRTT — the light-speed round-trip/propagation floor (does not grow with D);
• tprotocol-fixed — a fixed per-message protocol overhead (header, control/metadata, handshake)
that does not scale with the payload size; spec it as a fixed number of header bytes, not as
payload serialization;
• ttransfer = D/Beffective — the payload’s transfer time at the path’s effective goodput; payload
serialization is proportional to D and is already counted here, so it must not also appear
in a “fixed” term;
• tqueue — queueing/scheduling wait on the shared link (load-dependent; zero only on an idle
fabric).
The 20 ms used below is defined as a network-only retrieval round trip — the retrieval
path’s round-trip time on the fabric (the Ch 4 retrieval-latency class read as network time), not the
retrieval service’s full per-request duration and not a rack-line latency: the service’s server-side
processing time is excluded, so ttransfer = tnet − tRTT − tprotocol-fixed − tqueue does not absorb service
compute. A bare intra-rack RTT is far shorter, and the 20 ms contains ttransfer and tqueue in addition
to tRTT and tprotocol-fixed . Assuming an intra-rack 10 Gbps Ethernet backbone (10 Gbps = 1.25 GB/s):
Gper-req =

D
= 5 MB/0.02 s = 250 MB/s ≈ 2 Gbps
tnet

303

From Server to Fleet

For D = 5 MB (top-5 retrieval snippets) and tnet = 20 ms, Gper-req = 250 MB/s ≈ 2 Gbps is an
effective per-request goodput — payload ÷ observed round-trip duration — not the instantaneous
rate the link must carry: the instantaneous rate while the payload moves is D/ttransfer = D/(tnet −
tRTT − tprotocol-fixed − tqueue ) ≥ D/tnet , so 250 MB/s is a lower bound on the burst rate and the link
must be dimensioned for D/ttransfer . The two readings agree on the base case: moving 5 MB at the
fabric’s own 1.25 GB/s takes ttransfer = 5 MB ÷ 1.25 GB/s = 4 ms, comfortably inside the 20 ms observed
duration once tRTT + tprotocol-fixed + tqueue take their share.
The shared-link check is the aggregate offered byte rate against the link budget. The
fleet aggregate — the expected number of concurrent cross-host requests (ϕ · λ · tnet , by Little’s Law,
where λ is the request arrival rate) times that per-request rate — is
Bagg = ϕ · λ · D = 0.1 × 40 × 5 MB = 20 MB/s = 0.16 Gbps
i.e. 20 MB/s of offered bytes against the shared 10 Gbps (1.25 GB/s) link budget — 1.6% of
the link — so the base case is benign on the aggregate, and the per-request effective goodput (250
MB/s ≈ 2 Gbps) sits ~5× under the same link rate.
But if φ scales to 0.5 (many distributed queries) and D grows to 50 MB, the aggregate offered
byte rate becomes 0.5 × 40 × 50 = 1,000 MB/s = 1 GB/s — ~80% of the 1.25 GB/s link budget —
and the transfer leg alone needs ttransfer = 50 MB ÷ 1.25 GB/s = 40 ms, which no longer fits the 20
ms observed duration: sustaining 50 MB inside 20 ms would require D/tnet = 2,500 MB/s ≈ 20 Gbps,
i.e. a link faster than the 10 Gbps fabric. The aggregate check (φ·λ·D vs the link budget) scales with φ
and D; the per-request transfer leg (D/B_effective vs the observed duration) scales with D and B_
effective, not with φ.
This calculation shows that cross-host communication must be dimensioned on two separate
checks — the aggregate offered byte rate against the shared link budget (φ·λ·D vs 1.25 GB/s) and the
per-request transfer leg against the observed duration (D/Beffective vs tnet − tRTT − tprotocol-fixed − tqueue )
— the aggregate check (φ·λ·D vs the link budget) scales with φ and D, while the per-request transfer
leg (D/B_effective vs the observed duration) scales with D and B_effective, not with φ, even if the
base case appears benign. Varying D changes only the D-dependent D/Beffective transfer term; the
propagation and protocol-fixed terms stay constant, so there is no “fixed payload serialization”
residue. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
17.4.5. Request traffic and model collectives are different populations
The retrieval budget above follows request arrivals: a fraction of requests moves a payload between
hosts. A distributed model introduces different events. Tensor-parallel participants exchange partial
results at layer boundaries; expert-parallel participants dispatch and combine routed tokens. Their
payload and frequency follow the actual TP or EP communication group and execution schedule, not
the total number of serving hosts. KV transfer follows a further boundary: ownership of a request’s

From Server to Fleet

304

cached state. These populations need separate byte, frequency, and latency records before their loads
are combined on a shared link.1
Independent inference replicas do not perform a cross-fleet gradient all-reduce merely because
more hosts are added. Conversely, request-driven retrieval traffic is not the whole network budget
when a model spans devices or hosts. The capacity check accounts for each group’s traffic, simul­
taneous schedules, and shared-link contention. Only exposed communication on the critical path
adds directly to request latency; adding every collective duration again after counting overlapped
execution would double-count time. The earlier retrieval arithmetic remains a request-traffic example,
not a budget for all distributed-model communication. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
17.4.6. Counter-scenarios: KV is not always the driver
The canonical case is one regime — a mid-context, mid-rate RAG workload where the KV-residency
ceiling happens to be the binding constraint. Two counter-scenarios show that the method (compute
λ·W/C with the real service time) transfers while the conclusion (KV binds) does not. The formula
is the method; the binding term is per-workload.
Counter-scenario A — short context, high batch: KV is not the host-count driver. A
code-completion-style workload is a clear case: ~500-token input, ~100-token output, but a very high
arrival rate (say 200 rps peak) and a small model (7B, so weights are ~14 GB and the KV footprint per
token is far lower). Here two things happen. First, per-request KV is tiny — a 600-token max-context
against a small per-token κ is well under 1 GB, so the host holds hundreds of concurrent requests
at the KV screen; C is not the ceiling. Second, the binding term becomes decode bandwidth: per
decode step the weights are read once (~14 GB) and B tokens are produced, so the per-GPU decode
token rate ≈ B × HBM_BW ÷ weight_bytes, capped by compute and KV — at batch 1 that is ~239 tok/s
per GPU (one GPU serves the 7B model; ×8 if data-parallel replicated), at batch 100 ~23,900 tok/s per
GPU. At 200 rps × 100 output tokens the aggregate output-token demand is 20,000 tok/s — the same
per-GPU scope — which needs a batch large enough to clear it on one serving GPU; after bandwidth,
verify compute/KV headroom at the required batch. The host count is set by λ·O / (per-host token
rate), not by KV residency; one host here serves the model on one GPU, so the per-host rate is the
per-GPU rate above. The fleet formula is unchanged; the binding term is bandwidth, not memory.
Counter-scenario B — long context, low rate: memory dominates even below the KV
screen. A document-analysis workload is the opposite pole: ~128K-token input, ~50-token output,
but a low rate (say 2 rps). Here the per-request KV is enormous — 128K tokens against the canonical
κ is ~335 GB, which consumes most of the host’s ~436 GB KV budget (already net of the 140 GB
weights). Because even one request nearly fills the host, the fleet is sized almost one-request-per-host
1
