From Server to Fleet

despite the low rate. Here memory is not just a ceiling — it is the dominant term, and the canonical
brief-context C/W shorthand (which assumes many small requests share a host) does not apply at all.
The transferable lesson. In the canonical regime the host is KV-bound and sized by λ·W/C;
in counter-scenario A it is bandwidth-bound and sized by output-token rate; in counter-scenario
B it is memory-dominated and sized by aggregate context. The architect must identify which term
binds for the specific workload before applying any single sizing formula — that is what makes the
canonical scenario a method rather than a template.

17.5. Common Mistakes
1. Ignoring KV cache growth from agentic loops. A common mistake is to assume that
adding an agentic layer barely changes per-request resource usage. As shown, each turn
adds ~800 tokens of context, so KV per request grows linearly while concurrent‑request
capacity C = M_kv/(I(T)·κ) falls hyperbolically (as 1/I(T)), not linearly. Forgetting this leads to
under‑provisioning the fleet.
2. Over‑relying on sticky sessions without load‑balance analysis. Sticky sessions simplify
cross‑host communication but can create hot‑spot hosts if a few users generate disproportionate
traffic. Always measure the session‑affinity distribution on the actual workload. A Gini coef­
ficient exceeding 0.3 is an [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] example threshold, not
a universal constant — the trigger to abandon sticky sessions depends on the workload, the
tail-latency SLO, and the failure domain. Establish the skew threshold with a traffic replay/load
test and tune it to the SLO, not to a fixed 0.3; measure per-host queueing, p95/p99 latency, and
request drops to decide when stateless routing or session sharding is the appropriate response.
3. Using raw rps to size the fleet. Requests‑per‑second is necessary but not sufficient; the
product of rps × average latency gives concurrent load, which must fit within KV cache
capacity — and the KV screen must use λ × E[W_KV-resident] (the mean KV-holding time),
not the end-to-end latency. A host serving 40 rps at 0.5 s latency carries 20 concurrent requests,
whereas at 2 s latency it carries 80 — the same rps, very different resource usage.
4. Under‑estimating load‑balancer overhead. A 5% throughput reduction from the load‑bal­
ancer efficiency ρ = 0.95 — ρ is defined once, in Table 17-1, as the single LB/scheduling efficiency
factor that enters N = ⌈λ·W/(C·u·ρ)⌉, and this margin is that same ρ, not a second coefficient —
may seem small, but at the margin of capacity it can be the difference between fitting on N
hosts and needing N+1. Always provision with ρ explicitly in the formula.
5. Failing to model latency tail under spike traffic. GPU inference time is not constant;
under sustained high load, kernel time-slicing between concurrent GPU kernels, memory
fragmentation, and concurrent kernel launches can increase per‑token latency by 20–50%.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — a planning heuristic; measure the actual tail inflation on

From Server to Fleet

306

the target workload (Ch. 14) before sizing the safety margin; the linear model t = t_inference
+ t_tool is a lower bound; the architect should size the margin against the upper end of the
20–50% range (or measure the degradation on the target deployment) — start from 20% only as
a floor (a heuristic to be replaced by that measurement).

17.6. Architecture Consequence
Transitioning from one host to a fleet reshapes every layer of the system.
GPU fleet sizing. The number of hosts N must satisfy the service‑time‑augmented capacity
formula N = ⌈ λ_peak · W / (C · u · ρ) ⌉ (the minimum N — the provisioned fleet adds one spare on
top, the N−1 rule; the authoritative parameters are Table 17-1), where C depends on the agentic turn
distribution and W is E[WKV -resident ] — the mean KV-holding time, which here is proxied by the full
per-request service time (a proxy that rises with turns — each turn adds generated tokens, and adds
retrieval latency only while the KV block is retained; a tool gap during which the engine releases KV
belongs to We2e , not to W). Two effects compound as turns grow: C falls (more tokens → more KV
per request) and W rises (more per-turn retained time), so the KV‑resident population λ·W grows on
both sides. For the canonical customer‑facing peak (40 rps, W≈8.6 s), in‑flight ≈ 344 and N = ⌈344/17⌉
= 21 hosts at full utilization (31 at the 70% × 95% policy, 32 total with N−1) with FP16 KV; FP8 KV
cuts that to 15 working hosts at the 70% × 95% policy (10 hosts at full utilization; 16 total with
N−1).
Load‑balancer selection and configuration. The choice between hardware (F5, Cloud LB) and
software (NGINX, HAProxy) affects ρ and the session‑affinity model. Hardware L7 switches offer
better ρ (≈0.98) but less fine‑grained traffic‑shaping; software LBs offer ρ ≈ 0.95 but can implement
consistent hashing for session affinity. (a) if the session model requires affinity, the LB must support
it — consistent hashing or cookie/session pinning (verify hardware L7 support per platform); (b)
if stateless, use least-connections or power-of-two-choices so load follows capacity — do not use
consistent hashing. Keep the ρ values as the cost of each choice (0.98 vs 0.95 changes the host count
~3% at the canonical fleet size).
Cross-host data infrastructure. If any request type requires cross‑host communication (dis­
tributed retrieval, multi‑model orchestration, state sync), a dedicated backend network must be
provisioned. The minimum bandwidth is B_min = φ · λ · D (the fleet aggregate derived in §17.4.4 —
the expected concurrent cross‑host requests φ·λ·t_net times the per‑request effective goodput D/t_
net, which simplifies to φ·λ·D), and the fabric should provide at least 2×B_min for headroom. In the
canonical scenario with φ = 0.1, λ = 40 rps, D = 5 MB, B_min ≈ 0.16 Gbps (0.1 × 40 × 5 MB = 20 MB/s)
— an offered byte rate to be set against the shared 10 Gbps (1.25 GB/s) link budget, which it uses at
~1.6% — so a 10 Gbps intra-rack network has ample headroom for the aggregate; but as §17.4.4 notes,
the per‑request transfer leg (D/B_effective, whose observed-duration average D/t_net = 250 MB/s ≈
2 Gbps in the base case) must also fit a single link within the observed duration once a request is in

307

From Server to Fleet

flight, which is the binding constraint when φ or D grows. But the architect should instrument φ
and D from production telemetry and revisit the bandwidth provisioning quarterly.
Observability across the fleet. With N hosts, tracing a request end‑to‑end requires correlating
the LB routing decision, the selected host’s inference logs, and any cross‑host data calls. Structured
logging with a request‑ID field that propagates from the client through the LB to the host and back
is essential. Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger) should be enabled by default. Alerts should
trigger when per‑host concurrency exceeds 80% of C, when LB error rate exceeds 0.1%, or when
cross‑host bandwidth utilization exceeds 70%. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — tune against the
target stack.
Failover and redundancy. With N ≥ 2, the fleet provides automatic failover: if one host crashes,
the LB routes its traffic to the remaining N−1 hosts, reducing capacity by 1/N (N to N−1 hosts). For N
= 4 in the no-spare case (no N−1 reserve held back), a single‑host loss reduces capacity from 100%
to 75% (assuming equal load distribution) — under the chapter’s N−1 spare model (31 working → 32
total) one loss is absorbed without touching serving capacity. The architect must decide whether
this is acceptable or whether N must be larger (e.g., N = 6 for 83% residual capacity after one failure).
Health‑check frequency and graceful drain procedures affect the real-world failover time, typically
5–15 seconds [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] for software LBs with 2–5 s health-check intervals;
verify against the specific LB product’s documented failover and drain times before sizing the N−1
reserve.
Multi-region active-active availability is NOT priced in this chapter’s arithmetic. The
multi-region caveat of Ch 16 §16.3 applies verbatim to these host counts: every host count here — and
the N−1 failover/redundancy model above — is a single-region, N−1-only number (≈21 peak / 31
working / 32 with N−1 — the KV-residency screen at T=0 FP16, case-independent, numerically
equal to the case (iii) causal-triangle prefill screen; 22/33/34 under the case (ii) full-square
prefill compute screen), so the counts and the sizing arithmetic that hangs off them understate the
cost of the canonical workload’s own stated 99.9% availability requirement. Add a separate
multi-region capacity + replication cost line before the availability SLA can be considered met —
remembering the §16.3 split: per-region weight and index availability is mandatory, while liveKV replication across regions is an optional policy (clients may replay or recompute context in
the surviving region instead, within the recovery objectives).
DECISION STATE — CANDIDATE SCREENED; NOT COMMITTABLE — regional
availability, failover, SLO-goodput and matched-scope costs pending.
Every host count in this chapter is a screen, not a commitment: regional availability is
unsized and unpriced (Ch 16 §16.3), failover here means one lost host (N−1), not a lost
region, SLO-goodput at the target offered load is a Ch 14 measurement that has not
been taken, and the cost scopes behind these counts are not matched across delivery
modes (Ch 16 §16.3, Table 16-1). The counts therefore inform the candidate; they do not
close the spine loop’s Validate & Defend → Commit stages (Fig 1 — the Preface’s

From Server to Fleet

308

decision-loop figure), and no mode is selected on least cost from them. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[ASSUMPTION]

17.7. What We Still Don’t Know
Despite the arithmetic above, several questions remain open and would benefit from targeted
research:
• Turn-count distribution under fleet load. Do larger fleets (N ≫ 4 — the canonical 21/31/32,
or the 82/205/410 agentic fleets; N = 4 appears only in the Fig 17.1 burst-sizing example and the
§6 failover illustration) change the observed T distribution? This is an epistemic uncertainty
from unmeasured production traffic, not a sizing claim. Intuitively, more hosts reduce per-host
contention, potentially lowering latency and reducing the agentic loop depth, but empirical
measurement is needed.
• Latency amplification non-linearity. The agentic latency model from Chapter 19 frames
the added orchestration overhead as β(T) = 1 + (T·L_agent / L_base), which assumes constant
per‑turn orchestration overhead and a fixed base generation time. Under fleet scaling, GPU
saturation may make per‑turn overhead grow with concurrent requests, introducing convexity.
Empirical load‑testing across N = 1, 2, 4, 8 hosts is required.
• Optimal fleet size for cost vs. latency. The cost of adding a host is roughly the cost of
8×H100 (multi‑hundred-thousand dollars). The marginal latency improvement from the Nth
host diminishes (diminishing returns). A cost‑per‑latency‑improved curve would help the
architect justify fleet size to stakeholders.
• Cross‑host communication patterns at scale. The φ = 0.1 assumption may not hold for all
workloads (e.g., RAG over a shared index, distributed fine‑tuning). Real‑world measurement of
cross‑host traffic patterns is needed to size the backbone accurately.
• Context‑caching efficacy across a fleet. If many users query related topics, can a fleet‑wide
prefix cache (same-model, same-prefix hits only) or retrieval cache reduce the effective δ per
request? The savings could be substantial but require cross-host cache-invalidation protocols
for that prefix/retrieval cache, which are not yet well understood.

17.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Going Agentic: Service-Time-Aware Fleet Sizing
Scenario. An AI‑product company operates a fleet of 8×H100 hosts for the canonical traffic of 2,000
users at 10 rps average / 40 rps peak, 9,200 input + 300 output tokens, no agentic layer. After six
months, user growth pushes peak traffic to 100 rps, and the team introduces the agentic layer from
Chapter 19 with a maximum of 3 turns (median T = 1, 95th‑percentile T = 3, per the Ch 19 illustrative
turn-count distribution).
Initial sizing analysis (service-time-aware). At T = 3 (the 95th‑percentile, and the honest
stress‑cohort sizing point — “worst case” applies only to the 2% fallback route, F-01), I(3) = 9,200 +
3·800 + 3·65 + 300 = 12,095 tokens. With FP16 KV (κ = 2.62 MB/token), per‑request KV ≈ 31.7 GB, so

309

From Server to Fleet

KV‑residency capacity C = 436 GB ÷ 31.7 GB ≈ 13.8 concurrent requests per host (conservative integer
floor 13). But concurrency in flight is λ_admitted × W, where W is E[WKV -resident ] — proxied here
by the full service time under the stated KV-retention assumption — which grows with the agentic
turns. The evaluator (render/agent_trace.py) sums every invocation’s prefill: the T=3 trace has
four model calls (inputs 9,200 + 10,065 + 10,930 + 11,795 = 41,990), so under no prefix reuse W(3)
= (41,990/9,200)×1.08 + 0.025×495 + 3×0.133 ≈ 17.70 s (≈ 4.93 s of prefill across four calls + ~12.4 s
decode + ~0.4 s tool); under 100% prefix reuse only the final call’s new context is prefilled — 11,600
tokens, i.e. 2,400 new tokens (3 × 800 of retrieved context) once the 9,200-token prefix is served from
cache; the 195 generated γ tokens are not prefilled — giving W(3) ≈ 14.14 s. The tool leg here uses the
~133 ms/turn tool/retrieval rate; Chapter 19’s T·L_agent (~660 ms at T=3) is the orchestration-only
incremental overhead at a different per-turn rate, and a single model should use one rate consistently.
(Scope of this W in the KV screen: it is used as the conditional proxy for E[WKV -resident ] under the
explicit assumption that the scheduler keeps the KV block through the tool leg; if the engine releases
KV at the step boundary, the ~0.4 s tool term belongs to We2e only, and the in-flight counts below
fall correspondingly — the counts as written are the KV-held-through-tools case. Under no-reuse at
the 100‑rps peak, in‑flight ≈ 100 × 17.70 ≈ 1,770 requests; against C ≈ 13.8 per host (floor 13) and the
u×ρ policy, N ≈ ⌈1,770/(13 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈1,770/8.645⌉ ≈ 205 working hosts (≈ 164 at the reuse
W=14.14); at the 40‑rps peak, in‑flight ≈ 708 and N ≈ 82 working hosts (≈ 66 under reuse). These are
the honest arithmetic bounds the full service-time model produces — an rps-only estimate (peak rps
÷ the ~2.0 req/s per-host capacity) under-sizes hosts by roughly the service-time factor, because it
ignores both the decode duration and the re-prefill of each grown turn. (Introduced continuity note:
§17.3/§17.4 above present the earlier single-prefill in-flight figures for the non-agentic canonical
request (W = 8.6 s); this §17.8 update applies to the agentic T=3 scenario, and the non-agentic W =
8.6 s figures above stand for that scenario. It is not the incremental orchestration‑overhead figure of
~660 ms at T=3 that Chapter 19 reports as its T · Lagent ; the two are different quantities, and it is this
full W that drives concurrency and fleet size.)
KV compression changes the answer. Switching the KV cache to FP8 (κ ≈ 1.31 MB/token, raw
byte-halving — 50% of FP16) cuts per‑request KV at T=3 to ~15.85 GB and raises C to ≈27.5 per host
(436 ÷ 15.85 ≈ 27.5; conservative integer floor 27). Under no-reuse W(3) ≈ 17.70 s, so at the 100‑rps
peak in‑flight ≈ 100 × 17.70 ≈ 1,770 and N ≈ ⌈1,770/(27 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈1,770/17.955⌉ = ⌈98.58⌉
≈ 99 working hosts (≈ 79 under the reuse W=14.14; the u-only screen would read ~94, 66 at full
utilization (⌈1,770/27⌉ = ⌈65.56⌉)). Prefix caching can reduce repeated prefill work and share identical
cached prefixes when the engine supports that representation. Its additional capacity benefit depends
on prefix reuse and cache allocation; the reuse rows of Table 17-2 quantify the 100%-reuse point, and
no intermediate hit ratio is assumed here. KV precision and prefix caching are the primary levers
that make agentic fleets affordable, but even with both, an agentic 70B workload at 100 rps is a
multi‑dozen‑host fleet, not a handful.
Decision. At the 100-rps sizing traffic, the integer-slot FP8 bound under no-reuse is 99 working

From Server to Fleet

310

hosts at the 70% × 95% policy, plus one spare host for N−1 operation: 100 hosts in total; under
the 100%-reuse point it is 79 + 1 = 80 (⌈1,770/(27 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ + 1 and ⌈1,414/17.955⌉ + 1; the u-only
variants read ~94 + 1 / 75 + 1). This is a KV-residency planning minimum, not a validated deployment
size. Prefix caching can reduce the requirement further only at an explicitly named hit ratio; here the
reuse columns are the 100%-reuse point and no intermediate saving is assumed. The proposed design
treats the workload as stateless and uses NGINX with least-connections (power-of-two-choices) load
balancing — matching §2 and §6(b) — with OpenTelemetry tracing on each host. With the illustrative
φ = 0.05 — halved from §17.6’s φ = 0.1 to model a lower cross-host fraction at the grown 100-rps
traffic, an [ASSUMPTION] variant rather than a measured change — and D = 5 MB, the network
rule must also use the new 100-rps traffic: B_min = φ·λ·D = 0.05 × 100 × 5 MB = 25 MB/s = 0.20
Gbps. The 2×B_min headroom screen is 0.40 Gbps, below the existing 10 Gbps intra-rack link rate
(B_min is an offered byte rate against that 1.25 GB/s link budget); the per-request transfer leg must
also fit (§17.4.4). At 99 working hosts, the planned KV-slot occupancy is 1,770/(99 × 27) ≈ 66% under
no-reuse. This is not GPU compute utilization. A Chapter 14 deployment benchmark must validate
service time, SLO-goodput, failover behavior, and measured φ and D before hardware is committed.
End-to-end latency including agentic overhead remains an illustrative target until measured.
F-01 — distinguish the mean from the stress cohort and the tail. The T=3 columns
above are a conservative all-requests-at-T=3 stress cohort (the 95th-percentile turn count),
not the mean KV-resident population implied by the §19.8 turn distribution. Little’s Law needs the
mean E[WKV -resident ]; a percentile substituted into a mean equality yields a stress bound, not a
measured/typical population. Three distinct ledgers must be kept separate: (a) the distributionweighted mean KV residency and mean resident bytes, including the 2% fallback attempts (the §19.8
distribution-weighted ledger (Ch 19) gives mean W ≈ 12.71 s = 0.68×11.52 + 0.25×14.56 + 0.05×17.70 +
0.02×17.40, between the T=1 (11.52 s) and T=2 (14.56 s) values and lower than the T=3 stress figure);
(b) the T=3 stress cohort sized in the columns above (conservative upper bound on the KV-resident
population under the cap policy); (c) the extreme fallback route (3 failed attempted turns + the
single-shot) and its tail SLO. The columns above are honestly labeled as the stress cohort; they are not
claimed to be the distribution mean, nor a strict worst case if the 2% fallback jobs do multiple failed
invocations plus the final answer beyond the cap. E[bytes × time] is often a more informative memory
load than E[time] × p95 bytes; for host provisioning keep the discrete allocation/fragmentation gate
plus real trace admission tests (Chapter 14).
Lesson. The fleet decision is driven by KV‑residency capacity vs. service‑time‑scaled con­
currency (λ·W) — not by raw rps, and not by a per‑layer KV constant. The architect’s checklist:
(1) compute I(T) for the expected turn distribution, (2) derive per‑host concurrent capacity C from
the canonical per‑token KV (2 × layers × hidden × bytes), and (3) convert peak admitted rps into
KV‑resident concurrency via λ_admitted·E[W_KV-resident] using the mean KV‑holding time
(equal to the full service time only under the stated KV‑retention assumption). The full service time
is prefill + decode of all generated tokens plus per‑turn tool latency while KV is retained; with it, step

311

From Server to Fleet

(4) computes N = ⌈λ·W/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare (Table 17-1) — a capacity requirement, to be combined as
max(capacity, tail‑latency) before deployment. Steps (5) and (6): apply the cheapest capacity levers
first — KV precision (FP8), prefix caching, attention architecture (GQA/MQA) — before buying hosts,
and validate throughput and latency with a benchmark, not an assumption. A multi‑dozen‑host
FP8 fleet costs meaningful GPU capital, but avoids both wasteful over‑provisioning and a costly
re‑platform when traffic doubles.

chapter 18.
Operating Multiple Models

The Architect’s Question
How does an operator organize a fleet of complementary models—dense and sparse,
quantized and full-precision—so that every request reaches the right model at the right
cost, without over-provisioning or under-serving?
This chapter answers that question with real arithmetic, routing logic, and operational judgment.

18.1. Concept
A mixed-model fleet treats each model family as a resource with distinct cost, latency, and
capability profiles. Rather than running every request through a single 70B FP16 model on 8×H100,
we layer:
• Dense FP16 (baseline, high-quality)
• Dense 4-bit GGUF (lowest cost, edge-friendly; highest latency — see §18.3.2)
• MoE sparse (selective activation: fewer FLOPs per token at the same weight footprint; the
throughput advantage requires batching to amortize weight streaming, and per-request latency
can exceed a dense tier of the same size — cf. the 300 ms MoE figure in §18.3.2)
• Quantized variants (8-bit trade-offs; the 4-bit case is the Dense 4-bit GGUF row above)
The fleet operates on a routing function R(query) → model_id that maps incoming requests to
the cheapest model satisfying quality constraints.
Key design principles:
1. Cost-per-token is the primary unit of comparison across quantizations.

314

315

Operating Multiple Models

2. Latency-per-token determines interactive vs. batch placement.
3. Capability gaps (context window, tool-use, multilingual) dictate minimum model tiers.
4. Consolidation saves capex when overlap in workload profiles is high; separation preserves
isolation when workloads have divergent SLA or security needs.

The fleet operates as a cost-aware load balancer with three decision layers:

The weighting (α,β) is deployment-context dependent. Units and exercise of the gate: token_cost
is USD per 1M tokens (§18.3.2) and latency_cost is USD per ms of per-request service latency (or a
normalized latency score) — different units, so the gate is evaluated in the per-request additive form
cost = α·rate_tok·n_tok + β·rate_ms·n_ms (n_tok the request’s token count, n_ms its per-request
service latency; both terms USD per request), or equivalently by normalizing both terms to [0,1]
before weighting; α and β are then dimensionless weights with α + β = 1; the gate is exercised in
§18.3.4, where L̄ = Σ p_i·L_i ≈ 247 ms is checked against the ≤500 ms threshold before the cost ranking
is accepted. A chat UI tolerates ~200 ms of added service latency per request; a batch ETL job tolerates
~2 s per request but demands lower token cost. These are per-request service-latency thresholds for
the short-prompt routing scenario — the chat figure sits under the chapter’s ≤500 ms interactive
threshold (§18.3.4) — not the canonical TTFT/TPOT SLO (Ch 4); the canonical TPOT budget of ~25
ms is a per-token quantity and is not what these per-request figures measure.

18.3. Worked Example
Scenario: ~2,000 users, ~5% concurrent (≈100 simultaneous), ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak. Total
token volume per request: ~9,200 in + ~300 out. Base hardware: 8×H100, 640 GB total VRAM. Model

and does not numerically match the table; each basis moves independently if the fleet size,
the served volume, or the price inputs change. The §18.3.2 latency column is per-request

routed rows are re-priced on one basis (self-amortized per-1M on the stated hardware),

18.3.3. Routing arithmetic
Each request carries its full token profile together: 9,200 input + 300 output = 9,500 tokens. Requestlevel routing sends the entire request — input and output — to one model. A request cannot
have 70% of its input tokens answered by model A and the rest by model B, unless the architecture
explicitly supports model composition, cascade, or speculative decoding (a different mechanism we
do not assume here). Under ordinary routing, we therefore split by requests, not by in-tokens:
For 1,000 requests/hour (≈0.28 rps — a light illustrative load; the arithmetic is scale-invariant in
tokens):
• 70% of requests (700, ≈6.65M tokens) are routine → route to 70B 8-bit: 6.65M × $1.25 = $8.31
/ hr
• 20% of requests (200, ≈1.9M tokens) need high-quality reasoning → route to 70B MoE 8-bit:
1.9M × $1.00 = $1.90 / hr
• 10% of requests (100, ≈0.95M tokens) are complex / multilingual → route to 70B dense FP16:
0.95M × $2.50 = $2.38 / hr
(Each request’s output tokens are generated by the same model that processed its input. Routing
output tokens to a different model would require an explicit cascade/composition stage — e.g., a
generator plus a separate rewriter — which is a distinct architecture, not a free assumption.) The
4-bit GGUF tier (800 ms) is listed for completeness but is not routed to in this 70/20/10 split: at 800
ms it would miss the 500 ms interactive threshold, so the bulk goes to the 8-bit GPU tier (250 ms)
instead — the same SLO constraint the §18.8 mini-case works out in full.
Mixed-fleet hourly cost = $8.31 + $1.90 + $2.38 = $12.59 / hour vs. $23.75 / hour for single-FP16
(all 9.5M tokens at $2.50).
Monthly savings ≈ ($23.75 − $12.59) × 730 hr ≈ $8,147 / month (≈ 47% reduction) with com­
parable quality because the 8-bit model is assumed [ASSUMPTION] to meet quality thresholds for
≥90% of requests (no evaluation or benchmark is cited for this figure).
Escalation sensitivity (quality-failure rate → cost). If a share q of the 700 routine requests
fails the 8-bit quality bar and escalates to FP16, hourly cost rises by q × 6.65M × ($2.50 − $1.25)/1M ≈

321

Operating Multiple Models

q × $8.31/hr: at q = 10% the saving falls from $11.16/hr to ≈ $10.33/hr (≈ 43%), at q = 30% to ≈ $8.67/hr
(≈ 37%). The ≥90% quality [ASSUMPTION] above is what holds q at the low end; the savings are
conditional on a measured quality-failure rate, not on the price table alone.
Volume basis. The $8,147/month figure is the 0.28-rps illustration above, not a canonical-load
figure: at the canonical volume (6.24M requests/month × 9,500 tokens ≈ 5.93×10¹⁰ tokens) the same
per-token delta scales to ≈ $69,654/month ($148,200 single-FP16 − $78,546 mixed). The host counts
below are sized at the canonical 40-rps peak (344 requests in flight), so the saving and the host delta
sit on different bases — compare them at the canonical volume, or re-derive the saving at 40 rps.
Placement assumption, per-tier C and N, and the total-cost comparison. The savings
above are a token-rate delta only; a decision-grade comparison must add host amortization and
energy. Two placements are possible: (a) a shared 8×H100 pool holding every tier’s weights + KV,
or (b) dedicated host groups, one per tier. Under the shared pool the co-resident weights (~350 GB,
§18.3.1) cut pool KV to 640 − 350 − 64 = 226 GB, so C = ⌊226/24.89⌋ = 9 and N = ⌈344/9⌉ = 39 hosts
mixed (shared pool, no utilization derate) / ⌈344/(9 × 0.665)⌉ = 58 hosts mixed (with the 70%×95%
policy), against 21/31 single-model under the canonical C = 17 — 31 (no spare) / 32 (with the N−1
spare, the Ch 17 provisioned fleet). Under dedicated placement each tier gets its own group: 8-bit C
= ⌊506/24.89⌋ = 20 → 13 + 4 + 3 = 20 hosts / 32 with policy. The mixed fleet needs more hosts
than the single-model fleet under the shared placement (58 vs 31 — 27 extra hosts; 39 vs 21
— 18 extra — on the no-derate pair). Under the dedicated placement the no-policy pair falls below
the single-model fleet (20 vs 21) while the policy pair is marginally above it (32 vs 31) — the ledger
narrows rather than reverses. This worked example adopts the shared pool (the placement §18.3.1
describes), so the ~$8,147/month (≈ $98K/yr) token saving must be weighed against that placement’s
extra hosts’ amortization and energy: total cost = host amortization + energy + token cost, not token
cost alone. The sign of the host delta is a placement decision, not a property of consolidation.
18.3.4. Latency check
The per-request latency is that of the model serving it. The weighted-average request latency is

for a short-prompt routing scenario (the kind of request a router triages in milliseconds), used only to

that governs fleet sizing. The cost column, by contrast, is computed on the canonical 9.5K-token
request (6.65M tokens for 700 requests). A deployment benchmark (Ch 14) must supply the real
per-model service times before either column is used for a production decision.
The latency and capacity must also reconcile with the canonical workload’s KV residency (Chapter
17): routing 70% of requests to an 8-bit model that needs ≥2 GPUs (1×H100 holds the weights plus
only ~10 GB of KV — zero concurrent canonical requests, §18.3.1) changes the per-host KV ceiling
accordingly, and the fleet host count is set by the model each tier runs on. These are [ILLUSTRATIVE]
pricing and latency figures for Q4 2026; the architect re-runs the same arithmetic with measured
per-model cost/latency from a deployment benchmark (Chapter 14).
18.3.5. Consolidation vs. separation decision
• Consolidate when: workload profile overlap ≥70%, latency tolerance ≥300 ms, and cost dif­
ferential >30%. These thresholds are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] design criteria for the
worked example, not universal rules; a deployment should set its own consolidation thresholds
from its SLO, cost model and workload mix. Satisfied by construction in this scenario: our
scenario sits exactly at the threshold — it consolidates 70% of traffic to the dense 8-bit tier
— 90% to 8-bit variants once the 20% MoE 8-bit share is counted — at the ≥70% dense-8-bit
boundary, not above it, saving ~$11.16/hr ($23.75 − $12.59, the §18.3.3 derived figure). Referents:
“satisfied by construction” speaks to the ≥70% overlap and >30% cost-differential criteria; the
latency criterion is met against the ≤500 ms interactive threshold of §18.3.4, not the ~200 ms
chat tolerance quoted in §18.2 — L̄ ≈ 247 ms clears 500 ms and exceeds 200 ms, so consolidation
is eligible for a ≤500 ms per-request chat budget and would fail a 200 ms budget.
• Keep separate when: (a) security/classification policies require isolation, (b) workloads have
bimodal latency needs (some ≤50 ms, others batch-tolerant), or (c) model versioning cadence
differs (e.g., frequent fine-tuning on one family, stable other).
In our example, consolidation wins on token rate because the 8-bit and MoE tiers together capture
~90% of request classes at lower cost than FP16; the FP16 tier still handles the tail without contention.
But under the adopted shared placement of §18.3.3 the 18–27 extra hosts’ amortization plus energy
(≈$134–200K/mo at the Ch 16 per-host basis) exceeds the ≈$69.7K/mo saving, so the total-cost sign is
undetermined until a marginal per-host cost is supplied (break-even ≈ $69,654/18 ≈ $3,870/host/mo).
The FP16 tier has no separate reserve in this worked example: per §18.3.1 it shares the 640 GB pool —
140 GB of weights plus KV — and at the canonical 9.5K profile it cannot be a 2-GPU reserve, because a
2-GPU shard holds 160 GB − 140 GB = 20 GB of KV headroom against the 24.9 GB that one 9,500-token
request needs (κ = 2.62 MB/token, Ch 17). Two reserved GPUs suffice only for the ~250-token support
queries of §18.8, not for the canonical 9.5K request. Under the dedicated placement of §18.3.3 the

323

Operating Multiple Models

FP16 tier would instead get its own group (3 of the 20 hosts) — that group, not a 2-GPU reserve, is
what “handles the tail without contention” above.

18.5. Common Mistakes
1. Treating quantization as free. Quantization is not free: on CPU/GGUF it adds per-token
dequantization work (the §18.3.4 arithmetic shows why a CPU 4-bit tier cannot meet an
interactive SLO); on GPU it trades weight memory for lower-precision Tensor Core throughput
and sometimes a KV-format change, and either can cost quality on long-context tasks. Always
measure the quality hit before routing en masse.
2. One-size-fits-all routing. A static rule (“always use 8-bit”) fails when workload mix shifts
(e.g., seasonal increase in multilingual queries that need FP16 precision). Use a dynamic router
with feature-gate checks.
3. Ignoring capital amortization. FP16 on 8×H100 carries high upfront cost; annualize GPU
capex into the per-token rate and compare placements at the same volume. A mixed fleet does
not by itself reduce capital per token — under the shared placement of §18.3.3 it adds 18–27
hosts; it lowers cost per token only where the added hosts raise utilization of capacity that
would otherwise sit idle.
4. Over-provisioning the top tier. Keeping a full FP16 GPU idle “just in case” is expensive.
Keep just enough capacity for the tail (≈10% of peak rps — an [ILLUSTRATIVE] assumption to
be derived from the measured tail and the SLO, not a measured figure) and route the rest: N_
tail = ⌈λ_tail·W/(C·u·ρ)⌉ = ⌈4 × 8.6/(17 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈34.4/11.305⌉ ≈ 4 hosts at the canonical
40-rps peak (u = utilization target 0.70, ρ = policy yield 0.95, C = 17 is the single-model FP16
pool; the shared mixed pool’s C = 9 of §18.3.3 would roughly double this tail count).
5. No fallthrough plan. If the preferred model is at capacity, the router must have a next‑best
alternative ready; otherwise requests time out or queue indefinitely.
A routing candidate is a validated deployment variant, not only a model family. A lower-precision
variant can lower resource use, but its quality loss may appear selectively in reasoning, code, tool
arguments or long contexts. Retries and longer generations can consume the apparent savings. The
routing table therefore attaches quality and SLO evidence to the exact precision/backend combination,
and the fallback preserves the task’s acceptance conditions. A change to scales, excluded layers or
execution kernels creates a new candidate for validation; it does not inherit the previous candidate’s
quality curve automatically.

18.6. Architecture Consequence
A mixed-model fleet changes the architecture in three ways:

325

Operating Multiple Models

1. Router shim (HTTP middleware or gRPC interceptor) sits between the user API and the
model execution layer. It evaluates feature requirements, reads current capacity, and selects
model_id.
2. Capacity pool abstraction – rather than “GPU 0 runs model A,” the system tracks, per
placement, weights, reserved KV, free KV and the resulting concurrency C; the pool manager
places on KV headroom, not on weights.
3. Billing/telemetry pipeline – each request’s cost and latency are tagged with model_id,
enabling downstream dashboards and alerting (e.g., “cost per token rising above $0.0000025 —
population: every request routed by R() across all tiers, fleet-wide blended; threshold ≈1.9×
the §18.3.3 mixed-fleet average of $12.59/9.5M ≈ $0.000001325/token (the §18.3.2 FP16 rate of
$2.50/1M in per-token units; §18.8’s mini-case FP16 tier is quoted on its own per-token basis at
$0.003/token) — for 3 consecutive hours”).
The fleet operator becomes a cost‑latency steward rather than a single-model optimizer.
Qualification precedes placement and promotion
Placement starts with feasible configurations, not with a vendor label. A small local model can be a
candidate for an Intel GPU or an OpenVINO client path when its operators, memory budget and
service behavior pass the same gates as the central service.1 An integrated GPU and an NPU remain
separate choices even when they share a package and system memory. Their advertised compute
figures do not form one execution budget.2
A routing policy also needs the cost of failure. If a local attempt misses its contract and falls back
to a central service, both attempts contribute resource use and end-to-end delay. The fallback route
must preserve the data policy and still meet any applicable deadline. Promotion therefore follows a
canary on the exact model/backend configuration, with monitored cache behavior, correctness, tail
latency and rollback. Replacing a driver, kernel package or graph mode can change that configuration
even when the model identifier is unchanged.3

18.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• Quality–cost curves for new quantizations. As 3-bit and sub-4-bit GGUF models emerge, the
trade-off surface shifts; we need systematic human evals + automatic benchmarks (MT‑Bench
with a named judge model; FLAN-style held-out task sets — protocol to be specified) across
families.
• Optimal router policy for non‑stationary workloads. Reinforcement‑learning–based
routing that adapts α,β weights in real time is promising but underexplored in production
fleets.
• Cross-model distillation opportunities. (a) Does a smaller student distilled from a 70B FP16
teacher reach the quality bar that forces requests to the FP16 tier, and what is its serving cost
per token? (b) Separately, what quality is lost by quantizing that distilled student? Empirical
work needed.
• Edge–cloud continuum effects. When users bring their own 4-bit‑quantized local models
(via Ollama, etc.), the fleet routing must account for hybrid inbound/outbound token flows.

18.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: A Three-Tier Customer-Support Model Fleet
Deploy a three‑tier fleet for a customer‑support chatbot.
• Tier 1 (4-bit GGUF): Handles 80% of queries (FAQ, account lookup). Runs on edge nodes
(AMD Ryzen 7950X, 64 GB RAM). Cost: $0.0002/token, latency ~600 ms. Memory headroom: 35
GB of 4-bit weights in 64 GB RAM leaves ~29 GB for KV + runtime — 29/24.9 ≈ 1.16, i.e. an
upper bound of ~1 concurrent 9,500-token request’s KV, before any runtime/workspace reserve.
The §18.3.1 qualification footnotes (OpenVINO, Intel Core Ultra X9 388H, vLLM XPU) are a
general qualification procedure, not evidence for this AMD node.
• Tier 2 (70B 8-bit dense): Handles 15% of queries (order status, policy look-up). Runs on 1×H100
— unlike the canonical 9.5K request (§18.3.1, ≥2 GPUs), these ~250-token requests carry ~0.66
GB KV each, so 1×H100’s ~10 GB headroom holds ~15 concurrent requests (short-prompt-only
placement). Cost: $0.0015/token, latency ~250 ms.
• Tier 3 (70B FP16): Handles 5% of queries (complex escalations, multilingual). Runs on 2 GPUs
reserved. Cost: $0.003/token, latency ~120 ms.
Arithmetic: A small pilot deployment serving ~1,000 registered users at a modest, deliberately
low volume — 5,000 tokens/hour (each request averaging ~250 tokens gives roughly 20 requests/hour,

framework/runtime stack (e.g. torch==2.14.0):

Check the SLO before the cost claim. If we had used a single 70B FP16 model: 5,000 tokens/hr
× $0.003 = $15/hr → $10,950 / month (× 730 hr). The three-tier split looks like an $8,994 / month
(≈82%) saving — but the SLO gates the cost claim, and here it fails. Tier 1 (the cheapest, 4-bit
GGUF on CPU, ~600 ms) serves 80% of queries, so the p95 per-request latency is ~600 ms,
which violates the 500 ms SLO for the dominant tier. The split saves cost by routing the bulk to
a slow-but-cheap model — precisely the mean-vs-tail trap: the average does not look fine either —
0.80 × 600 + 0.15 × 250 + 0.05 × 120 = 523.5 ms > the 500 ms SLO — so both the mean and the p95 fail,
and the majority tier misses the deadline. The $8,994 / month saving is therefore conditional on first
making Tier 1 feasible.
Recalculated cost after substituting a feasible Tier 1. Replace the 4-bit GGUF (CPU, ~600
ms) with 8-bit quantization on a GPU (~250 ms, $0.0015/token — the same rate as Tier 2, which is
also 8-bit on 1×H100). Note the collapse: post-substitution Tier 1 is configuration-identical to Tier 2
(8-bit, 1×H100, $0.0015/token, ~250 ms), so 4,750 of 5,000 tokens/hr (95%) run on one configuration
and the three-tier fleet collapses to two distinct configurations. The 80% of queries now route at
$0.0015/token:
• Tier 1 (8-bit on GPU) processes 4,000 tokens/hr → $6.00
• Tier 2 (70B 8-bit dense) processes 750 tokens/hr → $1.13
• Tier 3 (70B FP16) processes 250 tokens/hr → $0.75
• Total hourly cost: $7.88 → $5,752 / month (× 730 hr).
The p95 is now ~250 ms (all tiers under 500 ms), so the SLO is met. The saving narrows from
$8,994 / month (≈82%) to $5,198 / month (≈47%) — still a clear win, but the SLO-constrained figure,
not the raw 82%, is the honest number. The correct order within the cost/SLO gate is: check the SLO,
then size the cost (the capability filter still comes first, per Fig 18.1 and Table 18-1). The routing
arithmetic shows the economic win; the SLO check is what keeps it honest, and it must come first in
the cost analysis.

chapter 19.
Agentic Systems

The Architect’s Question
In large-scale RQA (retrieval-augmented QA) pipelines serving thousands of users (tens to ~100
concurrent at the canonical 10 rps), the transition from static LLM calls to agentic orchestration
raises fundamental trade-offs: increased capability versus increased latency, higher per-request
token consumption versus better answers, and richer multi-step reasoning versus harder-to-debug
execution paths. This chapter addresses the architect’s central question: how to design agentic layers
that amplify intelligence without unsustainably inflating cost and latency.
Terminology. Throughout the book, “RAG question-answering workload” is the controlled term
for retrieval-augmented question answering; this chapter uses RQA for the retrieval-augmented QA
workload, single-shot or agentic (the retrieval leg plus one or more generation turns), and always
defines it on first use; “RAG” alone refers to the broader retrieval-augmented-generation family.
We begin from the canonical deployment scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 requests/second average
and ~40 requests/second peak. Each request carries ~9,200 input tokens and produces ~300 output
tokens. The base model is a 70B dense FP16 engine running on 8×H100 GPUs (640 GB total memory).
The agentic layer sits above this foundation, introducing tool use, retrieval, and multi-step reasoning.
The question we answer is how much additional overhead this layer introduces, whether the quality
gain justifies the cost, and how to size the infrastructure accordingly.

19.1. Concept
An agentic system is one in which the LLM does not merely complete a single prompt but

329

Agentic Systems

330

iteratively decides which actions to take — calling tools, querying databases, running checks, and
then reasoning about the results before producing a final answer. The core idioms are:
• Tool use: The model emits a structured call (often JSON) to invoke an external function — a
search API, a database query, a code interpreter, or a guardrail validator.
• Retrieval: Within each turn, the agent may trigger a vector search, re-rank results, and feed
the top-k passages back into the prompt.
• Multi-step reasoning: The agent maintains an internal “thought” chain, appending each new
observation and its interpretation before deciding on the next action.
• Guardrails: Pre- and post-hoc checks that validate whether the model’s intended action is
safe, on-topic, or within budget.
The agent loop terminates when a stop condition is met: a final answer is emitted, a maximum
turn count is exceeded, or a guardrail blocks further progress. This design pattern replaces the
“single-shot” prompt — one LLM call, one response — with a dynamic sequence of calls whose length
is data-dependent.
The architect must decide not only which tools the agent may call but also how to instrument
each call for latency and token accounting, and how to set termination thresholds so that the system
degrades gracefully under load.

19.2. Mental Model
The mental model we adopt visualizes the agent as a state machine with four recurring states:
Plan, Execute, Observe, and Decide. In each cycle:
1. Plan: The model reads the current context (original user query + accumulated observations)
and emits a plan — either “proceed with final answer” or “call tool X with parameters Y.”
2. Execute: The system routes the tool call to the appropriate backend, waits for results, and
formats them back into text.
3. Observe: The result text is appended to the conversation history, and the token count is
updated.
4. Decide: The model evaluates whether the observation resolves the user query or whether
another cycle is needed.
Plan and Decide are two evaluations of one model invocation per cycle (the Decide verdict is the
next cycle’s Plan input); the capacity model counts one LLM call per turn plus the terminal synthesis
call (§4).
This loop is deterministic in structure but data-dependent in length. A simple query (“What is
the capital of France?”) may terminate at Plan/Decide — the plan is “proceed with final answer,” so no
Observe round-trip is needed — while a complex RQA request (“Compare the performance of Model
A on dataset X against Model B on dataset Y, using the last three papers from arXiv as evidence”)
may traverse three or more cycles.

The critical insight for capacity planning is that each cycle incurs a fixed overhead: one LLM
inference turn plus any tool-call latency — in the simplified execution model this chapter prices; §4
generalizes it to an execution trace (a turn may contain zero or more model invocations and tool
calls). The variable portion is the number of cycles the model chooses. Our mental model therefore
separates fixed cost per turn from variable turn count, and we will quantify both in the next section.

19.3. Worked Example
Take a user query routed to an agentic RQA pipeline. The pipeline’s default policy is a maximum
of 4 turns; if the model has not terminated by then, the system returns a fallback answer “I’m
sorry, I couldn’t find a definitive answer within the allowed reasoning steps.” (Scope note on the
turn cap. This worked example uses a default cap of 4 to illustrate the binding worst case and the
token-amplification curve out to T = 4. The recommended operational policy — deployed in the §8
mini-case and used for fleet sizing in Chapter 17 — caps turns at 3, per the §4 guidance and the
95th-percentile sizing rule (size for the 95th-percentile turn count — §4’s illustrative distribution
gives p95 T = 3); that rule presupposes an uncensored turn distribution (cap disabled, or a shadow

run that observes the turns a capped deployment would have taken), so the distribution used here
is declared uncensored and illustrative — otherwise the cap must be presented as a policy choice,
not a number derived from censored telemetry; the 2% of requests that exceed the limit fall back to
single-shot. Table 19-1’s “T = 4 (over cap)” column is therefore an out-of-policy bounding case, not an
in-policy turn count.)
Call 1 (initial prompt):
• Input: 9,200 tokens (user query + retrieved passages)
• Model emits a tool-call: search(query="relevant concepts")
• System routes the call to the search backend, returns top-5 passages (≈ 800 tokens of snippets)
• Total tokens after Turn 0: 9,200 + 800 = 10,000
Call 2:
• Input: 10,000 tokens (history + new passages)
• Model emits a second tool-call: db_query(sql="SELECT ... WHERE condition")
• Latency: 85 ms (local PostgreSQL on H100 host) [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — no mea­

• Total tokens after Turn 1: 10,000 + 350 = 10,350

• Output: 300 tokens
• Conversation ends
This trace is 2 tool round-trips ⇒ T = 2 and 3 model invocations under §4’s convention.
Token accounting:
• Base single-shot: 9,200 input + 300 output = 9,500 tokens
• Agentic: 10,350 input + 300 output = 10,650 tokens
• Amplification factor: 10,650 / 9,500 ≈ 1.12× (this specific hand-worked trace, tool outputs 800 +
350; the per-turn convention of §4/Table 19-1 — δ=800 + γ=65 per turn — gives α(T=2) = (9,500
+ 2×865)/9,500 = 11,230/9,500 ≈ 1.18× — different conventions, not a discrepancy)
A harder query that exhausts all 4 turns is the upper-bound case. Using the chapter’s per-turn
convention (each turn adds δ≈800 tokens of retrieved context plus γ≈65 tokens of model-generated
reasoning), the token trajectory grows approximately linearly: after k turns, total input tokens ≈
9,200 + k·(800+65), and total output ≈ 300 (final answer) — the intermediate reasoning (≈65 tokens
per turn) is retained inside the input context above, not counted again as output. After 4 turns, input
≈ 9,200 + 4×800 + 4×65 = 12,660 tokens, output ≈ 300 tokens, giving a total of ~12,960 tokens. The
amplification factor vs. single-shot is 12,960 / 9,500 ≈ 1.36×.

Agentic Systems

This worked example demonstrates that the cost increase is moderate for short reasoning paths
but compounds as the agent loops deeper. The architect must weigh the probability of deep loops
against the budget per request.

19.4. Measurement
To plan capacity and set budgets, we derive three quantities from the example above and the
illustrative turn distribution below. A production deployment must estimate these quantities from its
own telemetry.
First, a scoping note that matters more than any single number: a production agent turn is not
guaranteed to be exactly “one LLM inference + one tool call.” A turn may contain zero or more model
invocations, parallel or chained tool calls, retrieval + reranking, model-generated reasoning, tool
output, context compaction, or cached prefixes.
Treating “1 turn = 1 LLM call + 1 tool call” is a simplified execution model, useful for first-pass
arithmetic but not the general agent model. A more faithful capacity model is an execution trace:
request → model invocation(s) → tool invocation(s) → observation(s) → model invocation(s) →
final response, with its own token and latency totals. The amplification framework below (token α,
latency β) is one concrete, simplified instantiation of that trace — it is what an architect can compute
before instrumenting a real system.
It must be validated against measured traces afterwards.
19.4.1. Per-agent-turn token amplification

adds δ tokens of retrieved context and γ tokens of model-generated reasoning. The total token count
after T turns is:
Total(T ) = (I0 + T · δ + T · γ) + Ofinal
where Ofinal is the final output (≈300 tokens). The per-turn amplification α is the ratio of total
tokens to the single-shot baseline I0 + Ofinal :

What α does and does not measure. α measures retained/accumulated task context under
the simplified turn model — the unique content that must be held (and, absent compaction, resent as
context) as the conversation grows. It is not the total model-processed or API-billed token multiplier:
if the model is invoked repeatedly on the growing prefix, that retained context may be counted in
multiple input calls, and the per-call outputs must be counted separately. So α ≈ 1.27× at T = 3 says
the context is ~27% larger than single-shot — it does not say the task costs 1.27× the API spend or
1.27× the prefill FLOPs. Compute actual task tokens by summing the inputs and outputs of every
model invocation, with cached-token accounting recorded separately:

• task_input = 9,200 + 10,065 + 10,930 + 11,795 = 41,990 — Σ pure per-call inputs; no output

cache rate schedule and lie between the two processed totals.
The δ tokens are generated once (as retrieval/tool output), then retained as part of later turns’
input context — they are counted once as output-of-tool and again (as carried context) in each later
call’s input. That is correct and intended, but it means total tokens ≠ context size: the amplification
α (retained context) and the task totals (Σ per-call) are explicitly different, and neither is the billed
amount without a cache/billing rule.

19.4.2. Tool-call latency budget
Crucially, the agentic layer adds latency on top of the base answer generation, not instead of it. We
keep two terms rigidly separate:
• Base inference latency Lbase — the time to generate the final answer itself. Under the
canonical model this is ~8.6 s: 1.08 s prefill (Ch 8) + ~7.5 s decode of the 300-token answer at
~25 ms/token (Ch 8). Every agentic request pays Lbase at least once for the final answer, and
pays additional decode time for the intermediate reasoning the loop generates (the T·γ tokens,
~1.6 s per turn at ~25 ms/token).
• Agent orchestration / tool-call overhead Lagent — the per-turn cost of the loop around
the model: per-invocation orchestration overhead — scheduling, KV-slot setup, kernel launch
— excluding model compute, plus the tool backend round-trip. On 8×H100 the per-turn agent
step is ~120 ms (typical) for a 10,000-token context; tool backends (search, SQL) add 50–150
ms depending on data volume. So per-turn orchestration overhead Lagent ≈ 120 + 100 ≈ 220
ms (typical/central estimate). Both inputs are engineering estimates for the canonical 8×H100
deployment, with no published measurement behind them [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION],
and they drive β, the p50/p90/p95 headline (220 / 440 / 660 ms), the W tool leg, and the §8
SLA scoping. Sensitivity: at λ_tool = 150 ms the per-turn overhead is 270 ms and the p95 loop
overhead rises to 810 ms. The 120 ms is orchestration around the model, not model compute:
at ~25 ms/token it would buy under 5 tokens, while each turn’s model work — prefill of the
grown prefix plus the 65-token γ decode (~1.6 s) — is counted in the full service time W below,
not in Lagent.

Lagent = λstep + λtool
where λstep ≈ 120 ms (per-invocation system overhead — scheduling, KV-cache slot allocation,
kernel launch — not model FLOP time; the model’s own per-turn work, prefill of the grown prefix +
decode of γ , is carried inside W , ≈ 2.9–3.3 s marginal per turn — W(1)−W(0) = 2.94 s … W(4)−W(3) =
3.25 s on the printed no-reuse values) and λtool ≈ 100 ms (typical, tool backend range 50–150 ms)
[ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION], both inputs being engineering estimates with no published source.
For T turns the added orchestration overhead is T · Lagent ≈ 220 ms at the median T = 1, ≈ 440 ms at
the 90th percentile T = 2, and ≈ 660 ms at the 95th-percentile T = 3. These percentiles are conditional
on a completed agent run (the §7/§8 convention; see §8 for the turn distribution). T is capped at
3; the 2% fallback adds zero turns to this incremental expectation, and its failed-attempt work is
counted unconditionally in the §8 fallback ledger. These are the incremental agent-orchestration
numbers, not the full request latency — see the next section.

Agentic Systems

19.4.3. Multi-step reasoning cost
The “cost” of multi-step reasoning has two facets: token amplification (already quantified as α)
and latency. The incremental added latency — the base generation plus the added orchestration
overhead — is:
Lorch (T ) = Lbase + T · Lagent
where Lbase ≈ 8.6 s is the canonical full answer generation (1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode of 300
output tokens) and T · Lagent is the added agent-orchestration overhead (≈ 220 ms per turn). So the
agentic layer does not replace the ~8.6 s generation with ~440 ms — it adds a few hundred milliseconds
of orchestration/tool overhead on top of a request that already takes ~8.6 s to generate its answer.
Scope note — two different quantities, separated in Table 19-1. The Lorch (T ) above holds the
base generation at the single-shot decode (300 output tokens) and adds only the per-turn orchestration
overhead; it deliberately isolates how much the agentic layer’s orchestration adds. The full agentic
service time — the quantity used for fleet sizing in Chapter 17 — must additionally account for (a) the
decode of the per-turn model-generated reasoning tokens (γ ≈ 65 tokens/turn, at ~25 ms/token ≈ 1.6
s/turn) and (b) the prefill of every call’s input. A T-turn trace is T+1 model invocations, and under
the no-prefix-cache (no-reuse) policy each invocation re-reads the grown prefix. The authoritative
evaluator (render/agent_trace.py) therefore sums the prefill of all calls, not just one:

At T = 3, β(3) is 1 + 660 ms / 8.6 s ≈ 1.08×: the orchestration-only component adds ~8% — the
orchestration component is ~8% of the base generation (β(3) = 1.08), while the full task slowdown
at T = 3 is ~2.06× (no-reuse). But β measures only the incremental orchestration overhead, not the
full task slowdown. The full service time of a three-turn task grows from ~8.6 s (single-shot) to ~17.70
s under no-reuse (~2.06×) once the per-turn reasoning decode (~65 γ tokens/turn) and the re-prefill
of every grown turn are counted — a full increase of ~9.1 s (to ~14.14 s / ~1.64× with 100% prefix
reuse, a full increase of ~5.5 s). So β is βorch (orchestration-only), and the true task-level multiplier
is Ltask E2E /Lbase ≈ 2.06× (no-reuse) at T = 3 (~1.64× with prefix reuse). The bound that actually
matters: the added orchestration overhead is ~220 ms per turn (budget it), while fleet sizing follows
the total request time — the ~17.70 s no-reuse full service time, not the ~8.6 s single-shot generation.
These derived quantities give the architect concrete numbers to set policies: cap T at 3 unless
the quality gain is statistically significant, and allocate ~220 ms per turn in the orchestration-latency
budget.

19.4.4. Internal depth, agent turns, and training rollouts
An internal depth iteration is not an agent turn. A recurrent model can repeat an internal block
within one model invocation without emitting a tool call. An agent turn can contain prefill, internal
computation, output generation, and tool interaction. A training rollout is a third object: a trajectory
collected for the training procedure, not a request-time turn budget. This distinction prevents a

Agentic Systems

340

training method or internal execution setting from being mistaken for the orchestration trace that
the fleet must serve.1
Sidebar — model qualification (evaluation detail; cf. the book’s model-selection chapter).
Model qualification records the benchmark harness, context policy, reasoning effort, sampling settings,
and success metric with the model revision. A best-of-several-trials result is not interchangeable with
pass-at-one. Averaging independent single-attempt success indicators can estimate pass-at-one only
under the declared sampling and task protocol. An advertised context window does not establish
useful long-context quality, target concurrency, or the cost of serving it. The deployment decision
follows measured task success, invocation traces, and SLO-goodput, not a model-family label alone.
§6’s p_success must be measured under the declared qualification protocol.

19.5. Common Mistakes
1. Unbounded or miscalibrated turn limits. Setting the maximum number of agent turns too
high for the task leads to runaway token consumption and latency spikes. A poorly scoped
tool can let a model loop until token or deadline limits stop the request. [HYPOTHESIS] The
right cap is task-calibrated: measure the distribution of useful completion turns, loop-failure
turns, and marginal value per turn for the workload, then set the cap where marginal value
drops off (the canonical policy caps at 3, with a 2% fallback to single-shot — §4, §8); the number
is a policy parameter, not a constant.
2. Neglecting token accounting per turn. Many architects track only the initial input tokens
and forget that each retrieval or tool call adds context that persists for all subsequent turns.
Turn T therefore sees an input base that grows linearly with T . Concretely the append-only
total is I₀ + T·δ + T·γ + O_final = 9,200 + 800T + 65T + 300, which at 2.62 MB/token takes FP16
KV from 24.9 GB (single-shot, 9,500 tokens) to 34.0 GB (four turns, 12,960 tokens).
3. Overlooking tool latency variance. A tool that typically responds in 30 ms may, under
cache misses or lock contention, take 2 s. Without a timeout and fallback, the entire agent loop
blocks. Always instrument timeouts and provide a “best-effort” fallback path.
4. Confusing ‘agentic’ with ‘more prompts’. Adding extra prompts without a structured loop
(Plan/Execute/Observe/Decide) does not give the model reasoning power; it just inflates token
count. The agentic value comes from the model’s ability to reinterpret prior observations and
decide the next action.
1

Geiping et al., Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach, arXiv:2502.05171v2,
17 February 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05171v2; Ornith Team, Ornith-1.5: From Self-Scaffolding to Self-Improvement,
August 2026, https://ornith.ai/ornith_1_5.html. These primary accounts distinguish recurrent internal computation and
training trajectories; neither establishes the request-time turn count of the book’s hypothetical agent; pass@k itself is
defined in Chen et al., Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code, arXiv:2107.03374 (2021). Sources inspected 28
October 2026 as part of the separately dated addendum, not a refresh of the August comparison tables.

341

Agentic Systems

5. Skipping guardrails. Without pre-call validation (e.g., query sanitization, budget checks)
and post-call verification (answer relevance, hallucination detection), agentic systems can
produce plausible but incorrect or unsafe outputs. Guardrails are not optional — they are the
safety net that makes bounded loops safe in production. A production agent needs explicit
termination, budget, recovery, and escalation policies: hard turn/token/cost/wall-time limits,
tool timeouts, cancellation, idempotency/retry discipline, state checkpointing, and human
escalation. A logical multi-step task may be resumed across bounded execution windows rather
than granted unlimited resources — guardrails make the loop safe, not unbounded.

19.6. Architecture Consequence
Introducing an agentic layer reshapes the system architecture in seven ways:
State-management policy sets the trajectory. Before quantifying context/KV growth, the
architect must decide the state-management policy, because that policy — not the model — determines
whether context grows unbounded. The quantitative path that follows (Fig 19.2) uses an appendonly bounding case with this exact retention policy: (i) the initial prompt is retained in full; (ii) each
turn’s tool outputs are retained in full (not externalized); (iii) the model’s per-turn reasoning tokens
are visible and retained in the context (not hidden); (iv) no prefix cache is assumed to be reused
across turns (each turn’s request is rebuilt from the full accumulated context); (v) no truncation or
compaction is applied. Under that policy the context is only ever appended and never evicted, so it is
the worst case — a deliberate upper bound, not the deployed design.
Two token counts must be kept distinct. The billable tokens (what the API charges, = Σ over
turns of the full accumulated context each turn sends — 41,990 input tokens for the T = 3 no-reuse
trace of §4, not the single final context of 12,095) and the KV-resident tokens (what occupies the
cache, = the same accumulated context under this no-reuse policy); the two differ by the Σ-per-call
vs peak-resident distinction even without caching; prefix caching additionally lowers the billable
count while the KV-resident count stays.
The durable lesson. The growth rate is set by the policy levers — summarization (compress the
accumulated history each turn), truncation (drop the oldest context beyond a budget), externalized
tool state (store retrieval results out-of-band rather than in-context), replay policy (re-derive rather
than retain), and cache policy (prefix caching, KV precision). A design that applies these levers can
hold context roughly flat while an append-only design grows it ~36% by turn 4; the append-only
number is the stress case that bounds what the system must tolerate if the levers fail, not the expected
operating point. Fig 19.3 then compares that bounding case with the compaction and cache-policy
levers named above and shows that they move different quantities, not different amounts of the same
one.
Inference scaling. The base model (70B FP16, 8×H100) must now serve variable-length contexts,
and — critically — the KV-residency conclusion is far more severe than a per-latency convenience
because the canonical per-token KV is ~2.62 MB/token (Chapter 7’s full-MHA reference geometry).

Agentic Systems

342

A request that triggers 4 agent turns carries ~12,960 tokens vs. 9,500 for single-shot (Table 19-1) —
that is not a “35% GPU memory” tweak but a move from ~24.9 GB KV per request (9,500 tokens
× 2.62 MB) to ~34.0 GB (12,960 ×2.62 MB) — roughly a 36% growth, on top of an already-large KV
footprint. At the canonical workload’s ~86 average in-flight requests at 10 rps (Lexec = λ × Wexec ≈
10 × 8.6 per Ch 4; distinct from the ~100 active-user population) with the median single-turn profile
(~27.2 GB/request at 10,365 tokens), using the base-system in-flight count (86 = 10 × 8.6, Ch 4) as a
lower bound — the agentic T = 1 service time W ≈ 11.52 s would raise in-flight to ~115 and aggregate
KV to ~3.1 TB — the aggregate KV alone is already ~86 × 24.9 GB ≈ 2.1 TB (single-shot profile) —
far beyond one host’s ~436 GB KV budget, so agents do not just stress memory, they force
a fleet (Chapter 17). The architect must therefore treat context growth as a first-order capacity
driver: cap T , quantize KV (FP8), or compact the accumulated context, as these levers can repeatedly
beat adding hosts on price — each relaxes the per-request KV ceiling without commissioning new
hardware; prefix caching is a separate lever that lowers recomputation and billable tokens but leaves
the request’s own resident KV unchanged (§6, Fig 19.3) (see Ch 25 §8 for the FP8 KV arithmetic:
at the single-shot 9,500-token request, 436 GB ÷ 12.45 GB ≈ 35 concurrent vs 17.5 at FP16; at the T
= 3 profile above the same budget gives ≈27.5 vs ≈13.8). Note we must be precise: the per-request
KV is set by the model’s canonical per-token KV (all layers), not by per-layer figures; the honest
number is tens of GB per request, which is exactly why agentic depth is a fleet-sizing problem. The
scheduling unit is the whole request, not the model call: the request holds its KV slot across every
tool round-trip, so a T = 3 request occupies capacity for W ≈ 17.70 s even though the GPU is idle for
the tool legs — concurrency is set by wall-clock occupancy, not by GPU-busy time. Agentic traffic is
structurally more prefill-heavy — the prefill-time/decode-time ratio rises from ≈0.14 (1.08 s / 7.5 s)
single-shot to ≈0.40 (4.93 s / 12.375 s) at T=3 (1 → T+1 = 4 prefills per request); the prefill/decode
token ratio likewise rises from 30.7 (9,200 / 300) single-shot to 84.8 (41,990 / 495) at T=3 — so chunked
prefill, prefix caching and prefill/decode scheduling that were optional for single-shot traffic become
first-order here (see Chs. 10/15).
Three policies, three different levers. The append-only bar is the stress case of Fig 19.2
— nothing is evicted, so the footprint grows ~36% by turn 4 (24.9 → 34.0 GB), driven purely by
cumulative context, not by extra requests. Compaction (summarize or truncate the accumulated
history each turn) moves the footprint itself and can hold it roughly flat. Prefix-cache eviction moves
neither: the request still carries the full accumulated context (34.0 GB at turn 4), so its own KV is
unchanged — what changes is the reusable cached prefix, which is freed and must be re-prefilled on
the next turn. Billable tokens and KV-resident tokens therefore diverge as soon as a prefix cache is in
play (the distinction drawn above). Only the append-only number is derived here; the two policy
bars are qualitative [ILLUSTRATIVE].
Task economics. The deepest shift an agentic workload imposes is a change in what the architect
optimizes. For conventional inference, the unit of cost is the token: the architect optimizes token
economics — cost per token, latency per token, KV per token. For an agentic system, the unit of

Why agentic depth is a fleet-sizing problem. Both the token count and the FP16 KV cache grow linearly

Append-only (the bounding case quantified in Fig 19.2) reaches 34.0 GB FP16 KV per request, +36%
over the 24.9 GB single-shot; compaction (summarize or truncate the accumulated history each turn)
bounds the footprint across turns at roughly the single-shot level — about 24.9 GB, 27% below the
append-only case; prefix-cache eviction leaves the request’s own context and KV unchanged (still
34.0 GB) while freeing cached prefix memory and costing a re-prefill. Assumption: each bar is a
counterfactual completed request after four turns (9,200 input + 300 output + 800 + 65 per turn), not
an intermediate state of a live agent; append-only [DERIVED] from Ch 19 arithmetic, the two policy
bars [ILLUSTRATIVE]. Caveat: only the append-only case is priced in this book — the other two
bars are qualitative.

value is the task: the architect optimizes task economics, because a task consumes a variable, datadependent number of model calls, tool calls, and tokens, and may fail. The right denominator is
therefore cost per successful task, not cost per token:

model calls/task × (uncached input tokens/call × $/in token
+ output tokens/call × $/out token
+ cached tokens/call × $/cached token)
+ tool calls/task × $/tool
cost per successful task ≈

+ retries/task × cost/retry
psuccess

where psuccess > 0 is the task success rate, the first term prices uncached input tokens per call
(the cached share is billed at its own rate and must not also be counted as input — cached is a subset
of carried input), and the tokens processed across the task’s calls are the execution-trace totals —
task_input 41,990 plus task_output 495 (§4 ledger), uncached — not the agentic factor α from Section
4, which is only the retained-context ratio (cumulative-context total vs the single-shot equivalent;
processed ≈ 4.47× vs α = 1.27×; the billed total depends on the provider’s cache-rate schedule and
lies between the two). Two consequences follow. First, a more expensive model that completes tasks
in one turn can be cheaper per successful task than a cheap model that needs three turns — the
amplification term can dominate the base price. Second, the success rate is as important as the
unit cost: a 10% cheaper pipeline that fails 5% more often can be net more expensive once retries
and human intervention are counted. This is a genuinely different objective from cheapest tokens,
and it is why agentic workloads cannot be priced or capacity-planned with the single-shot token
arithmetic alone. An architect should instrument tasks (success, turns, calls, retries) and optimize cost
per successful task, exactly as an architect of a deterministic service optimizes cost per completed
request.
Tool backend provisioning. Search indexes, SQL pools, and code interpreters become firstclass infrastructure components. Their capacity (concurrent queries, connection pool size, query
throughput) must be dimensioned alongside the LLM GPU pool. A bottleneck in the tool backend
will manifest as increased λtool , which directly inflates the per-turn loop overhead Lagent (§4), and
through it the full service time W .
Observability requirements. Each turn generates a tuple of (turn number, model input tokens,
model prefill time, model decode time — equivalently model output tokens, queueing latency, tool
call, tool latency, tool output tokens, decision); if the model latency is not timed directly it can be
derived from the recorded input/output token counts via the Ch 8 prefill model. Correlating these
tuples across turns for a single request, and across requests for the fleet, requires structured logging
and tracing. Without it, debugging why a request took ~11.5 s and consumed ~19,600 tokens is nearly
impossible.

Agentic Systems

346

Fallback & degradation pathways. Because the agentic layer introduces data-dependent depth,
the system must have graceful degradation: if the turn limit is reached, return the best partial answer
so far, or fall back to a simpler single-shot prompt. This preserves user experience even when the
agent fails to converge.

19.7. What We Still Don’t Know
Despite the quantified arithmetic above, several questions remain open and would benefit from
targeted research:
• Turn-count distribution shift with model scale. Do larger models (e.g., a 405B FP16 model)
exhibit different T distributions? Does the ability to “see more” reduce the need for multi-step
loops, or does the model reason more deeply and actually increase T ?
• Token amplification vs. answer quality curve. We can compute α(T) from the illustrative
token counts, but we have not firmly established the marginal quality gain per additional turn.
Is the 1.27× → 1.36× move from T = 3 to T = 4 worth the 7% token increase? A/B tests across
query categories would help.
• Latency tail under spike load. Our 95th-percentile added orchestration latency of ~660 ms
(T = 3, the scenario turn cap; conditional on a completed agent run, with the fallback-inclusive
ledger in §8 giving the same p95 but p99 = 860 ms) assumes GPU inference time is constant.
Under traffic spikes, GPU saturation can increase inference latency non-linearly. Empirical
measurement under controlled load is needed to validate the linear T·L model.
• Optimal tool design for minimal turn count. Some tools could return more comprehensive
results in a single call, reducing the need for multiple rounds. The design space of “rich
vs. narrow” tools and its impact on T is underexplored.
• Cross-user context caching. If many users ask related questions (e.g., “What does the policy
say about X?”), can we cache intermediate retrieval results and avoid redundant tool calls?
The savings could be substantial but require careful invalidation logic.

19.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Agentic Turn Distribution and KV Growth
Scenario. An enterprise RQA system serves 2,000 knowledge workers. The baseline single-shot
configuration uses a 70B FP16 model on 8×H100, with 9,200 input tokens and 300 output tokens, at
10 rps average / 40 rps peak. The team introduces an agentic layer with a maximum of 3 turns, using
the chapter’s per-turn convention (δ≈800 + γ≈65 ≈ 865 tokens/turn). The guardrail budget caps total
input at 13,000 tokens — a safety margin above the append-only worst case (12,660 at T = 4, Table
19-1), so the turn cap binds before the guardrail does.

back request’s own full service time (the §4 evaluator applied to the fallback trace: (39,395/9,200)×1.08
+ 0.025×495 + 3×0.133 ≈ 17.40 s model-side — prefill + decode + tool leg; W(3) = 17.70 s is on the same

is dominated by the ~8.6 s base generation (Ch 8), not the added orchestration; the ~220–660 ms
figures are the added agent/tool overhead, not the complete request latency. The complete request is
the full agentic service time W row of Table 19-1 — ~11.52 s at the median T = 1 and ~17.70 s at T = 3
under no-reuse (~10.43 s / ~14.14 s under 100% prefix reuse) — which is the quantity Chapter 17 sizes
the fleet against.
Architectural actions. The team sets the turn limit to 3, instruments each turn’s token and
orchestration latency, adds a context cache for the search tool, and adds prefix caching (or compaction)
for the grown prefix — at T = 3, processed tokens 4.47× → ≈1.27× and W 17.70 s → 14.14 s at 100%
reuse (billed lies between the two under the provider’s cache schedule — §4); prefix caching leaves
KV residency unchanged, while compaction reduces the resident context itself (it moves the footprint
— §6). With a cache hit rate of 30% on recurring queries, the newly-fetched portion of δ drops to
~560 tokens per turn (70% of 800; the cached 30% is not re-fetched) — a 30% cut in retrieval re-fetch
transport. Note: the retained context still carries the full 800 tokens per turn (cached or not), so
absent a concrete context-reduction policy this cache yields no LLM-token or KV-resident saving;
the re-fetch cost and the KV-resident length are distinct (see the billable-vs-KV-resident distinction
in §6). The median added orchestration overhead is still T = 1 → ~220 ms. The claim “meets an SLA
of <1 s” must be scoped carefully: the added agent-orchestration latency is comfortably under 1 s, but
the end-to-end request is ~9 s because of the base generation. The architect therefore scopes the <1
s SLA to orchestration overhead excluding final generation, and treats end-to-end as bounded by the
~8.6 s base generation in the incremental view (or by the full service time W ≈ 11.5 s at the median T
= 1 in the fleet-sizing view).

Lesson. The agentic layer had three distinct token effects that must be labeled separately: (a)
retained-context length grows ~12% distribution-weighted (α = 1.12×, from the expected 10,650
/ 9,500 — this is a weighted expectation over the §8 turn distribution; the per-turn α values are 1.09×
at T=1, 1.18× at T=2, 1.27× at T=3, 1.36× at T=4) — this is context, not processed or billed tokens; (b)
processed model tokens across all invocations grow ~152% per submitted request (2.52×, from the
distribution-weighted 100-request ledger: 23,927 / 9,500), because in this no-prefix-reuse request mix
the model re-reads the grown prefix on each call; (c) billed spend depends on the prefix-cache policy
and provider rates — under 100% prefix reuse only the incremental prefix is billed, under no-reuse
all of it is. It added, at the median T = 1, ~220 ms of orchestration latency (on top of an ~8.6 s base
generation), but improved answer correctness on multi-step reasoning queries by an estimated 22%
in an illustrative human-eval reading [ILLUSTRATIVE] scenario result, not a reported production
measurement. The trade-off is acceptable on the modeled terms only if the estimated correctness
gain holds — full service time rises from ~8.6 s to W(1) ≈ 11.52 s (+34%) and processed tokens to 2.52×,
against an estimated +22% correctness [ILLUSTRATIVE], a quantity §7’s open “Token amplification
vs. answer quality curve” question leaves unestablished; judged on orchestration overhead alone (220
ms) it would look far cheaper than it is; the verdict is against cost per successful task (§6), not the
~220 ms orchestration overhead — and context caching cut the retrieval re-fetch cost (transport only
— the retained context is unchanged). The architect’s key decisions were: (a) capping turns at 3, (b)
adding a search cache, and (c) providing a single-shot fallback when the limit is hit. Do not quote
the ~12% retained-context growth as a ~12% compute/cost increase — the processed-token
multiplier is ~2.52× in this no-reuse mix.
