chapter 20.
Fleet-Level Optimization

The Architect’s Question
As a RAG Q&A workload scales from a single host to a fleet of serving nodes, the architect must
confront a new set of trade-offs: how does aggregate throughput scale with added hardware, how
does scheduling latency affect user-perceived latency, and at what point does autoscaling cease to be
cost-effective? This chapter addresses these questions through concrete arithmetic, not hand-waving.

20.1. Concept
Fleet-level optimization treats the entire collection of serving hosts as a single resource pool rather
than independent islands. The central insight is that aggregate system throughput is not merely the
sum of individual host throughputs; it is modulated by scheduling overhead, network contention,
and the cost of moving data between hosts and storage. Two cost effects must be kept distinct. The
average cost per query declines only along the canonical 10 → 40 rps ramp, where fixed overhead
(model loading, infrastructure, staff) is spread across 4× the requests and across more SLO-compliant
completions per observation window (Ch 14’s goodput definition), cost per request may decline
until additional capacity steps dominate; adding idle hosts at fixed demand increases unit cost. The
marginal cost of each added host, however, is roughly constant in this model — one host buys ~2.0
req/s (17/8.6 = 1.977, [ANALYTICAL]) at ~$20/hr, so the marginal cost stays near ~$10 per req/s per
hour (Ch 17 §7 frames the Nth host as diminishing marginal benefit, not falling marginal cost). Unit
convention for this chapter: rps denotes an arrival rate and req/s a capacity rate; both are requests
per second. The economic lever is amortizing the fixed term, not the marginal one.

353

Fleet-Level Optimization

354

The key concepts are:
• Aggregate throughput: The total queries-per-second the fleet can sustain before latency SLO
violations.
• Scheduling overhead: The per-request cost of dispatching a query to an available host,
including placement decisions and data movement.
• Autoscaling break-even: The point at which growth in SLO-compliant completions per
observation window covers the next host’s fixed cost — average cost per query falls as fixed
costs amortize, while marginal cost per query stays roughly constant.

20.2. Mental Model
The mental model for fleet optimization replaces the single-host query pipeline with a two-level
hierarchy. At the lower level, each host processes queries using its GPU/CPU pipeline. At the upper
level, a scheduler routes incoming requests across hosts, handling load balancing, model parallelism
where needed, and graceful degradation under overload.
The scheduler’s decisions have direct impact on the tail of the latency distribution. Poor placement
can cause some hosts to saturate while others remain underutilized, inflating the 99th-percentile
latency even when aggregate throughput is ample. Conversely, intelligent scheduling — such as
consistent hashing for session affinity or predictive placement based on historical patterns — tends
to keep utilization more uniform across the fleet and reduces tail latency.
A critical assumption in this model is that the workload follows a known arrival process. For the
canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average and ~40 rps peak. With ~9,200 in-tokens and ~300
out-tokens per query, a ~8.6 s service time per request (1.08 s prefill + ~7.5 s decode), and a 70B dense
FP16 model running on 8×H100 (640 GB total HBM3), the fleet must sustain ~40 requests/s at peak,
which — by Little’s Law — corresponds to λ·W ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344 requests in flight (W here is Ch
17’s assumed mean KV-residency time E[W_KV-resident] ≈ 8.6 s, a conditional scenario proxy — not
the end-to-end W_e2e, which adds queue, tool and inter-turn time that, under the stated assumption,
holds no KV), not merely the ~100 concurrent users or the nominal 40 rps. The distinction between
“concurrent users” (a population), the arrival rate (rps), and in-flight requests (λ·W) is exactly what
Chapter 17 develops; it is the difference between sizing for a population and sizing a fleet against a
latency bound.

20.3. Worked Example
Take a fleet of N hosts, each with 8×H100 running a single 70B FP16 model instance. Two
capacities must be reconciled — throughput (tokens/s) and KV residency (concurrent requests) —
and neither can be reduced to a single “rps” constant, because rps is workload-specific (per-request
input/output tokens, context length, batch).

355

Fleet-Level Optimization

Latency floor first, then reconcile the two capacity bounds
A 300-output-token request at a ~25 ms/token decode rate (Chapter 8) takes ~7.5 s of generation
alone, plus 1.08 s prefill, so the service time is ~8.6 s per request (before tool calls). Two separate
ceilings bound how many requests a host can serve per second, and they must be reconciled — they
are not interchangeable.
Throughput bound (tokens/s)
A host sustains an illustrative ~35,000 tokens/s of total (prefill+decode) serving throughput — the
conservative low end of the ~35,000–56,000 tokens/s achievable range in Chapter 15 [ILLUSTRATIVE]
— distinct from the ~19,800 tokens/s prefill-only ideal in Chapter 8 (8 × 2,472 at 35% MFU), which counts
prefill compute alone. These two are not directly comparable as single numbers: ~35,000 is a
phase-mixed prefill+decode total and ~19,800 is a prefill-only figure. To compare them one
must first phase-resolve both, then compare prefill with prefill (the presented workload’s
prefill leg is 2.0 req/s × 9,200 = 18,400 input tokens/s) and decode with decode (2.0 × 300 =
600 output tokens/s); aggregating the two phases into one “total” rate requires an explicit
cost/phase-equivalence model. Dividing the total by the ~9,500 tokens/request gives ~3.7 requests/s
— but this is not achievable here, because it would require ~3.7 × 8.6 ≈ 32 concurrent requests in
flight, roughly double the host’s KV-residency ceiling (C ≈ 17.5, conservative integer floor 17, Chapter
17). The token-throughput figure is thus a non-binding upper edge for this canonical workload.
KV-residency / latency bound (Little’s Law)
The real ceiling is set by concurrency and KV residency time together: a host holds 17 whole
concurrent full-context requests (the ~17.5 KV ceiling, Chapter 17, floored to whole contexts — no
fractional admission) each for an assumed mean KV residency E[W_KV-resident] ≈ 8.6 s, so C/W
= 17 / 8.6 = 1.977 ≈ 2.0 requests/s [ANALYTICAL] at steady state — a KV-slot upper bound on
admitted rate (defined below).
The binding per-host rate is the minimum of the two — here the KV/latency bound under cases (i)
and (iii); a third, phase-resolved prefill-compute screen is evaluated below and binds under case (ii) (22
hosts raw, 23 with the ρ derate). This is exactly why a token-throughput number must not be divided
by tokens-per-request to manufacture an “rps” here: the units do cancel (tokens/s ÷ tokens/request =
requests/s), but the numerator is a phase-mixed prefill+decode total with no cost/phase-equivalence
model, and the ~3.7 req/s answer would need ~32 concurrent requests against the 17-slot host capacity.
The per-host request rate is a concurrency × service-time quantity — what makes the division wrong
here is what its numerator mixes and its answer assumes, not its units.

Fleet-Level Optimization

356

What the ~2.0 req/s figure is — and is not
The ~2.0 req/s figure is a KV-slot-based analytical UPPER bound on admitted request comple­
tion rate, conditional on an assumed mean KV residency time — a necessary capacity screen:
not a measured serving throughput, not a lower guaranteed rate, and not an SLO goodput. The lower
bound on host count derives FROM this upper bound on the per-host rate (⌈λ/(C/W)⌉ = ⌈λ·W/C⌉); it
is never a lower bound on the rate itself. It is achievable only if serving C concurrent sequences does
not inflate W beyond the assumed ~8.6 s, and neither a compute, bandwidth, nor scheduler constraint
binds first. In real continuous batching, W is a function of batch occupancy, scheduler policy, prefill
interference, decode batching, the arrival process, tensor-parallel communication, and the context
distribution — so C and W are not always independent constants. Treat ~2.0 req/s as an upper-bound
model, and require benchmarked goodput (Chapter 14) under the target arrival process for actual
fleet sizing. Planning-bound caveat: like the ~19,800 prefill tokens/s/host figure (Ch. 8, idealized
prefill only), the ~2.0 req/s/host figure is the KV-slot upper bound on admitted rate named above —
model-derived, not an implied deployed rate. No p95/p99 performance guarantee has been
shown for any of the host counts in this chapter; the p95/p99 tail latency and achieved goodput
must be measured on the target deployment (Chapter 14) before the governing 23-host sizing (21 =
the KV/Little screen under case (i); 22 = the ρ ≈ 0.95 derate of that screen — and, independently, the
raw full-square case (ii) prefill compute screen, which also gives 22 and rises to 23 with the same ρ
derate, the governing screen; 34 at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy against 32 for KV-only — Ch 17 Table
17-1, u and ρ independent) is treated as validated.
Simultaneous feasibility check (prefill + decode coexistence)
The ~2.0 req/s/host bound assumes prefill and decode run on the same host at the same time. Evaluated
at the displayed ~2.0 req/s — a deliberate stress screen, slightly above the unrounded 17/8.6 = 1.977 —
the prefill demand is 2.0 × 9,200 = 18,400 input tokens/s per host (§3). The idealized prefill ceiling
is 8 × 0.989 PF/s × 35% / (2 × 70e9) ≈ 19,780 tokens/s (Chapter 8, 35% MFU, prefill-only — case (i),
linear-only FLOP convention). Cross-note on MFU: Ch 20 uses the conservative 35% planning MFU
(Ch 8); Ch 22/24 use 40% sustained (Ch 24 §3.3) — the choice moves the case-(i) screen from 19 to 17
hosts. The ratio is 18,400 ÷ 19,780 ≈ 93% under case (i); under case (ii) (full-square, ×1.1723) the ceiling
falls to ≈16,870 linear-equivalent tokens/s and the ratio becomes 18,400 ÷ 16,870 ≈ 109% (the same

peak), and under case (iii) (causal-triangle, ×1.0861), ceiling ≈18,210 tokens/s, 18,400 ÷ 18,210 ≈101%
— above 100% the prefill leg alone does not fit at 2 req/s — so the ~7% headroom under case (i) is a

prefill ceiling under case (i). This is [ANALYTICAL] (Axis-3 measurement status; defined with the

a measured rate. The ~93% leaves very little headroom before decode coexistence, interference, and
the actual achieved MFU. Prefill and decode share the same hardware. Batch scheduling and decode

The additive form is a first-order capacity floor: scheduling, network-contention and data-movement

Scheduling overhead
A lightweight round-robin scheduler adds ~0.5 ms of dispatch latency per request [ILLUSTRATIVE]
— negligible next to a real 7.5 s decode. The governing target is absolute: < 100 ms p99 dispatch,
~1.2% of the canonical 8.6 s request and, equivalently, ≤ 5% of the 2 s TTFT SLO turn budget; the
fraction is derived from the absolute number, not a second constraint.
Autoscaling economics
Each 8×H100 host costs ~$20/hour (cloud, $2.50/GPU-hr canonical) or ~$8/hour amortized (owned)
— [ILLUSTRATIVE]. The marginal cost per additional req/s is $20 ÷ (req/s gained per host); the
economic lesson (declining average cost per request as fixed costs amortize across more requests)
is sound, but the exact per-req/s figure is only meaningful after the real per-host throughput is
benchmarked. Quantifying the break-even, with a fixed overhead of ~$40/hr (infrastructure and staff,
[ILLUSTRATIVE]): at the 40-rps peak the autoscaled fleet runs 21 hosts at (21 × $20 + $40) ÷ 144,000
requests/hr ≈ $3.19 per 1K requests, and at the 10-rps average it runs 6 hosts at (6 × $20 + $40) ÷
36,000 ≈ $4.44 per 1K — a ~28% average-cost decline across the 4× demand ramp while the marginal
$10.12 per req/s per hour is unchanged. The break-even against a statically provisioned 21-host fleet
($420/hr) sits at 19 hosts, i.e. sustained demand ≤ ~37.6 rps: above that, autoscaling costs more than
the peak-sized fleet it replaces.

A practical pitfall: measuring only aggregate req/s without tracking per-host variance can mask
saturation in individual nodes. Always report both the fleet-wide and per-host metrics.
Placement also determines the communication and failure domain. A slow or failed participant
can delay an entire model-parallel group while other replicas remain healthy. Group-level completion

tails, asynchronous failures and the affected requests therefore accompany per-host utilization. A
placement that improves average utilization but increases cross-group contention can reduce SLOgoodput; replica isolation and group recovery require measurement before they become fleet-capacity
assumptions.
The qualification gate in Chapter 18 applies before a configuration enters any capacity pool. A
fallback route consumes capacity too; its quality, deadline and data-policy constraints remain part of
the placement contract.

20.5. Common Mistakes
• Treating hosts as independent: Optimizing each host in isolation (e.g., tuning batch size per
host) inflates the variance in per-host service time; the fleet’s tail latency and the Table 20-1
utilization-variance target (< 0.2) are set by the slowest hosts, not by the average host.
• Overlooking data movement cost: In RAG workloads, the retrieved-context text that be­
comes the ~8,000-token portion of the ~9,200 input tokens per query must be fetched from a
vector database or cache over the network, while the ~300 out-tokens are generated entirely
on the host — only the final response needs to reach the user. The quantity that distinguishes
architectures is bytes fetched per query: if every host fetches independently, each query moves
its full context bytes, repeated for every query and every host. A shared cache layer or a
colocated store fetches each distinct context once and serves later hits locally, so the saving
is proportional to the cross-query context-overlap rate — not to a scaling exponent that is
identical under both schemes.
• Autoscaling too aggressively: Adding hosts at the first sign of latency increase can be
suboptimal if the bottleneck is scheduler throughput or cache contention, not compute capacity.
Measure the marginal cost of adding a host before triggering a scale-out event.
• Ignoring cold-start cost: When a host is freshly provisioned or re-warmed after idle, load­
ing the full model weights into HBM takes ~28–112 seconds [ILLUSTRATIVE] (a load-path
assumption for a ~140 GB model over a ~10–40 Gb/s (≈1.25–5 GB/s) path — 140 GB ÷ 28–112 s
≈ 5–1.25 GB/s, i.e. ≈40–10 Gb/s — not a hardware benchmark; distinct from the much shorter
KV-cache warm-up of ~2 s discussed in Chapter 15, which re-populates only the retained
KV state). Autoscaling policies must account for this weight-load warm-up window when
scaling out a fresh host; otherwise the fleet experiences a spike in error rate or timeout during
scale-out events.

361

Fleet-Level Optimization

20.6. Architecture Consequence
Fleet-level optimization reshapes the serving architecture in three ways:
1. Centralized scheduler: A lightweight service (e.g., based on etcd or a custom placement
engine) maintains real-time view of per-host utilization and makes dispatch decisions. This
service must be highly available, and its dispatch overhead should stay a small fraction of
the per-request SLO — for the canonical ~8.6 s service time, a sub-millisecond decision is
a comfortable target (the round-robin baseline adds ~0.5 ms, §3), not a universal necessity:
the binding constraint is that dispatch overhead not consume a meaningful share of the
request/turn SLO, which depends on routing frequency and scheduling architecture.
2. Data colocation: Vector indexes and model weights are stored close to the hosts that consume
them. This may mean running a local Qdrant or Milvus instance per host, or using a shared
object store (e.g., MinIO) with read-replicas per availability zone. The goal is to minimize the
distance — measured in network hops — between the scheduler’s placement decision and the
data fetch. But colocation is a trade, not a free win: a per-host index multiplies memory/storage,
consistency, ingestion, and operational cost across the fleet, and model-weight locality is a
different problem from vector-index locality. The right placement depends on the workload —
compare centralized retrieval, AZ-local retrieval, replicated indexes, and cached results, and
identify the traffic/latency point at which colocation’s access-latency saving outweighs its
replication cost. Do not conflate the two locality questions.
3. Graceful degradation: The fleet should have a mode where, under extreme overload, it serves
stale or truncated answers rather than failing entirely. This could mean returning the top-k
results from a cached embedding rather than recomputing, or surfacing a “try again” message
with an estimated wait time. The architectural contract must make this trade-off explicit so
product teams can set appropriate SLOs.
20.6.1. The useful completion is an accepted output
For a RAG fleet the useful completion is an accepted output — a response that passes the deadline,
integrity, quality, and safety gates in the observation window — so hosts are sized against accepted
outputs per observation window, not raw work; the rejection/OOM/cancellation counters and the
cost-per-accepted-completion basis follow that rule, and placement follows the measured-servicetime rule (place warm replicas where measured service time, not nominal load time, sets the request
path). The same accepted-completion goodput accounting applies to any fixed-output-contract
workload; a video-generation fleet is the clearest parallel beyond RAG — there the accepted output
is a clip passing the same four gates in the same observation window, raw work rates (frames/s,
clip-seconds/s) need a stated denominator and do not normalize the nonlinear attention cost, and
warm replicas trade idle cost for avoiding checkpoint downloads, initialization, compilation, and

Fleet-Level Optimization

362

encoder loading on the request path. For a RAG fleet architect the parallel is direct: both fleets
size hosts against accepted outputs in the observation window, not raw work, so the same capacity
screens and placement rules apply. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] proposed service accounting.

20.7. What We Still Don’t Know
Several open questions remain at the fleet level:
• Heterogeneous hardware: What happens when hosts mix H100, A100, and CPU-only nodes?
The scheduler must handle different throughput ceilings and memory capacities, and the
aggregate throughput calculation becomes a weighted sum rather than a simple multiple.
Real-world measurements of mixed-device fleets are scarce; most published benchmarking
uses homogeneous hardware, so the crossover point where heterogeneity hurts versus helps is
not well quantified.
• Multi-model serving: Ch 18 covers routing, tiering, and quantization trade-offs for mixed
model sizes; what this chapter leaves open is how to compute a fleet’s aggregate capacity when
per-host rates differ by model — the N × Q identity in §3 assumes a single Q — and how the
scheduler should place a request whose model is not resident on the least-loaded host without
breaking session affinity or the shared KV budget. Joint placement of heterogeneous model
sizes under one KV budget (Ch 18 §3.3) remains unresolved.
• Economic auto-scaling: The break-even point between owning hardware versus cloudon-demand depends on utilization patterns that are workload-specific. A fleet that runs at
20% utilization on average may be cheaper in the cloud; one at 80% utilization favors owned
hardware. The transition point is a function of capital expenditure amortization period, elec­
tricity cost, and the volatility of user demand. Published TCO analyses typically assume steady
utilization, but bursty workloads with short-lived spikes can make ownership risky unless
over-provisioned.
• Tail-latency arbitration: When two queries compete for the same GPU HBM bandwidth,
the 99th-percentile latency can spike disproportionately. We lack a general-purpose scheduler
policy that guarantees a target tail latency under arbitrary arrival patterns; this remains an
area of active research. Some systems use priority queues or token buckets to cap per-query
bandwidth, but these mechanisms add scheduling complexity and can increase median latency.
• Cross-query caching effects: RAG prompts share long leading prefixes across users asking
related questions, and the open quantity is the prefix-overlap distribution — shared leading
tokens as a fraction of a query’s prefill FLOPs. That fraction, not the raw token count, bounds
what prefix caching (Ch 15) can save. Charged against it is the cache-management cost: invali­
dation, cross-replica coherence, metadata, and the loss of batch-occupancy flexibility when

363

Fleet-Level Optimization

requests pin shared prefixes. We lack large-scale measurements of that overlap distribution
and of how much of the theoretical prefill saving survives the management cost. Reuse of
earlier outputs across askers is a separate question about answer quality and provenance, not a
KV-reuse question.

chapter 21.
The AI Factory: Turning Inference Into an
Industrial Process

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to treat AI delivery as an industrial process rather than a one-off
project: a repeatable factory with automated pipelines for data, evaluation, promotion, and rollback.
We will separate the three layers of the factory (the model lifecycle, the serving pipeline, and the
operations loop), then build the economics of promotion gating and retraining cadence for the
canonical workload. After this chapter, “we ship a better model” is a gated, measurable, reversible
event — not a risky redeploy.

21.1. Concept
The AI Factory is the discipline of making model delivery routine. We use the term as a generic
architectural concept — the idea that model delivery can be run as an industrial, gate-driven
process — not as any one vendor’s marketing vocabulary. It rests on three pillars:
1. Data pipeline — the automated intake, cleaning, versioning, and labelling of the data that
trains or evaluates the model. For a RAG system this includes the retrieval corpus, its freshness,
and its quality gates. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
2. Evaluation & promotion gate — a systematic process that scores a candidate model or
configuration against defined metrics (quality, latency, cost) on a held-out benchmark before it
can replace the incumbent in production. This is where Ch 14’s deployment benchmarking
becomes a recurring gate rather than a one-time event.

367

The AI Factory: Turning Inference Into an Industrial Process

368

3. Serve + observe + rollback — the serving layer (Ch 11) plus a feedback loop that mea­
sures real traffic, detects drift or regression, and can roll the production model back safely.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
The factory converts the architect’s recurring question from “should we adopt this model?” (a
one-off decision) into “does this candidate pass the automated gate?” (a routine, repeatable decision
with the same rigor every time).

21.2. Mental Model
The AI Factory is best read as a release pipeline with a quality gate placed before every
promotion, mirroring how software CI/CD gated deployments decades ago. Three mental moves:
• Models are artifacts like code. They get versioned, tested, reviewed, and promoted through
environments (staging → canary → production) with automated checks at each step — not
dropped into prod on a hunch.
• The gate is the memory of the factory. The evaluation suite and its thresholds encode
everything we’ve learned about what “good enough” means (Ch 4 capability, Ch 14 deployment).
If the gate is weak, the factory has no standards.
• Everything is reversible. A promotion that regresses metrics must be rollback-able in minutes.
The factory’s value is not eliminating errors but making them cheap and safe.
The factory’s shape is a pipeline with decisions: data in → train/fine-tune → evaluate →
push to canary → observe → promote or rollback → serve. Each arrow is a decision point, and each
decision point is where an architect has influence.

21.3. Worked Example
The example below works the economics of promotion gating on the canonical 70B RAG workload.
21.3.1. The Economics of Promotion Gating for the Canonical Workload
We show the factory’s value by comparing ungated and gated adoption of a candidate model on the
canonical 70B RAG workload (~10 rps average, 9.2K-in/ 300-out). [canonical scenario] (Ch 4, Table 4-2)
Setup. Suppose a new model candidate claims better retrieval-QA quality but no one has measured
its serving behavior. Two adoption paths:
• Ungated: deploy the candidate to all production traffic immediately. If it regresses (say p95
TTFT degrades because of a slower tokenizer, or quality drops on a subset), the service suffers
until rollback.
• Gated: run the candidate on a 5% canary for N hours, measure TTFT/goodput/quality against
the incumbent, promote only if it beats every threshold.

21.4. Measurement
The configuration qualification in Chapter 18 supplies the candidate identity for these gates:
model, precision, backend and relevant runtime versions. A changed execution path needs new
evidence; a previous model-level approval does not establish that the new configuration is safe to
promote.

The AI Factory: Turning Inference Into an Industrial Process

370

The factory is only as trustworthy as its gates. We measure four things continuously:
1. Gate pass rate — the share of candidates the gate admits. A rising rate can mean better candi­
dates or looser thresholds, so it is read only alongside the second number. False-promotion
rate — how often a gated change later regresses in production; only this one directly indicates
that the evaluation suite is losing fidelity.
2. Canary-to-production time and rollback time — the speed of promotion and escape; both
should be minutes, not days.
3. Model freshness / data staleness — time since the retrieval corpus or model was last validated;
drift detection feeds the retraining decision.
4. MTTR for a bad release — mean time to detect + rollback; the factory’s core reliability
number.

21.5. Common Mistakes
• No gate, or a decorative gate. An evaluation that always passes is worse than none because
it grants false confidence.
• Promoting on quality only. Quality passing but serving (Ch 14) regressing still breaks the
service; the gate must include deployment metrics.
• Assuming retraining cadence is “as often as possible.” More frequent retraining is not
free — it consumes compute, risk, and evaluation effort; the right cadence balances drift against
churn (the memory and compute a training run consumes — Ch 7 for the optimizer/activation
memory floor, Ch 8 for the FLOP budget — set the resource cost a cadence must fit).
• Skipping rollback rehearsal. A rollback that has never been exercised will fail precisely
when it is needed.
• Treating the factory as a build-once artifact. It is a living process that must absorb new
models, new metrics, and new data sources continuously.

21.6. Architecture Consequence
The AI Factory is the operational backbone that makes the book’s whole loop durable. Every
architectural decision recomputes through it: model selection (Ch 3/5) feeds the evaluation gate,
serving choices (Ch 11) determine canary mechanics, benchmarking (Ch 14) becomes the recurring
gate, TCO (Ch 16) sets how much gating overhead is affordable, and fleet operations (Ch 17–20)
provide the rollout/rollback surfaces. Without the factory, each chapter’s decision is a one-off; with
it, they compound into a system that gets better and safer every cycle.
Three components implement the factory: an evaluation runner that executes the gate, a canary
router that splits traffic between incumbent and candidate, and a rollback mechanism that restores
the last-known-good model. Three design decisions shape each promotion: gate granularity (what
the gate checks and how often), canary routing strategy (how traffic splits and for how long), and
the rollback trigger (which metric breach fires it). Each decision is a trade-off: a finer, slower gate

raises gate latency and delays promotion; a wider canary improves evaluation fidelity but exposes
more users.

21.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• The true cost of model churn (retraining + reeval + redeploy) per productivity gain is
[HYPOTHESIS] and workload-specific; there is no universal cadence.
• How well evaluation suites generalize across distribution shifts in real traffic is workloaddependent and evolves with traffic patterns — an ongoing verification requirement, not a gap
in this manuscript’s research; a suite tuned on last quarter’s data may misjudge this quarter’s
model.
• The right canary size for a given risk posture is [UNRESOLVED] per service; 5% worked
here but high-risk systems may need smaller, staged canaries.

372

21.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Vendor’s ‘Better Bench’: Canary and Roll­
back
A vendor pitches the architect a newer, cheaper model: “just swap it in — it scores better on the
bench.” A year ago the architect might have, and watched p95 TTFT silently drift past the SLO for a
week. Now the AI Factory is in place. The architect drops the candidate into the pipeline: the data
pipeline versions it, the evaluation gate scores it against quality AND the deployment benchmark
(TTFT/goodput/cost) on the canonical workload, and a 5% canary serves it for two hours. The gate
flags a quality regression on the legal-document subset the benchmark suite specifically covers —
a subset the vendor’s “better bench” never measured. The candidate improves quality on the main
subset but adds 240 ms to p95 TTFT; the canary has served 3,600 requests with 12 legal-subset
failures vs the incumbent’s 3 expected at α = 0.05 — the legal subset is ~10% of canary traffic (≈360
requests), the incumbent’s baseline failure rate on that subset is ~0.83% (3 in ≈360), and a one-sided
binomial test at α = 0.05 returns p ≈ 6.4×10⁻⁵, so the gate fires. The candidate also breaches the 2 s
p95 TTFT SLO on its own (1.9 s + 240 ms = 2.14 s), so the gate would have fired on the serving metric
even without the legal-subset regression. Given the §3 economics (a bad ungated release = 216,000
exposed requests ≈ $5,394 direct), should the architect promote, reject, or extend the canary to N
hours — and what blast radius does each choice bound? [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] The candidate
is rejected automatically, the incumbent stays, and the legal subset keeps working. No fire drill, no
manual heroics — the regression was contained to the canary (~12 legal-subset requests answered
wrongly) and production-wide exposure was avoided: the factory bounded the wrong vendor claim to
a ~3,600-request canary instead of 216,000 exposed requests, which is precisely what industrializing
the delivery loop is for.

21.9. Transition to Part VI
Parts I–V traced one engagement: token accounting defines workload demand; model architecture
sets compute and memory costs; parallelism adds communication; serving schedules shared resources;
fleet design determines capacity and cost — and the AI Factory, the operating layer those parts
build toward, governs the changes that follow. These mechanisms connect request-level behavior to
operational decisions.
Part VI applies these mechanisms to decisions under uncertainty rather than introducing another
subsystem. It makes the decision process explicit: state workload assumptions, compare alternatives
against resource bounds, and identify the measurements needed to resolve uncertainty. The next
chapters provide a worksheet for recording the decision, its assumptions, and its validation criteria.

part VI.
The Architect

chapter 22.
How to Think Like an AI Solution Architect

The Architect’s Question
Before any model is selected, any GPU is counted, any latency budget is allocated, the architect must
answer one question: what is the actual token-scale cost of delivering the stakeholder’s request? This
chapter exists to make that question automatic. We do not reach for vendor marketing numbers
or rule-of-thumb heuristics. Instead we trace a vague stakeholder ask — “we need a Q&A system
over our internal documents” — through a canonical loop that turns it into concrete architectural
bounds. The output is a set of derived quantities (token throughput, KV cache memory, prefill FLOPs,
decode bandwidth) that are verifiable, derived from first principles, and grounded in the canonical
~2,000-user, ~10 rps / ~40 rps peak, RAG Q&A, 70B dense FP16 scenario that every other chapter in
this handbook cites. The architect works through the canonical loop as a structured investigation,
and the chapter traces that reasoning step by step.

22.1. Concept
The unit we price, size, and optimize is the token. We established what a token is in Chapter 1 — not
a word, character, or byte, but whatever the model’s tokenizer carves text into via learned byte-pair
merging; that token counts are only approximately proportional to character counts, with a ratio
that depends on language, formatting and tokenizer version; and that “one token ≈ 4 characters” is a
rough rule for general-English prose, to be confirmed against the actual tokenizer before pricing
anything (Ch 1 §1). We do not restate that here; this chapter builds on it.
What Chapter 22 adds is not a re-derivation of the token but a re-framing of it as the input
to a decision loop. The architect treats a token as a metered unit of model I/O and accounting

374

375

How to Think Like an AI Solution Architect

— the way a kilowatt-hour meters electricity — not because one token is meaningful by itself, but
because every downstream cost and capacity number is denominated in it. The durable mental model,
unchanged from Chapter 1’s: tokens are the interface between a human’s request and a machine’s
arithmetic, and anything we are asked to size or price reduces to “how many tokens, in what context,
with what precision.” The loop below turns that unit into concrete bounds.

22.2. Mental Model
The prefill/decode split is the distinction the rest of the book builds on, and it was established
in Ch 2 §2 (in the canonical operating point, long-prompt prefill is compute-bound — a large burst
of FLOPs once per request — while low-batch decode is bandwidth-bound — a small amount of
work repeated for every output token). Ch 22 does not re-derive that distinction; it uses it. What
this chapter adds is the reasoning loop: the architect does not have to hold every quantity in their
head, because the loop turns a vague ask into a small, ordered set of token-scale bounds that the
downstream chapters price against. The mental model, distilled, is that the loop is the discipline —
derive the unit, then the traffic, then the split, in that order, so every later number is anchored rather
than guessed.

22.3. Worked Example — The Canonical Loop
We now demonstrate the canonical loop: turning a vague stakeholder ask into concrete bounds.
The stakeholder says: “We need a Q&A system over our internal documents. About 2,000 employees will
use it, they’ll ask questions throughout the day, and the answers should be accurate and fast.” From this
single sentence we will derive a full set of token-scale quantities that every downstream chapter will
price against.
Step 1 — Identify the unit. The ask mentions “Q&A over internal documents.” We do not assume
“one question = one page” or “one question = 500 words.” We go to the model’s tokenizer and ask: how
many tokens does a typical prompt contain? We extract representative prompts from the documented
corpus, run them through the tokenizer, and measure. In the canonical scenario, the prompt consists
of ~1,200 tokens of query text plus ~8,000 tokens of retrieved RAG context, yielding ~9,200 input
tokens. The answer generated is ~300 tokens. These are the book’s [canonical scenario] inputs
(Ch 4, Table 4-2) — an author-defined illustrative workload, not a vendor-reported [1P] figure, so
they are labeled [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION], not [1P].
Step 2 — Establish the traffic profile. The ask says “about 2,000 employees” and “throughout
the day.” We instrument or survey to find the per-user rate. The canonical scenario settles on ~10
requests/s average, with peaks of ~40 rps. These are declared traffic inputs [canonical scenario]
[ASSUMPTION], not derived from the user population (walk-through in Ch 4 §3).
Step 3 — Compute the token throughput. With I = 9,200 input tokens and O = 300 output
tokens per request, and λ = 10 req/s average:

Step 4 — Derive architecture-relevant quantities. The 30× input/output ratio is one of the
most important derived quantities here. It means this workload is input-heavy: the token budget is
dominated by prefill (processing the 9.2K prompt), not decode (generating the 300 answer tokens).
Combined with the canonical model, precision, serving, and SLO assumptions, this 30× ratio pushes
the design toward high prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure. The ratio alone does not settle
which resource dominates — that also depends on model architecture, attention/KV-head count,
precision, batching, hardware, kernel efficiency, prefix caching, and output-generation speed — but
under the canonical assumptions the prefill-compute and KV-capacity terms are where the pressure
lands, not decode bandwidth (the ~5.6 TB/s weight-read rate is a whole-model, host-level requirement
that tensor parallelism shards to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU on the canonical host, Ch 6 — a per-host
constraint, not a fleet-wide one). Every downstream chapter (memory, compute, cost) will price
against these derived numbers.
Step 5 — Record in Table 22-1. The full table of derived quantities appears below.
This loop — stakeholder ask → measured token counts → traffic profile → token through­
put → architecture-relevant derived quantities — is the canonical thought process an AI solution
architect runs, every time, before a single architecture decision is made. It is how we move from
“we need a Q&A system” to “at the canonical operating point our prefill will be compute-bound
at ~1.29 PFLOP per request (case (i), linear-only; ~1.5099 PFLOP under case (ii), Ch 8), and our
decode will be bandwidth-bound at a required weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s over each ~25 ms
token interval.” The loop is the chapter’s central contribution; the quantities that issue from it —
tagged [canonical scenario]/[ASSUMPTION]/[DERIVED]/[ILLUSTRATIVE] in Table 22-1 — are the
evidence that every following chapter trades on.

The loop on a second workload. The steps above are not specific to RAG Q&A, and the check
that they generalize is to run them on a differently shaped workload: a short-context chat assistant
with no retrieved context, ~400 input tokens and ~900 output tokens per turn. Step 1 still measures
tokens, Step 2 still settles a traffic profile, Step 3 still multiplies — but the input/output ratio is now
400 ÷ 900 ≈ 0.44× instead of 30×, so the workload is output-heavy, and Step 4 flips the verdict: prefill
compute collapses (2N·L at 400 tokens is ~0.056 PFLOP per request) while the decode leg carries the
weight-read rate (~140 GB per token over the ~25 ms interval, unchanged), and the prompt-only KV

GB prompt-only / ~24.9 GB end-of-turn for the canonical 9.2K/9.5K request. Nothing about the loop
changed; only which term dominates. That transferability — same order of steps, opposite conclusion
— is the content the loop is supposed to add, not the arithmetic itself.

separate: decode lands in the bandwidth-bound regime at low batch (Ch 6), prefill in the compute-bound
regime at long prompt (Ch 8) — each an operating-point property, not an identity.

22.4. Measurement
For the token-accounting step of this chapter’s method, measurement reduces to counting
tokens correctly, because a miscount at the input silently misprices everything downstream — and
only for that step: the end-to-end gates the book insists on elsewhere (the Ch 14 benchmark protocol,
measured SLO-goodput at the target offered load, regional availability, and the Ch 16 TCO gate) are
separate gates and remain unwaived here. Three things an architect can and should check:
1. Actual token count, not the rule of thumb. Run the model’s own tokenizer on representative
prompts from the actual traffic. The “4 chars ≈ 1 token” heuristic is for estimation only; real
counts differ by language, formatting, code, and tokenizer version. Measure on our traffic, not
the marketing figure.
2. Input vs output split. Measure both legs of the request (prompt tokens and generated tokens),
because they land on different bottlenecks — input on prefill compute and KV-cache capacity,
output on decode bandwidth — and on different cost line items. A request that is 90% input
and 10% output has a very different cost profile than one that is 50/50, even at the same total
token count.
3. Peak vs average context. Log the distribution of context lengths, not just the mean. A
workload that averages 9.2K input tokens but peaks at 32K (illustrative variant) has a very
different KV cache and latency profile. The 90th-percentile context length is often the number
the architect must design for.
This measurement habit is the token-level answer to the book’s recurring question, “what would

381

How to Think Like an AI Solution Architect

I actually measure here?” We measure token counts and their distribution, at the edge, before any
architecture decision is made.

22.5. Common Mistakes
• Assuming one token ≈ one word. That is not a dependable conversion. A token is often a
word fragment, not a whole word: a high-frequency English word is frequently one token, but
a longer or rarer word is usually split into several subword tokens, and code, numerics, and
non-Latin scripts routinely run several times the naive word-count estimate. Use the model’s
own tokenizer, or at most a ~4 English-characters/token rough estimate for general-English
prose only, and confirm against the actual tokenizer before pricing anything.
• Ignoring the input/output asymmetry. Treating a request as “one unit” hides that inputheavy workloads tend toward high prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure, while outputheavy ones are decode-bound (run-time per generated token) — opposite bottlenecks with
opposite fixes. (Note: “capacity pressure” is a memory-capacity constraint, not a memorybandwidth bound; see Ch 4/8.) The 30× input/output ratio in the canonical loop is the concrete
illustration of this principle.
• Quoting context window as free capacity. The window is an upper bound, not a recom­
mendation; using it fully is expensive. Keeping a 9.2K average inside a 128K window still costs
for the length we actually use.
• Trusting a vendor’s tokenizer count without checking. Tokenizer versions change and
report differently; measure on our traffic, not the marketing figure.
• Skipping the canonical loop. Assuming that the stakeholder’s description is sufficient to size
the system. The loop exists because vague asks almost always underspecify the token-scale
cost; skipping it produces architectures that fail latency or cost SLOs.

22.6. Architecture Consequence
The canonical loop’s derived quantities have immediate and concrete architecture consequences.
The 30× input/output ratio means this workload’s prefill phase dominates the compute budget:
~1.29 PFLOP of compute per request (case (i), linear-only; ~1.5099 PFLOP under case (ii)), and a KV
cache that grows with 9.2K input tokens. The decode phase, while smaller in total tokens, requires
a weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s sustained over each ~25 ms decode step (the ~140 GB weight-read
interval) — a whole-model figure (before tensor-parallel sharding); under the canonical 8×H100
tensor-parallel host the 140 GB is sharded, so each GPU streams only ~0.70 TB/s against its own 3.35
TB/s (Ch 6). The shard-invariant reason decode is memory-limited is its low arithmetic intensity

How to Think Like an AI Solution Architect

382

(~1.0 FLOP/byte), not the raw 5.6>3.35 comparison. (Note the units: 5.6 TB/s is a rate; the per-token
weight traffic is ~140 GB under the full-weight-read model, and rate = traffic / TPOT.)
These opposite bottlenecks lead to a central architectural decision: can we disaggregate prefill
and decode? If prefill needs FLOPS and decode needs bandwidth, a single homogeneous GPU
pool can be suboptimal. A two-pool architecture — a prefill cluster optimized for compute (more
GPUs, higher FLOPS, model parallelism) and a decode pool whose hardware property is HBM
bandwidth (faster HBM), managed with PagedAttention (KV allocation) and continuous batching
(scheduling) — software mechanisms that raise utilization, not bandwidth — is an architecture worth
benchmarking. Whether it needs fewer GPUs than a homogeneous design depends on achievable
utilization, duplicated model residency, KV-transfer cost, interconnect topology, workload shape,
burstiness, and the hardware assigned to each pool — those effects must be measured before the GPUcount conclusion is drawn. This is the central theme of Chapter 11 (Serving) and the prefill/decodedisaggregation pattern (Ch 12, candidate b). The architect who runs the canonical loop and records
the derived quantities in Table 22-1 is already positioned to make this decision with numbers, not
intuition.
Importantly, the loop does not end at a serving topology; it ends at a decision about where the
intelligence lives. A 70B dense pool on the fleet is one placement; an 8-bit or MoE variant, a retrievalfirst design that buys capability with context rather than parameters, a test-time-search loop that
spends compute on hard queries, or an agent runtime that orchestrates several specialized models
are all alternative placements of the same capability. The canonical loop’s derived quantities — token
throughput, KV footprint, prefill FLOPs, TCO — are precisely the numbers an architect uses to
compare those placements. So the full hierarchy the loop supports is:
Requirement → Workload → Intelligence (where the capability comes from) → System
→ Architecture → Fleet → Decision.
The Decision rung is where the loop’s output is committed — an ADR, an owner, a review trigger
(Chapters 25–26). Every earlier derived quantity exists to inform that final, committed decision, and
Appendix A’s closing question — where should the intelligence live? — is the architectural form of
that same question, made explicit at the top of the hierarchy rather than hidden at the bottom.
DECISION STATE — CANDIDATE SCREENED; NOT COMMITTABLE. Running
the loop on the canonical workload yields a screened candidate, not a commitment, so the
Decision rung records a HOLD — a legitimate, auditable outcome of this loop, and what
the example below records. The full callout (regional availability, failover, SLO-goodput
and matched-scope costs pending) is kept in Ch 25 §6.

• Context: The loop has produced capability, capacity and single-region cost screens: the

• Decision: None yet. The least-cost row — the cloud default paid-occupancy input at ~$14.04/1K

unmatched scopes, an unpriced availability requirement and unmeasured SLO-goodput.
• Rationale: A HOLD is the honest record when a hard nonfunctional requirement (regional
availability) is still unsized and the comparison basis is unequal; picking the cheapest row
would encode an input assumption as a decision.
• Alternatives considered: (1) select the least-cost mode now — rejected: the $87.6K line is a
paid-occupancy INPUT, not a measured duty cycle, and no row carries the 99.9% active-active
cost; (2) commit to self-host — rejected: its SLO-goodput pass is provisional until benchmarked

• Requirement coverage: multi-region active-active (99.9%): NOT VALIDATED / NOT
PRICED — no regional capacity, replication or region-failure test is in any number above; the
full requirement-coverage matrix is in the Ch 25 §6 copy of this record.
• Exit criteria / review trigger: (i) regional capacity sized and priced for the 99.9% active-active
SLA; (ii) a region-failure test defined — per-region weight/index availability mandatory,
live-KV replication optional (clients may replay or recompute context in the surviving
region within the recovery objectives, Ch 16 §16.3); (iii) measured p95 SLO-goodput at the
target offered load; (iv) a matched-scope re-run of the three modes.
• Evidence tags: [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — the three single-region cost rows are Ch
16 scenario inputs, not quotes; [DERIVED] — 6.24M req/mo and every $/1K division are Ch 16
arithmetic.

22.7. What We Still Don’t Know
This chapter’s numbers lean on the same open questions the book raises at the mechanism layer.
Rather than restating them, we point to the fuller treatment, then to the uncertainties that belong to
the loop itself:
• Sustained HBM bandwidth for weight-read kernels — discussed in Chapter 2 §7; the 3.35
TB/s H100 figure is a theoretical peak (published spec — FACT), while real serving kernels
may sustain less [HYPOTHESIS].
• Achieved prefill efficiency under continuous batching — Chapter 2 §7; 2 × params ×
tokens is exact per token and batching does not change it, but sustained MFU does, and it

How to Think Like an AI Solution Architect

384

swings the canonical prefill host count from ~1.6 (100% of peak) to ~4.1 (40% MFU) at average
load. [HYPOTHESIS]
• Effect of quantization on decode vs prefill — Chapter 2 §7; quantization shifts both
bottlenecks but the precise trade-off point is workload-dependent. [HYPOTHESIS]
• Cross-technology bandwidth numbers — Chapter 2 §7; HBM3e parts (e.g. H200) and the
MI300X (HBM3, ~5.3 TB/s) publish higher peaks, which would move the GPU-count equation
without changing the compute-bound vs bandwidth-bound classification. [HYPOTHESIS]
Three uncertainties are specific to this loop rather than to the mechanism layer, and none of
them is settled by the canonical scenario:
• Whether the measured token split generalizes beyond RAG. The 1,200-token query plus
8K retrieved context is one corpus shape; a short-context chat workload or a long-document
workload shifts the input/output ratio, and with it which leg is the bottleneck. [HYPOTHESIS]
• How the derived quantities move when the model is replaced. Swapping the 70B for
a smaller dense model moves the 2NL prefill term and the ~140 GB weight read roughly in
proportion to parameter count, but the KV-cache term by a different proportion, because it
scales with layer count × hidden (KV-head) size and context length rather than with parameters.
So the relative weight of the compute and bandwidth terms versus the KV-capacity term can
shift the binding constraint — without any change in traffic, and even though the prefillcompute and decode-bandwidth classifications themselves are unchanged. [HYPOTHESIS]
• Whether the loop’s inputs are stable upstream of it. The 8K retrieved context is an input
to the loop and a policy choice upstream of it; changing the chunking or retrieval policy
re-opens Step 1 and therefore every downstream number in Table 22-1. [HYPOTHESIS]

22.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Token-to-Fleet Thought Loop
The architect is still in the early design conversation about the internal Q&A tool described throughout
this handbook. The team has settled on a 70B-class dense model for accuracy, and they have a rough
traffic estimate: ~2,000 registered employees, with aggregate traffic matching the canonical scenario:
~10 rps average, ~40 rps peak, with prompts of ~1,200 tokens of query text plus ~8K retrieved context
and ~300 tokens of answer.
From the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 (values tabulated in Ch 4, Table 4-2) alone, the architect
can already state the hard numbers: each request carries ~9.2K input tokens and ~300 output tokens.
At 10 rps average, the system must sustain ~92,000 input tokens/s in prefill and ~3,000 output tokens/s
in decode (the Step 3 arithmetic of §3, tabulated in Table 22-1). The architect can also state the two
opposite bottlenecks: prefill will be compute-bound (~1.29 PFLOP per request at 9.2K input), and
decode will be bandwidth-bound (a ~140 GB/token weight-read requiring ~5.6 TB/s sustained over the
~25 ms decode interval — a whole-model figure (before tensor-parallel sharding); under the canonical
8×H100 host the 140 GB is sharded, so each GPU streams ~0.70 TB/s, and the shard-invariant cause is

385

How to Think Like an AI Solution Architect

the low ~1.0 FLOP/byte intensity, Ch 6). The team’s immediate architectural choice is whether to build
a single homogeneous GPU cluster or to separate prefill and decode pools — the arithmetic from this
chapter makes P/D disaggregation a candidate worth testing for either bottleneck; benchmarking
(Ch 14) and TCO (Ch 16) determine whether it wins, and the disaggregation option (Ch 12, candidate
b) is where to test it.
The peak, not the average, sizes the fleet. §3 sized prefill at the 10 rps average (10 × 1.288 =
12.88 PFLOP/s, ~1.6 hosts at peak, Ch 24 §3.3). At the 40 rps peak the same demand is 40 × 1.288 ≈
51.5 PFLOP/s — 6.5 hosts at 100% of the canonical aggregate host peak (8 × 0.989 = 7.91 PFLOPS), and
~16.3 hosts at 40% MFU (7.91 × 0.4 = 3.16 PFLOPS/host) — 16.3 rounded up is 17, since 16 × 3.164
PFLOPS/host = 50.6 PFLOP/s falls short of the 51.5 required. The KV budget binds at a similar scale:
Ch 17’s 436 GB of KV per host (640 − 140 − 64) ÷ 24.1 GB/request ≈ 18 in-flight requests per host, and
40 rps × 8.58 s ≈ 343 in flight needs ~19 hosts. Sizing on the average rate and meeting the peak would
need four times the fleet. The decision the team must make: does the homogeneous pool absorb
that 4× peak-to-average swing, or must prefill and decode be separated so each pool is sized for its
own leg? Two readings compete. (i) One pool is enough: if measured prefill occupancy at the peak
stays below the point where prefill steals decode’s bandwidth, a homogeneous cluster sized at ~17–19
hosts clears both budgets (prefill- or KV-bound depending on the KV budget, with a 21-host build
carrying the margin) and avoids duplicated model residency and KV-transfer cost. (ii) Separation
wins: if the measured prefill/decode GPU-time split shows each leg saturating at different times,
two pools let each be sized for its own peak and keep the TPOT budget off the prefill queue. The
loop does not settle it — it names what would. HOLD, with exit criteria: the P/D candidate (Ch 12,
candidate b) stays a candidate until (i) the measured prefill/decode GPU-time split at the 40 rps peak
is recorded (Ch 14 benchmark protocol), (ii) p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s and p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms are met by each
candidate configuration at the offered load, and (iii) the KV-transfer cost and duplicated-residency
penalty of the two-pool option are priced against the homogeneous alternative (Ch 16 TCO gate).
Before the memory-sizing step — the KV and residency arithmetic Chapter 7 already built —
the architect locks in one more number: the tokens-per-request split. This is the currency every
downstream chapter will price against, and it has already been established as ~9.2K input + ~300
output per request. The rest of the design — model fitting, memory budget, latency budget, cost —
can now proceed in token-denominated terms.

chapter 23.

Working With Customers: From Vague Ask to
Defensible Scope

The Architect’s Question
After this chapter we should be able to sit with a customer or stakeholder who says “we want to
build something with AI” and turn that vague ambition into a bounded, measurable, defensible scope.
We will apply the book’s core loop in a conversational setting: ask the questions that surface the real
workload (Ch 4), the quality bar (Ch 3/5), the latency and cost constraints, and the operational reality
— then restate the requirement in terms we can architect against. After this chapter, “let’s go build
an AI thing” becomes “here are the bounds, the SLO, and the open questions” — and the customer
knows exactly what they asked for.

23.1. Concept
Most AI projects fail in requirements, not in technology. [HYPOTHESIS] The root cause is a category
error: the customer and the architect mean different things by the same words. “Fast,” “good,” “smart,”
and “it should just work” are not contracts; they are vibes. The architect’s first job is to convert vibes
into quantified, testable bounds using the disciplines of the earlier chapters.
The conversion rests on one idea: most consequential architectural decisions should trace back
to an explicit number or constraint, many of which the customer can see. Whether the model is 7B
or 70B, whether we self-host or use an API, whether we cache, quantize, or disaggregate — all of it is
decided by six numbers we can extract from a customer conversation:

386

387

Working With Customers: From Vague Ask to Defensible Scope

1. The traffic — how many users, at what concurrency, with what peak-to-average ratio (Ch
4/Ch 17).
2. The token profile — what inputs look like, how long contexts are, the input/output ratio (Ch
4/Ch 6).
3. The latency/SLO — what “fast” means, the percentile and the budget (Ch 6).
4. The quality bar — what “good enough” means on this task, on their data (Ch 3/Ch 5/Ch 14).
5. The cost ceiling — the money they can spend, and whether that implies self-host or API (Ch
16).
6. The operational reality — data privacy, geography, available staff, time-to-value (Ch 13/Ch
21/Ch 24).

23.2. Mental Model
The customer conversation is really about buying information, not delivering answers. We
are not in the room to impress; we are in the room to learn the six numbers. Three mental moves
keep the conversation productive:
• The Socratic funnel. Start broad (“what problem are we solving?”) and narrow through a
scripted set of questions that each commit the customer to a concrete bound. Every “vague”
answer gets followed by a request for magnitude: “roughly how many users?” “what’s the
slowest acceptable answer?”
• The mirror test. Restate their words back as a quantified requirement and check they still
agree. “So: ~2,000 users, under 2 seconds to first token, on company-internal data — did I get
that right?” The restatement is where scope actually gets locked.
• The two-window honesty. Separate what the customer thinks (goals) from what the system
can guarantee (SLOs). Goals are aspirations; SLOs are contracts. Confusing them breeds many
fee disputes and scope fights.

23.3. Worked Example
23.3.1. The Requirements Dialogue: Turning “an internal AI assistant” Into Bounds
(Worked example dialogue — illustrative, not reference.) An internal-platform lead says: “We want
an AI assistant for our sales teams — it should answer questions from our product docs and CRM
data, and it should be fast.” [ILLUSTRATIVE] (Scenario provenance — a constructed worked-example
dialogue, not a secondary source; the provenance/status label axes are defined in the Sources chapter.)
Architect: “How many people will use it, and how often?” Lead: “~2,000 on the platform; maybe
5% are in it at once at peaks.” Architect: “So ~100 concurrent at peak — that’s users with the tool
open, not requests in flight — and realistically only a fraction of those are firing requests at any
moment. Roughly how many questions per second at the busiest minute?” Lead: “If everyone on the
sales floor asked at once, maybe 40 a second.” Architect: “And an average minute, not the busiest —

roughly how many?” Lead: “Maybe 10 a second on a normal day, with bursts around launches.” →

pages in a typical prompt, how many retrieved chunks, and how long is the answer you’d send back?”
Lead: “Specs run two to three pages, maybe a handful of retrieved sections; the answer is a paragraph
or two.” → Bound 2: long ~9,200-token inputs with retrieval, ~300-token outputs. (A page

Architect (mirror): “So to lock it: ~2,000 sales users, ~10 rps average / 40 peak, prompts with

data is regulated, and within a self-host budget. Have I captured it?” Lead: “Yes — that’s exactly it.”
Reading the result. The vague ask collapsed into the exact canonical workload this book has
architected end-to-end — a 70B-class model (the candidate tier the quality bound points to, pending
the 50-question benchmark — Ch 5’s selection rule is to pick the smallest tier that clears the quality
bar) served on 8×H100 hosts, a ~21–32-host fleet at the canonical peak (Ch 17/20/24) — becomes a
candidate architecture whose memory fit can be derived and whose latency, throughput, quality, and
peak-load behavior must then be validated (Ch 2–16 derive the constraints; the deployment has to
be benchmarked and measured against them, as Ch 24’s red-team pass shows). The conversation
did not sell a model; it exposed the numbers that then narrowed the candidate set, and left the actual
validation to the measurement phase. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] (worked example, not reference)

23.4. Measurement
The requirements dialogue has its own quality metrics:
1. Bound coverage — did the conversation surface all six numbers (traffic, tokens, SLO, quality,
cost, ops)? Missing one is a future scope surprise.
2. Customer buy-in — did the mirrored restatement get an explicit “yes”? An unconfirmed
restatement is not a scope.
3. Decision lead time — how quickly the six bounds let us produce a defensible draft architecture.
The whole point is that extracting numbers, not more meetings, unlocks the design.
4. Assumption log — every guess we made that the customer did not explicitly confirm, tracked
as [UNRESOLVED] items, not silent defaults.

23.5. Common Mistakes
• Selling before scoping. Pitching a model or a price before extracting the six numbers commits
us to an answer we cannot yet defend.
• Accepting aspirations as SLOs. “Make it fast” is a goal; “p95 TTFT under 2 s” is a contract.
Write the contract.
• Letting the customer choose the technology. “We want a 70B model” is a solution, not a
requirement; the architect derives the model from the bounds (Ch 5), not from the customer’s
guess.
• Ignoring the operational constraint. “It has to be on-prem / private / no cloud” often decides
more than any performance number — surface it early.
• Not logging assumptions. Every silence becomes a hidden assumption that surfaces as a
dispute later. Write them down as [UNRESOLVED] items.

Working With Customers: From Vague Ask to Defensible Scope

390

23.6. Architecture Consequence
The requirements conversation is where the book’s entire loop is fed. The six bounds it extracts
are exactly the inputs Ch 1–17 consume: traffic feeds capacity (Ch 17), tokens feed KV/memory (Ch
7), quality feeds model selection (Ch 5), latency feeds serving (Ch 11), cost feeds TCO (Ch 16), and
the operational constraint picks the tier (Ch 13). A good requirements session is not a warm-up to
architecture — it is the first chapter of the architecture, and every downstream decision traces back
to the numbers it locked. [ILLUSTRATIVE] (scenario provenance — the same worked-example dialogue
as §23.3, not a secondary source)

23.7. What We Still Don’t Know
• How accurate the customer’s own-told numbers are (“40 rps peak”) is [UNRESOLVED];
peak estimates are notoriously optimistic and should be triangulated with real logs where
possible.
• Whether the quality bar once defined stays stable is [HYPOTHESIS]; as users adopt the
tool, their expectations and the data they query both shift.
• The right number of questions to lock quality is [UNRESOLVED]; 50 worked here as a
representative proxy but a larger, task-distributed set is stronger.

23.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The ‘Next Month’ Customer Portal: Require­
ments Dialogue
A CTO emails the architect: “We heard LLMs are great — let’s put one on our customer portal to
answer support tickets. Shipping it next month.” Rather than confirm the launch date, the architect
books a 30-minute session and runs the funnel. It emerges the portal gets ~5 rps average but 200-rps
bursts during outage events (traffic), tickets are short (~500 tokens, not retrieval-heavy), quality
means “resolve the ticket, not just answer” (a capability that rules out an answer-only model — in
this scenario the architect puts 7B-class forward as the candidate to test first, on the Ch 5 rule of the
smallest tier that clears the quality bar, with the pilot’s pass criterion stated as ~60% of baseline tickets
resolved without escalation (illustrative threshold, set with the customer before the pilot); the short
~500-token tickets keep the KV footprint and per-host memory small, which is a memory argument
for the smaller tier, not a capability one), the SLO is 3 s because users are already frustrated (latency),
and — critically — the portal sits on regulated payment data so nothing leaves the premises (ops).
The mirrored restatement turns “let’s ship AI next month” into “a 7B-class model on one on-prem
GPU, resolving baseline tickets under 3 s, with a 200-rps burst buffer, quality-gated on real resolved
tickets — and a two-week pilot on 5% of tickets to confirm the resolution quality before full rollout.”
The burst buffer, spelled out. The buffer is an arrival-rate buffer: bursts of duration D queue
and drain at rate r, a decode-only ceiling of 100% MFU (≤141 rps — 7B FP16, ~500 output tokens/request,
H100); with the ~500-token prefill included the total request rate is ~71 rps at 100% MFU (~21–28 rps
at 30–40% MFU), so r = 50 in the worked example below is an optimistic decode-only illustration

(approval workflows, audit, compliance), integration (auth, API, data pipelines), failure recovery
(RTO/RPO, backup, failover), and human review (escalation, override, sign-off) — those are out of
scope for this chapter (see Ch 13/Ch 21), not covered here; this figure focuses on the architecturalbounds questions. [ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual

success, data, constraints, what must be quantified) → quantified bounds → the decisions those bounds
unlock. The full worked example (figure plus the §23.3 dialogue and Table 23-1) surfaces the six

ops/tier, TCO), and the worked example in §23.3 supplies the sixth (quality bar — Table 23-1, the

Working With Customers: From Vague Ask to Defensible Scope

392

and the measured per-host rate must replace it before the burst budget is trusted. Max queue wait ≈
D·(200−r)/r must stay inside the 3 s SLO — so state D, the buffer depth D·(200−r) requests, and choose:
(a) add capacity, (b) add admission control, or (c) scope the SLO to non-burst traffic. Worked: D = 1 s
at 200 rps → 200 requests arrive, 50 served during the burst; queue depth at burst end = (200−50) × 1
= 150 requests; drained at ~50 rps in 150/50 = 3 s; max queue wait = 3 s, so the last-arriving request
completes at 3 s plus its own service time — past the 3 s SLO; total time from burst start = 4 s (1
s burst + 3 s drain) — burst-window requests miss the 3 s SLO, so the burst runs under a separate
queue-and-drain degraded-mode SLO (option c).
Architect (mirror, closing): “So what we’ve locked: 3 s p95 SLO on non-burst traffic; above ~50
rps the burst is served under the queue-and-drain degraded mode, with admission control capping
the queue at the depth the 3 s drain allows, and that degraded-mode target is written into the contract
as a separate SLO. Sign off on that split?” CTO: “Yes — non-burst 3 s, bursts best-effort with the
queue visible. That’s the scope.”
The customer’s vague excitement became a defensible, bounded, shippable scope — the 3 s SLO
scoped to non-burst traffic, the burst served under the queue-and-drain degraded mode — and the
architect is already architecting, not guessing.

chapter 24.
Red Team / Green Team

The Architect’s Question
How do we rigorously evaluate the security, safety, and robustness of a RAG-enabled model fleet
before it reaches production users — and how do we measure that evaluation with quantitative
derived quantities that stand up to scrutiny?

24.1. Concept
Red Team / Green Team is a structured adversarial evaluation pattern borrowed from military
wargaming and software security. The Green Team builds and operates the system; the Red Team
attempts to break it. In the context of a RAG + model fleet architecture, the Red Team probes the
system across the five layers of §2 (prompt, retrieval, tool use, model behavior, fleet orchestration),
which group into three attack surfaces: prompt injection, RAG corruption, and system-level exploits.
1. Prompt injection — crafting user inputs that bypass safety guardrails and extract restricted
outputs.
2. RAG corruption — injecting malicious or misleading documents into the retrieval corpus to
shift model behavior.
3. System-level exploits — targeting tool use, function calling, and plugin boundaries to achieve
unintended actions.
The Green Team responds by hardening defenses, refining detection, and quantifying coverage.
The cycle repeats until the residual attack surface is within the agreed threshold.
This chapter assumes a canonical deployment: ~2,000 registered users (an illustrative ~100 active
users, not a simultaneous-request count; arrival rate and execution occupancy are separate quantities

393

Red Team / Green Team

394

in Chapter 4), a 70B dense FP16 base model, and a RAG pipeline with vector search over a curated
corpus. The Red Team / Green Team process is not a one-time audit; it is an ongoing practice
embedded in the deployment lifecycle.

The Green Team tracks each probe’s outcome as a FACT (observed, verifiable event), DERIVED
(computed from lower-level data), or HYPOTHESIS (unverified but testable claim). These are
epistemic-status labels; provenance and measurement status are separate axes defined in the Sources
chapter. Each reported metric also needs its underlying observation, calculation, or stated assumption.
