The Verification target column states thresholds to be met, not FACTs; the cost row’s cell carries
its own DERIVED provenance label. On cost, the capstone separates the two bases (R-01): the “Modeled
example” cell is a marginal-generation-work statement — at a 35% semantic-cache hit ratio, ~35% of
queries skip generation entirely, so the marginal generation work is ~65% of the uncached value. This is
not an all-in self-hosted TCO reduction: the §16 fleet is a fixed set of hosts whose capex/opex (hardware
amortization, site power, the fixed $10,000/mo staff allocation) does not fall with cache hits unless the
fleet is also re-sized, so one must not multiply the §16 all-in $0.02497/request ($24.97 per 1,000 requests,
Ch 16) by a fraction of requests. The hosted-API cost is a separate basis: $0.0116/request (unrounded
$0.01164 ≈ $11.6 per 1,000 requests, Ch 4 — the mid-tier API at $1.20/$2.00 per 1M), which is not Ch 16’s
frontier-class ~$20.8 per 1,000 ($0.0208/request at $2/$8 per 1M, the managed-API price ADR 0015 carries):
both are per-request managed-API prices at the canonical 9,200/300 token mix and 6.24M requests/mo,
but at different model tiers, so the two API figures are not interchangeable either; per Ch 4’s basis note,
the two cost bases are not interchangeable — the self-host figure is an illustrative included-cost rate and
the API figure is a mid-tier managed-API list price, so the two scopes are not comparable unconditionally.
A defensible cost statement keeps (A) marginal generation work, (B) variable metered API spend, and (C)
all-in self-hosted TCO as separate units and denominators (see §26.8). Provenance note: the “Modeled
example” column is a worked-out illustrative instance, not gathered telemetry. The values in it
(~29% SM util, 35% hit ratio, 7% fallback) are scenario outputs chosen to illustrate how the pattern library
is applied and validated — each carries its measurement point: Step 1’s 45% SM-utilization baseline is

437

The Solution Architect’s Toolkit + Patterns Library

assumed at the uncached ~2.0 rps offered rate (R-07: assumed baseline input, not a measured FACT),
and the ~29% is the same definition at the cached ~1.3 rps engine load (45% × 1.3/2.0 ≈ 29%, scaled with
engine load), so the before/after direction matches the cache’s mechanism — lower engine load cannot
raise SM utilization — and one load test must measure both under a single SM-utilization definition;
they are not FACTs measured on a deployed system, and the marginal-work saving (not an all-in TCO
number) is what a real deployment must confirm from a recorded load test. Use a blank instrumentation
template to record the real FACTs separately.
Takeaway (Fig 26.2): the three patterns compose to mean TTFT ~180 ms and p99 TTFT ~250 ms
(−44% vs the ~450 ms uncached baseline, not a blended average) — the cache sets both numbers under
the two-point model of Step 2, while the circuit breaker is idle below the ~2.0 rps per-host ceiling
and guards the saturation excursions it exists for, with its ~7% shed share tracked separately — that
7% sits outside the two-point latency model, which carries no shed population; cost is reported as
marginal generation work — ~35% of queries skip generation at the assumed hit ratio — not as an
all-in TCO reduction (the §16 fixed fleet’s capex/opex does not fall with cache hits unless the fleet is
also re-sized; see §26.8). Scope: full arithmetic in §26.8; a weighted average of component latencies is
a mean, not a quantile — under the hit-50 ms / miss-250 ms model p99 = 250 ms. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
conceptual].
A note on utilization targets. The “SM util < 80%” row is an operational guardrail for this specific
workload, not a universal performance criterion. A GPU has many utilization figures — SM utilization,
tensor-core utilization, HBM bandwidth utilization, NVLink utilization, memory-capacity occupancy
— and which one matters is set by the workload’s dominant constraint, not by the hardware (Ch. 8).
Under an SLO-satisfying state, a GPU can sit at very different utilizations depending on whether the
workload is prefill-bound (compute) or decode-bound (bandwidth/memory). The architect’s question
is therefore not “is utilization high enough?” but “which resource is saturated when the SLO
is satisfied, and does the pattern keep the fleet the right side of that saturation?” In this
instance ~29% SM utilization with p99 within SLO is healthy headroom; in a heavier-throughput
workload the same ~29% could mean under-provisioning. State the SLO-bound resource, not a bare
percentage.

a pattern template with seven table columns covering eight fields (problem solved and triggering
symptom share one column): name, problem solved, triggering symptom, mechanism, minimal FACT
set, trade-off, conditions of failure, and chapter pointer. Patterns A–C from §3 are the first three
entries. §8 Step 4 records the capstone’s filled-in instance as Table 26-2. The two model-selection
patterns that Ch 5 files here close the catalog.

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture
Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

Snapshot: 2026-08-30 technical evidence snapshot, compiled from the first-party
technical reports and model cards listed in A.10 (First-hand Sources), with sepa­
rately dated 2026-09-27 and 2026-10-28 addenda. The body of this handbook works
through durable mechanisms — tokens, memory floors, rooflines, parallelism, KV arith­
metic — that do not change; this appendix reads the 2026 frontier (DeepSeek-V4, Kimi
K3, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, GLM-5.3-Flash) as one signal about where those mechanisms
are heading, and every mechanism below maps back to a chapter. The four-family com­
parison and the First-hand Sources list reflect nothing released after 2026-08-30; reverify
vendor claims against the cited first-party sources before any procurement or deploy­
ment decision, and once more immediately before publication. Dated service-status
corrections live with the post-snapshot notes below. This is a framework walkthrough
on a changing frontier, not a current model leaderboard.

A.1. The Signal in One Paragraph
Four 2026 frontier open models we surveyed converge on a second-order architectural pattern —
one that improves efficiency (more context, cheaper tokens) rather than raw capability —
which we read as an interpretation rather than an established historical fact. We should be precise
about what kind of gain each lever delivers. The common error is to read architecture innovation
as raw capability. In our interpretation, it is mostly efficiency (more context, less cost per token)
that comes out of the attention and MoE changes below, not intelligence. The capability story —
reasoning, post-training, test-time compute — lives elsewhere (A.8), and carries at least as much of
the frontier’s real progress. We separate the two explicitly.

Definition of “active” (what counts in the activated-parameter numerator, and what it does not
mean). Here “active” (equivalently “activated”) means the parameters that participate in the forward
pass for a given token: the routed experts dispatched for that token, the shared/always-on experts,
and the attention and embedding/head parameters that run for every token. It is not the same as
any of these: (a) resident parameters — the full expert + attention + embedding fabric that must be

445

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

held in memory (or sharded/offloaded), which is the total-parameter count, not the active count; (b)
per-token FLOPs, since activation count is not a proxy for compute cost under softmax-routing and
layered dispatch; (c) KV or attention-state sparsity, which is a different quantity (see the GQA/MLA
discussion in Ch 7); and (d) achievable serving speed — a low active fraction does not translate
proportionally into a faster served rate, because total-weight residency, expert routing/traffic, and
attention cost still dominate. The four families use different expert counts, dispatch schemes, and
embedding splits (Qwen’s N-gram embedding table and MTP module are excluded from both the
numerator and the denominator below — see the Fig A.1 note — so the Qwen figure is a backbone-only
ratio, not a fraction of the deployed parameter inventory; the table is offloadable), so the active
fractions below are comparable only after this definition is fixed; the numbers are not a drop-in
cross-model ranking of serving cost. (Here “active” contrasts total vs activated parameters — see the
model/MoE discussion in Ch 3 and the GQA/MHA KV discussion in Ch 7.) [1P]
Frontier MoE sparsity in 2026. Kimi K3 is the extreme case: 2.8 T total / 104 B active (~3.7% active);
DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284 B/13 B (~4.6%); GLM-5.3-Flash 320 B/18 B (~5.6%); Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125 B/6
B (~4.8% — backbone-only ratio: the denominator is the 125 B backbone; the separate 51 B n-gram
embedding and 4 B MTP modules are excluded from both numerator and denominator, so this is a
backbone fraction, not a fraction of the complete deployed parameter inventory). Active-parameter
fraction in each of these four frontier MoE families is in the single digits — the anchor for the Ch10 expertparallelism serving calculus. [1P] arXiv:2606.19348; arXiv:2607.24653; HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next; HF
zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash
Three efficiency levers the 2026 frontier families pulled (items 1-2 in all four entries; item 3 is
reported unevenly across the surveyed families and is a capability lever, not an efficiency one):
1. Hybrid attention as the new KV lever — an efficiency lever, not (by itself) a capability
lever. Each of the four surveyed frontier families re-engineered attention to shrink longcontext cost at the mechanism level — compressed/sparse hybrids (DeepSeek CSA+HCA),
delta+sparse (Qwen Gated DeltaNet + QSA), delta/residual (Kimi KDA + AttnRes), sparse+linear
(GLM). KV cache is no longer a fixed per-token constant we only quantize; it is a design
surface the model vendor already optimized. The intended benefit is to preserve useful model
capability while reducing long-context inference cost and/or extending practical context length
— indispensable, but it does not by itself make the model smarter. Capability gains come from
the post-training/reasoning stack in A.8.
2. MoE sparsity went extreme — the capacity-per-FLOP lever. Active-parameter fractions
fell to single digits (Kimi 104B of 2.8T; Qwen 6B of 125B). In our reading, one could argue MoE is
a larger architectural innovation than attention: it lets a lab grow knowledge/capacity without
proportionally growing FLOPs per token. We read this as a driving reason the 2026 open
landscape is heavily MoE-oriented. Expert parallelism and fused cross-expert communication
moved from a footnote to a serving-critical capability.
3. Training stack as a first-class result. Training-stable optimizers (Muon, reported for

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

446

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next; no surveyed family reports an equivalent optimizer swap in the August
snapshot) and post-training RL (GRPO, async RL — named across the surveyed families without
per-family attribution in the snapshot) are now reported as core architecture, not tooling — a
capability-ledger item (A.8), not an efficiency lever.
Items 1-2 form the cost/context ledger of the frontier. The capability ledger — reasoning, posttraining, test-time compute, agent harness — is where most of the qualitative improvement actually
lives (A.8). Distinguishing efficiency levers from capability levers is the architect’s first move when
reading any new model card.

A.2. How to read this appendix: Observed, Interpretation, Hypothesis
This appendix surveys vendor-reported material, so we are careful to separate three layers of
statement that are easy to blur — especially in a fast-moving field full of first/“most-efficient”/3Tclass claims:
• Observed — what the vendor’s technical report or model card actually states (e.g., “DeepSeekV4 reports a reduced KV footprint”). This is [1P] fact about the claim, not the same as the third
layer.
• Interpretation — our read of what architectural mechanism the report demonstrates (e.g.,
“the KV reduction suggests the model changes how attention stores state”). This is analysis,
ours, and could be wrong.
• Hypothesis — a prediction about consequence we draw for serving architecture (e.g., “we
expect long-context serving to become more memory-comfortable at equal context”). This is a
testable prediction — a hypothesis — not a fact.
When we write “a number of frontier models converge” or “one could argue MoE is a larger
architectural innovation,” read those as Interpretation / Hypothesis — defensible reads of the
frontier signal, not independent measurements. Vendor numbers stay tagged [1P] and flagged verifyon-own-hardware; our reads sit one register lower and should be read with the same skepticism we
ask of any vendor claim. The practical rule: if it’s a percentage from a report, it’s Observed [1P]; if it’s
a claim about what the industry trend means, it’s ours — treat it as analysis, tune it against the reader’s
real workload.
Mapping onto the book’s evidence taxonomy. These three reader-friendly layers are an
on-ramp to, not a replacement for, the three-axis taxonomy used throughout the book (provenance ×
epistemic status × measurement status): Axis 1 provenance [1P]/[2°]/[LAB]/[ILLUSTRATIVE] × Axis
2 status [FACT]/[DERIVED]/[ASSUMPTION]/[HYPOTHESIS]/[UNRESOLVED], with Axis 3 riding
along. ([FACT] means established for its stated scope: a measured runtime quantity in the body
chapters, or a documented first-hand record here — Axis 1 [1P]/[2°] carries who established it.) The
workload-scoping marker [canonical scenario] rides alongside these: it marks values drawn from
the canonical enterprise Q&A scenario defined in Ch 4, not a separate epistemic status.

447

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

• Observed ↔ [1P] · [FACT] — the vendor’s stated claim, a fact about the claim.
• Interpretation ↔ [INTERPRETATION] — an explicit analysis/interpretation marker for
the book’s own read of the evidence. It is not a sixth arithmetic status and adds nothing to Axis
2 (where a three-axis status is required, an interpretation is recorded as [ASSUMPTION] — a
stated reading, not a measurement — with [INTERPRETATION] marking it inline): [DERIVED]
stays reserved for reproducible calculation (a number anyone can recompute from stated inputs),
and testable predictions use [HYPOTHESIS]. (Where the book’s taxonomy would label the
same passage [ILLUSTRATIVE], note that; the appendix uses “interpretation” as plain prose
for an analytical read, never a sanctioned arithmetic status.)
• Hypothesis ↔ [HYPOTHESIS] — a testable prediction, exactly the taxonomy’s
[HYPOTHESIS].
• Measurement status ↔ Axis 3 — ANALYTICAL / ILLUSTRATIVE / MODELED / MEASURED
(or [UNMEASURED] where the stage is not yet determined): how far the number has climbed
the measurement-status hierarchy, defined in the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility chapter.
The appendix’s labels are the human-friendly framing; the three-axis labels are the precise
book-wide convention. They should never conflict.
One fact, three registers (worked contrast). Take the same Qwen3.8-Flash-Next figure three
ways: (a) numeric ratio — “6 B ÷ 125 B = 4.8% active” is [DERIVED]: reproducible calculation from
stated inputs, anyone can re-run it; (b) descriptive interpretation — “sparsity this extreme makes
long-context serving a memory problem before a compute problem” is [INTERPRETATION]: our
read of what the number means, analysis that could be wrong and earns no arithmetic status; (c)
measurable prediction — “at equal context, serving this model becomes more memory-comfortable”
is [HYPOTHESIS]: a testable prediction you can check on your own hardware. Only (a) is [DERIVED].
This is a dated field guide, not an evergreen ranking. The four-family comparison is a
snapshot as of the 2026-08-30 cutoff (with separately dated September and October observations, plus
the 2026-11-01 service-status re-verification, outside the comparison). A later edition re-verifies the
vendor reports and may change the families, numbers, or the comparison; the ranking here is not a
permanent verdict. Reproduction status is recorded per family in the First-hand Sources list (A.10):
each entry carries its source URL/identifier and release date where recorded; a general compiled
note states that all parameters/claims are vendor-reported [1P] and pending independent check, and
the per-entry verification status lives in the sources.csv manifest. Where a number has not been
independently validated, it is flagged — do not treat a model-card figure as an audited measurement.
The vendor-fact / author-interpretation / hypothesis layers above, plus the per-family reproduction
status, are the four columns a reader needs; a sources.csv manifest (source URL, accessed date,
model variant, reported baseline, verification status) accompanies the repository’s render/ material
for the fast-changing Appendix A claims.

A.3. DeepSeek-V4 — Making Long Context Cheap by Re-Architecting Attention
Decisive fact [1P] — arXiv:2606.19348; HF deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro: V4-Pro is 1.6 T total
/ 49 B activated, V4-Flash 284 B / 13 B activated, both 1M-token context, MIT-licensed. Its hybrid
attention combines Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA).
At 1M context, DeepSeek reports ~27% (Pro) / ~10% (Flash) of V3.2’s single-token inference
FLOPs and ~10% / ~7% of its KV cache.
What this means for the architect (ties to Ch7 Memory, Ch8 Compute). In our reading of
the vendor reports, this is a strong confirmation that KV-per-token is a moving target. Chapter 7’s
arithmetic (per-token × context) is a floor for a given architecture; DeepSeek shows the constant
factor itself can be cut ~10–14× across the V4 variants (the ~14× end is V4-Flash’s ~7%-of-V3.2
single-token KV, A.7) through attention re-architecture alone — the saving comes from the attention
mechanism within each variant, not from a change of that variant’s own parameter count; note the
V4 variants themselves differ in size (V4-Pro 1.6 T vs V4-Flash 284 B, above) and each ratio is that
variant’s vendor-reported figure against its own stated V3.2 baseline, so do not read the ~10–14×
band as a same-size comparison. The architectural decision shifts from “how much KV memory does
this context need?” to “which KV scheme does this model use, and is its vendor-published saving
reproducible on my serving stack?”
Service status (dated, outside the snapshot; re-verified 2026-11-01). These variant names
have moved since the cutoff: see the 2026-09-10 / 2026-09-14 service-status caveat at the top of this
appendix — V4-Flash and V4-Flash-Vision-Exp are retired (their API names temporarily route to
V4.1-Flash), while V4-Pro remains available: the 2026-09-10 announcement that all deepseek-v4pro requests would route to V4.1-Flash from 2026-09-14 was superseded by DeepSeek’s current API

change log, which decides to continue V4-Pro API service after 2026-09-14 with the billing method
unchanged (change log retrieved 2026-11-01). The V4-Flash alias routing says nothing about V4-Pro’s
availability — the two are separate service facts. The [1P] figures above remain the historical record
of what DeepSeek reported by 2026-08-30; the successor’s constants are in the 2026-10-28 V4.1-Flash
note.

A.4. Kimi K3 — Vendor-Reported First Open 3T-Class Model, and the MoE-Sparsity
Extreme
Decisive fact [1P] — arXiv:2607.24653; HF moonshotai/Kimi-K3: 2.8 T total / 104 B activated,
native vision, 1M context. Built on Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) + Attention Residuals (AttnRes),
with Stable LatentMoE activating just 16 of 896 routed experts per token. Claims ~2.5× scaling
efficiency over Kimi K2. Weights are QAT-trained from SFT onward with MXFP4 weights / MXFP8
activations. Full weights are released — per the vendor, the first open 3T-class model.
What this means for the architect (ties to Ch3 Model, Ch10 Parallelism). A model whose
total size is 2.8 T but whose activated footprint is 104 B is a clear illustration of Ch3’s total-vs-activated

449

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

distinction and Ch10’s expert-parallelism doctrine. Serving Kimi K3 requires accommodating the 2.8
T total parameter fabric across the serving system (the full expert set must reside somewhere unless
an explicit offload/load-on-demand architecture is used) while only ~104 B parameters participate in
the computation of a given token. The architectural problem is therefore simultaneously one of total
weight residency/distribution and active-weight communication/computation — sharding
and scheduling the expert fabric, plus the KV for our context. The decision surface is expert-parallel
communication and fused cross-expert kernels, not only raw capacity — total weight residency of
the 2.8 T fabric is the capacity half of the same decision.

A.5. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — A Vendor-Framed Qwen4 Architecture Preview, Pri­
oritizing Cost-Performance
Decisive fact [1P] — HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next; GitHub QwenLM/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:
125 B MoE total / 6 B activated, plus a separate 51 B of N-gram embedding parameters (offloadable
to host memory). Native 262 K context (YaRN to 1M). Hybrid attention: Gated DeltaNet (GDN)
+ Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA), where QSA operates at the micro-block level; Gated Residual
widens the residual stream; 512 MoE experts (10 routed + 1 shared per token); Muon + AdamW.
Reported training cost ~1/9 of Qwen3.7-Plus (vendor-stated basis; the unit is not specified in the
snapshot sources).
What this means for the architect (ties to Ch3, Ch5 Model Selection, Ch16 TCO). Qwen’s
technical report, 26 August 2026, describes the n-gram tables as held off the accelerator and prefetched
from host memory. This is a vendor-reported mechanism, not only an architectural inference. Its effect
on a particular deployment still depends on placement, bandwidth, overlap and engine support; the
report does not establish a general serving-performance result for every backend. The 125B backbone,
separate 51B n-gram tables and separately listed MTP module remain distinct parts of the residency
inventory. Model selection therefore weighs heterogeneous memory and the supported transfer path
alongside total and active parameters. [1P][FACT] mechanism; deployment consequence [DERIVED].

A.6. GLM-5.3-Flash — Vendor-Reported First Natively Multimodal GLM,
Efficiency-Branded
Decisive fact [1P] — HF zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash; Z.ai release article, 2026-08-26: 320 B total
/ 18 B activated, 1M native context. Per the vendor, the first natively multimodal model in the
GLM-5 series (text/image/video). It combines sparse and linear attention (first in the series per the
vendor), Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), W8A8 quantization with mixed-cache
(INT8/FP8/BF16), and Encode-Prefill-Decode serving (a vendor serving mode that separates token
encoding from the prefill and decode phases). The release article compares it with GLM-5.3 using
attention compute per head per layer and average BF16 KV cache per layer. On those normalized

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

450

measures, it reports 3.0× lower attention compute and a 4.4× lower KV cache. These are not wholemodel FLOP or total-cache ratios, and they do not establish an end-to-end speedup. The February
GLM-5 parent report, arXiv:2602.15763, is not the source of these Flash-specific ratios. MIT weights.
Z.ai positions it as approaching Claude Opus 4.8 on coding/agentic at ~1/10 the price.
What this means for the architect (ties to Ch7 Memory, Ch8 Compute, Ch19 Agentic).
GLM’s coupling of hybrid attention with native multimodality shows the model border is remaking:
“LLM” and “vision/video model” are converging in a single weight set, which changes workload
characterization (Ch4) — a multimodal prompt has a different token/KV profile than text-only. And
mHC + attention-mixing being reported as scaling-efficiency results reinforces Ch8’s point that
compute arithmetic is architecture-specific, not universal.
Post-snapshot observation (recorded 2026-09-27; outside the 2026-08-30 compile-date
envelope). Beyond the four families above, Ornith-1.5-397B (released 2026-08-19 by DeepReinforce /
ornith-ai) ships as another natively multimodal frontier model: 397 B MoE, ~262 K context, MIT

weights, image-input via the inherited Qwen3.5 vision tower. We verified the image-input path
end-to-end with a live API call carrying a base64-encoded PNG as image_url content: the model’s
own reasoning trace referenced the rendered pixels (a white-square test and a red/blue half-image
test both answered correctly). This is a [LAB] author observation — a single first-person
capability probe: one API call carrying two ad-hoc image fixtures (a white-square test and
a red/blue half-image test), which establishes only that one function path (image input)
is reachable. It is not a benchmark, not comparable across models, and not reproducible
without re-running the call: the exact model/API ID, sampling settings, prompt/image fixtures,
and (credential-redacted) API response are not published as a reproducibility capsule, and the probe
says nothing about benchmark quality, throughput, or cost. It must not be read as evidence for any
comparative claim about Ornith-1.5-397B relative to the four families (which it is not a part of), nor
as a measurement of capability or quality. It is recorded as a single-path capability hint and cited as
an observational sidebar, not promoted into the four-family comparative figures or the First-hand
Sources list above, both of which retain the 2026-08-30 compile-date stamp. Treat as a hint that the
natively multimodal frontier continues to widen between snapshots — exactly the trajectory the
four-family narrative above predicts.

A.7. What This Means for the Handbook’s Canonical Arithmetic
Same message as Fig 7.1’s GQA line, taken to the frontier: the per-token KV and FLOP “constants”
of Chapter 7/8 are not universal — they are the canonical full-MHA conservative upper-bound
teaching model, which hybrid attention re-architects down at the mechanism. Each row is a model’s
vendor-reported ratio of its own stated reference (e.g. DeepSeek V4 vs V3.2); they do not share a
common denominator, so they must not be read as percentages of a single baseline. The canonical
70B dense full-MHA model is the book’s foundational teaching model, not the denominator for these
percentages. An architect who re-derives them per candidate model avoids both over- (sizing a model

The book’s canonical scenario is a 70B dense FP16, ~9.2K-token RAG workload on 8×H100. The
2026 frontier does not invalidate it — it refines the interpretation an architect should carry:
• The KV constant (Ch7: ~2.62 MB/token FP16; ~1.31 MB/token 8-bit) derives from the canonical
full-MHA conservative upper-bound teaching model. (The 8-bit figure is the raw tensor bytehalving bound: ~1.31 MB/token, exactly 50% of FP16, which is what the fleet-sizing chapters
use. vLLM’s widely cited 54% is a decode inter-token-latency slope from its Llama-3.1-8B Table
3 [S6] — a latency metric, not a memory ratio; there is no vendor-measured FP8 KV memory
footprint for the configurations cited in this book, and any allocator block/metadata overhead
is not vendor-measured. The 8-bit KV constants are [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED].) Hybridattention models cut it ~4–14× at the mechanism in the named configurations — from
GLM’s 4.4× normalized per-layer KV measure to DeepSeek’s ~7%-of-V3.2 single-token
KV (≈14×) — different scopes (per-layer normalized vs single-token KV at 1M context),
not directly comparable — a band across models, not a universal constant, so “context
fits on N GPUs” must be re-derived per model, not looked up once. [1P]
• The roofline (Ch8) still holds; what changed is where a frontier model’s prefill/decode ride it.
Vendor-reported FLOP/KV reductions are [1P] first-party claims but not yet independently
reproduced — an architect should re-run Ch8’s measurement on the candidate model be­
fore betting capacity. Evidence status: first-party vendor claim; deployment-specific result not
independently reproduced.
• The MoE memory decision (Ch10) is jointly dominated by total-weight residency/sharding,
active-parameter compute, KV footprint, and expert-fabric communication. Extreme sparsity
reduces per-token compute; it does not eliminate total-weight residency, which still scales with
the full parameter count unless experts are explicitly offloaded (sharding changes per-device
residency, not the aggregate). [1P]
None of this changes the book’s mechanisms; it changes the constants an architect plugs into
them. This is exactly why we wrote the arithmetic as verifiable, first-principles reasoning rather
than as a fixed catalog of numbers.

A.8. Where 2026 Capability Actually Comes From (beyond Architecture)
A recurring error — easy to fall into after reading four new model cards — is to attribute frontier
gains to the attention mechanism splashed across the front page. The industry is converging not just
on architectures (MoE + efficient attention + very long context) but on a multi-layered recipe in which
architecture is one ingredient, and arguably not the dominant one. A qualitative decomposition of
the recipe:

A frequently underestimated layer is the one the model card almost never shows: posttraining. Two models with broadly similar architectures and pre-training can end up materially
different when one went through mediocre post-training and the other excellent. The recipe — the
same families every lab now runs — is what carries much of the qualitative gap:
• RLVR / reinforcement learning for reasoning
• synthetic reasoning data
• verifier-based training
• preference optimization
• curriculum learning
• tool-use training and agent trajectories
• coding-specific trajectories
• multimodal reasoning
• long-horizon interaction training
This is why architecture alone never tells an architect how good a frontier model is, and why the
decision can no longer stop at “which model” — the marginal capability may live in the post-training
and the runtime that wraps it.
From a single model to a whole system. The earlier stages (Transformer, Efficient, MoE) are
efficiency-led — they make inference affordable and raise capacity-per-FLOP. The later stages (Rea­
soning, Test-Time Compute, Tool-Using, Agent, Agent System, Agent Fleet) are capability-led — they
raise effective intelligence. [ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual
This chain is the spine of this handbook — from a single model’s tokens (Ch1–9) to parallelism
(Ch10), serving (Ch11–16), and finally the fleet of specialized models and agents (Ch17–26). It also

explains why two models with broadly similar base architectures can have very different practical

is now architecturally decisive.

A.9. The Frontier Question: Where Should Intelligence Live?
The most useful lens for an AI Solution Architect in 2026 is not “which attention mechanism does
the model card list?” but where the intelligence and the compute budget should be placed:
The placement ladder. Every placement layer that can carry intelligence is a place the architect
may choose to push capability or cost; this book gives the arithmetic and decision framework for each
(Ch3/7/8 weights & attention, Ch10 MoE routing, Ch19/21 post-training, Ch8/20 test-time, Ch19/24
tools, Ch17–20 runtime, Ch18/20 fleet). [ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual
Every placement layer maps to chapters in this book:
• Inside weights (dense capacity) — Ch3 Model, Ch8 Compute
• Inside attention (context / efficiency) — Ch7 Memory, Ch8 Compute
• Inside MoE routing (capacity per FLOP) — Ch10 Parallelism
• Inside post-training (reasoning, RL, verification) — Ch19 Agentic, Ch21 AI Factory
• Inside test-time search (adaptive inference, more compute on hard tasks) — Ch8 Compute,
Ch20 Fleet-Level Optimization
• Inside tools (compute allocated via a harness) — Ch19 Agentic, Ch24 Red/Green Team
• Inside the agent runtime (persistent state, runbooks, execution control) — Ch17–20, Ch24
• Across a fleet of specialized models — Ch18 Operating Multiple Models, Ch20 Fleet-Level
Optimization
Deciding where intelligence lives — rather than which attention variant a model card lists — is the
actual job of an AI Solution Architect. The frontier of 2026 makes that explicit: DeepSeek-V4-Flash
vs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next vs a fleet of specialized agents on a 2×DGX cluster are no longer merely
model choices; they are placement-of-intelligence choices whose economics this handbook’s chapters
give the tools to evaluate.

Architecture dimensions and executed depth — 2026-10-28
This update is separate from the four-family comparison compiled through 30 August 2026. A retrieval
date is not a release date. Some examples below were available before that comparison; others are later
releases or later paper revisions. The purpose is to examine mechanisms that change a deployment
decision, not to extend a model ranking.

459

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

Three independent dimensions
A model description now needs at least three independent dimensions: parameter allocation, historystate representation, and execution depth. Dense feed-forward layers can coexist with recurrent
token mixing. Sparse experts can coexist with global attention. Shared weights can execute repeatedly
within one token prediction. None of these properties determines the others.
Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B is a useful counterexample to the idea that a dense model must use conven­

tional full attention throughout. Its card describes dense feed-forward layers and native image/video
understanding. Its language configuration contains 48 Gated DeltaNet layers and 16 full-attention
layers. DeltaNet updates a recurrent history state; the full-attention layers retain a separate historydependent KV component. Dense parameter allocation therefore does not imply a full-MHA cache
formula.1
A different form of recurrence repeats a shared core over the current representation. Huginn and
Ouro provide public research examples. Their shared weights reduce the unique parameter inventory
relative to an equally deep untied network. The repeated executions still consume compute. Attention
states can also differ between iterations, even when the weights are identical. These research artifacts
are not evidence that adaptive-depth production serving is already routine.2,3

Phase and storage tier matter
deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash changes more than one constant. Its vendor report describes

a Causal Encoder-Decoder with 552B backbone parameters and a separate 196B Engram component
(the vendor’s compressed history-state module). It reports 8B activated parameters per token during
prefill and 16B during decode. A single active-parameter figure would obscure this phase difference.
These counts describe the vendor’s computation paths; they do not establish an elapsed-time ratio.4
The report also separates memory objects. Cross-layer reuse and FP4 main-KV storage produce a
vendor-reported global HBM KV footprint of 890 bytes per token [1P] (mechanisms named above;
the snapshot sources do not publish the layer/head geometry needed to re-derive the number). This
is not total request memory. Bounded sliding-window state, weights, workspaces, and allocation
overhead remain separate. The reported persistent-cache reduction to approximately one-eighth of
DeepSeek-V4-Flash concerns host or SSD storage under SWA Bounded Replay. It is not the same
metric as global HBM KV.
The transferable rule is to account for each independently stored state, its update rule, and
its location. Sparse attention that reads selected history entries need not store only those entries.
Cross-layer consumers can share one stored object. A local window can bound live state while prefix
restoration still incurs storage or recomputation. Capacity across several accelerators also does not
establish that each rank fits its assigned weights and state.
4

DeepSeek-AI, “DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression,” Abstract and §§2.1–2.4, 3.2:
[A-S23]. Model card: [A-S24]. The numerical memory and activation claims are vendor-reported, not independently
reproduced.

A stopping rule is not yet a runtime saving
Huginn’s model card requires a recurrence-aware cache so that later core passes do not overwrite
earlier KV entries. It also labels its per-token adaptive-compute facility a zero-shot proof of concept.
Its stopping criteria include changes in latent state, output distributions, and prediction stability.5
Ouro’s revised paper studies learned exit decisions and cache sharing. It reports that prefill needs
distinct iteration caches in the evaluated setting, while selected decode-only sharing strategies can
reduce the cache component. These are phase-specific experiments, not a universal reduction in
whole-request memory.6
The released runtime path also matters. In the Ouro implementation retrieved for this update,
the core loop computes all configured iterations before the language-model wrapper selects an exit
representation. That path does not demonstrate skipped core computation merely because an earlier
representation is selected. The model card separately states that its vLLM path does not support
adaptive exit. A paper’s stopping policy, a reference implementation, and an optimized serving engine
are different evidence objects.7,8
A deployment evaluation would therefore record actual core executions, state bytes, and perstage time alongside quality. Variable-depth scheduling could change batch efficiency and latency
tails. That consequence remains a testable hypothesis until measured on the intended engine and
workload.
Figure A.5 separates the parameter object from its invocations and the invocations from their
cached histories. The lower lanes make the stopping boundary explicit. Only the upper lane avoids
the final pass. The exit index in the drawing is illustrative; it does not prescribe a quality-preserving
stopping rule for either research model.
With separate caches, an iteration index is part of the state identity. Reusing the same weight
pointer does not make different hidden representations interchangeable. A cache-sharing policy
changes that assumption and needs its own phase-specific evidence. An adaptive stopping rule also
needs an accuracy target: stable logits or a small latent-state change is a stopping signal, not proof

of correct reasoning. These distinctions keep a research mechanism from being promoted into a
production efficiency claim without the intervening engine and workload evidence.9,10
Training loops are not inference loops
Ornith-1.5 provides a useful boundary case. Its report describes joint improvement of training tasks,
scaffolds, and solution rollouts. The released family builds on existing architectures with additional
training. This is evidence about the training and evaluation system, not proof of shared-depth
recurrence or online weight updates during a user request.11
The same distinction applies within a vendor’s product family. Z.ai describes GLM-5.3 as using
the GLM-5.2 base with post-training gains, while GLM-5.3-Flash starts from a newly trained base
and a redesigned hybrid architecture. The exact variant determines which explanation applies.12
“Flash” does not identify a common architecture or a small resident model. The open-weight
examples combine different expert layouts, compressed or local attention, multimodal encoders,
and drafting mechanisms. For gemini-3.8-flash, the public documentation establishes a service
interface and token limits, but the sources examined here do not establish its exact parameter
inventory or KV layout. Service price and product naming cannot fill that gap.13
Quantization implementation observations — 2026-10-28
These observations concern pinned October implementations, not support at the August cutoff. No
backend performance was measured for this note.
Current implementations illustrate why representation and execution are separate. At vLLM
commit 41dd82e6a7392ead33b1e8a7d175442511e488ca, NVFP4 has a CUTLASS low-bit path, a
Marlin W4A16 path and a higher-precision emulation path. Its MXFP4 Marlin code explicitly ignores
a requested activation-quantization configuration because that kernel is weight-only. These are
different execution experiments even when the stored weights use the same named representation.
They are code observations, not benchmarks or proof that a particular installed release selects the
native path. [1P][FACT] (NVFP4 CUTLASS; NVFP4 Marlin; MXFP4 Marlin.)
The same separation appears in GGML/llama.cpp. At the pinned revision in the source ledger,
block_q4_K occupies 144 bytes for 256 values: 4.5 effective bits/value. Q4_K_M, however, selects a

mixture of tensor encodings and can promote selected tensors to Q6_K. IQ encodings have their
own grid, sign, lookup and scale layouts; their imatrix requirements are type-specific. The complete

model’s average precision therefore follows a tensor inventory, not one block’s byte rate. GGML’s

Post-training calibration and training-based recovery also describe different work. PTQ estimates
quantization parameters without a full model-training run; the particular algorithm can search scales
or compensate weight errors. QAT updates model parameters while accounting for quantization
effects. QAD additionally uses teacher targets to recover behavior. That recovery consumes training
compute and memory, and a favorable fake-quant evaluation still needs confirmation after export
through the real serving kernels. Calibration, recovery and inference therefore receive separate
resource ledgers and separate quality records. [1P][DERIVED] (Model Optimizer QAT/QAD example,
pinned revision.)
An NVFP4 training recipe need not have the same storage arrangement as a one-dimensional
inference storage budget. Transformer Engine documents two-dimensional 16×16 weight scaling,
as well as gradient-specific stochastic rounding, transformations for weight-gradient computation
and high-precision treatment of sensitive layers. These are additional recipe choices, not properties
supplied by the four-bit value code. Training can also require multiple tensor orientations, higherprecision state and temporary buffers. The unique scale information of a 2D block is therefore not a
prediction of resident training memory, nor a reason to reuse an inference footprint as the training
budget. [1P][DERIVED] (Transformer Engine NVFP4.)
OCP MicroXcaling 1.1 is dated 2026-10-09 and renames E8M0 to UE8M0 while clarifying con­
version and boundary behavior. That revision is later than the book’s cutoff. The August snapshot
retains the 1.0 E8M0 terminology; later terminology is identified here with its revision date. Current
Model Optimizer recipes also combine AWQ-lite error control with either INT4 or NVFP4 repre­
sentations. This is evidence that the method and representation are combinable axes, not that every
method/container/backend combination is available. [1P][FACT] (OCP MicroXcaling 1.1; INT4 AWQ
preset; NVFP4 AWQ preset.)
Diffusion language generation — 2026-10-28
This observation is outside Appendix A’s frozen 2026-08-30 comparison. It does not update that
four-family table or treat a present-day source as proof of its historical contents.
Public artifacts now support more than one diffusion-language deployment pattern. LLaDA
and Dream publish open checkpoints and generation code for masked/refinement-based language
generation; their announcement, paper and checkpoint-revision dates are separate provenance
events. LLaDA2.2 adds bounded block editing. DiffusionGemma is an explicitly experimental open
release. Mercury 3 is a vendor-documented closed API release dated 2026-10-19; its internal schedule,
precision and hardware allocation have not been independently established here. Gemini Diffusion’s
official page describes an experimental demo. What did not change after 2026-08-30 is the

465

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

mechanism: masked/refinement generation, block-level editing, renoising without MASK and
block-causal state reuse are treated paper by paper in §7A below, and this note records only the
release and support delta. These records establish different release and support boundaries, not a
common production-readiness level. [1P][FACT]14
The inspected SGLang revision, a1966e1b5d8b750b494d7e53cca1d2464f960038, illustrates
why engine names are insufficient. Its Gemma4Renoise path (a named model-variant serving recipe in
the engine) disables radix caching and chunked prefill, rejects quantized loading and pipeline/context
parallelism, and accepts only specified attention backends. Its recipe rejects grammar/logit-bias
requests. Vendor low-precision performance claims do not override those implementation restrictions.
Conversely, the source contains an attention-backend-specific graph path, so an older recipe’s eageronly shorthand is not a timeless limitation. These are static source observations, not a successful
local deployment test. [1P][FACT]15
The strongest evidence supports conditional hypotheses, not a speed ranking (§7A carries
the mechanism; this note carries only what the post-2026-08-30 sources add to it). Google’s own
DiffusionGemma report describes a low-concurrency benefit while acknowledging lower overall
quality and potentially higher serving costs. Earlier LLaDA results differ by task. Recent cache/verify
work compares against particular diffusion baselines and does not establish an equivalent gain over an
optimized AR service. Published evaluations also identify format, replanning and exploration failures
in earlier models; those findings cannot be projected unchanged onto later releases. The durable
conclusion is to compare matched-quality service frontiers, with explicit cache and commitment
semantics. [1P][FACT] (source-reported, not locally reproduced); [2°][FACT]16

A.9.1.

470

From corruption to learned generation

A diffusion model learns to reverse a specified corruption process. In a continuous denoising diffusion
model, the forward process progressively adds noise to data. Training constructs corrupted examples
and teaches a model to predict information needed for the reverse process, such as the added noise
(Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models). At generation time, sampling starts from a simple prior
and repeatedly applies learned reverse updates. The forward process is not an inference pipeline
that first corrupts the requested answer: the answer is not available during generation. The forward
process defines the learning problem. [1P][FACT]
Score-based formulations express related dynamics through the score, the gradient of the log
density of perturbed data (Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equa­
tions). The associated reverse-time stochastic differential equation and probability-flow ordinary
differential equation provide different sampling trajectories. In the ideal formulation they can share
time-marginal distributions; this does not make their finite-step numerical errors, randomness
or network-evaluation counts identical. A deterministic solver can still require many sequential
evaluations. [1P][FACT]
Text requires a discrete construction because token IDs are categories, not continuous pixel values.
Discrete diffusion defines corruption through transitions between categorical states. Uniform token
replacement and an absorbing MASK state are different choices (Structured Denoising Diffusion
Models in Discrete State-Spaces). In masked diffusion, training hides selected tokens and learns to
recover them from the visible sequence. MDLM (Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language
Models) and LLaDA (Large Language Diffusion Models, generation code) connect this procedure to
diffusion likelihood objectives; it is not merely a fixed-rate masked-language-model loss with a new
name. LLaDA samples mask rates and weights the masked-token loss accordingly. Its conditional
fine-tuning leaves the prompt clean while corrupting the response. This teaches the reverse model to
reconstruct an answer conditioned on a known request. [1P][FACT]
Flow matching belongs next to this discussion, but not inside a synonym list. It regresses a vector
field on a chosen probability path (Flow Matching for Generative Modeling); the family of paths can
include diffusion paths and can extend beyond them. Rectified flow uses straight interpolants to
learn transport and can iteratively rectify the coupling (Flow Straight and Fast). Straight training
interpolants do not guarantee that any trained model has perfectly straight generation trajectories
or equal-quality one-step sampling. The shared systems question is repeated model evaluation along
a path. The objectives and samplers remain distinct. [1P][FACT]

471

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

A.9.2.

A language-generation trajectory

A basic masked language sampler allocates an output canvas containing unresolved positions. Each
evaluation predicts token distributions using the current canvas and the prompt. The sampler accepts
some predictions and leaves other positions unresolved. A confidence policy may accept several
positions at once, so generation need not advance strictly left to right. In the inspected LLaDA base
sampler (observation 2026-10-28), already accepted token IDs are retained; remasking low-confidence
candidates does not mean that every accepted token is repeatedly edited. The configured output
capacity and evaluation schedule still determine work even when later display logic removes an EOS
suffix. [1P][FACT]
Parallel predictions are not free joint reasoning. Several position-wise predictions from one
canvas evaluation are conditioned on the old canvas, not necessarily on one another’s newly sampled
values. Individually plausible tokens can form an implausible combination. Confidence thresholds,
extra rounds and verification can improve this tradeoff, but they change the amount of work and
may change task quality. A lower iteration count is therefore not a quality-neutral implementation
improvement by default. [1P][FACT]
The inference loop is also not an agent loop. An agent turn may invoke a model, inspect a tool
result and decide its next action. A diffusion round updates an internal output state. An autoregressive
model with a long chain of thought remains autoregressive. A diffusion draft model can also propose
blocks for an autoregressive verifier, as in DFlash; that combination does not turn the verifier’s target
distribution into a fully diffusion-based language model. [1P][FACT]
A.9.3.

State reuse follows dependency boundaries

The ordinary causal-cache argument depends on a fixed prefix. Later output tokens cannot change an
earlier token’s causal hidden state. Under bidirectional attention, an unchanged token ID can acquire a
different representation when another canvas position changes. Its previous K/V tensors can therefore
be stale even though its spelling is unchanged. Approximate cache policies exploit empirical stability,
delayed caching or selective refresh; those policies require quality and refresh-cost measurements.
Fast-dLLM and dKV-Cache are concrete examples, not proof that ordinary autoregressive caching
transfers unchanged. [1P][FACT]
A block-causal model creates a stronger boundary. Earlier finalized blocks cannot depend on later
blocks, while the active block can use bidirectional attention internally (Block Diffusion). The runtime
can reuse correctly finalized prefix state and repeatedly recompute the active block. Finalization
must make cached state correspond to the accepted block contents; accepting token IDs alone is not
always enough. DiffusionGemma (model card, Google release post) uses a related separation between
cached encoded context and a mutable decoder canvas, then encodes the completed canvas before
continuing. These are architectural boundaries, not a universal property of the word “diffusion.” [1P]
[FACT]

Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families

472

Not every language diffusion process starts from MASK or only fills holes. Uniform-state renois­
ing can begin with ordinary token states. Editing models can replace accepted tokens or perform
insertion/deletion operations within a bounded block. LLaDA2.2 (paper, checkpoint) restores its
configured block length after such operations; this is not an unbounded global canvas. A stopping rule
may test unresolved positions, stability, confidence, EOS or an iteration limit. These are operational
termination rules, not proofs of semantic correctness. [1P][FACT]
The architectural consequence is conditional, and it is the reason Ch 3 §1 only scopes this material,
with the paper-by-paper treatment collected here as durable background rather than in a serving
chapter. Parallel positions can improve matrix utilization at low request concurrency, but repeated
evaluation can increase total compute and communications. Block size changes both parallel work
and the delay before commitment. A useful deployment comparison therefore fixes the task-quality
requirement first, then measures the inference schedule, peak state and committed-output latency
together. The token remains the application interface; the execution trace connects that interface to
resources. [DERIVED]
A.9.4.

Noise-stage expert selection (Wan2.2 A14B)

If both expert checkpoints remain on GPU, both occupy weight memory even though only one expert
runs in a branch evaluation. Explicit offload changes that placement: it introduces a weight-transfer
operation and may lengthen the transition or interfere with other transfers. It does not change the
model into a smaller checkpoint. The two noise stages also do not imply equal numbers of scheduler
timesteps. [1P][FACT]
A.9.5.

Deriving attention FLOPs for a whole-clip video workload (Wan2.2 TI2V-5B)

The same derive-then-decide move applies to a workload that evaluates all of its token positions
together rather than one per step: the budget below is derived from counted dimensions, not from a
duration label. This example applies the Ch 8 §1 principle (fewer sequential evaluations ≠ less total
work) to a whole-clip denoiser, where 50 timesteps × 2 CFG branches = 100 evaluations each process
all 27,280 tokens simultaneously.
A worked example makes the new work unit concrete. We use Wan2.2 TI2V-5B in its text-to-video
path, not the A14B expert model. Its configuration specifies a dense transformer with hidden width
3,072, 30 layers, and 24 attention heads. The VAE has 48 latent channels and temporal/spatial strides
of 4, 16, and 16. The denoiser patches the latent video by (1,2,2). The release’s “720P” example is
precisely 1,280 × 704 pixels, 121 frames, at 24 frames/s. The dimensions, rather than the marketing
resolution label, determine the budget. [1P][FACT] (Wan2.2 TI2V-5B configuration, pinned revision
1ea34ff, retrieved 2026-10-28; Diffusers transformer config).

Fig 8.3 in Ch 8 shows the data path. The prompt passes through UMT5-XXL. An optional image
follows a separate reference-conditioning path. The T2V calculation below does not add that I2V
branch to its state budget. Initial noise spans the entire latent video. Each scheduler step calls the

Total trajectory work. At this shape the attention core requires 9,144,709,939,200 FLOP per
layer, or about 9.145 TFLOP. Across 30 layers it requires about 274.341 TFLOP per branch evaluation.
The inspected upstream loop evaluates conditional and unconditional predictions separately at each
of its 50 default scheduler timesteps (same pinned revision 1ea34ff). That is 100 single-sample
branch evaluations, giving about 27.434 PFLOP of attention-core work over the trajectory. This
is not the whole model’s FLOP count and is not a GPU execution time. A runtime may batch the
two branches into one forward call without removing their two-sample arithmetic. [1P][DERIVED]
(configuration; sampling loop).
Memory boundary. The memory calculation has an equally important boundary. One hypo­
thetical BF16 hidden tensor contains N × d × 2 = 167,608,320 bytes. Materializing one BF16 score
tensor for 24 heads would require 24 × N 2 × 2 = 35,721,523,200 bytes, or about 33.268 GiB. This is
a hypothetical implementation choice, not a claim that FlashAttention allocates such a tensor. Tiled
exact attention avoids retaining the full score matrix while still performing the pairwise work. The
upstream code creates initial latent noise in FP32, so assigning BF16 to every live tensor would also
undercount state. [1P][DERIVED] (attention module; sampling loop).

474

Sensitivity. This explains the architectural consequence. Extending 121 to 241 frames changes
the temporal latent count from 31 to 61. Token count rises by about 1.968×; the dense pairwise term
rises by about 3.872×. Doubling both spatial dimensions gives four times the tokens and sixteen times
the pairwise work. These are algebraic sensitivities, not claims that either larger workload meets
the release’s quality or memory envelope. A request limit expressed only in clip-seconds misses this
distinction. [1P][DERIVED]
At 24 frames/s, 121 frames also exposes a measurement convention. The final frame’s timestamp is
5 seconds after the first. A constant-frame-duration container spans 121/24, or about 5.0417 seconds.
A service contract needs one convention. “Five-second clip,” “121 frames,” and “27,280 transformer
tokens (patch positions)” describe related but different quantities. [DERIVED]

Glossary of Acronyms and Common Terms

Model fundamentals
• tokenization / tokenizer — splitting text into the model’s vocabulary of integer IDs; a token
is whatever the model’s tokenizer decided to carve the text into (learned BPE-style merges),
so token counts are tokenizer-dependent — run the model’s own tokenizer on representative
traffic rather than a characters-per-token rule of thumb (Ch 1).
• embedding — the lookup that maps each discrete token ID to the dense vector the model
actually operates on; the pipeline is text → tokenizer → IDs → embedding → attention → KV
cache (Ch 1).
• attention — the mechanism that compares each token’s query (Q) against every prior key (K)
and blends the values (V) by those scores; a processed token’s K/V never change, which is why
they are cached (the KV cache) rather than recomputed each step (Ch 2).
• logits — the model’s raw, unnormalized per-vocabulary scores at a generation step; the sampler
turns them into the next token (Ch 2).
Inference and serving
• TTFT — time to first token: latency from request to the first output token (prefill-dominated).
• TPOT — time per output token: steady-state decode latency per token.
• ITL — inter-token latency: the decode phase’s per-token lag, including any queueing/scheduling
gap between emitted tokens. The book writes “TPOT/ITL” for one canonical per-token metric;
where a source separates them, TPOT is the bounded steady-state value and ITL the tailsensitive per-token value that also carries that gap.
• tail latency — latency at the high percentiles of the distribution (p95/p99), set by the slow­
est requests rather than the typical one; the SLOs in this book are written against the tail
(TTFT/TPOT p95/p99), so a median that meets its budget says nothing about the tail (Ch 20).
• prefill — the pass that processes the prompt tokens and builds the KV cache/state. Often the
compute-bound pass in high-arithmetic-intensity regimes, but the compute- vs bandwidthbound classification is a function of model, sequence length, batch, kernel, and device operating
point (Ch 8, §8.2). Long-context and large-batch regimes can shift where it sits on the roofline.

475

Glossary

476

• decode — the autoregressive pass that generates the output one token at a time from the built
state. Often memory-bandwidth-bound at low batch (small arithmetic intensity per emitted
token), but not invariably so; large-batch and bandwidth-friendly regimes can move it. Refer to
the operating-point discussion in Ch 8, §8.2 for the conditional, not unconditional, classification.
• goodput — useful throughput: throughput that meets the latency/quality bar, discounting
failures.
• P/D disaggregation — running prefill (P) and decode (D) on separate pools/services.
• continuous batching — scheduling new requests into a running decode batch so the GPU is
kept busy token-by-token rather than waiting for an entire batch to finish; raises throughput
at some latency cost.
• chunked prefill — splitting a long prompt’s prefill into sub-blocks interleaved with decode
work, so a long prompt does not monopolize the GPU and stall latency-sensitive decode.
• FlashAttention — an I/O-aware attention kernel that tiles/fuses the Q·K·V computation
through fast on-chip storage, reducing HBM traffic while preserving the same attention
mathematics.
• PagedAttention — a memory-management strategy for the KV cache that allocates key/value
blocks in non-contiguous pages, reducing fragmentation and enabling near-full memory
utilization.
• speculative decoding — a draft model proposes a candidate sequence that the target model
verifies in parallel, accepting matching tokens to raise effective throughput at the cost of draft
+ verification compute.
• MFU — model FLOPs utilization: achieved model FLOPs as a fraction of hardware peak; a
compute-efficiency ratio for a run (the worked examples assume 35%), not a host-occupancy
number — see Utilization and efficiency below for how it differs from u, ρ and offered-load
utilization.
• RPS / QPS — requests per second / queries per second: a rate of incoming work, the primary
input to a capacity model.
• concurrency — the number of requests in flight (being served) at the same time; distinct from
concurrent users, which is a population measure, and related to the arrival rate by Little’s law
(in-flight ≈ λW ) (Ch 17, 20).
Memory and attention
• KV cache — the keys/values of past tokens retained so attention need not recompute.
• KV quantization — reducing the bytes per K/V element (e.g. FP16 → FP8), not the number of
K/V entries; the canonical raw byte-halving is 2.62 → 1.31 MB/token (exactly 50%), a raw-array
figure that is not a vendor-measured engine footprint, and the vLLM FP8-KV blog’s 54% is a
decode-ITL latency slope, not a memory ratio (Ch 2, 6, 7; S6).
• KV offloading — moving some KV state out of GPU HBM (to host DRAM/SSD), trading
capacity against transfer latency; it does not shrink the state itself (that is quantization), and the

477

Glossary

cited 2–22× TTFT range is a particular warm-cache reuse benchmark, not a generic cold-cache
improvement (Ch 2, 6; S7).
• GQA — grouped-query attention; MQA — multi-query attention; MHA — multi-head attention;
MLA — multi-head latent attention: a compressed per-token KV (K/V stored in a low-rank
latent space), so KV per token still grows with context but at fewer bytes/token than full MHA
(Ch 1, 8; App. A).
• APC / RadixAttention / prefix cache — caching of shared prompt prefixes to avoid recom­
putation.
• prompt caching — the provider-facing name for the prefix caching above: reusing the KV of a
shared prompt prefix across requests. Not a separate mechanism (Ch 2); kept as its own entry
because providers document and bill it as a feature.
• cache hit / miss — a cache hit serves a request (or a shared prefix) from cached state without
recomputing it; a miss must be computed (or re-prefilled); the hit ratio (hits ÷ requests) is the
FACT from which the prefix- and semantic-cache arithmetic starts (Ch 15, 19, 26).
• TTL — time-to-live: how long a cached entry stays valid before it must be refreshed or evicted;
the semantic response cache uses a 5-min TTL, and its hit ratio is measured at TTL=T (Ch 26).
• LRU — least-recently-used: the eviction policy that discards the least recently used cache entry
first (Ch 26, Table 26-2).
• HBM — high-bandwidth memory: the large, relatively slow-capacity memory attached to a
GPU (distinct from fast on-chip SRAM).
• arithmetic intensity — FLOPs moved per byte read from memory (FLOP/byte); the quantity
that determines whether a kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound.
• MoE — mixture of experts: a sparse model that routes each token to a subset of expert layers,
cutting compute-per-token without reducing the parameter count or (necessarily) the KV
cache.
Parallelism and flows
• TP — tensor parallelism; PP — pipeline parallelism; DP — data parallelism; EP — expert
parallelism; FSDP — fully sharded data parallelism (shards the model weights, gradients and
optimizer state across ranks, reducing per-rank memory vs full-replica DP); CP — context
parallelism (shards the sequence dimension across ranks when a single context is too long for
one rank).
• all-reduce — the collective that aggregates (e.g. sums) a tensor across ranks so every rank
ends with the same reduced value; used to share gradients, activations, or states.
• RQO — Reasoned Quality Optimization: the discipline of improving the quality of an architec­
ture decision by forcing the articulation of alternatives and evidence, so the trade-off surface
is explicit and the reasons are verifiable; ADRs are where it is recorded (Ch 25 §6).
System and economics

Glossary

478

• SLO — service-level objective (the latency/availability target committed to); SLA — service-level
agreement.
• TCO — total cost of ownership (capex + opex + staff + energy over a horizon).
• PUE — power usage effectiveness: total facility power over IT equipment power.
• ADR — architecture decision record: a short write-up of a design choice and its rationale.
• RAG — retrieval-augmented generation: augment generation with retrieved context.
• PIES — prompt-injection exposure surface: the count of distinct prompt-pattern classes an
adversary can submit through all user-facing entry points, with “distinct” fixed by an authorchosen normalized-edit-distance threshold stated before any number appears; a local, authordefined operational proxy for one deployment, not a standardized or portable security metric
(Ch 24).
• NED / normalized Levenshtein (normalized edit distance, NLE) — string distance scaled
to [0,1] by the longer string’s length; it is the deduplication criterion behind PIES (two probe
patterns count as the same class within NLE ≤ 0.25) (Ch 24).
• MTTR — mean time to recover from a bad release: mean time to detect + roll back; the factory
loop’s core reliability number (Ch 21).
• FAISS — a vector-similarity index library for nearest-neighbor embedding retrieval; the RAG
corpus-policy example moves the retrieval index from a pure FAISS index to a provenanceaware store (Ch 24).
Notation used in the arithmetic
• PFLOP — peta-FLOPs; FLOP/param — floating-point operations per parameter per forward
pass (≈2 for a matmul).
• roofline — a capacity model that plots achievable performance (FLOP/s) against arithmetic
intensity; a kernel sits on a bandwidth-bound line below the ridge point and a compute-bound
plateau above it. The ridge point is the arithmetic intensity at which a machine transitions
from memory-bound to compute-bound (peak FLOP/s ÷ peak bandwidth).
• GB vs GiB — decimal vs binary units: 1 GB = 109 , 1 GiB = 230 . The book uses decimal GB
unless stated.
• CDF — cumulative distribution function: F (x) is the probability a draw is at most x; the
capstone’s two-point latency model gives F (50) = 0.35 and F (250) = 1.0, which separates
the 180 ms mean from the 250 ms p99 (Ch 26).
• tokens/s — throughput in tokens per second; token/request — average tokens per request (a
workload property).
• κ (kappa) — per-token KV cache footprint in bytes/token (e.g. ≈2.62 MB/token FP16 for the
canonical full-MHA 70B; κ = 2 × nlayers × dhidden × bytes). Used in the KV-residency and
concurrency arithmetic (Ch 7, 17).
• KV-heads (nKV-heads ) — the number of key/value heads per layer; with head dimension dhead ,

479

Glossary

nKV-heads × dhead = dhidden for full MHA, and fewer KV-heads than query heads for GQA/MQA
(Ch 1, 3, 7).
• ρ (rho) — the effective throughput fraction after load-balancer and scheduling effects (the
fraction of theoretical peak a host actually sustains under the chosen LB/fleet configuration);
used with the capacity formula (Ch 17).
Utilization and efficiency — four quantities that are not MFU
• utilization target (u) — the policy ceiling on how full a host may run (0.70, Table 17-1); a
chosen provisioning input, not a measurement.
• scheduling efficiency (ρ) — the separate load-balancer/scheduling loss applied on top of
u (0.95: health checks, affinity skew, LB CPU); u and ρ multiply the denominator as two
independent factors, never nested (Ch 17, §17.4; the same symbol as ρ (rho) under Notation
above).
• offered-load utilization (occupancy) — served ÷ provisioned at the operating point (Ch 16,
Note 16.1-1: “Utilization = served ÷ provisioned”); how full the fleet runs under the offered
load — an occupancy ratio, not a compute-efficiency ratio.
• qualitative scenario indicators — hand-designed ordinal labels such as Table 15-1’s Illustra­
tive load pressure (a 0–100 dimensionless score with no FLOP numerator or denominator); a
teaching aid, deliberately not an MFU and not a measured utilization.
Quote which quantity — memory and latency distinctions
• raw bytes / allocated cache / observed resident memory — the three accounting boundaries
of any footprint number (Ch 7, §7.4): raw bytes is the logical K/V payload (2.62 MB/token FP16
canonical; 1.31 MB/token at 8-bit raw byte-halving), allocated cache is what the engine reserves
(paged blocks plus scale/offset metadata and allocator rounding, so allocated ≥ raw), observed
resident memory is what the device reports in use. Name which one a footprint counts.
• active weights vs resident weights — active is the set touched per token (the ∼12.8B-active
MoE reads ∼25.6 GB of weights per token); resident is the full weight bytes held in HBM (∼140
GB FP16 for the dense 70B, ∼94 GB for the ∼47B MoE’s full expert set) (Ch 3).
• residency duration vs end-to-end latency — residency duration is the time state actually
occupies the accelerator: the mean KV-holding time E[WKV -resident ] in the provisioning
formula, or weight residency; end-to-end latency is request-to-last-token wall time as the user
sees it (We2e , tool and orchestration overhead included), which is not the W in the KV formula
(Ch 17). SLO-goodput is neither latency: it is the goodput that meets the latency/quality bar
(above).
Where an acronym is ambiguous or its definition is load-bearing, the body defines it at first use and the
relevant chapter develops the consequence.
